items.title: How it works
items.text: Conference programs are long. KubeCon has more than 500 sessions, and an IETF meeting has more than 1,000 active drafts in the tracked working groups. This site keeps the few items that matter to one reader. That reader is a product manager who works on physical datacenter networking, cloud-native networking, network security, and identity.

items.title: The pipeline
items.text:
flowchart LR
  F["Conference program"] --> P["Digest prompt"]
  P --> T["ToFaRev: shortlist, select, write"]
  T --> R["Pull request review"]
  R --> W["This site"]
  1. Discover. A weekly job checks each recurring conference for new editions and adds the confirmed ones to the registry.
  2. Fetch. After an event ends, a fetcher reads its published program: papers, talks, or drafts, with abstracts and links. Some sites block cloud IP addresses. For these sites, the owner runs the fetch from a laptop.
  3. Compose. The program goes into a prompt with the reader profile, guidance for the conference type, and the output rules.
  4. Write. ToFaRev runs the prompt in GitHub Actions with zai-org/GLM-5.3 on Nebius Token Factory. Large programs go through stages. First, batches of the program are shortlisted in parallel. Then the final picks are selected. Last, the digest is written from the selected items. ToFaRev reads the papers and slides that the picks link to, and gives their text to the writer. The writer can also fetch each pick's talk page.
  5. Check. Code, not the model, does the last checks. It removes any link that is not in the program and flags headings that do not match a program item. It also confirms that every tier is present.
  6. Link. Code, not the model, adds a row of links to every pick: the abstract page, the paper, the slides and the recording. They come from the program and the talk's own page. A recording found by search is added only when its title, its channel and its upload date all match the talk and the event.
  7. Review and publish. ToFaRev opens a pull request with the digest. When it is merged, the digest appears here and the tracking issue closes.
  8. Refresh. Recordings and slides often appear weeks after an event. Every week, for four months after each conference, the links are checked again. New ones arrive in a small pull request; the write-ups do not change.

items.title: Reading a digest
items.text:
Tier Meaning Core Directly about datacenter and WAN networking, cloud-native networking, network security, or identity. Adjacent Relevant to the broader field: useful context, or likely to matter soon. Wildcard Two to four items outside these interests that are novel or show where the field is going. Themes The patterns across the whole program.

Each pick starts with its links: Abstract (the talk or paper page, which usually lists every material), Paper, Slides and Recording, as far as they are published. A talk recording also shows a thumbnail: click it to play the talk on the page. For IETF drafts the links are the Draft, its Slides, the Session recording of the working group meeting and the session Materials.

Each pick has the same parts. Why tells you why it is worth your time. What gives the contribution in plain terms, and How gives the mechanism. Where applicable tells you whether the work is general or specific to one organization, vendor, or deployment. A write-up marked from abstract only had no fuller source available. Links come from the program, so a pick without a link had none.

items.title: ASPA in the RPKI Dashboard
items.text:
APRICOT 2026 (Jakarta) — Operator digest Core pick Jakarta · 12 February 2026

Slides

Tim Bruijnzeels, RIPE

PDF

  • Why: ASPA is the mechanism operators will be asked to deploy after ROV; this is the clearest available explanation of its verification semantics — what it catches, what it deliberately tolerates, and how it fails.
  • What: A worked tutorial of ASPA (AS Provider Authorisations): objects like ROAs, signed by the customer-AS holder, authorizing one or more provider ASes. Routes learned from customers are invalid if a hop is proven "Not Provider"; the system supports partial deployment (no attestation = fail open, as does an RPKI validation problem itself), and it detects valley-free violations by constructing the longest UP ramp (customer→provider from the origin) and DOWN ramp (provider→customer from the receiver) and rejecting paths with a gap — i.e., route leaks — regardless of whether the cause is accident, leak, or spoofing.
  • How: Object structure and path-verification logic presented through concrete examples (spoofed-origin and leaked-path cases), matching what the RIPE RPKI Dashboard now surfaces.
  • Where applicable: Protocol-level and vendor-neutral; broadly applicable. Deployment is early (ARIN brought ASPA online for its own services 20 January 2026, per the ARIN update in the same program), so this is the right time to learn the semantics before it lands in dashboards you use.

items.title: Authenticating networks with RPKI RSC
items.text:
APRICOT 2026 (Jakarta) — Operator digest Adjacent pick Jakarta · 12 February 2026

Slides

Arnold Nipper, DE-CIX (with Yolandi Cloete)

PDF

  • Why: Machine-verifiable proof that the party you're talking to controls the network resources it claims — network identity, which rhymes with the workload-identity problem in other domains.
  • What: PeeringDB is introducing signup authentication for networks via RPKI RSC (RPKI Signed Checklists) in March 2026, and the talk solicits community input on follow-on features: whether to surface how and when a network authenticated, and whether to support periodic re-authentication.
  • How: RSC objects let a resource holder sign an arbitrary checklist of their holdings; PeeringDB will use them to verify that a PeeringDB record is created by whoever actually holds the ASN/prefixes. (APNIC's annual report in the same program notes RSC objects are now provided in its RPKI services too.)
  • Where applicable: PeeringDB-specific rollout, but the pattern — cryptographic resource-holder authentication replacing manual LOA/email verification — is general, and directly relevant to anyone building inter-org trust flows. Caveat: this is a thin lightning talk and the deck ends with a sponsorship pitch; the signal is the feature, not the depth.

items.title: BGP in 2025
items.text:
APRICOT 2026 (Jakarta) — Operator digest Core pick Jakarta · 12 February 2026

Slides

Geoffrey Huston, APNIC

PDF

  • Why: The annual reference for DFZ scale, churn, and the year's notable routing events — baseline data for FIB/TCAM planning and for understanding routing-system fragility.
  • What: The IPv4 DFZ exceeded 1M entries for all BGP peers in 2025; headline events include the July 7 Ramses exchange fire in Cairo (four deaths, visible disruption in BGP), and Amazon's AS16509 swinging from 50M to 158M advertised addresses during the year — including a -15.8M withdrawal on 4 November and a +15.1M re-announcement on 10 December. The advertised IPv4 table actually shrank by 11M /32s over the year while unadvertised space grew by 10M; RIR allocations continue to be outpaced by recovery. Top churn tables (China Mobile +13k prefixes, USDA's odd 3,122-prefix behavior, Cox, Amazon) give a feel for who is re-de-aggregating.
  • How: Longitudinal analysis across every routing peer of RouteViews and RIPE RIS: FIB counts, advertised address span, update/churn dynamics, two decades of comparison.
  • Where applicable: Global and vendor-neutral; the numbers are what they are. Most useful as planning input (FIB growth, prefix-churn tolerance) and as a reminder that single-actor behavior can move the global table by millions of addresses in a day.

items.title: bgproutes.io: A Next-Generation BGP Data Collection Platform
items.text:
APRICOT 2026 (Jakarta) — Operator digest Core pick Jakarta · 12 February 2026

Slides Recording

Thomas Holterbach, University of Strasbourg (with Thomas Alfroy, Cristel Pelsser)

VideoPDF

  • Why: RIPE RIS and RouteViews only collect best-path announcements; monitoring hijacks, leaks, and policy behavior needs more, and this platform — running for a year — shows how to get it.
  • What: A next-gen BGP collection platform prioritizing accurate real-time/short-term monitoring and perpetual retention (where RIS/RouteViews historically prioritized coverage). After one year it receives data from ~70 contributing networks and, critically, aggregates everything already collected by RIPE RIS, RouteViews, PCH, and CGTF into a single database, then exposes it via API and dashboards.
  • How: Three coverage ingredients: (1) automated peering establishment — operators authenticate via PeeringDB and fill in a form to start a session; (2) aggregation of existing collectors; (3) BGP Monitoring Protocol to collect beyond best-path (routes from multiple peers at multiple decision-process stages) — operationally, a small number of BMP sessions already yields a large number of additional vantage points. Every collected route gets RPKI and ASPA validation, with results exposed to users, which makes the platform a live testbed for assessing whether those mechanisms actually work at scale.
  • Where applicable: Community infrastructure, partially APNIC Foundation funded; usable by any operator or researcher today (contribute a session, or just consume). Complements rather than replaces RIS/RouteViews.
path: bgproutes.io: A Next-Generation BGP Data Collection Platform

items.title: Building an OOB network
items.text:
APRICOT 2026 (Jakarta) — Operator digest Adjacent pick Jakarta · 12 February 2026

Slides

Phil Mawson, Vocus

PDF

  • Why: The management plane is what saves you when the data plane is down — this is a multi-year, build-it-again carrier case study with real design decisions, prompted by exactly the class of outage (Optus AS7474 national outage, November 2023; Meta, October 2021) that makes OOB non-negotiable.
  • What: Vocus' consolidation of many inherited bespoke OOB solutions into a dedicated national OOB MPLS network, built alongside a new zero-touch-provisioned aggregation network.
  • How: Key rules: OOB must not rely on any founder IP network; per-state regions with route-reflector pairs; OSPF as IGP; own transmission interstate with diverse paths and metro dark-fiber rings. Equipment: Juniper ACX7024/SRX345 routers, EX3400/4100 switches, Opengear console servers. International sites use Megaport Layer-2 VXC back to an Australian headend (cheaper than 10G waves). Extras worth stealing: a third-party transit VPN concentrator as break-glass if AS4826 dies entirely, geographically diverse bastion hosts in three cities, and printed break-glass local credentials locked away for when your auth servers are unreachable.
  • Where applicable: Vocus-specific in its parts list and assumptions (they own Australian transmission), but the design principles — independence from the production network, geographic diversity, break-glass auth — transfer to any operator or large DC operator. Budget math differs if you must buy OOB transport.

items.title: Can RPKI help mitigate social engineering attacks?
items.text:
APRICOT 2026 (Jakarta) — Operator digest Adjacent pick Jakarta · 12 February 2026

Slides

Sanjaya, APNIC (with Carlos Martinez, LACNIC)

PDF

  • Why: A rare public postmortem of a hijack executed through humans, not protocol weakness — and a direct answer to whether RPKI would have stopped it.
  • What: LACNIC address space was hijacked intermittently in July 2025 by a rogue AS with a repeat-offender history across multiple RIR regions. The investigation (LACNIC → APNIC → APJII/IDNIC) found the bad actor had hijacked the ASN itself and convinced a multinational transit provider to provision transit using forged company letterhead and a faked domain — short random BGP advertisements followed. The transit provider terminated service on the victim's report; the case was jointly written up as a community case study.
  • How: Incident timeline and escalation-path walkthrough; the stated lessons map the defenses: a ROA with correct maxlength prevents the prefix hijack, and ASPA blocks unauthorized upstream providers — the exact door the attacker walked through.
  • Where applicable: General — any resource holder. Its main value is the honest gap analysis: ROV stops origin forgery but not social engineering at your transit provider; ASPA (or contractual LOA verification) is the missing control.
path: Can RPKI help mitigate social engineering attacks?

items.title: Channelmania! – future proof your DWDM network topology while keeping it flexible for 1.6T
items.text:
APRICOT 2026 (Jakarta) — Operator digest Core pick Jakarta · 12 February 2026

Slides

Thomas Weible, FLEXOPTIX

PDF

  • Why: Choosing grid spacing and filters today determines whether your DWDM plant can carry 800G/1.6T superchannels tomorrow — a topology/spectrum planning problem IP engineers now own under IPoDWDM.
  • What: An argument that coherent detection changes the rules: because a coherent receiver is "blind" to anything but its own wavelength, you can build filterless/colorless topologies and combine sub-bands through cheap 1x4 splitters and ordinary 50 GHz muxes. The concrete recommendation is 400 GHz COTS muxes (12 channels in C-band vs. the classic 96x50 GHz) to future-proof for 1.6T while remaining backward compatible with legacy 50 GHz services.
  • How: Walks from OOK/direct-detection limits through higher-order modulation (16-constellation, dual-polarization, 425Gbps at 53.125 GBd), balanced receivers, phase- and polarization-diversity coherent detection, homodyne/heterodyne/intradyne tradeoffs, and ends with a "make a frequency plan for your spans" design methodology — think in THz/GHz, not nm or channel numbers.
  • Where applicable: General DWDM design guidance for operators planning or refactoring their own optical plant; vendor-presented (FLEXOPTIX), so the COTS-component framing is self-interested, but the physics and filter-sizing argument are vendor-neutral. Assumes coherent optics end-to-end.
path: Channelmania! – future proof your DWDM network topology while keeping it flexible for 1.6T

items.title: Conference Network Report
items.text:
APRICOT 2026 (Jakarta) — Operator digest Adjacent pick Jakarta · 12 February 2026

Slides

Yoshinobu Matsuzaki, IIJ (APRICOT Technical Committee)

PDF

  • Why: A compact live postmortem from running a real network under load — including an IPv6-mostly deployment with measured client behavior and a genuinely unusual BGP debugging story.
  • What: The APRICOT 2026 NOC ran dual transit (Lintasarta, Envision) plus Starlink backup, Akvorado NetFlow analysis, and an IPv6-mostly design: 609 unique MACs, 70% of clients (431) operated IPv6-only via NAT64 (DHCPv4 option 108 signaling), 30% dual-stack, 300 Mbps peak. Incidents and fixes: WiFi channel overload at the opening plenary; a BGP "ghost route" — their prefixes showed globally reachable via route-views/RIS but lacked actual reachability, traced to a longer-than-expected AS_PATH left over from an earlier temporary announcement, cleared by contacting ASes on the path (one had a config bug); a rogue AP broadcasting the same SSID/password outside controller management, fixed by a reset; and intermittent public-DNS resolution failures on IPv4 queries with RD=1, fixed by offering local resolvers via RDNSS/DHCP.
  • How: Straightforward ops: PREF64/NAT64 for the v6-only tier, per-incident triage with community help on the ghost route.
  • Where applicable: Conference scale, but the lessons — IPv6-mostly is now viable for 70% of unmanaged clients, stale AS_PATHs can linger as ghost routes after withdrawals, rogue APs happen even with a controller — transfer directly to enterprise and campus networks.

items.title: Debugging Routing & Forwarding Using RIPE Atlas
items.text:
APRICOT 2026 (Jakarta) — Operator digest Adjacent pick Jakarta · 12 February 2026

Slides

Randy Bush, Internet Initiative Japan

PDF

  • Why: Two real cases where external vantage points found in minutes what provider NOCs couldn't find in weeks — cheap, adoptable debugging technique.
  • What: Case 1: a serial-console server on a colo LAN became unreachable; the provider's week of debugging failed, one Atlas global/random traceroute found the problem (with hover-text and clickable hop detail as the "smoking gun"), fixed within an hour. Case 2: a friend's IPv6 was unrouted for months while the ISP NOC saw nothing; 15 Atlas probes inside that same ISP exposed the internal routing problem to a senior engineer within hours.
  • How: RIPE Atlas (12,000+ probes) one-off measurements and traceroute visualizations, plus the measurement API for automation. Bush closes with a challenge: build an AI front-end that takes a problem description and drives the Atlas API to diagnose it — a nice framing of where troubleshooting tooling is heading.
  • Where applicable: Anyone; free to use if you host a probe (membership not required). Scale- and vendor-agnostic.
path: Debugging Routing & Forwarding Using RIPE Atlas

items.title: Exploring the Blind Spot of Internet Exchange Point Route Servers
items.text:
APRICOT 2026 (Jakarta) — Operator digest Core pick Jakarta · 12 February 2026

Slides

Stefano Servillo, University of Rome "La Sapienza" (with Spadaccino, Konstantaras, Luciani, Cuomo)

PDF

  • Why: A formally defined, quantified vulnerability in the IRR-based route-server filtering that most of the world's IXPs rely on — directly relevant to routing security practice.
  • What: The blind spot: IRR validation via AS-SET expansion builds a prefix list per peer but never binds prefixes to their legitimate origin AS, so a prefix covered by a route object under any AS that appears in a member's AS-SET is accepted by the route server regardless of who really owns it. Stale AS-SETs make this worse: of ~130k allocated ASes only ~77k are active, so AS-SETs routinely contain unallocated, private, or inactive ASes whose route objects can weaponize the gap. The team demonstrates prefix hijacking through this path, quantifies prevalence across a large set of IXPs, and validates with real route-server data from AMS-IX and NAMEX.
  • How: Feasibility analysis defines the conditions (prefix not ROA-covered, update not filtered by intermediate ASes, origin AS in a member's AS-SET but not required to be there, etc.), followed by control-plane data analysis; practical countermeasures to strengthen RS filtering are proposed.
  • Where applicable: Applies to any IXP or operator doing IRR-based filtering anywhere; RPKI ROAs close the hole for covered prefixes, which sharpens the case for ROA coverage as hijack insurance rather than just leak hygiene. Research-grade but with production validation.
path: Exploring the Blind Spot of Internet Exchange Point Route Servers

items.title: Getting 1+ Tbps from an x86 server
items.text:
APRICOT 2026 (Jakarta) — Operator digest Core pick Jakarta · 12 February 2026

Slides

Branimir Rajtar, 5x9 Networks

PDF

  • Why: The datapath-internals story of the year at this conference — what it actually takes to make commodity x86 forward at terabit rates, relevant to anyone building or evaluating software dataplanes (vBNG, vEPC, NFV).
  • What: The evolution of a virtualized BNG from many small 4-vCPU forwarder VMs to a single "Big VM" forwarder, ending at 200 Mpps per CPU and 1.6 Tbps on one server (~600 W). Includes an honest comparison table: ASIC white-label switching (multi-terabit, low flexibility, ~30k subscribers) vs. x86 (~1 Tbps and improving, ~200k subscribers, high flexibility, C/DPDK/eBPF/P4 development).
  • How: SR-IOV plus Intel DPDK to bypass host kernel and drivers; systematic optimization in waves — newer hardware (+30%), deep DPDK/BIOS/PCIe/NIC tuning (+30%), then vTune-guided code-level redesigns driven by CPU cache behavior and PCIe bottlenecks. The horizontal-scaling small-VM design was abandoned because per-instance overhead dominated. CUPS architecture (dashboard/controller/forwarder) throughout.
  • Where applicable: vBNG/BRAS is the use case and the headline numbers are tied to their specific hardware generations; the methodology (measure, profile, redesign around cache/PCIe) transfers to any DPDK dataplane effort.
path: Getting 1+ Tbps from an x86 server

items.title: IP Networking in Deep Space
items.text:
APRICOT 2026 (Jakarta) — Operator digest Wildcard pick Jakarta · 12 February 2026

Slides

Marc Blanchet, Viagenie

PDF

  • Why: Not operationally relevant, but the most instructive stress test of the IP suite's assumptions you'll read this year — what breaks when RTT is minutes and links vanish for hours.
  • What: An architecture for Moon and Mars networks in which every link carries IP: 3GPP (5G/6G) and 802.11/WiFi on the surface, CCSDS for deep space, spacecraft onboard networks also IP — creating a single Layer-3 network end to end, aligned with NASA's LunaNet interoperability specification. The core problems: Earth-Moon ~2 s one-way delay, Earth-Mars 4–22 minutes, and intermittence (an orbiter passing behind a body turns a 2-second path into a 2-hour gap; until full laser-linked constellations exist, disruptions are the norm).
  • How: Three key adaptations, with simulations confirming suitability: (1) temporary buffering of IP packets on forwarders with intermittent links; (2) configuring QUIC with parameters matching the expected round-trip time; (3) configuring application timeouts. Everything else follows from accepting asynchronous operation as the paradigm — no interactivity, no fast remote management.
  • Where applicable: Space-specific by subject, but the delay/disruption-tolerance findings translate to any store-and-forward or high-latency environment, and the QUIC-parameter work is a concrete example of transport tuning under extreme RTT.

items.title: IPoDWDM in 2026
items.text:
APRICOT 2026 (Jakarta) — Operator digest Core pick Jakarta · 12 February 2026

Slides

Mark Tinka, TransmissionCo

PDF

  • Why: IPoDWDM failed once (2000s: proprietary, fixed, power-hungry line cards) and is now succeeding — this talk explains exactly what changed and who is deploying it, which matters for anyone planning DC/WAN interconnect on dark fiber or short DWDM spans.
  • What: A state-of-the-market walkthrough of routed optical networking built on MSA coherent pluggables. Per CignalAI data cited, coherent pluggables outsold proprietary embedded optics 2:1 in 2025, and most 400G-ZR shipments have gone into hyperscaler IPoDWDM deployments; hyperscalers are converging on OSFP for 800G-ZR for thermal reasons. Includes a live reference network: a 130 km span in Cape Town built from a Juniper ACX7300 router with 2x 400G-ZR+ QSFP-DD plugs plus a third-party open line system — no transponder tier.
  • How: Coherent pluggables (100G-ZR QSFP28, 400G/800G-ZR QSFP-DD/OSFP) put DWDM line-side optics directly in standard router/switch ports, on dark fiber or integrated with a line system for reach; line- and client-side mix on the same card; disaggregation removes the optic from the host platform. Pluggable transponders are positioned as the bridge for operators who still want Layer-1 aggregation/demarcation/protection.
  • Where applicable: Broadly applicable technique, not org-specific — driven by hyperscaler economics but now accessible to any operator with dark fiber or short spans. Presented by a vendor-side MD, but the deck is grounded in third-party market data and a real multi-vendor deployment rather than a product pitch.

items.title: IX.br São Paulo: Migration to SRv6 EVPN
items.text:
APRICOT 2026 (Jakarta) — Operator digest Core pick Jakarta · 12 February 2026

Slides

Julio Sirota, NIC.br

PDF

  • Why: A production migration template for anyone running a large L2 fabric (IXP peering LAN or DC) on aging LDP+VPLS: flood-based MAC learning, ARP/ND storms, and unknown-unicast flooding are exactly the failure modes EVPN was built to fix.
  • What: The completed migration of IX.br São Paulo (one of the world's largest IX fabrics) from LDP+VPLS to SRv6 EVPN. Concrete results: 84% of equipment (97% of capacity) now on EVPN CSID SRv6 with proxy ARP/ND, unknown-unicast flood eliminated, and a large measured drop in ARP/Neighbor Solicitation volume — including visible reduction in CPU load on participant routers.
  • How: RFC 8560 "VPLS and EVPN seamless integration" allowed PE-by-PE replacement with the core forwarding both MPLS and IPv6/SRv6 labels during migration, no gateway needed. Proxy ARP/ND uses the RFC 9047 ARP/ND Extended Community with the Immutable flag so static entries prevail over dynamic ones, which both kills broadcast storms and prevents participants answering ARP/ND for IPs that are not theirs (spoofing protection).
  • Where applicable: IX.br-specific production story, but the mechanism is standard-track (RFC 8560, RFC 9047) and broadly applicable to any VPLS estate with SRv6-capable PEs. The seamless-migration trick (dual-plane forwarding, one box at a time) is the transferable part.
path: IX.br São Paulo: Migration to SRv6 EVPN

items.title: Keynote: The Agentic Shift: The Internet Industry Reimagined
items.text:
APRICOT 2026 (Jakarta) — Operator digest Wildcard pick Jakarta · 12 February 2026

Mukhammad Andri Setiawan, Universitas Islam Indonesia

  • Why: The direction-of-field keynote: autonomous agents as operators of infrastructure — the world the IETF's WEBBOTAUTH and CATALIST efforts (see the IETF update above) are being chartered for.
  • What: An argument that the industry is shifting from manual configuration to networks configured by agents, code generated without SQL, and ops moving from hands-on engineering to high-level coordination — with roles emerging for the next decade: "Agent Shepherds" guiding agent swarms, "Sovereignty Architects" for ethical/policy frameworks, and "Compute Brokers" managing agent-economy compute. Also covers bias and accuracy risks, and "AI sovereignty" as a national capability.
  • How: Futures-style synthesis rather than a technical method; the same speaker's IPv6-renumbering study elsewhere in the program grounds the claim empirically (AI-assisted configuration cut measured cognitive workload ~65–72% and task time dramatically in a small within-subjects experiment, while organizational readiness lagged).
  • Where applicable: Broad and speculative, but the trajectory it names — identity, authorization, and supervision for non-human actors — is exactly where the identity portion of this reader's portfolio is heading. (from abstract only)
path: Keynote: The Agentic Shift: The Internet Industry Reimagined

items.title: MESec: Minimal-Exposure AS-Path Verification against BGP Post-ROV Attacks
items.text:
APRICOT 2026 (Jakarta) — Operator digest Core pick Jakarta · 12 February 2026

Slides

Jiangou Zhan, Tsinghua University

PDF

  • Why: With ~49% of IPv4 prefixes ROA-protected and ~37% of ASes doing ROV, attackers move to path manipulation and route leaks — but ASPA's requirement to publish customer-provider relationships globally is commercially toxic. This is the sharpest articulation of that adoption dilemma at the conference, with a real alternative.
  • What: MEASPV, a framework that decouples path validation from topology disclosure: relationship attestations are visible only to designated trusted validators, never broadcast. Evaluation shows a security posture comparable to standard ASPA against post-ROV threats, with minimal information exposure and incremental deployability (no BGP-4 message changes).
  • How: Validator-assisted, three phases: trust establishment (ASes share encrypted, authenticated neighbor-relationship data with chosen validators), path verification on each BGP UPDATE (validators return Type-I high-trust direct reports plus Type-II public-data checks from CAIDA/RouteViews; results aggregate into a score from Strong-Valid to Strong-Suspect), and secure route selection using the score as a BGP decision-process tie-breaker. Caching of per-pair scores (1–5 day refresh, path score = minimum) keeps latency and control traffic low. The authors also prove a lower bound: any effective defense must expose relationship data to at least one third-party verifier — the question is how few.
  • Where applicable: Research framework, not deployed; requires a trusted-validator ecosystem. Conceptually important for anyone designing ASPA-adjacent or attestation-based path security, including in private fabrics where a neutral validator is easier to stand up.
path: MESec: Minimal-Exposure AS-Path Verification against BGP Post-ROV Attacks

items.title: sidrops IETF UPDATE
items.text:
APRICOT 2026 (Jakarta) — Operator digest Adjacent pick Jakarta · 12 February 2026

Slides

Tom Harrison, APNIC

PDF

  • Why: The plumbing of RPKI distribution is being redesigned; if you operate relying parties or a publication point, this affects you.
  • What: Three sidrops work items: the Erik synchronization protocol (draft-ietf-sidrops-rpki-erik-protocol), NRO Trust Anchor Constraints, and Best Current Practices for RPKI publication servers.
  • How: Erik is the interesting one — today every relying party fetches from every publication point (an M:N problem that worsens over time, where one slow PP holds up an RP's whole validation run). An Erik relay, runnable by anybody, fetches from PPs and serves RPs over the new protocol: PPs go from handling thousands of RPs to ~20 relays in full deployment. It also fixes RRDP's encoding waste (base64 adds 33%, XML another ~10%), serves raw DER objects, and uses Merkle trees to support cheap diffs and individual-file repair — eliminating the "delta failed, re-fetch a 100 MB snapshot" thundering herd (the deck shows a 102 MB snapshot vs. a 68 KB delta).
  • Where applicable: All RPKI operators; deployable incrementally alongside rsync/RRDP. Reference implementations exist (rpkitouch relay, public relay instance).

items.title: To Space and Back: Integrating Next-Generation Terrestrial and Satellite Communication Networks
items.text:
APRICOT 2026 (Jakarta) — Operator digest Wildcard pick Jakarta · 12 February 2026

Slides

Katarina Stefanović, Telecom Serbia

PDF

  • Why: A surprising measured result: LEO satellite paths, though physically longer, can beat terrestrial mobile networks on long-haul latency and stability — with real data, not vendor claims.
  • What: A 7-day continuous RIPE Atlas measurement campaign comparing Starlink LEO connectivity against 4G/5G mobile networks across multiple European countries, targeting an APNIC-hosted host in Singapore: Starlink consistently showed lower and more stable long-haul RTT (enabled by backbone efficiency and evolving inter-satellite-laser routing), while mobile networks showed higher jitter and EPC-driven processing delays despite shorter physical paths.
  • How: Atlas probes measuring long-haul RTT, hop-count behavior, intercontinental routing paths, and jitter distribution; plus an architecture deep-dive into LEO mesh topology, ground stations, laser inter-satellite link types (intra-plane, inter-plane, crossing-plane), and NTN–TN interoperability per 3GPP TR 38.811 — including how beam handovers, congestion, atmosphere, and PoP presence shape user experience.
  • Where applicable: Results are European-vantage and Starlink-specific; the framework (measurement-based comparison rather than assumptions) is general. Relevant to anyone evaluating LEO as a WAN or resilience path, and to the interconnection-panel question of whether LEO edges change regional peering economics.
path: To Space and Back: Integrating Next-Generation Terrestrial and Satellite Communication Networks

items.title: What’s new at the IETF?
items.text:
APRICOT 2026 (Jakarta) — Operator digest Core pick Jakarta · 12 February 2026

Slides

Paresh Khatri, Nokia (delivered with Warren Kumari, Dhruv Dhody, and Suresh Krishnan, IAB)

PDF

  • Why: The standards radar this cycle is unusually relevant: three of the newly chartered working groups touch attestation, bot/agent authentication, and PKI — squarely in identity territory — alongside routing and ops topics.
  • What: New WGs: Secure Evidence and Attestation Transport (SEAT), Domain Connection (DCONN), Open Cloud Mesh (OCM), Web Bot Auth (WEBBOTAUTH), and PKI, Logs, And Tree Signatures (PLANTS); Authenticated Transfer (ATP) in chartering. BoFs at IETF 125: CATALIST (coordinating AI agent-to-agent communications work) and ONSEN (operationalizing service abstractions). Also reports the IAB workshop on IP address geolocation concluding that IP is a weak, overloaded geolocation signal (anycast, satellite, overlays) — a useful data point for anyone building location-dependent policy.
  • How: An operator-oriented survey of IETF structure (areas, ~125 WGs, IRTF, IAB) and where the new work landed, aimed at helping operators track what will hit their networks.
  • Where applicable: Broadly applicable; for this reader, WEBBOTAUTH and CATALIST are the items to watch for agentic/workload identity, and SEAT/PLANTS for attestation-transport plumbing.

items.title: Advisory Council Working Group Updates
items.text:
ARIN 57 Public Policy and Members Meeting digest Adjacent pick 22 April 2026

Slides Recording

Douglas Camin, Alison Wood, and Matthew Wilder, ARIN Advisory Council

VideoPDF

  • Why: The forward worklist for number-resource policy — a cheap way to see which NRPM sections will be churned over the next 12–18 months.
  • What: The Policy Experience Report Working Group's "What's Hot" list: eliminating NRPM 8.5.7 (alternative additional IPv4 transfer criteria, judged redundant and little-used); simplifying the IPv6 initial allocation formula in 6.5.2.1; reconciling inter-RIR transfer discrepancies in 8.4 (needs-based requirements differ across RIRs, creating asymmetric transfer flows); and consolidating the overlapping IPv4 direct-allocation sections (4.1.8, 4.4, 4.10). The Policy Engagement WG is surveying the community on modernizing participation beyond the mailing list / meeting format.
  • How: Status reports on working-group deliberation — no mechanism, but each item names the section and the observed problem.
  • Where applicable: ARIN-region policy process. The inter-RIR transfer asymmetry item is the one with the most practical consequence for multi-region footprint planning.

items.title: Engineering Update
items.text:
ARIN 57 Public Policy and Members Meeting digest Core pick 22 April 2026

Slides Recording

Mark Kosters, ARIN (CTO)

VideoPDF

  • Why: Densely useful for three of the PM's interests at once: identity (ARIN's own MFA mix), physical DC work (ARIN's data center migration), and routing security infrastructure (RPKI trust anchor constraints, ASPA, and the planned retirement of legacy directory services).
  • What: The operational report on ARIN's public services. Highlights: MFA adoption across 53,065 users is 61% TOTP, 36% SMS, and only 3% FIDO2 — a sobering data point for anyone betting on passkey adoption in registry-adjacent systems; all authorizations have moved into ARIN Online (email-based approvals retired); ASPA support released; RPKI Trust Anchor Constraints work is underway, leveraging extended stats and extended transfer logs to attest registry contents per the IETF constraining-trust-anchors draft (already implemented in rpki-client); a consultation is planned on retiring RWhois and Whois-RWS, collapsing four directory-service interfaces (Whois, RWhois, Whois-RWS, RDAP) down toward RDAP.
  • How: On infrastructure, ARIN moved its computer room from HQ to a new Northern Virginia data center, replaced end-of-life hardware, and now runs public-facing services on Red Hat OpenShift with services under OpenShift KubeVirt virtual machines, with Prometheus monitoring displacing Sensu. RRDP is now the largest public-facing traffic class at 46.6% — a signal of how RPKI repo synchronization has become the dominant directory workload.
  • Where applicable: ARIN-specific as an implementation, but the pattern — registry services re-platformed onto hosted Kubernetes with VMs for legacy services, and protocol-surface reduction (retiring RWhois/Whois-RWS in favor of RDAP) — is a template any infrastructure registry operator (including internal IPAM/identity services) can study. The FIDO2-at-3% figure is a broadly citable adoption reality check.

items.title: Grant Reports
items.text:
ARIN 57 Public Policy and Members Meeting digest Core pick 22 April 2026

Slides Recording

Harlen Stenn (Network Time Foundation), James Harr (Internet2), Matt Griswold (20C)

VideoPDF

  • Why: Three community-grant reports, and the middle one is a genuinely reusable operator tool: a cheap, pre-configured device that stands up IPv6-only/IPv6-mostly test environments — the exact environments that are otherwise a multi-week lab project.
  • What: (1) Internet2's IPv6 Test Pod: a sub-$150 device, funded by a $16,000 grant (follow-on to $7,000 in 2023), that creates dual-stack, NAT64/DNS64, IPv6-mostly (DHCPv4 Option 108), and IPv6-only wired/wifi networks over an IPv6 tunnel, pre-configured and distributed free to participants (45 units delivered, 20 more in April). Testing to date includes the Windows 11 CLAT private preview, NetworkManager 1.58 CLAT support, and HPN-SSH Happy Eyeballs behavior. (2) NTF's grant adds native Markdown output to GNU AutoGen to unify NTP documentation formats. (3) 20C's "From Raw to Ready" delivers a web UI (reg.fullctl.io) over regCtl, which normalizes RDAP responses across RIRs into consistent object views.
  • How: The pod encapsulates the hard-to-assemble mix — NAT64 (poorly supported on low-end platforms), DNS64, PREF64, and Option 108 signaling — so a developer, IT support team, or network engineer can test client behavior in a v6-only environment without building the bed themselves. The rationale laid out is worth internalizing: dual-stack hides problems (Happy Eyeballs), doubles address pools and firewall policies, and makes troubleshooting ambiguous.
  • Where applicable: The pod is available by application (ipv6-pod.info) to anyone in the ARIN community — this is the transferable piece. The AutoGen and regCtl work is niche but the RDAP normalizer is handy for anyone scripting against registry data across RIRs.

items.title: KEYNOTE: Demystifying RPKI: Exploring Tools to Simplify ROA Planning and Visualize Validation
items.text:
ARIN 57 Public Policy and Members Meeting digest Core pick 22 April 2026

Slides Recording

Steve Wallace, Internet2 (NSF-supported, OAC-2530871)

VideoPDF

  • Why: ROA creation is the single biggest friction point in RPKI adoption — operators fear creating a ROA that accidentally invalidates their own (or a customer's) more-specific announcements. This is a set of free, working tools that directly address that fear, plus an early look at ASPA object planning.
  • What: Three web tools hosted at rootbeer.internet2.edu: an RPKI-ROA Planner that computes candidate ROAs for a prefix and the safest order to create them; an RPKI-ROA Visualizer that walks through Route Origin Validation bit by bit (useful for training staff who don't intuit maxLength semantics); and an experimental RPKI-ASPA Planner that suggests a draft ASPA object for an ASN.
  • How: The ROA Planner correlates three data sources — IRR route objects, currently observed Internet routes, and historical routing data — to derive the set of plausible origins for a prefix, then lets the user pick which apply and sequences ROA creation to avoid transient Invalid states. The ASPA Planner builds its suggestion from CAIDA AS-relationship data ("and some magic," per the speaker).
  • Where applicable: Broadly applicable to any operator with ARIN-region resources; the tools are public and free. The ASPA Planner is explicitly experimental and should be treated as a starting draft, not a turnkey ASPA — ASPA semantics are still moving through the IETF.
path: KEYNOTE: Demystifying RPKI: Exploring Tools to Simplify ROA Planning and Visualize Validation

items.title: KEYNOTE: The Nine Lives of an Early Adopter: Leading Cats to Water in the IPv6 Era
items.text:
ARIN 57 Public Policy and Members Meeting digest Core pick 22 April 2026

Slides Recording

Nick Burlagio (Planning and Architecture) and Inder Monga (Executive Director), ESnet

VideoPDF

  • Why: ESnet is one of the few production networks that has actually gone IPv6-only on its management plane (with the ESnet6 buildout, completed 2022), and this keynote frames the "why now" argument in terms directly relevant to cloud-native and agentic workloads. It is a rare operator talk where the transition strategy, not the nostalgia, is the payload.
  • What: A history-to-present narrative of ESnet's IPv6 journey — 6Bone participant, 6REN founder, recipient of the first production IPv6 allocation from ARIN in 1999 — culminating in ESnet6, which runs an IPv6-only management plane with comprehensive automation and visibility. The forward-looking argument: AI agents on the network need simplicity (elimination of middleboxes), one consistent addressing scheme for end-to-end automation, and any-to-any hyper-connectivity — none of which survive NAT and dual-stack sprawl.
  • How: Primarily a strategy and lessons talk rather than a mechanism talk (the deck walks the 1995–2026 timeline of IPv6 touchpoints). The concrete operational takeaway is the IPv6-only management plane as proof that a large WAN can run single-stack for infrastructure traffic even while carrying dual-stack customer traffic.
  • Where applicable: ESnet-scale (DOE national labs, 100G/400G backbone) is specific, but the management-plane-first pattern is broadly transferable — it's the least risky place to go v6-only and it forces the tooling/automation to become v6-native. The agentic-workload argument is relevant to anyone planning for machine-dense networks.
path: KEYNOTE: The Nine Lives of an Early Adopter: Leading Cats to Water in the IPv6 Era

items.title: Number Resource Organization Number Council and RIR Governance Document Status Update
items.text:
ARIN 57 Public Policy and Members Meeting digest Wildcard pick 22 April 2026

Slides Recording

Amy Potter, ASO AC Vice Chair / NRO NC

VideoPDF

  • Why: Not technical, but this is the rewrite of the constitutional document of the RIR system — including, for the first time, how an RIR gets derecognized and what happens to its registry in an emergency. After the AFRINIC governance crisis, this is where the field is heading institutionally, and it will shape who holds and administers number resources globally.
  • What: A status report on Version 2 of the "RIR Governance Document" (the ICP-2 replacement), targeting finalization by Q4 2026. Key mechanics agreed or in drafting: recognition of a new RIR at "unanimity minus one" (with conflict-of-interest handling); targeted compliance reviews initiable by any group of RIRs, by 25% of an RIR's membership (or 2,000 members, whichever is lower), or by ICANN; regular audits at least every 5 years; and an Emergency Continuity procedure allowing an affected RIR to trigger continuity for itself (or others/ICANN at sub-unanimity), with an "Emergency Operator" taking over the affected RIR's services, staged transfer, and no cap on renewals.
  • How: Multi-round global consultation (298 RIR questionnaire responses, two public comment rounds), with substantive issues tracked in published status reports.
  • Where applicable: Global RIR system governance — affects every resource holder indirectly, and directly if you operate in a region whose RIR ever enters distress. The Emergency Operator concept is the piece to watch: it is effectively a pre-agreed continuity plan for the Internet's number registry.
path: Number Resource Organization Number Council and RIR Governance Document Status Update

items.title: Policy Block: Draft Policy ARIN-2025-3: Change Section 9 Out Of Region Use Minimum Criteria
items.text:
ARIN 57 Public Policy and Members Meeting digest Adjacent pick 22 April 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Gerry George (with Matthew Wilder), ARIN Advisory Council

VideoPDF

  • Why: A live example of how a seemingly small threshold change (/22 → /24) can materially shift address-market behavior — the staff review itself says so.
  • What: Reduces the in-region IPv4 utilization required to justify out-of-region use from a /22 to a /24. Staff and Legal review flags the consequence explicitly: nothing in Section 9 caps out-of-region use, so a single in-region /24 could in practice unlock substantially larger blocks for deployment entirely outside the ARIN region; staff anticipate a significant increase in IPv4 waitlist volume and ticket workload.
  • How: A one-line NRPM text change, with the "real and substantial connection" requirement as the only remaining guard.
  • Where applicable: ARIN-region policy, but relevant to any multi-region operator's IPv4 planning: if adopted, it lowers the entry cost for using ARIN as the source of globally-deployed space, and community feedback notes it could push organizations with heavy out-of-region growth toward other RIRs.
path: Policy Block: Draft Policy ARIN-2025-3: Change Section 9 Out Of Region Use Minimum Criteria

items.title: Policy Block: Draft Policy ARIN-2025-8: Reserve 4.10 Space for In-Region Use
items.text:
ARIN 57 Public Policy and Members Meeting digest Adjacent pick 22 April 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

E. Marie Brierley (with Kaitlyn Pellak), ARIN Advisory Council

VideoPDF

  • Why: The policy counterpart to the RIO fraud report — 4.10 space (the IPv4 block reserved to facilitate IPv6 deployment) is one of the documented abuse vectors, and this codifies the in-region restriction.
  • What: Amends Section 4.10 to state the set-aside is dedicated to facilitating IPv6 deployment within the ARIN service area. Staff review confirms this codifies existing practice with no operational impact. The live controversy is scope: PPML commenters noted the vague wording could block legitimate uses — e.g., an org with a globally-used ARIN IPv6 allocation using its 4.10 IPv4 to provide NAT64 for that global v6 space.
  • How: A two-word textual amendment; the interesting question posed to the community is whether "only" should be specified.
  • Where applicable: ARIN-region policy; matters mainly to orgs holding or seeking 4.10 space — which, per the RIO report, includes the more inventive lessees.
path: Policy Block: Draft Policy ARIN-2025-8: Reserve 4.10 Space for In-Region Use

items.title: Policy Block: Draft Policy ARIN-2026-1: Taking IP To Other Planets (TIPTOP)
items.text:
ARIN 57 Public Policy and Members Meeting digest Wildcard pick 22 April 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Alison Wood (with Brian Jones), ARIN Advisory Council

VideoPDF

  • Why: The first formal attempt to recognize off-Earth use cases in any RIR's policy manual, and a genuinely novel addressing problem: how do you allocate IP space for a topology whose "regions" are gravity wells? For anyone who thinks about aggregation and hierarchical addressing, this is a fun and occasionally rigorous stress test of the concepts.
  • What: A draft policy, proposed jointly with the IETF TIPTOP working group (see draft-li-tiptop-address-space and draft-many-tiptop-ip-architecture), to let ARIN allocate address space to Extra-Terrestrial Networks (defined as beyond the GEO arc — LEO and GEO excluded). It proposes hierarchically organizing allocations by "Celestial Region" (Moon, Earth-Moon Lagrange points, asteroid belt, planetary systems), prefers IPv6 with a /48 minimum, employs sparse allocation within the ETN block for growth, and relaxes utilization verification where "active host" checks are impractical for high-latency nodes.
  • How: Topology-aligned aggregation: agencies currently select space ad hoc from multiple RIRs, forcing disaggregated announcements when deep-space networks interconnect; contiguous per-region blocks would let each gravity well aggregate to a single route advertised back to terrestrial ground stations.
  • Where applicable: Not implementable as written — staff and legal review is explicit that it presumes unsatisfied prerequisites: an IETF determination, an IANA allocation, an ARIN Board finding that serving as (even interim) deep-space registry fits ARIN's mission, and concurrence of the other RIRs. Near-term demand is small and specialized. The precedent (first off-Earth recognition in RIR policy) and the routing-scalability framing are the real content.
path: Policy Block: Draft Policy ARIN-2026-1: Taking IP To Other Planets (TIPTOP)

items.title: Policy Implementation and Experience Report
items.text:
ARIN 57 Public Policy and Members Meeting digest Adjacent pick 22 April 2026

Slides Recording

John Sweeting, ARIN (Chief Experience Officer)

VideoPDF

  • Why: Where policy text meets operational reality — the most interesting part is ARIN staff's frank account of IPv4 leasing and inter-RIR transfer arbitrage, which affects the market everyone buys address space in.
  • What: Three items. (1) AFRINIC's inter-RIR transfer policy was ratified 4 February 2026; ARIN staff have reviewed it as reciprocal and will allow IPv4/ASN transfers to and from AFRINIC once AFRINIC implements. (2) On LACNIC's new third-party sub-assignment (leasing) policy: ARIN does not consider leasing to be efficient needs-based utilization for transfers (NRPM 8.⅜.4) or waitlist qualification — and staff have observed ARIN-originated space appearing on leasing platforms in other regions after inter-RIR transfer. (3) Options floated for encouraging IPv6 adoption: requiring demonstrated IPv6 deployment for IPv4 waitlist access.
  • How: A staff-practice report rather than a new mechanism; the leverage points are transfer approval criteria and waitlist eligibility rules.
  • Where applicable: Relevant to anyone acquiring or transferring IPv4 in the ARIN region, and to anyone modeling IPv4 market behavior across RIRs. The AFRINIC change materially alters the global transfer map.

items.title: Registry Integrity and Oversight
items.text:
ARIN 57 Public Policy and Members Meeting digest Adjacent pick 22 April 2026

Slides Recording

Reese Radcliffe, ARIN (Senior Manager, Registry Integrity and Oversight)

VideoPDF

  • Why: The operational security underside of the registry: how number-resource fraud actually manifests, with numbers. Directly relevant to anyone whose address space could be hijacked or whose counterparties might not be who they claim.
  • What: A threat-landscape and casework report. Notable findings: of out-of-region organizations creating ARIN Org IDs "to expand into the region," roughly 30% are found announcing ARIN resources out-of-region within 60 days; ~240 Org Creates per month, of which ~35 are escalated to RIO, with 42% of those being out-of-region expansion attempts; NRPM 4.10 (IPv4-to-facilitate-IPv6) space is abused via out-of-region announcement, reassignment to customers, leasing, or announcing with no associated IPv6; 223 policy non-compliance reports were received in 2025, of which 28 were actionable.
  • How: RIO runs escalated review of suspicious Org Creates, Section 12 audits with video identity verification, fraud investigation, and law-enforcement collaboration, plus inter-RIR knowledge sharing.
  • Where applicable: ARIN-specific process, but the threat taxonomy (entity fraud, unauthorized reassignment, out-of-region leakage, IRR misinformation) is the same one any resource holder or IX should assume exists. The 30%-within-60-days figure is a good calibration for how quickly out-of-region misuse follows a new Org ID.

items.title: Routing Security Update
items.text:
ARIN 57 Public Policy and Members Meeting digest Core pick 22 April 2026

Slides Recording

Brad Gorman, ARIN (Director, Customer Technical Services)

VideoPDF

  • Why: The best single data source on where RPKI actually stands in the ARIN region — which is directly actionable when prioritizing your own ROA coverage and when deciding how much to lean on ROV in filtering. Also the first production deployment of ASPA objects worth watching.
  • What: A quarter-over-quarter adoption report plus new features. Key numbers (NIST RPKI monitor, 1 April): global RPKI validity has climbed steadily through Q1 2026, with IPv4 and IPv6 both in the roughly 60–66% range. In-region: 8,403 organizations registered for ARIN RPKI services (25% growth since Q1 2025), 98% of them on Hosted RPKI — but ~15% of registered orgs have never created a single ROA, only 50% of RPKI-eligible IPv4 blocks are covered by ROAs, and 54% of ARIN-registered IPv4 blocks seen in announcements are RPKI Valid. ASPAs are live in production (198+ created and trending up), enabling IETF draft testing with real data. An upcoming "RPKI Routing Intelligence" feature will show orgs their prefixes as seen in the global BGP table, explain why announcements are Invalid or Not Found, and simulate the effect of proposed ROA changes.
  • How: The update combines NRO/NIST monitoring data with ARIN's own registry cross-referencing (allocations under agreement vs. ROA coverage vs. announcements). The Routing Intelligence feature is essentially a BGP-table diff against your resource certificate with counterfactual analysis.
  • Where applicable: The stats are ARIN-region-specific, but the gap they expose (signup ≠ protection; the bottleneck is ROA coverage, not registration) generalizes. The Routing Intelligence preview matters to any ARIN resource holder; worth benchmarking your own coverage against the 50%-of-eligible-blocks regional figure.

items.title: Address Supporting Organization Address Council (ASO AC) Update
items.text:
ARIN 58 Public Policy and Members Meeting digest Wildcard pick 23 October 2026

Slides Recording

Kevin Blumberg (ASO AC / NRO NC)

VideoPDF

  • Why: Not a technical talk, but it covers a genuine structural shift in Internet governance: the multi-year ICP-2 rewrite that will define how an RIR can be audited, placed under emergency operation, or derecognized. That's the failure-domain design of the registry system itself — worth one read even for a purely technical PM.
  • What: Status of the RIR Governance Document: a recommended draft published 1 September 2026 after two consultation rounds, now with ICANN for consideration after productive discussions at ICANN 87. Key changes: a five-year regular audit cycle, a distinct Compliance Review process with misuse safeguards, Rehabilitation Plans as the preferred path, a Temporary Emergency Continuity Arrangement an affected RIR can initiate for its own services (90-day limit, two-thirds RIR threshold), a derecognition process requiring two-thirds RIR support excluding the subject RIR, and amendment freezes during emergency arrangements or pending derecognition.
  • How: Multi-stakeholder consultation timeline running since October 2024; open mailing lists and ASO AC teleconferences; Oscar Robles selected to fill the vacant ICANN Board Seat 9.
  • Where applicable: Governance-level; affects all five RIRs. No operator action, but it is the framework that would govern any future RIR failure — the "datacenter redundancy plan" equivalent for the registry layer.
path: Address Supporting Organization Address Council (ASO AC) Update

items.title: ARIN Directory Services Roadmap
items.text:
ARIN 58 Public Policy and Members Meeting digest Adjacent pick 23 October 2026

Slides Recording

Hollis Kara (ARIN, Director of Communications)

VideoPDF

  • Why: Directory-data consolidation onto RDAP touches the PM's directory/identity instincts, and the Port 43 WHOIS debate is a live case study in legacy-protocol retirement politics — relevant to anyone whose tooling still scripts whois.
  • What: Outcome of a community consultation on retiring three legacy services in favor of RDAP as ARIN's single directory protocol. RWhois: uncontested, retiring on a 365-day countdown after a migration tool ships. Whois-RWS: uncontested in principle, API sunset set for July 2026/2027 path (July 2027 per deck), gated on RDAP closing one parity gap (CIDR more-specifics / hierarchy walking); web UI to run in parallel with a beta Advanced RDAP Search for ~6 months. Port 43 WHOIS: real opposition — of 43 substantive comments, 24 opposed or wanted a much longer transition (56% against), 11 supported, 8 neutral — so ARIN paused and will reconsult once RDAP clients ship by default in OS distributions.
  • How: Analysis grounded in actual query traffic (79% IP lookups, 9% ASN, 10% org) and a candid visibility caveat: the top queriers all resolve to cloud provider addresses, so ARIN can't see the real end users. Engineering judged a WHOIS-compatible proxy in front of RDAP to cost more operational risk than keeping native WHOIS running longer — the reason the proxy compromise was rejected.
  • Where applicable: Anyone with scripts or products querying ARIN directory data. The security argument (unauthenticated, unencrypted, MITM-tamperable) vs. the ecosystem-readiness argument (RDAP clients not yet default in OS distros) is the transferable lesson for any forced protocol migration.

items.title: Data Accuracy Update
items.text:
ARIN 58 Public Policy and Members Meeting digest Core pick 23 October 2026

Slides Recording

John Sweeting (ARIN, Chief Experience Officer)

VideoPDF

  • Why: Registry accuracy is network security infrastructure — the stated objectives are preventing resource hijacking and supporting law enforcement. For anyone building systems that consume WHOIS/RDAP data or dealing with hijacked/legacy space, the mechanics of how ARIN is cleaning up non-agreement holdings are directly relevant.
  • What: Progress report on driving the remaining "not under agreement" space to zero: 372,877 /24-equivalents remain outside agreements (Q3 2026), down 26,313 quarter-over-quarter and down 81% since Q1 2024; 16,212 legacy CIDR blocks; 2,195 /24-equivalents already returned to the IPv4 waitlist. A Q4 2025 step change brought 1.28M /24-equivalents under RSAs in one quarter. The remaining center of gravity: 715 /16-sized blocks hold 49.1% of the outstanding space, and just 23 blocks of /15 or larger hold 38% of it.
  • How: A cohort model. Cohort 1 (2,660 orgs with zero usable contact info) gets services stopped, a 12-month quarantine hold, then release via the waitlist with rights extinguished. Cohort 2 (10,218 orgs with contacts pending verification) gets targeted outreach and DAP contact validation; organizations whose contacts prove inaccurate fall back to Cohort 1. The /16 population is managed as a named list with account-level engagement.
  • Where applicable: ARIN-registry-specific, but the quarantine-then-rights-extinguishment pattern for unreachable holders is a notable operational model for any registry-like system. The 49%-in-/16s concentration means most remaining work is a small number of very large legacy accounts.

items.title: IPv6 Task Force
items.text:
ARIN 58 Public Policy and Members Meeting digest Core pick 23 October 2026

Slides Recording

Lee Howard (ARIN Board of Trustees)

VideoPDF

  • Why: The task force's framing is a real shift: IPv6 adoption is "no longer principally a matter of awareness" — the remaining problem is practical deployment obstacles (IPv6-mostly, network autonomy, host/network readiness). That's exactly the territory a networking PM lives in, and ARIN is soliciting input on how to structure the program.
  • What: A Board-chartered task force (SP 1.5) recommending the structure of an ARIN IPv6 program: identifying and prioritizing deployment obstacles, a community peer-support platform for IPv6 problems (with moderation model and code of conduct), and metrics of success. Existing efforts include an IPv6 address-planning e-learning course, outreach focused on "IPv6 Mostly" and network autonomy, and business-case/case-study blog series.
  • How: Program plan for engagement and problem-solving, a community interaction tool for peer support, and advice on longer-term advocacy including government/public-sector engagement. Task force members are Lee Howard, Rob Seastrom, and Tina Morris, and they are explicitly asking for input on program structure and how to record and prioritize issues.
  • Where applicable: ARIN-region outreach, but the obstacle catalog and peer-support approach are generally applicable. The notable argument in the deck: single-stack is better than dual-stack and you can't single-stack on IPv4 — plus fraud pressure on the residual IPv4 market as a driver.

items.title: Policy Block 1: Recommended Draft Policy ARIN-2025-1
items.text:
ARIN 58 Public Policy and Members Meeting digest Adjacent pick 23 October 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Leif Sawyer (Advisory Council; co-drafted with Elizabeth Goodson)

VideoPDF

  • Why: Defines who counts as an LIR vs. an ISP across the whole policy manual — which determines which allocation rules apply to the PM's org and its customers.
  • What: Creates an explicit ISP definition (connectivity, web services, colocation, dedicated/VPS, VPNs), rewrites the LIR definition (LIRs include but aren't limited to large enterprises, universities, and ISPs), and replaces "ISP" with "LIR" throughout the NRPM — treating ISP as a type of LIR, not an equivalent.
  • How: Terminology harmonization; notably it states all LIRs without IPv4 automatically qualify for an initial /24 (up to /22 with a 24-month plan). Staff estimate six months to implement due to docs/systems updates; no material change to how requests are evaluated.
  • Where applicable: ARIN-region allocation eligibility. Relevant to enterprises and universities that didn't previously self-identify as LIRs — they're now explicitly in scope.

items.title: Policy Block 1: Recommended Draft Policy ARIN-2025-3
items.text:
ARIN 58 Public Policy and Members Meeting digest Adjacent pick 23 October 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Gerry George (Advisory Council; co-drafted with Matthew Wilder)

VideoPDF

  • Why: The out-of-region-use rules govern when ARIN space can be deployed outside the ARIN region — a real constraint for anycast or multinational deployments rooted in ARIN allocations.
  • What: Lowers the in-region IPv4 utilization threshold to justify out-of-region use from /22 to /24. Staff review flags the sharp edge: with no maximum on out-of-region requests, a single in-region /24 could unlock substantially larger blocks deployed entirely outside the region. An amendment also bars using out-of-region justification for waitlist, micro-allocation (4.4), and IPv6-deployment (4.10) space — which drew community objection as an unrelated, precedent-setting restriction on waitlist eligibility by intended use.
  • How: Single-text threshold change with carve-outs; implementable in 3 months.
  • Where applicable: ARIN-region resource holders with any non-ARIN-region deployment; the community fight over the waitlist restriction is the part worth watching.

items.title: Policy Block 1: Recommended Draft Policy ARIN-2025-7
items.text:
ARIN 58 Public Policy and Members Meeting digest Adjacent pick 23 October 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Lily Botsyoe (Advisory Council; co-presented with Leif Sawyer)

VideoPDF

  • Why: A concrete IPAM rule fix — the sizing table for IPv6 end-user allocations — that any org planning IPv6 address structure should know is changing.
  • What: Fixes a math loophole in NRPM 6.5.8.2: the "75% of /48s in a prefix" rule accidentally qualified single-site organizations for a /44, contradicting the examples. The revision makes a single site = /48, with 2–12 sites = /44, 13–192 = /40, 193–3,072 = /36, 3,073–49,152 = /32, and renames "assignment" to "allocation" throughout to match current ARIN practice.
  • How: Pure text clarification; staff review says no operational change, implementable in 3 months, strong community support.
  • Where applicable: Any ARIN-region org requesting IPv6 end-user allocations; the nibble-boundary site-count table is the durable takeaway for IPv6 address planning.
path: Policy Block 1: Recommended Draft Policy ARIN-2025-7

items.title: Policy Block 1: Recommended Draft Policy ARIN-2025-8
items.text:
ARIN 58 Public Policy and Members Meeting digest Adjacent pick 23 October 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Kaitlyn Pellak (Advisory Council; co-drafted with E. Marie Brierley)

VideoPDF

  • Why: Closes an abuse vector in the last ARIN-controlled IPv4 pool — relevant to anyone tracking where fraudulent IPv4 leasing/announcement pressure comes from.
  • What: Codifies that 4.10 space (dedicated IPv4 allocations to facilitate IPv6 deployment) may only be used within the ARIN service region, adding "within the ARIN service area" to NRPM 4.10. ARIN's Registry Integrity Report identified 4.10 as the highest-target pool for fraud: announced out of region, reassigned to customers, leased, or announced with no associated IPv6.
  • How: One-sentence amendment codifying existing staff practice; implementable in 3 months, overwhelmingly positive meeting feedback.
  • Where applicable: 4.10-space holders only, but a useful data point on which IPv4 pools fraudsters target as scarcity deepens.
