items.title: Policy Block 2: Draft Policy ARIN 2026-1
items.text:
ARIN 58 Public Policy and Members Meeting digest Wildcard pick 23 October 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Alison Wood (Advisory Council; co-drafted with Brian Jones)

VideoPDF

  • Why: The most novel thing in the program: a first-of-its-kind proposal to allocate IP address space for networks beyond Earth orbit, with topological aggregation by celestial region. Even in draft form, it signals where hierarchical addressing thought is heading and is tightly coupled to a live IETF working group.
  • What: "Taking IP To Other Planets" (TIPTOP) would let ARIN allocate IPv4/IPv6 for extra-terrestrial networks (beyond GEO — the Moon, Mars, Lagrange points), organized hierarchically by celestial region so lunar/planetary prefixes can aggregate into single advertisements back to terrestrial ground stations. Staff's verdict: not implementable as written — it presumes IETF determination that dedicated space is needed, IANA allocation, RIR concurrence on who runs the registry, and a Board mission-scope decision. Meanwhile the IETF TIPTOP WG advanced its use-case and IP-architecture documents, and a joint IPv6 address-space draft (draft-limarsjenwar-tiptop-address-space-00, by Li, Eubanks, Atkinson, Kumari, and Linkova) was published 15 September, asking IANA for dedicated space with suballocation per celestial body and the NRO to determine allocation within celestial bodies.
  • How: Policy defines an Extra-Terrestrial Network, a dedicated allocation pool, sparse allocation within the ETN block to allow growth without fragmentation, and utilization exceptions where "active host" verification is impractical (high-latency cold-storage nodes, orbital relays).
  • Where applicable: Aspirational and multi-year; contingent on IETF/IANA/NRO process. Watch it as an addressing-architecture thought experiment — aggregation-by-gravity-well is the interesting design idea, and the deep-space transport assumptions (intermittent links, buffering, long delay) are in the WG documents.

items.title: Policy Block 2: Draft Policy ARIN 2026-2
items.text:
ARIN 58 Public Policy and Members Meeting digest Core pick 23 October 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Matthew Wilder (Advisory Council; co-drafted with Alicia Trotman)

VideoPDF

  • Why: This is a proposal to rewrite the entire IPv6 allocation framework from formula-based sizing to documented network plans. If the PM's organization (or its customers) ever requests IPv6 space from ARIN, this changes what "justification" means — it effectively makes IPAM discipline the allocation criterion.
  • What: A full revision of NRPM Section 6.5 that replaces rigid sizing calculations, utilization thresholds, and IPv4-dependent qualification with a planning-based evaluation model. Requests must include a network plan identifying typical assignment sizes (/48, /56, /64), the addressing hierarchy, and projected utilization at 1-, 2-, and 5-year horizons. Subsequent allocations require 75% assignment of the prefix units in the 2-year plan plus evidence deployment matched the submitted hierarchy, with ARIN issuing additional space contiguously to protect aggregation. Deployment must begin within 12 months of issuance. Community survey at the meeting: 40% support, 40% oppose, 20% neutral — genuinely contested.
  • How: The mechanism shifts review from arithmetic (e.g., the 75%-of-/48s nibble-boundary rules elsewhere in Section 6.5) to evaluating a documented plan: hierarchy, aggregation strategy, and growth projections over defined time horizons, applied consistently to LIR and end-user/PI allocations.
  • Where applicable: Applies to ARIN-region IPv6 allocations only, but the shift from formula-based to plan-based justification is a direction other RIRs watch. Broadly applicable to any org requesting space; the open community question — should ARIN require network plans, and does ARIN need to define what a plan is — is where the practical friction will land.

items.title: Policy Block 2: Draft Policy ARIN 2026-5
items.text:
ARIN 58 Public Policy and Members Meeting digest Adjacent pick 23 October 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Gus Reese (Advisory Council; co-drafted with Bill Herrin)

VideoPDF

  • Why: Directly resolves the anycast ambiguity: the question of whether geographically diverse (anycast) use of ARIN space counts as "out of region" has been a recurring community concern.
  • What: Adds a definition of Out Of Region Use to the NRPM: "the sole use of ARIN-allocated resources in locations outside the ARIN service region" — explicitly excluding simultaneous use of a resource both inside and outside the region.
  • How: One definitional section; new to the PPML as of September 2026, feedback pending.
  • Where applicable: Any ARIN resource holder doing anycast or multi-region deployment — this is the clarification that keeps anycast out of Section 9's restrictions.

items.title: Policy Implementation and Experience Report
items.text:
ARIN 58 Public Policy and Members Meeting digest Adjacent pick 23 October 2026

Slides Recording

John Sweeting (ARIN, Chief Experience Officer)

VideoPDF

  • Why: The rare policy session with quantified operational results, and the waitlist/transfer mechanics matter to any org acquiring or moving IPv4 space.
  • What: Three implementation reviews. (1) The waitlist multi-block question: policy forces single contiguous blocks, so an org qualifying for a /22 that accepts down to a /24 gets one /24 even when four noncontiguous /24s are free — staff asked the community whether that restriction, aggregation-driven, is still necessary. (2) The NRPM 8.⅜.4 12-month recipient-to-source wait is invisible in the recipient-facing policy text, causing surprises. (3) ARIN-2025-2 (implemented 3 March 2026) removed the "within the last two versions" RSA constraint: of 490 transfer-participating orgs in the first six months, 72 were spared a new RSA — faster transfers, less legal overhead (vs. 11.7% forced re-signing in the prior six months).
  • How: Staff-experience reporting with before/after ticket-level numbers, feeding directly into new policy proposals (several ARIN-2025/2026 items originated here).
  • Where applicable: ARIN-region transfer and waitlist operations; broadly relevant as a model of policy-implementation feedback loops.

items.title: Routing Security Update
items.text:
ARIN 58 Public Policy and Members Meeting digest Core pick 23 October 2026

Slides Recording

Brad Gorman, ARIN (Director of Customer Technical Services)

VideoPDF

  • Why: Routing security is squarely in the PM's network-security remit, and this is the one session with hard adoption data and a preview of ASPAs — the next RPKI object after ROAs. It also matters for anyone building products that depend on customers having their RPKI in order.
  • What: A data-driven status report on RPKI adoption in the ARIN region plus ARIN's RPKI roadmap. Headline numbers: 9,673 organizations registered for RPKI (up 27% year over year), but roughly 1 in 7 hosted-RPKI organizations has never created a single ROA — "registered is not the same as protected." 59.4% of ARIN-registered IPv4 blocks seen in announcements are RPKI Valid. Globally, 3,389 ASPAs (Autonomous System Provider Authorizations) now exist across the five RIR repositories (2,081 at RIPE NCC, 685 at ARIN), and all five RIRs will support ASPA creation by end of 2026 as the RFC finishes ratification.
  • How: The adoption analysis slices coverage by entity type (government vs. education vs. commercial) and by geography within the ARIN region, isolating where ROA coverage lags. On the tooling side, ARIN is building "BGP Insight": correlating prefixes on a resource certificate with what's actually seen in the global BGP table, explaining Invalid/Not Found states, showing the impact of proposed ROA changes before they're made, and presenting paths to a Valid state. Also in flight: ASPA info in the RPKI changelog, new Reg-RWS RESTful API capabilities, and inter-RIR work toward RPKI feature parity.
  • Where applicable: RPKI validity and ASPA trends are global; the hosted/delegated/repository service tiers and the adoption figures are ARIN-region-specific. ASPA momentum is the transferable takeaway for any operator doing BGP security planning in 2027 — the object class is about to become generally creatable across all RIRs.

items.title: Architecture and Troubleshooting: A Guide to AWS Peering
items.text:
AusNOG 2026 digest Adjacent pick 5 September 2026

Slides Recording

Chitiz Shrestha - Amazon Web Services (AWS)

VideoPDF

  • Why: Useful for anyone interconnecting with AWS — which spans the PM's DC/WAN interconnect interest — as it explains how AWS actually runs and troubleshoots peering, and what will break maintenance operations on their side.
  • What: AWS's peering operation explained: AS16509 (public peering), 14618, 7224 (Direct Connect); selective, IX-centric peering (175 IXs, 189 interconnection facilities); regional route scoping — peers receive region-specific routes to localize traffic and keep it off the AWS backbone. Capability matrix: AS-path prepending is their primary TE; RPKI/ROA filtering yes; MD5 optional; BFD and BGP communities not supported. Operational content: common issues (link errors, discards, session flapping, non-optimal paths); auto-mitigation with the caveat that "taking the wrong action can be worse than taking no action"; the maintenance workflow (drain via BGP filtering / IGP metric poisoning before work); a hard rule that peers must not static-route to AWS (it breaks their zero-traffic-then-deploy model); and self-service diagnostics — the EC2 reachability checker (first triage step: if the test host is reachable, the problem is WAF/security groups, not peering), RIPE Atlas probes hosted on EC2 (reverse traces, since AWS has no looking glass), and NLNOG Ring nodes. Provisioning is portal-automated (interconnect.amazon with PeeringDB auth) with pre-deployment checks (RPKI validation, no private ASN, stable sessions) and auto-disconnect of dead sessions.
  • How: Explanation of their internal model plus concrete self-service tooling a peer can use before escalating.
  • Where applicable: Only relevant if you peer or interconnect with AWS. It is a hyperscaler explaining its own operational contract — informative context, not a transferable technique.
path: Architecture and Troubleshooting: A Guide to AWS Peering

items.title: Assurance on a budget
items.text:
AusNOG 2026 digest Adjacent pick 5 September 2026

Slides Recording

Tim Warnock - Superloop

VideoPDF

  • Why: A catalog of low-cost lab techniques for validating vendor claims, supplier conformance, and regressions — exactly the kind of tooling others can adopt, and the talk openly exists because "vendors often tell porkies about capabilities."
  • What: How Superloop built an assurance lab on MikroTik CCRs, x86 compute, and open-source software: bulk traffic generation (MikroTik traffic-gen, snake tests that loop ports and multiply traffic uplinks — with pitfalls: rate adaptation hammers buffers, invalid MACs, generated frames with bad CRCs); RtBrick BNG Blaster for emulating PPPoE/IPoE subscribers at scale (tested to 32k sessions on a 10-core server; a multi-hour 4,000-session / 48k pps full-duplex test with zero flaps ran on an HP T740 thin client under Proxmox); MikroTik vCPE for simulating Q-in-Q DHCP subscribers with per-subscriber option-82; ROS7 "fantasy routing" for RIB/FIB stress testing (with the real insight that not all TCAM is the same — LEM vs LPM vs eTCAM, IPv4 vs IPv6 key sizes); scripted Python PCAP generation for traffic no tool produces (16,000 ICMP requests, each with unique source IP, MAC, S-TAG/C-TAG, and valid CRC); tcpreplay/MikroTik PCAP injection with speed control; thousands of RFC-compliant DHCP requests to test CoPP. Process advice: keep a problem register, maintain a regression suite with reference PCAPs.
  • How: Cheap hardware + open-source tooling, with concrete configs and commands in the deck.
  • Where applicable: Any operator without a vendor-grade test lab. The NBN TC4 conformance specifics are Australian, but the techniques are general.

items.title: ...because copy+paste isn't a network configuration strategy - automation for amateurs
items.text:
AusNOG 2026 digest Core pick 5 September 2026

Slides Recording

James Morgan - VERNet (presented with Mitch Blair, VERNet, per the slides)

VideoPDF

  • Why: A 15-person research network replaced CLI copy-paste and spreadsheet IPAM with NetBox-as-source-of-truth and full configuration generation — a complete, honest, adoptable automation pattern touching IPAM, a core PM interest.
  • What: VERNet's journey from 2019 ("configs lived on devices, IPAM was a classy spreadsheet, everyone gets read/write") to today: NetBox holds IPAM, L2/L3 hardware inventory, OOB, racks, and config metadata; ConnectMaster holds fiber plant; the OSS holds customer/service records. Golden configs were rebuilt from first principles (a box with no services, plus role-dictated sections); services were classified and their differences turned into properties; Jinja templates (in Git, synced to NetBox) render full device configs. The pipeline: device state change in NetBox → generated candidate config → diffed against the approved repo → pull request → on approval, AWX/Ansible pushes a full overwrite with on-box validation, automatic rollback on failed checks, and commit-confirm; scheduled AWX jobs track drift (running vs approved config) and open GitHub issues on divergence. Refreshingly honest about pain: the first generated config errors out, the second is six lines, "by about the 12th generation you'll get a full config," and the diffing phase surfaced hundreds of edge cases and embarrassing legacy mistakes nobody owned.
  • How: NetBox + Git + GitHub Actions + AWX + Ansible; config templates inherit; review shifts from config diffs to template diffs; fewer people need write access; provisioning a new box takes minutes.
  • Where applicable: Small and mid-size networks of any vendor mix. Explicitly framed as "if we can do this, you absolutely can" — though they candidly note they haven't yet decided whether their particular sync approach works for them. Adopt the pattern, not their exact choices.
path: ...because copy+paste isn't a network configuration strategy - automation for amateurs

items.title: BGP EVPN. A view from the field
items.text:
AusNOG 2026 digest Core pick 5 September 2026

Slides Recording

Alex Mitev - Cisco System

VideoPDF

  • Why: EVPN is consolidating L2/L3 service delivery and DCI under one BGP control plane, and this is a field-density walkthrough of design options and — most valuably — in-service migration paths from legacy redundancy schemes. Relevant to both DC fabric and telco access work.
  • What: The core framing: EVPN (RFC 7432/7623/8214/9135) replaces MC-LAG/ICCP, ICCP-SM, nV Edge, and VPLS flood-and-learn by moving coordination into BGP — deleting peer-links and sync protocols, eliminating split-brain, enabling N-way multi-vendor multihoming; risk changes shape ("more failure events, smaller blast radius — each one survivable"). Multihoming modes mapped: all-active (per-flow), single-active (per-VLAN), port-active (per-port), plus single-flow-active for L2 ring protocols (G.8032/STP-AG). Migration recipes with actual IOS-XR config: MC-LAG → port-active EVPN (no CE change, NDF sets LACP out-of-service, then ICCP removed); VPLS → EVPN (add EVI, PEs auto-discover, pseudowires shut down; both VFIs and EVIs default to split-horizon group 1 so no PE forwards between them during transition); VPWS seamless integration where EVPN VPWS is preferred over the legacy PW when both exist for the same AC; nV Edge is the one migration requiring downtime (de-clustering). Also covers hierarchical EVPN (EVPN-HE) with P-bit/B-bit service carving, flexible cross-connects to bundle thousands of services into fewer tunnels (cutting BGP state and OAM), and real Australian use cases: RSPs delivering BNG services over EVPN with SRG-driven service carving, and wholesale fan-in (thousands of L2 sub-ifs onto BNG pairs) solved via VLAN-aware FXC and L2 NNI handoff.
  • How: Config-level sequencing and DF-election/service-carving modes (preference-based, access-driven, srg-driven) with show-command output from a lab.
  • Where applicable: SP access/aggregation and enterprise DCI. This is a Cisco SE session with IOS-XR-specific configs — vendor-flavored, but the design concepts and migration orderings are multi-vendor standards work and directly reusable.
path: BGP EVPN. A view from the field

items.title: Channelmania! – future proof your DWDM network topology while keeping it flexible for 1.6T
items.text:
AusNOG 2026 digest Core pick 5 September 2026

Slides Recording

Thomas Weible - Flexoptix

VideoPDF

  • Why: DWDM topology planning for the 800G/1.6T coherent era — squarely in the PM's physical WAN interconnect interest. This is about how to structure a C-band plant so future superchannels don't strand you.
  • What: An argument for planning DWDM networks in frequency terms (THz/GHz) rather than channel numbers or wavelengths, and for a "colorless," flexible architecture: carve the C-band into 12 × 400 GHz subbands using low-cost PLC 1×4 splitters to combine TX / split RX, and run each subband through ordinary 50 GHz DWDM MUX/DeMUX. This yields DIY coherent superchannels (425 Gbps @ 53.125 GBd dual-polarization 16-QAM per the deck) that can be re-arranged as optics evolve. The deck also notes ~100 GHz spacing as the observed optimum (attributed to Blake Willis), 800G ZR+ in DD/OSFP form factors arriving, 12.8T liquid-cooled XPO optics approaching, 300 GHz options appearing, and that coherent BIDI needs a second laser for the RX local oscillator.
  • How: Coherent intradyne detection with phase- and polarization-diversity balanced receivers; higher-order modulation constellations (4 bits/symbol × 2 polarizations); superchannels assembled from COTS PLC splitters plus standard DWDM muxes; "make a frequency plan for your spans."
  • Where applicable: Operators building or re-planning their own DWDM plant. This is a vendor session (Flexoptix sells tunable optics), but the frequency-plan method and superchannel construction approach are vendor-neutral engineering. The slide text is fragmentary and fast-paced; expect the talk to be denser than the deck.
path: Channelmania! – future proof your DWDM network topology while keeping it flexible for 1.6T

items.title: Migrating a Large Telco Networks IGP from OSPF/OSPFv3 to ISIS
items.text:
AusNOG 2026 digest Core pick 5 September 2026

Slides Recording

Sam Faunt - Aussie Broadband

VideoPDF

  • Why: IGP migrations at telco scale are rare war stories with real failure detail — core routing/WAN interest, and a candid postmortem-style account of what broke.
  • What: Aussie Broadband moved its backbone IGP from OSPF/OSPFv3 (two processes for two address families) to IS-IS, motivated by one protocol for v4+v6, unifying the IGP across AS4764 and AS9268, segment routing readiness, and vendor support. Method: lab first (convergence testing, choosing FRR/SRLG-disjoint/node-protection/microloop-avoidance features, prefix policy — loopbacks only vs loopbacks + links, OSPF/IS-IS coexistence on the same box, cross-platform behavior); deploy IS-IS alongside running OSPF; cut over by lowering OSPF/OSPFv3 admin distance below IS-IS so IS-IS takes over. AS4764 cut over cleanly. During AS9268, traffic blackholed — the RIB still preferred OSPF for some loopbacks; they assumed stale routes, rebooted the core router, and it did not come back. The network was eventually migrated fully to IS-IS.
  • How: Admin-distance-based cutover with both IGPs running simultaneously; phased AS-by-AS; lab validation before deployment.
  • Where applicable: SP/telco backbones running dual OSPFv2/v3. The specific blackhole and failed reboot are org- and platform-specific, but the lab-first, coexistence-then-cutover method is broadly transferable. The slides are thin on detail — the talk is likely richer than the deck.
path: Migrating a Large Telco Networks IGP from OSPF/OSPFv3 to ISIS

items.title: Mission Possible: Disabling IPv4 on Google Enterprise Network
items.text:
AusNOG 2026 digest Core pick 5 September 2026

Slides Recording

Jen Linkova - Google

VideoPDF

  • What: Google's production rollout of "IPv6-mostly" networks (RFC 8925 DHCPv4 Option 108) across its enterprise network: clients that signal Option 108 receive no IPv4 address and run IPv6-only with NAT64, PREF64 signalled in Router Advertisements (RFC 8781/9872), DNS64, and CLAT (464XLAT, RFC 6877) for IPv4-literal and legacy apps. Rollout ran March–December 2023 (pilot → greenfields first → incremental 10%→100% of existing subnets). Results: no blocking issues; Apple/Android/ChromeOS devices went IPv6-only automatically; 75–80% of hosts became IPv6-only; DHCPv4 utilization dropped 3–4× on WiFi segments; 500K+ IPv4 addresses reclaimed (a /19 was downsized to /22). Documented pitfalls: devices with disabled/link-local-only IPv6, extension-header filtering breaking ESP (VPN, WiFi calling), APs blocking multiple IPv6 addresses (and multiple EVPN Type-2 routes), tethering/hosts-as-routers breaking, and Happy Eyeballs masking IPv6 bugs ("users do not report problems; network bugs remain unfixed").
  • Why: IPv4 reclamation is a live operational problem everywhere; this is the most complete public deployment data on the IPv6-mostly pattern, and it's directly relevant to IPAM and enterprise addressing strategy.
  • How: Standard-track mechanisms only — Option 108 in DHCPDISCOVER/REQUEST parameter list, NAT64 at site edge, RA-signalled PREF64, CLAT on the client; the dedicated IPv6-only SSID/VLAN approach is explicitly rejected (user confusion, higher IPv4 consumption, low issue visibility).
  • Where applicable: Enterprise/campus wired + wireless with central DHCPv4 and SLAAC. The specific numbers are Google-scale, but the technique is deployable now wherever clients are Apple/Android/ChromeOS (they send Option 108 by default); Linux requires manual opt-in; Windows is the open gap. Prerequisite: IPv6 must already genuinely work.
path: Mission Possible: Disabling IPv4 on Google Enterprise Network

items.title: Optimizing Traffic Flow with Akamai
items.text:
AusNOG 2026 digest Adjacent pick 5 September 2026

Slides Recording

Kams Yeung - Akamai

VideoPDF

  • Why: Understanding why conventional BGP traffic engineering does not move a major CDN is operationally important for capacity planning and interconnect strategy at any eyeball network.
  • What: Akamai maps users via DNS (unicast, per-requester answers based on latency, throughput, loss, server load, cache policy) — not anycast — so AS-path prepending, MED, and more-specific advertisements all do nothing. Clusters are islands (no inter-cluster backbone) with preference on-net cache > PNI > IX > transit. Operator guidance: run your own recursive resolvers with anycast IPs and per-location external IPs (mapping follows the resolver's IP), ACL them, never rewrite Akamai hostnames' TTLs, or else use Google/OpenDNS with ECS; announce complete and consistent prefixes (both DNS and end-user ranges) or risk whole-ASN blocking; carry everything you announce — no holes or filtered /24s, since Akamai edge routers don't hold full tables; don't filter or rate-limit ICMP (used for performance monitoring); avoid CGNAT (or use 100.64.0.0/10 and place caches outside CGNAT); and enable IPv6 — Australia sits at 30.1% adoption, ranked #69, with Telstra at 60.3% and TPG at 24.7%.
  • How: Explanation of the mapping system followed by a concrete do/don't list for ISPs.
  • Where applicable: Networks delivering Akamai-served content (i.e., most eyeball ISPs). A vendor session, but framed as operational guidance rather than a product pitch.

items.title: Our journey on "how we are modernising our network"
items.text:
AusNOG 2026 digest Adjacent pick 5 September 2026

Slides Recording

Richard Vander Reyden - Optus

VideoPDF

  • Why: A large telco's target-state architecture is a useful directional signal for where SP fabrics are heading — SRv6, IGP consolidation, core separation — even if the specifics don't transfer.
  • What: A history (Bay Networks → Cisco 7200/7500/GSR → Juniper M320/MX960/PTX; VPLS → Seamless MPLS) and a pointed critique of the current state: internet traffic (~90% of volume) sharing a complex telco core (OSPF + LDP + iBGP/eBGP-LU) with in-band management. The target state: internet core separated from telco core, IS-IS + SRv6 end to end (already IS-IS + SR-MPLS in access), dual-vendor dual-plane core, defined interconnects, VxLAN in access, built for 400/800G colored optics, and a dedicated OOB management network (star topology, dual SYD/MEL hubs, carrier-diverse paths). On operations: from manual CLI (typo-outages, no rollback, knowledge silos) to CI/CD with atomic commits and automatic rollback, Git + NetBox + NSO as single source of truth, one YAML intent layer across Cisco/Juniper, continuous drift detection, AI anomaly detection with humans deciding.
  • How: Architecture-program level description; the deck contains little implementation detail.
  • Where applicable: Optus-specific scale and topology — a direction signal, not a copyable design. Pair with the Aussie Broadband IGP talk for the IS-IS/SR trend.
path: Our journey on "how we are modernising our network"

items.title: Rethinking Address Reality: IPv4 Utilisation and Proxy Network Exposure in Australia
items.text:
AusNOG 2026 digest Core pick 5 September 2026

Slides Recording

Aftab Siddiqui - APNIC Foundation

VideoPDF

  • Why: Two halves, both valuable: ground-truthing Australian IPv4 holdings/geolocation (registry data vs reality), and a genuinely novel measurement of residential proxy networks — including a NetFlow-based detection technique consumer ISPs can deploy today. The proxy half is a network-security problem that lands on operators' laps.
  • What: Part 1: NRO delegation data shows Australia actually holds ~45.9M IPv4 addresses (179K /24s, 9,867 delegations) vs what APNIC REX presents; transfer analysis shows Australia is a net exporter of IPv4 (net −500 transfers / −2.1M addresses over ten years). Only 5.3% of AU delegations publish RFC 8805 geofeeds (94.7% silent), with common breakage (GitHub blob URLs returning HTML, dead URLs); cross-checking commercial (IPinfo) vs geofeed data shows 99.97% country agreement but only ~80.5% city agreement, with commercial data biased toward capitals. Part 2: instrumented five residential proxy providers (Oxylabs, IPRoyal, FloppyData, Shifter, Bright Data) with ~500K requests, 28,217 unique exit IPs across Sydney/Melbourne/Brisbane: 2,747 IPs appeared in ≥2 providers (Oxylabs–Shifter overlap largest at 1,375); exits concentrate in consumer ASNs (Telstra 6,668, TPG 4,776, Optus 3,099, Aussie Broadband 2,571, Starlink 1,925); and TCP timestamp-rate fingerprinting (fitting TSval slope within connections) clustered exits into ~1000/300/250/100 Hz families (70.8% at ~1000 Hz) — a device-class signal the proxy relay cannot fake because the exit's own kernel builds the segments. The exits never fetched any sub-resource (zero of five tracking pixels loaded).
  • How: Per-provider hostnames + per-request tokens to join client and server logs; SYN pcap analysis (TTL, MSS, window, TCP option order); timestamp-rate fitting requiring ≥3 samples over 250 ms; browser fingerprint page. Operator guidance: proxy SDKs hold persistent outbound connections from consumer CPE to a small set of gateways — visible in NetFlow as long-lived flows to the same destinations from thousands of unrelated subscriber lines, no DPI needed.
  • Where applicable: The dataset and geofeed findings are Australia-specific; the measurement methodology and the NetFlow detection guidance transfer to any consumer ISP. Provider device-count claims quoted from vendor marketing are explicitly unverified.
path: Rethinking Address Reality: IPv4 Utilisation and Proxy Network Exposure in Australia

items.title: Return loss problems associated with faster optical networks
items.text:
AusNOG 2026 digest Core pick 5 September 2026

Slides Recording

Takaya Nakagawa - NTT Advanced Technology Corporation

VideoPDF

  • Why: As links move from 10G to 100G/400G and beyond, reflections at connector points — not just insertion loss — become an error source. This is core physical-layer optics knowledge for anyone running DC or WAN fiber plants, and it comes with real experimental data rather than folklore.
  • What: A controlled demonstration that 100GBASE-LR4 links develop bit errors when total return loss degrades below the IEEE limit (21 dB) across multiple connection points. A single poor (<21 dB) connection point did not immediately produce errors, but three poor points did, via multiple reflections between connectors (eye closure, jitter, rising BER). BER worsens as received power drops, and the three transceivers tested showed materially different tolerance to poor return loss. The talk also catalogues causes: dust contamination takes a clean connector pair from 0.05 dB IL / 52.6 dB RL to 1.1 dB / 22.7 dB; hand oil to 44.2 dB RL; a partially seated connector hit 13.8 dB RL; legacy PC polishing only guarantees ~25 dB. Notably, poor reflection points spaced 20 km apart produced no errors — the reflected signal is attenuated over distance.
  • How: Testbed of a 100GBASE-LR4 link with variable optical attenuator and deliberately poor connectors, measuring eye diagrams and BER across three transceiver vendors; PAM4 (400G+) flagged as even more exposed since it is now mainstream.
  • Where applicable: Any single-mode plant with dense patching — meet-me rooms, DC cross-connects, ROADM/MUX shelves — especially at 100G+ and at low receive power. Broadly applicable physics, though NTT-AT sells connector cleaning/polishing products, so the "Clean Before Connect" conclusion aligns with their business.
path: Return loss problems associated with faster optical networks

items.title: Revocation
items.text:
AusNOG 2026 digest Core pick 5 September 2026

Slides Recording

Geoff Huston - APNIC

VideoPDF

  • Why: Directly in the PM's identity/authentication core. PKI revocation assumptions underpin everything from Web TLS to workload identity — and this talk empirically shows revocation does not work in practice.
  • What: A live experiment: generate a Let's Encrypt certificate, revoke it, wait weeks, and check browsers. Only Firefox had learned of the revocation; Chrome (which disabled OCSP in 2012 and never supported Must-Staple) and Safari (CRLset-style downloads plus stapled OCSP) did not. The talk walks the whole failure chain: CRLs are too large and weekly-fresh (a DigiCert example with 17,527 entries); OCSP adds latency, leaks client activity to the CA, concentrated load (Akamai once answered ⅔ of Let's Encrypt OCSP), and forces fail-open (DDoS vector) or fail-closed (availability vector) choices; stapling adds nothing because a server holding a revoked cert would never staple its own revocation. Conclusion: revocation is unfixable within X.509 — shorter cert lifetimes bound the damage but CA infrastructure can't scale to hour-long lifetimes. The provocative alternative: DANE — put DNSSEC-signed public keys in the DNS with TTL-scale freshness and staple the DNSSEC chain into the TLS handshake, eliminating the CA third party entirely.
  • How: Demonstration-first methodology (generate/revoke/wait/check across Chrome, Safari, Firefox), plus a structural analysis of CRL/OCSP/stapling mechanics.
  • Where applicable: Universal for anyone depending on Web PKI or designing certificate-based workload/agent identity. The DANE proposal is contrarian and has no browser support — treat it as direction-setting, not deployable. Highly relevant to short-lived-certificate designs (SPIFFE-style) where "we'll just revoke" is a non-answer.

items.title: Rural Fibre Co
items.text:
AusNOG 2026 digest Wildcard pick 5 September 2026

Slides Recording

Phil Britt - Rural Fibre Co

VideoPDF

  • Why: Outside the PM's core areas, but two things here are genuinely novel signals: operational software built by a network engineer with Claude Code in eight weeks, and hard economics on vertically integrated fiber builds.
  • What: A 16-month-old Gippsland FTTP overbuilder: 1,431 premises passed, 430 connected, 130 km of duct, built by 42 people, targeting 10,000 passed by mid-2029. Key choices: Nokia end-to-end stack (Lightspan MF-2 OLT, Altiplano, 7750 SR-1s) chosen partly so the network is saleable without the founder; a wholesale product deliberately shaped like NBN's (QinQ S-tag/C-tag from ONT to RSP handoff, AVC-style IDs in DHCP option 82) because every Australian RSP already has those integrations — "inventing a better product would mean asking every RSP to build a new integration for a network with 1,431 premises." Automation: no human touches an order until the technician knocks on the door; the design system generates all construction tasks, work orders, inventory, and purchase orders ("the design is the work orders"). The workforce management system was built in eight weeks by a network engineer with Claude Code — zero developers, no PMO — and drill productivity tripled (250 → 775 m/day total) attributed to visibility and gamification rather than the machinery. Take-up against NBN fixed wireless reached 52% at ~9 months. Hard lesson: an unlocated NBN duct got drilled through, taking down ~3,000 premises; asset-locating checks are now enforced in software, blocking tasks until completed.
  • How: Vertical integration across design → civils → splicing → network → provisioning → billing to eliminate margin stacking and coordination tax; software-enforced process gates.
  • Where applicable: The regulatory frame (Part 8 superfast broadband obligations, TEBA/POI, open-access wholesale) and the NBN-overbuild economics are Australian. The transferable ideas are the AI-assisted software build and design-as-single-source-of-truth.

items.title: Securing modern telco networks
items.text:
AusNOG 2026 digest Core pick 5 September 2026

Slides Recording

Patrick Ohearn - AARNet Pty Ltd

VideoPDF

  • Why: A practitioner's prioritized view of what actually matters in SP security right now — fundamentals, PQC, routing security, and the AI vulnerability-discovery wave — directly in the PM's network security core.
  • What: A survey of telco security practice, organized by layer: fundamentals (backups, SSO/RBAC, MFA on external paths, segmentation, per-device credentials, never sharing auth between corporate and telco domains, JIT access, one-time break-glass creds, jumphost controls); NOS hygiene (consistent config/software deployment, vendor hardening guides, disable telnet, CoPP/RE filters, alert on reboots and firmware/software changes, investigate all coredumps); supply chain (signed package updates, trusted computing, vetted suppliers, less second-hand gear, secure shipping); hardware (SecureBoot, physical security, real-time inventory change logging, passive asset monitoring, cameras); OSS/BSS (billing is a prime target, CDRs and metadata are espionage targets, JIT for external vendors/contractors, audit SaaS access). Notable current items: frontier-lab security models (Cisco, Juniper/HPE, Nokia working with frontier labs) have surfaced ~10,000 high/critical vulnerabilities; patch velocity is rising to fortnightly NOS updates; transport encryption should be pushed at L1 (OTNSec, WDM encryption) through L4; PQC is coming sooner than expected and impacts SecureBoot/package signing (potentially requiring new hardware) more than transport; routing security = RPKI, route filtering, BGP enforce-first-AS, OTC (RFC 9234), and ASPA (draft — APNIC support as of July 2026). Core message: fundamentals matter most; vendor QA is lagging; make encryption a purchase criterion.
  • How: A field-informed checklist rather than a single mechanism, closing with industry collaboration (peer telcos, ASD/Home Affairs, conference lists).
  • Where applicable: Broadly applicable to any SP/telco; the regulation references (SOCI/TSRMP, CI Fortify) are Australian-specific, but the technical content is general.

items.title: The CDN Landscape Revisited: Static, Live, and AI
items.text:
AusNOG 2026 digest Wildcard pick 5 September 2026

Slides Recording

Steve Meuse - Kentik

VideoPDF

  • Why: Not a core PM area, but it carries a genuinely surprising empirical result — AI traffic on real networks is still tiny — plus the clearest available account of CDN market consolidation.
  • What: Since 2023: Stackpath exited, Lumen's CDN was dismantled, and Edgio went Chapter 11 (AS22822 dark), with roughly 15% market share mostly absorbed by Akamai. Content delivery is commoditized (transit price pressure, no differentiation, hyperscaler bundles); survivors are re-tooling into edge compute/GPU platforms — the deck maps Cloudflare, Akamai, Fastly, and GCore product timelines (Workers → containers → inference; Akamai's Linode/Ondat/Geko/NVIDIA Blackwell), with the strategic asymmetry that CDNs can't match hyperscaler capital but pay zero egress. Live events: mega-streams (72.5M concurrent, T20 World Cup) were handled fine; the Jake Paul–Mike Tyson failure (60M streams, 2.5–3× normal peak) was not the network — interconnect and cache capacity had headroom, root cause suspected on the streaming/replication side, no Netflix postmortem. The AI surprise: on a large US SP, video is Tb/s while AI in August 2025 measured in hundreds of Mb/s (~1.5 Gb/s in 2026 samples) — the exec-level panic is hype-cycle artifact, not operational concern; inference is served largely via Cloudflare/Google (Anthropic's $1.8B/7yr Akamai deal noted), and the unknown is agent-driven traffic directionality (per the Schaeffer NANOG keynote), which is not yet visible in flow data.
  • How: Kentik OTT mapping (DNS queries joined with flow data) plus flow-based unique-destination-IP counts as a user proxy.
  • Where applicable: Industry-level perspective grounded in Kentik's customer visibility (US-weighted). Best used to calibrate capacity-planning and AI-traffic assumptions.
path: The CDN Landscape Revisited: Static, Live, and AI

items.title: A Marathon and Not a Sprint: Lessons Learnt from Trying (and sometimes succeeding!) to Automate Enterprise Campus Networks
items.text:
AutoCon 3 (Prague) — Operator digest Adjacent pick Prague · 28–30 May 2025

Slides Recording

Robert Mertling-Blake, AEG (entertainment venues worldwide)

VideoPPTX

  • Why: An unusually honest "we are not fully automated and here's why" operator story — the failure-mode content the operator-program criteria ask for, with lessons that transfer even to non-campus environments.
  • What: AEG's journey automating campus networks across 100+ venues (>800 switches, thousands of APs), including the drivers, failures, and what finally worked.
  • How: Key lessons from the slides: assurance matters more than self-healing when the event must work (their golden rule); DCIM cable documentation at remote/unmanned sites dramatically improved remote-hands resolution; "source of record" framing gets buy-in where "source of truth" evangelism doesn't; doing automation perfectly became the enemy of doing any automation (a rushed greenfield deployment without physical connectivity or PNP time); buy the SoR-driven process wins — NetBox-driven config generation, Oxidized backups, monitoring and DDI creation that manual SOPs always missed. They deliberately keep DDI changes non-event-driven while tooling confidence grows, and deploy sacrificial old kit during construction to eat the dust.
  • Where applicable: Campus/venue-specific in details, but the meta-lessons (pick fewer battles, alignment with site refreshes, data quality as the persistent constraint) transfer to any heterogeneous multi-site estate.
path: A Marathon and Not a Sprint: Lessons Learnt from Trying (and sometimes succeeding!) to Automate Enterprise Campus Networks

items.title: An Epic Journey: Automating networks with Terraform
items.text:
AutoCon 3 (Prague) — Operator digest Core pick Prague · 28–30 May 2025

Slides Recording

Eduardo Pozo

VideoPPTX

  • Why: A concrete, numbers-backed account of Terraform at datacenter scale — including where it hurts (provider bugs, plan times, state risks) — which is rare and directly useful for DC automation decisions.
  • What: Using Terraform as the primary automation tool across oil, health, and enterprise projects, including migrating a large multi-site datacenter to fully automated deployment.
  • How: The slides quantify the pain: a 500+ leaf, 4-location, 2000+ VLAN fabric; a full terraform plan against an empty APIC (Cisco ACI, ~5334 resources) took 45 minutes, cut to 19 minutes by moving data transformation (dedups via set(), key lookups, validation) out of Terraform into Python. Honest coverage of vendor provider reality: "vendors say yes yes, it just doesn't work," API bugs, 12+ month-old issues, no CRUD — and the mitigations (contribute, pressure the vendor, hybrid approach, fork the provider). Also state loss/locking, apply-can-destroy surprises driven by provider quality, and preferring pipelines straight to infrastructure over controller-mediated paths where possible.
  • Where applicable: The specific numbers are ACI/APIC-specific, but the lessons (stateful tools at DC scale, controller API limits vs. parallelism, keeping computation out of your IaC layer) apply to any large fabric automation effort.
path: An Epic Journey: Automating networks with Terraform

items.title: Automation Transforms $70 APs into Enterprise-Grade Networks
items.text:
AutoCon 3 (Prague) — Operator digest Core pick Prague · 28–30 May 2025

Slides Recording

Henry Haller, Telecom Infrastructure Project (TIP) OpenWiFi

VideoPPTX

  • Why: Under the WLAN packaging, this is one of the few sessions about device identity at fleet scale — per-device certificate generation, CA signing, and mutual TLS between controller and devices, i.e., the bootstrapping problem familiar from SPIFFE/SPIRE workload identity, applied to hardware.
  • What: An open-source lifecycle system (TIP OpenWiFi) that takes commodity $70 access points from zero-touch adoption to provisioned enterprise WLANs, covering WPA⅔, PSK/mPSK-RADIUS, OWE, GRE tunneling, and multi-band configs.
  • How: WAPs generate SSL certificates on adoption and submit them to a CA for signing; the certificates then authenticate the devices to the OpenWiFi Gateway via mutual TLS, creating a web of trust, with CA management included. Provisioning is driven by operator intent via JSON API transactions to the gateway and WebSocket transactions from gateway to APs. The source slides add operational lessons: immediate UI feedback and robust logging/error reporting matter because end-user feedback arrives late and through many layers.
  • Where applicable: The software is TIP OpenWiFi-specific, but the onboarding pattern — device-generated keys, CA signing, mTLS control channel — is the template for any commodity-hardware fleet (including cameras, sensors, and DC out-of-band gear).
path: Automation Transforms $70 APs into Enterprise-Grade Networks

items.title: Building Trustworthy Network Automation, From Principles to Practice
items.text:
AutoCon 3 (Prague) — Operator digest Adjacent pick Prague · 28–30 May 2025

Slides Recording

Damien Garros

VideoPPTX

  • Why: The trust problem is why automation adoption stalls — teams don't delegate critical network operations to systems whose failure behavior they can't predict. This is the cleanest principles-to-patterns treatment at the conference.
  • What: A framework of design principles that make automation trustworthy, explicitly "built on mistakes, refined by experience": idempotency, dry-run, transactional commit/rollback, declarative over imperative workflows, version control, and testing.
  • How: The slides include a useful comparison table: imperative workflows make idempotency, dry-run, and transactionality hard; declarative makes them easy; version control gives all three nearly free. Patterns shown: dry-run before apply, diff-based changes, state verification, grouping changes so they either all commit or all roll back, plus process advice (enforce business process in workflows, safe defaults, "integrate what you can, build what you must").
  • Where applicable: Broadly applicable, tool-agnostic; these principles map onto any automation stack (Nornir, Ansible, Terraform, orchestrators).
path: Building Trustworthy Network Automation, From Principles to Practice

items.title: Coding for infrastructure is just coding, on how we moved from a script based model to an object oriented architecture
items.text:
AutoCon 3 (Prague) — Operator digest Core pick Prague · 28–30 May 2025

Slides Recording

Antonio Balmaseda & Alberto Villegas Erce, Roche

VideoPPTX

  • Why: The second of two talks at this conference independently reaching the same conclusion about optical automation (Roche's optical network uses the same devices as ESnet and GEANT). Together they read as a mini-postmortem of Ansible-and-controller-based approaches to transport automation.
  • What: Roche Pharma's move from scattered per-engineer scripts and Ansible playbooks to an object-oriented, model/controller/view architecture built on the Workflow Orchestrator framework, expected in production by the conference date.
  • How: Abstract service models with Python clients talking directly to devices (RESTCONF, TL1 for ROADMs); hardware changes only require adding implementations via Python single-dispatch, giving clean boundaries between abstract intent and device config. Concrete results from the slides: 6000 backups in 20 minutes (down from 3 hours), and 200 devices patched unattended over a weekend with no CLI access. Massive changes now ship as a JSON file plus Jinja templates through a merge request.
  • Where applicable: Roche-specific scale (worldwide multi-vendor network, thousands of devices), but the pattern — abandon YAML-nesting for real code when logic gets complex, keep Ansible only for what it's good at (backups, compliance, OS upgrades) — is broadly applicable.
path: Coding for infrastructure is just coding, on how we moved from a script based model to an object oriented architecture

items.title: From Clicks to Code: Optical Network Automation Journey at GARR
items.text:
AutoCon 3 (Prague) — Operator digest Core pick Prague · 28–30 May 2025

Slides Recording

Matteo Colantonio, GARR (Italian research and education network)

VideoPPTX

  • Why: Physical-layer transport (optical circuits, transponders, ROADMs) is the least-automated part of most networks, and this is a rare honest account of why the usual automation stack fails there and what actually works. Directly relevant to anyone with DC/WAN interconnect responsibilities.
  • What: GARR's progression from Ansible/AWX and the vendor controller's northbound API to a workflow-orchestrator architecture that talks directly to optical devices, now in early production use.
  • How: Ansible handled basic transponder upgrades but collapsed on complex logic — restarting cards one-by-one and verifying service recovery required three nested YAMLs with include statements. The vendor controller API was a stripped-down version of the GUI: missing key features, and useless for circuits crossing multiple line systems (mixed-platform ROADM metro regions). The pivot: build abstract service models plus Python clients speaking the same southbound interfaces the vendor controller uses (RESTCONF, TL1 shell for ROADMs), separating intent from device-specific configuration.
  • Where applicable: GARR-specific in topology (research backbone, mixed optical platforms), but the lessons — vendor NBIs as a bottleneck, direct device control, incremental automation starting with critical services — transfer to any optical/WAN environment. The observation that optical networks' GUI-centric (not CLI-centric) history changes the automation starting point is a genuinely useful framing.
path: From Clicks to Code: Optical Network Automation Journey at GARR

items.title: Going beyond show commands and screen scraping with BMP
items.text:
AutoCon 3 (Prague) — Operator digest Core pick Prague · 28–30 May 2025

Slides Recording

Bart Dorlandt (freelance network automation engineer, Netherlands)

VideoPPTX

  • Why: Verifying that BGP announcements you configured actually propagated and passed import policy is a classic gap; most shops do it with screen scraping. BMP (BGP Monitoring Protocol) is the right tool and this gives the architecture and the scaling numbers.
  • What: A production pipeline for pre- and post-policy BGP data: router → BMP collector → Kafka → consumer → database → API, replacing screen scraping of show commands for customer-facing verification.
  • How: The initial consumer managed 30 msg/sec — nowhere near enough for millions of RIB entries — and was rewritten with a pool of async Kafka producers, reaching 45,000 msg/sec. Hard lessons: every stage (collector, consumer, DB) can be crippled by too much data, so filter early, deduplicate, and decide what you actually need; peer-down notifications are the critical code path; the BMP collector implementation used was incomplete and needed patches (Kafka TLS, Docker).
  • Where applicable: Broadly applicable wherever BGP policy correctness needs verification (peering, DC fabrics, WAN). The pipeline is buildable from open components but the scaling numbers are one implementation's — treat 30→45k msg/sec as directional, not a benchmark.
path: Going beyond show commands and screen scraping with BMP

items.title: Mastering Network Operations: The Power of Abstraction
items.text:
AutoCon 3 (Prague) — Operator digest Adjacent pick Prague · 28–30 May 2025

Slides Recording

Jaakko Rautanen

VideoPPTX

  • Why: The concrete "how do I actually build abstract services" talk the design-first theme needs — with a working production stack, an open-sourced plugin, and a demo that goes from three inputs to deployed MPLS L3VPN service.
  • What: A layered automation stack in which NetBox-native data is detailed state, and a new top layer of "abstract services" (NetBox plugins) collapses daily operations to a handful of variables per service.
  • How: An example "Virtual Network" service (VRF + customer MPLS-site attachments) needs dozens of correctly-allocated details (prefixes, VLANs, loopbacks, route-targets, ASNs); the abstract model reduces user input to name, template, and site attachment, with all other values allocated automatically from template-defined ranges. Config delivery uses NetBox Config Templates (Jinja), deployment varies by vendor, and a diff view against live state precedes a one-click push. The team open-sourced the Ninja NetBox plugin for generating interactive diagrams or any text output from Jinja. Lessons: purge arbitrary encoding rules from IP/VLAN schemes, go declarative (they replace entire device configs each push), keep models generic with templates.
  • Where applicable: The implementation is a media-network MPLS/VPN environment, but the pattern (service abstraction layer over NetBox, template-driven allocation, full-config declarative pushes) is directly adoptable by anyone already running NetBox.
path: Mastering Network Operations: The Power of Abstraction

items.title: Network Event Correlation. Stories to keep you awake
items.text:
AutoCon 3 (Prague) — Operator digest Wildcard pick Prague · 28–30 May 2025

Slides Recording

Javier Antich

VideoPPTX

  • Why: A refreshingly blunt "why event correlation mostly doesn't work" talk, with a taxonomy of where rules end and ML/neuro-symbolic approaches begin — relevant to anyone drowning in NOC alert noise.
  • What: An honest dissection of operational noise-reduction approaches — what correlation can and cannot do today, war stories, and a proposal for doing better.
  • How: The slides frame correlation as static rules (e.g., link_down + OSPF_Down on same device/interface → correlated) over normalized inventory data, and lay out a two-column map of automation vs. autonomy across operations: static thresholds → ML goal-deviation tracking, rules-based correlation → neuro-symbolic AI, rules-based closed-loop and compliance → goal-driven autonomous agents.
  • Where applicable: Tool-agnostic and broadly relevant; the AI/autonomy roadmap is a vendor-independent framework, though the neuro-symbolic claims are forward-looking rather than shipped.
path: Network Event Correlation. Stories to keep you awake

items.title: Pls stop exposing your... secrets
items.text:
AutoCon 3 (Prague) — Operator digest Core pick Prague · 28–30 May 2025

Slides Recording

John Howard

VideoPPTX

  • Why: Hard-coded credentials and verify=False on REST calls are endemic in network automation code, and the automation toolchain itself becomes an attack surface — squarely a network-security concern for the PM.
  • What: A fast tour of HashiCorp Vault's built-in secret engines, showing a PoC instance that removes hard-coded creds from automation scripts at team scale.
  • How: Standing up a Vault PoC and using a couple of its built-in engines to centralize secrets consumed by automation pipelines, addressing both the accidental-exposure problem and the DevSecOps friction it causes. (From abstract only — lightning-talk depth.)
  • Where applicable: Broadly applicable; this is a generic, adoptable pattern rather than an org-specific one. Watch for the usual caveat that Vault itself becomes Tier-0 infrastructure your automation now depends on.

items.title: Start at the Beginning; Automating Network Design
items.text:
AutoCon 3 (Prague) — Operator digest Adjacent pick Prague · 28–30 May 2025

Slides Recording

Claudia de Luna (Opening Keynote)

VideoPPTX

  • Why: This sets the thesis the rest of the conference keeps echoing: automation's next bottleneck is upstream of operations, in design. If the PM's teams produce monolithic diagrams and Word documents, this names the problem precisely.
  • What: An argument that the fixation on "source of truth" is a symptom of starting midstream; the real anchor is programmatically consumable design data — patterns, data models, structured data — from which diagrams, documentation, configurations, and build guides all derive.
  • How: Conceptual keynote, not an implementation: reframe design artifacts as structured data that everything else flows from, and spotlight existing work in that direction. (From abstract only.)
  • Where applicable: Universal framing; pairs naturally with the Design-Driven Automation and Abstraction talks below.
path: Start at the Beginning; Automating Network Design

items.title: Taking Automation to next level: Drive your network with Microservices
items.text:
AutoCon 3 (Prague) — Operator digest Adjacent pick Prague · 28–30 May 2025

Slides Recording

Shirish Basant Rai, Colt Technology

VideoPPTX

  • Why: Colt is a real carrier doing event-driven microservices for network automation aligned to TMF ODA NaaS standards — a useful signal of where operator automation architectures (and NaaS standardization) are heading.
  • What: Colt's evolution from a simple workflow-engine architecture to an event-driven microservices model, and how that architecture naturally aligned with TMF ODA NaaS.
  • How: Separation of concerns into microservices, asynchronous workflow and service-orchestration complexity hidden from consumers, code promotion without service disruption, and faster development cycles. (From abstract only — no usable source text, so expect architecture philosophy rather than deployment detail.)
  • Where applicable: Colt-specific scale (global carrier, NaaS ambitions); the microservices event-driven pattern is heavy machinery for smaller estates, but the TMF ODA alignment angle matters to anyone selling or consuming NaaS-style interconnect.

items.title: Teaching "old" LLMs new tricks
items.text:
AutoCon 3 (Prague) — Operator digest Wildcard pick Prague · 28–30 May 2025

Slides Recording

Urs Baumann

VideoPPTX

  • Why: Not about networking per se, but a signal of where network automation tooling is heading: specialized models fine-tuned for automation tasks. Worth a look even for a skeptic of LLM-for-netops.
  • What: A method for making general-purpose LLMs accurate on specialized network automation tasks without datacenter-scale training budgets, plus a practical fine-tuning pipeline.
  • How: LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) fine-tuning — adding small trainable weight matrices to a frozen base model — which sharply reduces the compute needed to specialize an LLM, applied to network-automation tasks. (From abstract only — the slide text didn't extract.)
  • Where applicable: The technique is general; the constraint is having a task set worth fine-tuning for and the discipline to evaluate accuracy claims honestly. Interesting more as a direction than a deployable today.

items.title: The Road to EVPN: Automated Service Migrations
items.text:
AutoCon 3 (Prague) — Operator digest Core pick Prague · 28–30 May 2025

Slides Recording

Luke Gollan, Megaport

VideoPPTX

  • Why: Migrating a live global network to EVPN with automated service cutover is squarely in the PM's EVPN/BGP and interconnect territory, and this covers the whole arc: architecture, config rollout, then customer service migration with minimal disruption.
  • What: Megaport's end-to-end story of automated EVPN deployment across a global telco network, from design through rollout to migrating production services, plus customer/support-facing migration tooling.
  • How: Object-driven database generating device configs; NETCONF operations to configure, log, and track changes; diversity zones to contain blast radius; APIs and message queuing to trigger migrations; explicit phased migration steps with rehearsed rollback; tooling to track network changes and keep business stakeholders informed. (From abstract only — no usable source text.)
  • Where applicable: Megaport-specific (global NaaS/telco topology, dense service inventory), but the checklist — rehearsed rollback, diversity zones, event-driven migration triggers, stakeholder-visible risk — is a transferable migration methodology for any EVPN or fabric migration.

items.title: The Why, What, and How about Design-Driven Automation
items.text:
AutoCon 3 (Prague) — Operator digest Adjacent pick Prague · 28–30 May 2025

Slides Recording

Christian Adell Querol, Network to Code

VideoPPTX

  • Why: The most concrete instantiation of the keynote's thesis: treat design as executable, versioned, decommissionable data rather than documentation. Includes a working open-source implementation.
  • What: A framework where a network service catalog (minimal validated inputs + template logic + external context) drives a PLAN, a builder creates tracked/connected/rollbackable data, and that service data becomes the single reference for orchestration, automation (Nornir/Ansible/Terraform engines), and observability.
  • How: Demonstrated with Nautobot's Design Builder (which the speaker contributes to): a PoP deployment created from just name + size with architectural validation; a second design creating a VRF, prefix from a pool, and a cable; design updates that understand what changes (prefix preserved, cable re-pointed); clean decommissioning reverting created objects; and every change tracked as a commit. Key argument: test the design, not just the implementation — if the design is deterministic, deployments don't need per-instance review, the way nobody reviews a PR when someone launches a VPC.
  • Where applicable: The demo is Nautobot-specific, but the concepts (minimal input, design-as-data, traceable provenance, dry-run, full lifecycle through decommission) port to other SoT platforms. Speaker is vendor-affiliated (Network to Code) yet the talk is substantially technique-first.
path: The Why, What, and How about Design-Driven Automation

items.title: Transforming Network Automation with Temporal
items.text:
AutoCon 3 (Prague) — Operator digest Adjacent pick Prague · 28–30 May 2025

Slides Recording

Naveen Achyuta

VideoPPTX

  • Why: Durable-execution workflow engines are how other industries solved long-running, failure-prone, stateful orchestration — exactly what network change automation is. Temporal is underused in networking and this is a solid architectural introduction.
  • What: An introduction of Temporal to network automation: architecture, why durable execution fits network use cases (provisioning, config management, automated remediation, human-in-the-loop), and how it compares to what teams hand-roll today.
  • How: Tasks are ordinary code ("activities") whose state is persisted by the Temporal service (history service shards, matching service task queues, distributed workers) — workflows are guaranteed to run to completion, resuming where they left off after failures, with built-in tracing and audit trails. The slides show a practical trigger path (NetBox webhook → workflow) and per-step timing for optimization, plus a GitHub starter repo. Explicit caveat given: don't use it for simple tasks; it earns its keep at scale and resiliency requirements.
  • Where applicable: General-purpose; the main adoption constraint is running another stateful service well, which small teams may find heavy.

  • Why: SONiC fragmentation across distributions is a real operational problem for multi-vendor cloud and AI infrastructure provisioning — and AI-cluster fabric provisioning is exactly where this is biting hardest right now.
  • What: A demonstration of how traditional IaC tools can drive abstractions that generate actual device configurations across multiple SONiC platforms, instead of writing per-flavor configs.
