items.title: Rethinking Identity, Policy, and Access Control (IPAC) for Agentic AI - BRKETI-2623
items.text:
Cisco Live Europe 2026 (Amsterdam) digest Core pick Amsterdam · 31 March 2026

Abstract

Marcelo Yannuzzi (Cisco)

  • Why: Agentic identity is where the PM's identity work is heading, and this is one of the first vendor architectures that names the actual problem: current IAM scopes, scopes authorization around humans and static service accounts, not autonomous NL-driven entities acting at machine speed.
  • What: The technology gaps in today's IAM for agentic AI, and a proposed IPAC architecture covering: dynamic trust establishment among users, agents, and MCP servers (Just-In-Time identification, Multi-Factor Verification across domains), policy that defines what autonomous entities may do without a human in the loop, and granular authorization for entities communicating in natural language — with a demo and pointers to Cisco's open-source efforts (from abstract only).
  • How: Architecture-plus-demo: identify the gaps (static identity, human-in-loop assumptions), then layer JIT identification and policy enforcement over agent/MCP interactions.
  • Where applicable: Early-stage/forward-looking — this is where the field is going rather than where it is. Note the SPIFFE/SPIRE-shaped hole: workload-identity primitives would be the natural substrate, worth probing in Q&A. Cisco "innovations and open source efforts" means expect some product framing.
path: Rethinking Identity, Policy, and Access Control (IPAC) for Agentic AI - BRKETI-2623

items.title: The New, QUIC Based Encrypted Protocol Stack Taking over the Internet and How to Deal with It - BRKSPM-2024
items.text:
Cisco Live Europe 2026 (Amsterdam) digest Core pick Amsterdam · 31 March 2026

Abstract

Andreas Enotiadis (Cisco), Bart Van de Velde (Cisco)

  • Why: QUIC + HTTP/3 + DoH + ECH is dismantling the visibility and traffic-management assumptions most network and security infrastructure was built on. The abstract cites QUIC at ~50% of total traffic, doubling every 18 months — a structural shift, not an SP niche topic.
  • What: How the QUIC-based encrypted stack is constructed and evolving, its behavior in terms of visibility and flow control, its impact on infrastructure elements, and the techniques providers can use to keep pace — traffic visibility, QoE monitoring/management, and efficient use of 5G spectrum (from abstract only).
  • How: Protocol-level decomposition: TLS 1.3 encryption removing application visibility, congestion management moving into the application, applications disintermediating the network.
  • Where applicable: Framed for service providers, but the visibility loss applies to any enterprise DC or security team doing traffic inspection, QoS, or telemetry on the wire.
path: The New, QUIC Based Encrypted Protocol Stack Taking over the Internet and How to Deal with It - BRKSPM-2024

items.title: VXLAN EVPN: A Deep Dive into Packet Forwarding - BRKDCN-3966
items.text:
Cisco Live Europe 2026 (Amsterdam) digest Core pick Amsterdam · 31 March 2026

Abstract

Lukas Krattiger (Cisco)

  • Why: EVPN is the dominant DC overlay control plane and datapath-debugging knowledge is where most operational pain lives. This is a datapath-internals talk, not an EVPN primer.
  • What: A packet-by-packet walkthrough of VXLAN EVPN forwarding — routing, bridging, and multi-destination handling from ingress VTEP through to egress VTEP and beyond (from abstract only).
  • How: "Day in the life of a packet" structure following a concrete frame through the overlay.
  • Where applicable: Any VXLAN EVPN fabric (Nexus 9K baseline is Cisco's, but the mechanics are standard). Assumes working EVPN knowledge.
path: VXLAN EVPN: A Deep Dive into Packet Forwarding - BRKDCN-3966

items.title: 400G, 800G, and Terabit Pluggable Optics: What You Need to Know - BRKOPT-2699

Mark Nowell (Cisco), Errol Roberts (Cisco)

items.text:
Cisco Live US 2026 (Las Vegas) — for Networking / Security / Identity PM digest Wildcard pick Las Vegas · 30 June 2026

Ramana Kompella (Cisco)

items.title: AI Gave Every Attacker a Kubernetes Playbook. Isovalent Takes It Away - PSOSEC-2345
items.text:
Cisco Live US 2026 (Las Vegas) — for Networking / Security / Identity PM digest Adjacent pick Las Vegas · 30 June 2026

Abstract

Duffie Cooley (Cisco)

  • Why: A PSO product pitch, but the underlying pattern — identity-aware (not IP-aware) network policy in K8s — is core to where this PM's cloud-native-security interests are heading.

items.title: Beyond the (Switch)-Port: Exploring the World of Host Networking - BRKNWT-2620
items.text:
Cisco Live US 2026 (Las Vegas) — for Networking / Security / Identity PM digest Core pick Las Vegas · 30 June 2026

Abstract

Bruce McDougall (Cisco), Chris Lapp (Cisco)

  • Why: Host-side networking is where this PM's physical and cloud-native interests converge — kernel bypass, eBPF datapaths, CNI performance, and SmartNICs in one arc.
  • What: A tour from the ToR switch port down into the host: native OS packet paths, hypervisor networking, the Kubernetes CNI ecosystem, and emerging sub-100µs host-networking techniques (from abstract only).
  • How: Compares virtio/SR-IOV and vSwitch options (OVS, VPP), benchmarks CNI choices — Calico "just routes," Cilium's eBPF policy datapaths, VPP-backed CNIs for terabit throughput — and looks ahead at XDP/AF_XDP kernel bypass, eBPF congestion control, and SmartNICs fusing packet processing with AI inference.

path: Beyond the (Switch)-Port: Exploring the World of Host Networking - BRKNWT-2620

items.title: Building AI/ML Fabrics at Hyperscale: Architecture Evolutions, Challenges, Open Standards, Performance Characterization and Validation on Cisco SiliconOne-based Platforms. - BRKMSI-2014
items.text:
Cisco Live US 2026 (Las Vegas) — for Networking / Security / Identity PM digest Core pick Las Vegas · 30 June 2026

Abstract

Masiuddin Mohammed (Cisco), Evan Knipp (Cisco)

  • Why: The single densest architectural map of where AI-scale DC fabrics are going — cluster size, topology generations, and DCI constraints are exactly the design questions a physical-networking PM needs answered.
  • What: A trace of AI fabric evolution from 4K/16K-GPU leaf-spine, to 64K-GPU Disaggregated Scheduled Fabric (DSF) two-tier with super-spines, to >200K-GPU three-tier scale-out, plus multi-DC DCI interconnect; paired with a benchmarking methodology for validating these fabrics (from abstract only).

Validation is done in production-like environments using open, standards-aligned test practices to minimize test drift.
  • Where applicable: Cisco-specific (Silicon One platforms) and hyperscaler-derived, but the topology taxonomy, failure-mode catalog, and benchmark methodology generalize to any large AI fabric build.
path: Building AI/ML Fabrics at Hyperscale: Architecture Evolutions, Challenges, Open Standards, Performance Characterization and Validation on Cisco SiliconOne-based Platforms. - BRKMSI-2014

items.title: Cisco Nexus 9000 Architecture - BRKDCN-3939
items.text:
Cisco Live US 2026 (Las Vegas) — for Networking / Security / Identity PM digest Core pick Las Vegas · 30 June 2026

Faraz Taifehesmatian (Cisco)

items.title: Control your destiny in the token-based AI economy with pluggable optics innovations - PSOMSI-1005
items.text:
Cisco Live US 2026 (Las Vegas) — for Networking / Security / Identity PM digest Adjacent pick Las Vegas · 30 June 2026

Ray Nering (Cisco), Yoav Schreiber (Cisco)

items.title: Designing RoCEv2 Networks for Distributed AI Training with Cisco Nexus 9000 - BRKDCN-2688
items.text:
Cisco Live US 2026 (Las Vegas) — for Networking / Security / Identity PM digest Core pick Las Vegas · 30 June 2026

Praveen Poojary (Cisco)

path: Designing RoCEv2 Networks for Distributed AI Training with Cisco Nexus 9000 - BRKDCN-2688

items.title: Failure Patterns in Modern Distributed Systems: Lessons from Major Internet Outages - BRKOPS-2000
items.text:

Mike Hicks (Cisco)

path: Failure Patterns in Modern Distributed Systems: Lessons from Major Internet Outages - BRKOPS-2000

items.title: Hijacking Trust: Weaponizing Stolen Cookies and Tokens - BRKSEC-2132
items.text:
Cisco Live US 2026 (Las Vegas) — for Networking / Security / Identity PM digest Core pick Las Vegas · 30 June 2026

Abstract

Stefan Duernberger (Cisco)

  • Why: Session/token theft is the dominant real-world auth attack vector, and this session covers the modern defensive stack — passkeys, token binding, shared signals — directly on this PM's identity interests.
  • What: How stolen cookies and tokens are weaponized, and the countermeasures: passkeys (FIDO/WebAuthn), OAuth 2.0 and OIDC flows, Google's Device-Bound Session Credentials (DBSC), Cisco Duo Passport, and the Shared Signals and Events (SSE) framework (from abstract only).
  • How: Walks implementation of each mechanism and how they combine in a Zero Trust architecture to kill replayable bearer credentials.
  • Where applicable: Standards-based and broadly applicable (DBSC is a browser standard-in-progress, SSE is OpenID Foundation work); the Duo Passport portion is product-specific.
path: Hijacking Trust: Weaponizing Stolen Cookies and Tokens - BRKSEC-2132

items.title: Hunting the Invisible Army: Visibility for AI Agents & Non-human Identities - BRKSEC-2067
items.text:
Cisco Live US 2026 (Las Vegas) — for Networking / Security / Identity PM digest Core pick Las Vegas · 30 June 2026

Abstract

Tal Kronrod (Cisco)

  • Why: NHI explosion is the identity story of the cycle; traditional ITDR built for humans misses machine-speed, broad-permission identities.
  • What: A framework and product demonstration (Cisco Identity Intelligence) for unified visibility and threat detection/response across service accounts, workloads, and autonomous AI agents in cloud, on-prem, and SaaS (from abstract only).
  • How: Applies identity intelligence — correlating inherited permissions, credential usage, and behavior — to detect threats from NHIs that never trip human-focused anomaly detection.
  • Where applicable: The NHI problem is universal, but the demo is Cisco's Identity Intelligence product; the framework's portability to other ITDR tooling should be probed.
path: Hunting the Invisible Army: Visibility for AI Agents & Non-human Identities - BRKSEC-2067

items.title: Life of a Packet in Kubernetes: A Network Engineer's Guide - BRKCLD-3734
items.text:
Cisco Live US 2026 (Las Vegas) — for Networking / Security / Identity PM digest Core pick Las Vegas · 30 June 2026

Abstract

Nico Vibert (Cisco)

  • Why: A datapath-internals walkthrough of Kubernetes networking using Isovalent Cilium — squarely on this PM's core cloud-native interests (eBPF, Gateway API, overlays, BGP).
  • What: A full trace of a packet through a Kubernetes cluster — across nodes, overlays, policy, and egress — using Cilium as the dataplane, with live demos (from abstract only).
  • How: Unpacks VXLAN/Geneve overlays, Gateway API, Egress Gateway, BGP routing, IPsec encryption, Direct Server Return, multi-cluster Cluster Mesh, plus performance features BIG TCP and topology-aware traffic engineering; observability via Hubble, Cilium CLI, and Wireshark.
  • Where applicable: Cilium/Isovalent-centric but the K8s networking constructs (Gateway API, CNI, multicluster) are vendor-neutral; advanced session, assumes routing/overlay/LB fluency.
path: Life of a Packet in Kubernetes: A Network Engineer's Guide - BRKCLD-3734

items.title: Modern Multi-Homing in VXLAN EVPN: Enabling vPC and ESI+ in Today's Data Centers - BRKDCN-2940
items.text:
Cisco Live US 2026 (Las Vegas) — for Networking / Security / Identity PM digest Core pick Las Vegas · 30 June 2026

Abstract

Parth Patel (Cisco)

  • Why: EVPN ESI multihoming landing in NX-OS 10.6.1 is a real control-plane shift for Cisco fabrics; the vPC-vs-ESI trade-off is a live design decision.
  • What: A comparison of classic vPC and the new EVPN ESI multihoming (ESI+), covering how each works, what changes with ESI+, and when to choose one over the other (from abstract only).
  • How: Real design examples and packet-flow comparisons, framed around fabric scale, resiliency requirements, and operational model. Assumes prior vPC-VTEP knowledge.
  • Where applicable: NX-OS fabrics specifically; the ESI-MH model itself is the IETF standard mechanism also used by other vendors and SONiC, so the concepts travel well.
path: Modern Multi-Homing in VXLAN EVPN: Enabling vPC and ESI+ in Today's Data Centers - BRKDCN-2940

items.title: Pig-in-the-Middle - TLS Decryption and Encrypted Visibility Engine Deep Dive on Cisco Secure Firewall - BRKSEC-3320
items.text:
Cisco Live US 2026 (Las Vegas) — for Networking / Security / Identity PM digest Core pick Las Vegas · 30 June 2026

Abstract

Carol Trincia Dsouza (Cisco)

  • Why: Encrypted Client Hello plus post-quantum crypto is about to break passive TLS interception — a network-security sea change this PM needs to plan for.
  • What: A deep dive on the modern encryption stack as seen from the firewall: ECH, domain fronting, evasive VPNs, fake TLS, QUIC decryption, and how the Encrypted Visibility Engine fingerprints the source process of an encrypted connection without decrypting anything (from abstract only).
  • How: Live demos of decryption configuration (TLS and QUIC) and of encrypted-traffic analysis, including how a free CDN account can stack QUIC + ECH + encrypted DNS + post-quantum crypto into an opaque connection, and what that means for decryption policy.
  • Where applicable: Cisco Secure Firewall product context, but the threat/visibility analysis (ECH, PQ, QUIC obfuscation) is broadly relevant to any TLS-inspecting security stack.
path: Pig-in-the-Middle - TLS Decryption and Encrypted Visibility Engine Deep Dive on Cisco Secure Firewall - BRKSEC-3320

items.title: Real World Deployments: Architectural lessons learnt from a 100+ Node AI Factory Deployment - BRKXAR-2039
items.text:
Cisco Live US 2026 (Las Vegas) — for Networking / Security / Identity PM digest Core pick Las Vegas · 30 June 2026

Abstract

Dave Lucas (Cisco), Nandu Shankar (Cisco)

  • Why: The closest thing in this program to an end-user case study with failure discussion — a real integration bring-up, not a clean-room reference architecture.
  • What: Lessons from standing up a 100+ node "AI factory" spanning compute, network, and storage, with dual GPU vendors, virtual and containerized workloads, RDMA-accelerated storage with GPUDirect, multi-tenant security, and a scalable RoCE front and back-end fabric (from abstract only).
  • How: Explicitly covers the failure modes that don't appear in config guides: multi-OS GPU driver inconsistencies, RoCE fabric optimization, cross-vendor GPU networking quirks, shared-services dependencies, cabling/topology missteps, and typical bottlenecks.
  • Where applicable: Deployment-specific (one environment, Cisco-built), but the cross-vendor integration pitfalls are broadly instructive for anyone running mixed-GPU AI infrastructure.
path: Real World Deployments: Architectural lessons learnt from a 100+ Node AI Factory Deployment - BRKXAR-2039

items.title: Reclaiming Your Agency: MCP, OAuth 2.1 and the Power to Automate Anything - BRKSEC-2065
items.text:
Cisco Live US 2026 (Las Vegas) — for Networking / Security / Identity PM digest Core pick Las Vegas · 30 June 2026

Abstract

Jeremiah Williams (Cisco)

  • Why: Agentic identity is an emerging core interest, and this is the standards-level session — MCP authorization, OAuth 2.1, fine-grained authorization — rather than a product pitch.
  • What: How the emerging agentic-AI security stack works: Model Context Protocol (MCP), OAuth 2.1, fine-grained authorization, and related mechanisms for controlling what autonomous agents can access and do (from abstract only).
  • How: Explores how these standards combine to give agents delegated, scoped, auditable access to business applications — and notes the same machinery applies to human identity.
  • Where applicable: Standards-track and vendor-neutral (MCP, OAuth 2.1, fine-grained authz are IETF/OpenAI-ecosystem work); product agnosticism should be verified in the deck.
path: Reclaiming Your Agency: MCP, OAuth 2.1 and the Power to Automate Anything - BRKSEC-2065

items.title: Safeguarding the Internet's Backbone: Unleashing the Power of RPKI for Unbreakable IPv4 and IPv6 BGP Security - BRKENT-2179
items.text:
Cisco Live US 2026 (Las Vegas) — for Networking / Security / Identity PM digest Core pick Las Vegas · 30 June 2026

Abstract

Jeffry Handal (Cisco), John Shea (Cisco)

  • Why: RPKI deployment is the practical, deployable answer to BGP hijacking — core internet-routing security with direct DC/WAN interconnect relevance.
  • What: Real-world BGP hijack incidents (criminal and nation-state) analyzed against what RPKI and related BGP capabilities would have prevented, plus deployment strategies and working configuration examples to start an RPKI rollout (from abstract only).
  • How: Route Origin Validation mechanics, deployment patterns (full vs partial ROV), and complementary BGP security capabilities.
  • Where applicable: Any organization operating BGP and announcing prefixes — vendor tooling is Cisco IOS-XR/IOS-XE but RPKI/RFC 6811 is standards-based and cross-vendor.
path: Safeguarding the Internet's Backbone: Unleashing the Power of RPKI for Unbreakable IPv4 and IPv6 BGP Security - BRKENT-2179

items.title: Silicon One Unveiled: Diving into the power of Cisco silicon - BRKNWT-2624
items.text:
Cisco Live US 2026 (Las Vegas) — for Networking / Security / Identity PM digest Core pick Las Vegas · 30 June 2026

Abstract

Ramesh Sivakolundu (Cisco), Dave Zacks (Cisco)

  • Why: Silicon One is the unifying silicon across Cisco's enterprise, SP, and AI portfolios; understanding its design rationale is directly relevant to physical DC networking decisions.
  • What: A deep-dive into how Silicon One is architected and why — the design choices, distinguishing features, and how its capabilities map to different network roles. Caveat: the abstract is noticeably hype-toned ("fast-paced... you will be glad you did!") and carries no specific technical claims, so depth must be verified in the room or on the recording (from abstract only).
  • How: Presented as silicon design-and-engineering rationale — not just feature lists but the why behind implementation choices, and how those translate into deployable designs.
  • Where applicable: Cisco silicon-specific; valuable mainly as the architectural underpinning for the AI-fabric and routing sessions above.
path: Silicon One Unveiled: Diving into the power of Cisco silicon - BRKNWT-2624

items.title: The Network Capability AI Has Been Waiting For - BRKPAR-1026
items.text:
Cisco Live US 2026 (Las Vegas) — for Networking / Security / Identity PM digest Wildcard pick Las Vegas · 30 June 2026

Abstract

Nikhil Handigol (Forward)

  • Why: A partner session, but it points at a genuinely novel operational pattern: a mathematically accurate network digital twin as the reasoning layer for both human changes and autonomous AI agents.
  • What: Demonstration of pre-deployment verification of routing and firewall changes on a formal network model, catching regressions before production, and automated end-to-end impact assessment replacing manual approval cycles (from abstract only).
  • How: Formal verification of network state and behavior (the Forward Networks model-checking lineage) applied as the guardrail that lets AI agents act on production networks with verified-before-risk confidence.
  • Where applicable: Formal-model based, vendor- and device-neutral in principle (Forward ingests multi-vendor configs); the AI-agent-trust framing is early but directly relevant to where network automation is heading.
path: The Network Capability AI Has Been Waiting For - BRKPAR-1026

items.title: The New, QUIC Based Encrypted Protocol Stack Taking over the Internet and How to Deal with It - BRKSPM-2024
items.text:
Cisco Live US 2026 (Las Vegas) — for Networking / Security / Identity PM digest Adjacent pick Las Vegas · 30 June 2026

Abstract

Andreas Enotiadis (Cisco), Bart Van de Velde (Cisco)

  • Why: Adjacent rather than core because of its service-provider framing, but the QUIC/HTTP-3/DoH/ECH stack it describes is the same visibility threat covered in BRKSEC-3320, with protocol-internals depth.
  • What: How the QUIC-based stack (QUIC + HTTP/3 + DoH + eSNI/ECH) is constructed and evolving — already claimed at ~50% of traffic and doubling every 18 months — and why it obsoletes the assumptions SP networks are built on: encryption kills application visibility, and congestion management moves into the application (from abstract only).
  • How: Analysis of the stack's visibility and flow-control behavior plus SP-side countermeasures for traffic visibility, QoE monitoring, and efficient use of scarce resources like 5G spectrum.
  • Where applicable: SP networks primarily; the protocol analysis applies to any operator of middleboxes and QoS infrastructure facing QUIC traffic.
path: The New, QUIC Based Encrypted Protocol Stack Taking over the Internet and How to Deal with It - BRKSPM-2024

items.text:
Cisco Live US 2026 (Las Vegas) — for Networking / Security / Identity PM digest Core pick Las Vegas · 30 June 2026

Abstract

VASU Thatipalli (Cisco)

  • Why: SONiC is where open-source NOS development is actually happening; a TAC-lead troubleshooting session is a good signal of how production-mature SONiC on Cisco silicon has become.
  • What: Operational and control-plane debugging of BGP, ACLs, and VXLAN in SONiC environments, plus a structured troubleshooting framework covering data plane, control plane, and root-cause analysis (from abstract only).
  • How: SONiC CLI techniques and log analysis to isolate faults in production-scale deployments.
  • Where applicable: Cisco 8000 + SONiC deployments; the framework and CLI methods apply to SONiC generally, and the session doubles as a maturity readout for disaggregated switching.
path: Troubleshooting SONIC on Cisco 8000: Learn how to Troubleshoot BGP, ACL, VxLAN on SONIC - TACMSI-2001

items.title: Unifying Kubernetes and the Data Center: Isovalent Private Networks over EVPN/VXLAN - BRKDCN-3668
items.text:
Cisco Live US 2026 (Las Vegas) — for Networking / Security / Identity PM digest Core pick Las Vegas · 30 June 2026

Abstract

Marcos Hernández (Cisco)

  • Why: Bridges this PM's two worlds — K8s networking and DC EVPN fabric — with concrete control-plane and datapath mechanisms rather than hand-waving about "integration."
  • What: A blueprint for integrating Isovalent Private Networks (Cilium-based K8s) with external EVPN/VXLAN fabrics, including underlay/overlay connectivity, BGP control-plane setup, EVPN route-type advertisements, VRF instantiation, and VTEP configuration on both sides (from abstract only).
  • How: Details the specific route advertisements and datapath programming needed to stretch logical L2/L3 networks between Kubernetes and the Cisco fabric, and how the result supports distributed AI/ML application designs.
  • Where applicable: Isovalent + Cisco NX-OS/ACI-style fabrics specifically; the EVPN-into-K8s pattern is generalizable to any CNI that can speak BGP/EVPN.
path: Unifying Kubernetes and the Data Center: Isovalent Private Networks over EVPN/VXLAN - BRKDCN-3668

items.title: VXLAN EVPN: A Deep Dive into Packet Forwarding - BRKDCN-3966
items.text:
Cisco Live US 2026 (Las Vegas) — for Networking / Security / Identity PM digest Core pick Las Vegas · 30 June 2026

Abstract

Lukas Krattiger (Cisco)

  • Why: EVPN/VXLAN datapath internals are a core interest — this is the "follow the packet" internals session, not a feature overview.
  • What: A day-in-the-life walkthrough of a VXLAN EVPN packet: routing and bridging behavior, and multi-destination (BUM) traffic handling, from ingress VTEP to egress VTEP and beyond (from abstract only).
  • How: Step-by-step datapath trace of encap/decap, ARP suppression, and multicast replication mechanics on the fabric.
  • Where applicable: Any VXLAN EVPN fabric; mechanism-focused rather than product-specific.
path: VXLAN EVPN: A Deep Dive into Packet Forwarding - BRKDCN-3966

items.text:
Cisco Live US 2026 (Las Vegas) — for Networking / Security / Identity PM digest Core pick Las Vegas · 30 June 2026

Abstract

Sabitha Krishnamurthy (Cisco)

  • Why: AGNTCY is a Linux Foundation open-source project defining agent interoperability infrastructure including agent identity — the federation/identity layer this PM tracks (analogous to SPIFFE's role for workloads).
  • What: An introduction to the Internet of Agents and AGNTCY.org's four core technologies: agent directory, agent identity, SLIM messaging, and observability — the shared substrate for cross-environment agent discovery, trust, and communication (from abstract only).
  • How: Technical overview plus practical multi-agent use cases demonstrated with shared code.
  • Where applicable: Open-source (Linux Foundation) and cross-vendor by design; early-stage, so expect evolving specs rather than settled interfaces.
path: Your AI Agents Don't Talk to My AI Agents - Let's Fix That! - BRKETI-1009

items.title: Zero Trust for Agents - PSOSEC-2344
items.text:
Cisco Live US 2026 (Las Vegas) — for Networking / Security / Identity PM digest Adjacent pick Las Vegas · 30 June 2026

Abstract

Tsailing Merrem (Cisco), Prabhu Barathi (Cisco)

  • Why: Down-ranked from core: this is product-positioning for Cisco's Zero Trust portfolio applied to agents, and the more substantive agentic-identity coverage is in BRKSEC-2065 and BRKSEC-2067.
  • What: The argument that autonomous agents become the "ultimate insider" without fine-grained authorization, and how Cisco is extending its Zero Trust access architecture to enforce scope, access control, and data security for an agentic workforce (from abstract only).
  • How: Extends existing Zero Trust enforcement points (identity-aware proxy/access) to agent identities and their permitted actions rather than just access.
  • Where applicable: Cisco Zero Trust portfolio-specific; useful mainly as a readout of how a major vendor plans to operationalize agent authorization.

items.title: ASPA: the new protocol for improving BGP routing security
items.text:
DKNOG16 — Operator Track (Scandic Copenhagen, Mar 5–6, 2026) digest Core pick Scandic Copenhagen · 6 March 2026

Abstract Recording

Ondřej Caletka (RIPE NCC)

Video

  • Why: Routing security is moving from origin validation to partial path validation, and ASPA deployment decisions are landing on BGP operators now — directly within the PM's network-security scope.
  • What: An introduction to Autonomous System Provider Authorization, the next RPKI feature being deployed after Route Origin Authorization: each AS can cryptographically declare which ASes are expected to provide it transit, and operators performing ASPA validation can drop routes arriving via unauthorized providers. (from abstract only)
  • How: RPKI-signed provider-authorization objects let validators check a received route's propagation path against the declared transit graph, catching route leaks and hijacks propagated through unauthorized providers — complementing, not replacing, ROV.
  • Where applicable: Any BGP operator — transit, enterprise, or DC — building on existing RPKI/ROV deployments. Deployment is early, so the practical constraints (who signs objects, which platforms validate) are the things to listen for. RIPE NCC is a registry, not a vendor, so no product-pitch risk.
path: ASPA: the new protocol for improving BGP routing security

items.title: Auto-bandwidth for SR-TE
items.text:
DKNOG16 — Operator Track (Scandic Copenhagen, Mar 5–6, 2026) digest Core pick Scandic Copenhagen · 6 March 2026

Abstract Recording

Dmytro Shypovalov (Vegvisir Systems)

Video

  • Why: Bandwidth-aware SR-TE has been vendor-locked to date; this is an open-standard, multi-vendor prototype with an open-source component — the kind of adoptable tooling that matters for anyone running SR policies across a WAN or DC interconnect.
  • What: A prototype auto-bandwidth solution for Segment Routing Traffic Engineering that is open-standard and multi-vendor (in contrast to existing vendor-specific mechanisms), plus an open-source "SR-TE bandwidth sampler" that collects SR policy counters via gNMI, calculates traffic rates, and converts them into BGP-LS format per RFC 9857. (from abstract only)
  • How: Streaming telemetry of SR policy counters (gNMI) → traffic-rate computation → BGP-LS encoding per RFC 9857, so the SR-TE control plane or controller can resize policies from measured load without any vendor-proprietary signaling.
  • Where applicable: Networks running SR policies — SP WANs and large DC-interconnect fabrics; requires gNMI-capable devices and BGP-LS support for the relevant encodings. It is explicitly a prototype, so expect a demo and roadmap rather than production tooling. Vegvisir Systems is a vendor in this space, but the open-source sampler lowers the pitch risk; evaluate the open components on their own merits.

items.title: Automate what makes sense: Data, principles and practice
items.text:
DKNOG16 — Operator Track (Scandic Copenhagen, Mar 5–6, 2026) digest Adjacent pick Scandic Copenhagen · 6 March 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Brian Jeggesen (no affiliation listed)

VideoPPTX

  • Why: Diagnoses the commonest automation failure mode — tools are fine, the organization stalls — and gives a concrete starting step rather than a framework pitch.
  • What: An explanation of why "automate what makes sense" becomes a permanent excuse to automate nothing: unclear definitions of "safe" and "correct," fragile inputs, and changes that can't be proven before shipping. Offers a pragmatic path to make automation a normal way of working, with guardrails and evidence instead of optimism, and a first step implementable immediately. (from abstract only)
  • How: Principles-and-practice approach — pre-ship proof of correctness, guardrails, and incremental confidence-building rather than heroic one-off projects.
  • Where applicable: Any network organization; general technique with no scale or topology dependency.
path: Automate what makes sense: Data, principles and practice

items.title: Channelmania! – future proof your DWDM network topology while keeping it flexible for 1.6T
items.text:
DKNOG16 — Operator Track (Scandic Copenhagen, Mar 5–6, 2026) digest Core pick Scandic Copenhagen · 6 March 2026

Abstract Recording

Thomas Weible (no affiliation listed; material made with FLEXOPTIX Research)

Video

  • Why: Grid and spectrum planning for 800G/1.6T superchannels is a near-term, irreversible decision for anyone owning DWDM for DC/WAN interconnect; filter choices made today can lock a network out of 1.6T tomorrow.
  • What: A case for moving DWDM channel plans to larger grids (up to 400GHz, with COTS filters) to accommodate 400G/800G/1.6T coherent superchannels, while retaining backward compatibility with legacy 50GHz services — and an argument that IP engineers must now understand coherent optics in the IPoDWDM era. (from abstract only)
  • How: High-baud coherent superchannels need far more spectrum than legacy 50/100GHz slots; coherent detection being "blind" to anything but its own wavelength enables filterless topologies, but at the cost of flexibility. Wider COTS filters both open the growth path to 1.6T and coexist with legacy narrow-grid services.
  • Where applicable: Operators of their own DWDM/IPoDWDM infrastructure — DC interconnect, metro, and regional transport. Networks locked into 50GHz-gridded plants face the harder migration. The content is standard transport engineering despite the FLEXOPTIX Research affiliation; discount for any product positioning around their filter/solution portfolio.
path: Channelmania! – future proof your DWDM network topology while keeping it flexible for 1.6T

items.title: Command-Line to Codebase: Learning Software to Expand Your Engineering Toolkit
items.text:
DKNOG16 — Operator Track (Scandic Copenhagen, Mar 5–6, 2026) digest Adjacent pick Scandic Copenhagen · 6 March 2026

Abstract Recording

Thomas Kjær (no affiliation listed)

Video

  • Why: A replicable method for network engineers building small software tools, anchored on ECMP troubleshooting — a problem anyone running DC fabrics knows is painful and manual.
  • What: The story of building a small ECMP-aware probing tool while learning a new programming language, starting from familiar tools (traceroute, Wireshark, RFCs). The contribution is the method, not the tool: start in a domain you trust, measure everything, build in small slices, test one change at a time, explain results to yourself as you go. (from abstract only)
  • How: Incrementally translating a manual troubleshooting workflow into code, with validation steps at each slice.
  • Where applicable: Any network engineer; ECMP troubleshooting is universal. Light on novel technical results — the value is the low-risk method for starting and sustaining small tool projects.
path: Command-Line to Codebase: Learning Software to Expand Your Engineering Toolkit

items.title: Geopolitics and Digital Sovereignty in Greenland
items.text:
DKNOG16 — Operator Track (Scandic Copenhagen, Mar 5–6, 2026) digest Wildcard pick Scandic Copenhagen · 6 March 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Signe Ravn-Højgaard (Tænketanken Digital Infrastruktur)

VideoPPTX

  • Why: An extreme-case stress test of resilience design: an entire national ecosystem hanging off two submarine cables with routing terminating abroad. It exposes failure modes (single-corridor dependence, no traffic localization) that softer versions exist in most networks.
  • What: An examination of Greenland's structural dependence on U.S.-controlled infrastructure across multiple layers: two submarine cables plus limited satellite links, routing and traffic flows largely terminating outside Greenland, and minimal local traffic localization — and how that constrained path diversity intersects with heightened geopolitical attention. (from abstract only)
  • How: Case analysis of connectivity topology and traffic flows (15-minute short talk).
  • Where applicable: Greenland-specific, but the failure patterns — path diversity below the redundancy threshold, external hosting, no local traffic retention — generalize directly to any WAN resilience review. A good forcing function for asking "what is our two-cable equivalent?"
path: Geopolitics and Digital Sovereignty in Greenland

items.title: How far can you get with IX Route Servers?
items.text:
DKNOG16 — Operator Track (Scandic Copenhagen, Mar 5–6, 2026) digest Adjacent pick Scandic Copenhagen · 6 March 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Ben Cartwright-Cox (bgp.tools)

VideoPPTX

  • Why: Peers rarely question whether route server routes are actually imported; this replaces that folklore with measurement across many exchanges. Evidence-based peering strategy at a large scale.
  • What: A quantification of route server effectiveness — how relevant they are, how many participants actually import from them, and who those importers are — using the bgp.tools route collector network's deployment footprint across many internet exchanges. (from abstract only)
  • How: Collector-based observation at many IX fabrics, comparing routes offered by route servers against what participant networks actually accept.
  • Where applicable: IXP participants of all sizes; findings depend on bgp.tools's collector footprint (large but not exhaustive). Useful input for deciding how much to invest in bilateral peering vs. relying on the RS.
path: How far can you get with IX Route Servers?

items.title: Introduction to Design-Driven Network Automation
items.text:
DKNOG16 — Operator Track (Scandic Copenhagen, Mar 5–6, 2026) digest Adjacent pick Scandic Copenhagen · 6 March 2026

Abstract Recording

Mark Coleman (no affiliation listed)

Video

  • Why: The design/intent layer above config generation is where network automation platforms are converging; this gives the conceptual grounding and — usefully — covers where the approach still fails.
  • What: Design-driven automation treats the high-level design as a first-class artifact: an explicit model of topology, roles, relationships, and constraints, independent of any device configuration. Traces the idea from early topology-aware NMS and fabric controllers to modern intent-based systems, and covers how state, drift, refactoring, and unplanned change are reasoned about from a design model. (from abstract only)
  • How: Modeling and reasoning mechanics rather than a specific tool — how networks are represented as designs and how change over time is interpreted against them.
  • Where applicable: Networks at the scale or complexity where per-device config models break down; relevant to DC fabrics and multi-site estates alike. Conceptual survey; judge it by the "where it still struggles" section.

items.title: IXP+ based observations on peering and routing changes after Middle East cable outages
items.text:
DKNOG16 — Operator Track (Scandic Copenhagen, Mar 5–6, 2026) digest Core pick Scandic Copenhagen · 6 March 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Kaj Kjellgren and Bernd Speiss (DE-CIX)

VideoPPTX

  • Why: A physical-layer failure with measurable routing consequences — exactly the kind of concrete postmortem that transfers across environments. Relevant to anyone whose traffic depends on intercontinental cable paths.
  • What: Observations from DE-CIX data of trends and changes in routing and traffic after the cable cuts near the shore of Yemen in September, explicitly framed as do's and don'ts for routing setup, with the authors arguing the findings hold globally. (from abstract only)
  • How: IXP-side analysis of traffic volumes, route announcements, and peering behavior before and after the cuts — who rerouted successfully, who lacked alternate paths, and what the shifts revealed about regional routing setups.
  • Where applicable: The specific observations are tied to the Middle East corridor and DE-CIX's vantage points (single-IX perspective), but the resilience lessons — path diversity, alternate peering, routing hygiene under failure — apply to any operator with intercontinental dependencies.
path: IXP+ based observations on peering and routing changes after Middle East cable outages

items.title: Merging Service Provider Networks
items.text:
DKNOG16 — Operator Track (Scandic Copenhagen, Mar 5–6, 2026) digest Adjacent pick Scandic Copenhagen · 6 March 2026

Abstract Recording

Bastian Hoss and Markus Jungbluth (Xantaro Deutschland GmbH)

Video

  • Why: SP consolidation makes IP/MPLS integration a recurring real-world project, and this is practice-based technical content (architecture, routing, interop pitfalls) rather than a methodology pitch.
  • What: A technical walkthrough of merging distinct IP/MPLS network infrastructures: the general project approach, key architectural considerations, and challenges in routing-protocol integration and vendor interoperability, based on past project experience. (from abstract only)
  • How: Experience-driven — lessons from actual merge projects rather than a single mechanism.
  • Where applicable: Service-provider mergers and acquisitions; the routing-protocol and interop pitfalls also apply to enterprises consolidating DC fabrics after acquisitions. The underlying projects are unnamed, so treat specifics as consultancy experience; the pitfall list is the transferable part.

items.title: Network Automation in the Modern Age
items.text:
DKNOG16 — Operator Track (Scandic Copenhagen, Mar 5–6, 2026) digest Adjacent pick Scandic Copenhagen · 6 March 2026

Abstract Recording

Marcus Stoegbauer and Veit Heller (no affiliation listed)

Video

  • Why: The "source of truth / data model" problem is the current wall in netops automation — most teams past the template stage hit it. This names the next stage rather than selling a tool.
  • What: A reflective talk tracing automation from template-pushing to variable storage in documentation systems/DCIMs, arguing the next stage demands modeling the world explicitly, unconstrained by DCIM limits — and that automation designers now need deeper data-modeling skills than the tools teach. Explicitly a conversation-opener, with a glimpse of an early draft solution. (from abstract only)
  • How: Conceptual — decoupling the network's world-model from the documentation system that stores it; no finished tool is presented.
  • Where applicable: Any netops team that has outgrown templates and found its DCIM's model shaping (and limiting) its automation. Conceptual rather than deployable; the value is the framing and the community discussion it opens.
path: Network Automation in the Modern Age

items.title: Sovereignty for whom? Between digital (in)dependence and Big Tech expansionism
items.text:
DKNOG16 — Operator Track (Scandic Copenhagen, Mar 5–6, 2026) digest Wildcard pick Scandic Copenhagen · 6 March 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Signe Sophus Lai and Sofie Flensburg (University of Copenhagen)

VideoPPTX

  • Why: Not technical, but it argues the sovereignty debate is missing the layer the PM works on — who owns the submarine cables and routing economics underneath "sovereign cloud" marketing. Strategic context for infrastructure decisions, from researchers who focus on the physical layer.
  • What: An academic analysis of how "digital sovereignty" is deployed politically — by governments (including Denmark's "liberation" of the public sector) and by hyperscalers selling sovereignty as a service — arguing that a persistent focus on applications and services over underlying infrastructure obscures the real power structures. Illustrates with research on global submarine data cable ownership changes and the conditions around global internet routing. (from abstract only)
  • How: Social-science research synthesis — stakeholder analysis of the sovereignty debate tied to concrete infrastructure examples.
  • Where applicable: EU/Danish policy and procurement context; strategic framing rather than operational technique. Worth the PM's time precisely because it connects cable ownership and routing to the policy language increasingly attached to infrastructure budgets.
path: Sovereignty for whom? Between digital (in)dependence and Big Tech expansionism

items.title: Understanding and optimising transceiver efficiency using internal metrics for improved power savings
items.text:
DKNOG16 — Operator Track (Scandic Copenhagen, Mar 5–6, 2026) digest Core pick Scandic Copenhagen · 6 March 2026

Abstract Recording

Gerhard Stein (Flexoptix GmbH)

Video

  • Why: Transceiver power draw is a growing slice of DC and WAN opex, and this is one of the few talks showing how to extract savings from data the optics already expose — no hardware swap required. Squarely in the PM's physical-optics territory.
  • What: An analysis of Versatile Diagnostics Monitoring (VDM) metrics in modern (>100G) optical transceivers, focused on Thermoelectric Cooler (TEC) current, correlated with temperature and cable length, to find operating conditions that minimize power while holding performance. Software prototypes were built to evaluate and visualize transceiver efficiency in Watts using real-world VDM data. (from abstract only)
  • How: TEC current acts as a proxy for how hard the module is working to hold its temperature setpoint; correlating it with temperature and cable length across real deployment data reveals which optics and link types operate inefficiently and quantifies the per-link watts.
  • Where applicable: Any fleet of >100G pluggables that expose VDM — the metrics come from the transceiver, not a specific switch, so the technique is broadly transferable to DC, metro, and WAN optics. Caveat: the speaker is from a transceiver vendor, so expect some product framing around a genuinely vendor-neutral technique.
path: Understanding and optimising transceiver efficiency using internal metrics for improved power savings

items.title: Who put the "inter" in internet?
items.text:
DKNOG16 — Operator Track (Scandic Copenhagen, Mar 5–6, 2026) digest Wildcard pick Scandic Copenhagen · 6 March 2026

Abstract Recording

Poul-Henning Kamp (no affiliation listed)

Video

  • Why: The conference keynote (60 minutes) by Poul-Henning Kamp, a veteran of internet infrastructure and FreeBSD; his keynotes reliably challenge assumptions about how the internet's interconnection and economics actually work, and the title suggests exactly that target.
  • What: No description was published at the time of this digest ("More to come" in the program); the title points to a critical examination of what the "inter" in internet — interconnection and its ownership — actually consists of. Slides and a recording are attached to the event page, so the content can be reviewed after the fact. This item cannot be assessed beyond title and speaker.
  • How: Unknown — no abstract available; do not assume content from the title.
  • Where applicable: Unknown given the missing description; keynote length (1 hour, per the event page) and speaker track record alone justify attention.

items.title: A comprehensive analysis of the IRR landscape
items.text:
GRNOG 20 digest Adjacent pick 30 June 2026

Abstract Slides

Stavros Konstantaras (AMS-IX)

PPTX

  • Why: IRR (Internet Routing Registry) data is still what most networks generate route filters from, and its well-known staleness/inconsistency is a routing-security hygiene problem that also affects RPKI deployment. A comprehensive analysis — with the program having no abstract — suggests a data study across registries (RIPE, RADB, ARIN, etc.): freshness, coverage vs. RPKI, hijack-attributable errors. That's evidence, not anecdote — the kind of cross-environment content the PM should watch.
  • What: A landscape-scale analysis of IRR data quality and coverage, from AMS-IX (which has both exchange-point visibility and a public IRR mirror) (program text only).
  • How: Unknown; presumably registry-scraping and cross-correlation of route/route6 objects against observed announcements and/or RPKI ROAs.
  • Where applicable: Any operator that uses IRR-derived filters (near-universal). The findings should be broadly applicable; note AMS-IX's vantage point means analysis is anchored on the European exchange ecosystem.
path: A comprehensive analysis of the IRR landscape

items.title: Agentic AI in Networking
items.text:
GRNOG 20 digest Wildcard pick 30 June 2026

Abstract Slides

Ioannis Kaminaras, Kostas Gerakaris (Uni Systems)

PPTX

  • Why: Agentic AI — autonomous LLM agents that plan and execute multi-step network changes — is the emerging subfield where the PM's identity interests (agentic/workload identity) meet their networking interests. This is an early, practitioner-level look at the concept from a systems integrator (Uni Systems), useful for understanding what's being attempted in the field today (and what its authorization/trust-model problems are).
  • What: An overview of agentic AI applied to networking operations (program text and deck metadata only — no abstract).
  • How: Unknown; expect LLM-agent architectures (tool use, planning loops) applied to network operations tasks like configuration, troubleshooting, or assurance.
  • Where applicable: Conceptual relevance to any network team; approach is vendor- and lab-stage, so treat claims of production maturity with skepticism. Notably, running agents that make network changes raises exactly the identity/authorization questions the PM works on — a natural cross-reference with the WebPKI talk.

items.title: ASPA and Roles: What's up with that?
items.text:
GRNOG 20 digest Core pick 30 June 2026

Abstract

Antonis Chariton (AS4601 | Cisco)

  • Why: Routing security is a core interest, and ASPA (Autonomous System Provider Authorization) is the current frontier of RPKI-based BGP security — the mechanism that extends protection beyond ROAs/origin validation to AS-path verification. "Roles" refers to the ASPA registration taxonomy (e.g., provider vs. peer relationships) that has been actively debated in the RPKI working group. A talk titled "What's up with that?" from an operator/standardista (Chariton runs AS4601/Packet Clearing House infrastructure and works on RPKI tooling) is likely a candid status-and-interop report, exactly the kind of transferable operational content this program should surface.
  • What: An update on ASPA adoption, the roles model in RPKI, and the practical questions operators face when registering ASPA records and enabling AS-path verification (program text and speaker metadata only).
  • How: Presumably: RPKI-signed ASPA objects binding a customer AS to its authorized providers, plus BGP AS-path verification at receiving ASes, with discussion of the role registration semantics that caused deployment confusion.
  • Where applicable: Any operator running BGP with RPKI ROV today. Broadly applicable and standards-based (not org-specific), though real-world enforcement value depends on upstream adoption rates — which is likely the crux of the talk.
path: ASPA and Roles: What's up with that?

items.title: Balkan Digital Gateway: Enhancing Greece's Regional Connectivity
items.text:
GRNOG 20 digest Adjacent pick 30 June 2026

Abstract

Polina Kudriashova, Valentin Velichkov

  • Why: Regional fiber/cross-border connectivity projects shape the physical WAN topology that interconnects Greek (and Balkan) datacenters and IXs. For a PM whose remit includes physical DC/WAN interconnect, hearing where new regional capacity is being built — and its latency/route-diversity implications — is useful planning context, even if the talk is more project-update than deep technical.
  • What: An overview of the Balkan Digital Gateway initiative and Greece's position as a regional interconnect hub (program text and deck metadata only).
  • How: Unknown; expect maps of new/expanded routes and interconnection points rather than protocol-level detail.
  • Where applicable: Directly relevant only to operators with SE-European footprint or Greece-landing infrastructure; project- and geography-specific, and pitched at policy/funding-body level rather than engineer level.
path: Balkan Digital Gateway: Enhancing Greece's Regional Connectivity

items.title: DNS4EU Public DNS Resolver Infrastructure
items.text:
GRNOG 20 digest Adjacent pick 30 June 2026

Abstract

Panagiotis Palias (Whalebone)

  • Why: DNS4EU is the European Commission-backed public DNS resolver platform — a multi-node, privacy-focused resolver alternative to 8.8.8.8/1.1.1.1. For a PM watching internet infrastructure, this is a real-world case study in operating geographically distributed resolver infrastructure with policy/filtering layers, and it carries sovereignty/identity implications (who resolves your names).
  • What: The architecture and operation of the DNS4EU public resolver infrastructure, presented by Whalebone, one of the platform's operators (program text only).
  • How: Unknown; presumably anycast/distributed resolver nodes, filtering and malware-blocking policy tiers, and privacy handling, though details aren't in the program.
  • Where applicable: Relevant as operational context for anyone running or evaluating public recursive DNS; specific to the DNS4EU consortium's design — treat the numbers (deployment size, load) as org-specific rather than transferable benchmarks.

items.title: EVPN – One Control Plane to Rule Them All
items.text:
GRNOG 20 digest Core pick 30 June 2026

Abstract

Patrick Prangl (Arista Networks)

  • Why: EVPN is the de facto control plane for modern physical DC fabrics (VXLAN overlays, multi-dimensional ECMP, integrated bridging/routing) — directly in the PM's physical DC networking core. The "one control plane" framing speaks to a live operational debate: collapsing L2/L3/overlay/underlay services onto a single BGP-based control plane instead of stitching VLANs + IGP + separate overlay signaling.
  • What: A position/tutorial-style talk arguing for EVPN as the unified control plane across datacenter (and possibly WAN) services, per the title and the speaker's vendor affiliation (program text only).
  • How: Unknown from the program; expect BGP EVPN route types, VXLAN overlay with an underlay, and EVPN's L2/L3 service models (E-LAN/E-Tree, IRB) as the framing.
  • Where applicable: Applicable to any multi-tenant or leaf-spine DC being designed or refreshed. Caveat: the speaker is from Arista, so treat this as a vendor-lensed architectural pitch — worth watching for the conceptual argument (consolidated control plane, one failure domain to reason about), not for vendor-neutral tradeoffs.

items.title: Infrahub: Next-gen data management platform for Design-Driven Automation
items.text:
GRNOG 20 digest Adjacent pick 30 June 2026

Abstract

Pete Crocker (OpsMill)

  • Why: Network automation source-of-truth is a persistent operational problem. "Design-driven automation" — declarative, design-first intent feeding validation and provisioning — is the current generation's answer to the limits of pure inventory-SoT tools (NetBox-style) and bespoke scripts. Tooling that others can adopt is explicitly what this operator program should surface.
  • What: A talk introducing Infrahub, OpsMill's data-management platform for network automation: managing the intended design (schemas, relationships, hierarchical data) and driving automation from it (program text only — no abstract, and the event page shows no presentation materials and "Not scheduled", which suggests this session may have been cut or not yet scheduled; verify before seeking the recording).
  • How: Presumably a graph/schema-oriented data model with versioning and constraints, integrated into provisioning pipelines rather than a flat IPAM inventory.
  • Where applicable: Any network team building declarative automation. Caveat: the speaker is from the vendor itself, so expect product framing; the transferable content is the design-driven paradigm, which can be evaluated independently of the product.
path: Infrahub: Next-gen data management platform for Design-Driven Automation

items.title: MPTE update
items.text:
GRNOG 20 digest Core pick 30 June 2026

Abstract Slides

Dr Kireeti Kompella (HPE Networking)

PPTX

  • Why: Kompella is one of the principal authors of the MPLS and segment-routing protocol family, and "MPTE" refers to the emerging multi-path traffic engineering work (the successor direction to per-flow SR-TE and PRECISION-style path steering) being pursued in the IETF SPRING/RTGWG space. DC/WAN interconnect and TE internals are core to this PM. An "update" from the author himself is a first-hand read on where large-scale path steering is heading — worth the slot even with no abstract.
  • What: A progress report on the MPTE architecture — steering traffic across multiple paths with fine granularity, aimed at fixing what per-destination ECMP and heavy per-flow TE can't do well (program text and speaker metadata only; the MPTE.pptx deck exists but was not readable here).
  • How: Presumably the MPTE label/segment approach: encoding per-path/per-flow steering state compactly so a single tunnel can carry many flows with independent placement, without per-flow session state in the core.
  • Where applicable: Operators with SR-MPLS or SRv6 underlays, or building DC-to-WAN fabrics that need granular steering (elephant/mice separation, non-minimal path routing, loss-aware placement). Vendor-neutral in intent (it is IETF-track work presented by a long-time individual contributor), but expect it to reflect HPE's implementation timeline.

items.title: The Future of Network Visibility: LLM and Intelligent Monitoring
items.text:
GRNOG 20 digest Wildcard pick 30 June 2026

Abstract

Luca Deri (ntop)

Seeing that lineage pivot to LLM-driven monitoring is a strong signal of where observability tooling is heading: natural-language querying of flow data, automated anomaly explanation, and conversational triage. Not a fit for the PM's core topics, but a genuine "I wouldn't have searched for this, but…" pick.
  • What: A look at integrating LLMs into network monitoring/visibility tooling (program text only).
  • How: Unknown; presumably pairing ntop flow/packet telemetry with LLM-driven summarization, query, and root-cause suggestion.
  • Where applicable: Any operator with flow visibility (NetFlow/IPFIX). Caveat: ntop is a vendor of monitoring tooling, so the talk may double as product positioning — the signal is the direction, not the specific integration.

items.text:
GRNOG 20 digest Core pick 30 June 2026

Abstract Slides

Dimitris Zacharopoulos

PPTX

  • Why: Certificate automation and lifecycle agility sits squarely in the PM's identity/PKI interests. WebPKI is the trust root for TLS everywhere — DC, cloud, and enterprise — and the operational pain of short-lived certs, ACME, and CA/B Forum rule changes is shared across every environment.
  • What: The attached deck is titled HARICA_GRNOG_20.pptx, strongly suggesting this is a talk by the HARICA CA (the Greek academic/regional certificate authority) about the state of WebPKI, certificate automation, and the push for faster certificate issuance/rotation cycles (program text and slide metadata only).

items.title: A New Paradigm: Verifiable AI
items.text:
GTC 2026 — Networking, Security, and Identity digest Core pick San Jose · 16–19 March 2026

Abstract Recording

Ofir Arkin (NVIDIA), Jonathan Dotan (EQTY Lab), Caroline Yap (Sovereign AI) — Talk, Wednesday, March 18

Video

items.title: Accelerated Networking for AI Infrastructure
items.text:
GTC 2026 — Networking, Security, and Identity digest Core pick San Jose · 16–19 March 2026

Abstract

Nawar Nawar (NVIDIA) — Full-Day Workshop, Sunday, March 15

  • Why: This is the one hands-on session covering all three communication domains of an AI factory — and the PM's physical-DC interest means the labs (not the slides) are the value.
  • What: A full-day DLI workshop that walks through the essential communication paths in AI-factory deployments and then has attendees configure key pieces in guided labs. (from abstract only)
  • How: Level-set lecture plus bring-your-own-laptop labs: east-west GPU-to-GPU across racks over InfiniBand, north-south and storage connectivity over Spectrum-X Ethernet, and low-latency, high-bandwidth NVLink within a rack. Prerequisites are intermediate TCP/IP (L2/L3, iperf, Wireshark, CLI).
  • Where applicable: Entirely NVIDIA-stack specific (InfiniBand, Spectrum-X, NVLink). Costs a full day; worth it only if hands-on exposure to these fabrics is otherwise hard to get.

items.title: Achieve Truly Serverless GPUs With libfuse, CRIU, and CUDA-Checkpoint
items.text:
GTC 2026 — Networking, Security, and Identity digest Wildcard pick San Jose · 16–19 March 2026

Abstract

Charles Frye (Modal) — Talk, Tuesday, March 17

  • Why: Serverless inference only works if GPU containers boot fast — and the checkpoint/restore mash (CRIU + CUDA-Checkpoint + libfuse) used to get there is genuinely novel systems work the PM wouldn't naturally search for.
  • What: The techniques Modal developed to speed up GPU container boots and achieve truly serverless execution for workloads across thousands of GPUs. (from abstract only)
  • How: Process checkpoint/restore via CRIU combined with CUDA-Checkpoint for GPU state and libfuse for filesystem setup — the abstract names the tools but not the measured boot-time gains.
  • Where applicable: Modal's platform at thousands-of-GPUs scale; the techniques generalize to any system that needs fast cold-start of GPU replicas.
path: Achieve Truly Serverless GPUs With libfuse, CRIU, and CUDA-Checkpoint

items.title: Break Communication Barriers: Scale AI and HPC with NCCL, NIXL, and NVSHMEM
items.text:
GTC 2026 — Networking, Security, and Identity digest Core pick San Jose · 16–19 March 2026

Abstract

Matthew Nicely (NVIDIA) — Talk, Thursday, March 19

  • Why: The internals of the GPU communication stack — symmetric memory, copy-engine collectives, zero-SM communication, and NIXL's tier-spanning async transfers — are datapath and RDMA-adjacent content central to the PM's interests.
  • What: A year of evolution across the three libraries: NCCL added Symmetric Memory and Copy Engine collectives enabling zero-SM communication; NVSHMEM enhanced GPU-initiated operations in the Python ecosystem; NIXL emerged for inference, providing async noncontiguous transfers across memory tiers (HBM, DRAM, local/networked storage) with GDS, UCX, and S3 backends. Plus developer-level material: custom NCCL collectives, KV-cache and storage innovations in NIXL, expert-parallelism patterns, and Spectrum-X plugins for multi-site scale-across. (from abstract only)
  • How: Library-level mechanisms per above; the zero-SM collectives and NIXL's cross-tier transfers are the pieces that matter for disaggregated inference architectures.
  • Where applicable: NVIDIA GPU clusters — vendor stack, but the de facto standard for GPU collective communication; the NIXL/disaggregated-inference material applies wherever KV cache and weights move between memory tiers over a fabric.
path: Break Communication Barriers: Scale AI and HPC with NCCL, NIXL, and NVSHMEM

items.title: Build a High-Performance Research Cluster
items.text:
GTC 2026 — Networking, Security, and Identity digest Core pick San Jose · 16–19 March 2026

Abstract

Chris Turpin, Jerome Vienne (Qube Research & Technologies) — Talk, Monday, March 16

  • What: An end-to-end design walkthrough of a high-performance research cluster using B200 HGX and Spectrum-X, covering NVLink/NVSwitch topologies, intra- and inter-host multi-GPU communication, and validation with real workloads, plus "hard-won lessons": observability patterns, common misconfigurations, and troubleshooting techniques. (from abstract only)
  • How: Design decisions validated against real workloads rather than synthetic microbenchmarks; the troubleshooting content implies real incidents, though the abstract doesn't quantify them.
  • Where applicable: QRT-specific (quant research) cluster on the NVIDIA HGX + Spectrum-X stack; the design and ops lessons transfer well to similar on-prem HGX-class builds.

items.title: Build a Software-Defined Multi-Tenant NVLinked Cluster
items.text:
GTC 2026 — Networking, Security, and Identity digest Core pick San Jose · 16–19 March 2026

Abstract

Adam Tetelman (NVIDIA), Alex Saroyan (Netris), Lukas Gentele (vCluster Labs) — Talk, Thursday, March 19

  • Why: The one session in this set that stitches cloud-native tooling (Netris network automation, vCluster tenancy) onto an NVL GPU cluster — directly relevant to the PM's Kubernetes-networking and fabric-automation interests.
  • What: A reference architecture for a single enterprise-grade, software-defined, multi-tenant NVL GPU cluster, examined across infrastructure, platform, and software layers, with a concrete example integrating Run:ai, Base Command Manager, vCluster, and Netris to handle production requirements: stricter security, operational rigor, and a broad user base. (from abstract only)

  • Where applicable: Tied to specific vendor products (Run:ai, BCM, vCluster, Netris) on NVIDIA NVL hardware; the multi-tenant-GPU-cluster pattern itself is broadly applicable to R&D clusters going to production.

items.title: Build Secure AI Infrastructure With DOCA
items.text:
GTC 2026 — Networking, Security, and Identity digest Core pick San Jose · 16–19 March 2026

Abstract

Ofir Arkin, Ariel Kit (NVIDIA) — Talk, Tuesday, March 17

  • Why: Line-rate network security enforced from the DPU without host agents or touching protected workloads is the strongest network-security offering in this program — and it extends toward prompt-level defenses and agentic-workflow security, both new territory.
  • What: The DOCA security stack (microservices, frameworks, APIs) running on BlueField: granular network security policy at line rate, real-time detection and blocking of threats to AI workloads, prompt-level defenses, and security for agentic workflows — framed as protecting AI without consuming compute or hurting token economics. (from abstract only)
  • How: BlueField enforces policy in the datapath at line rate, independent of host software; the prompt-level and agentic components are the newest claims and the least mechanistically described in the abstract.
  • Where applicable: Requires NVIDIA BlueField DPUs; NVIDIA-centric stack. The line-rate policy piece is proven ground; treat the prompt-level and agentic-security claims as early and demand the mechanism.
path: Build Secure AI Infrastructure With DOCA

items.title: Building Sovereign AI: Scaling 100B+ Model Training on NVIDIA Blackwell Infrastructure (Presented by Lablup, Inc.)
items.text:
GTC 2026 — Networking, Security, and Identity digest Core pick San Jose · 16–19 March 2026

Abstract Recording

Jeongkyu Shin (Lablup, Inc.) — Theater Talk, Wednesday, March 18

Video

  • Why: The most concretely operational talk in the pre-selection: named failure modes (NCCL timeouts, 10x storage degradation from an NFS driver bug, MXFP8 precision instability on Blackwell) and network tuning (RoCE and InfiniBand) on a 500+ B200 national-scale cluster.
  • What: Hands-on experience training 100B+ parameter models from scratch on more than 500 B200 GPUs in a sovereign AI initiative: fault-tolerant orchestration, storage I/O optimization, NCCL tuning, automated failure recovery, resolution of a 10x storage slowdown traced to NFS driver issues, MXFP8 stability work, and RoCE/InfiniBand network tuning done through cross-vendor collaboration. (from abstract only)
  • How: A resilient stack with automated failure recovery, exploiting LLM training's parallelism characteristics for large-capacity fault tolerance and data-driven fault demarcation and localization.
  • Where applicable: Lablup's deployment in a Korean national sovereign-AI initiative; NVIDIA Blackwell with both RoCE and InfiniBand fabrics present. The failure-and-fix detail is what makes it valuable; scale (hundreds, not tens of thousands, of GPUs) makes it relatable to enterprise builds.

items.title: Enable Enterprise AI Factories With Secure, High-Performance Networking
items.text:
GTC 2026 — Networking, Security, and Identity digest Core pick San Jose · 16–19 March 2026

Abstract

Yael Shenhav (NVIDIA), Chris Wright (Red Hat) — Talk, Monday, March 16

  • Why: DPU-based isolation — separating infrastructure services from user workloads to shrink attack surface — is squarely the PM's network-security interest, and Red Hat's CTO co-presenting signals real enterprise pull.
  • What: How Red Hat OpenShift, NVIDIA BlueField DPUs, and high-performance Ethernet fabrics combine into enterprise AI infrastructure, with DPU-based isolation enforcing policy boundaries between infrastructure and tenant workloads. (from abstract only)

  • Where applicable: Requires the OpenShift + BlueField + NVIDIA Ethernet stack; enterprise (not hyperscale) focus. Product-pitch elements are real, but the DPU-isolation pattern is broadly relevant to multi-tenant AI platforms.
path: Enable Enterprise AI Factories With Secure, High-Performance Networking

items.title: Enhance Data Center Efficiency and Throughput by Co-Scheduling on NVIDIA CPU+GPU Systems
items.text:
GTC 2026 — Networking, Security, and Identity digest Core pick San Jose · 16–19 March 2026

Abstract

Brian Austin (NERSC), Mathias Wagner (NVIDIA) — Talk, Thursday, March 19

  • Why: Utilization economics for coherent CPU-GPU systems, with concrete isolation mechanisms the PM can use directly — cgroups, ARM MPAM cache/memory-bandwidth partitioning, and InfiniBand QoS for network traffic separation.
  • What: Co-scheduling CPU-only, partially accelerated, and fully GPU-accelerated jobs on the same coherent CPU-GPU nodes to boost throughput and energy efficiency, removing the need for dedicated per-workload clusters, with workload studies for NERSC's upcoming Doudna system and projected utilization/efficiency gains. (from abstract only)
  • How: Isolation via CPU affinity (cgroups), cache and memory-bandwidth partitioning through ARM's MPAM extensions, and InfiniBand QoS for network separation; plus methodology for identifying co-scheduling candidates and designing scheduling policies users will accept.
  • Where applicable: NERSC HPC context (Doudna, Grace-based coherent nodes), but cgroups/MPAM/IB-QoS are general techniques for any shared GPU fabric; the policy/ incentive discussion is broadly applicable to mixed-workload clusters.
path: Enhance Data Center Efficiency and Throughput by Co-Scheduling on NVIDIA CPU+GPU Systems

items.title: From Kernels to Clusters: How PyTorch Powers High-Performance AI (Presented by Meta)

items.title: How AI Factories Can Shift-left to Accelerate Infrastructure and Ecosystems Readiness

Amit Katz (NVIDIA), Harshdeep Banwait (CoreWeave) — Talk, Wednesday, March 18

items.title: Quantum and HPC at Riken: The Sum is Greater than Its Parts

Satoshi Matsuoka, Mitsuhisa Sato (Riken) — Talk, Tuesday, March 17

items.title: Safety in the OpenClaw Era
items.text:
GTC 2026 — Networking, Security, and Identity digest Core pick San Jose · 16–19 March 2026

Abstract

Elia Zaitsev (CrowdStrike), Ali Golshan (NVIDIA), Amit Zavery (ServiceNow), Francis deSouza (Google Cloud) — Panel, Monday, March 16

  • Why: Autonomous agents that hold credentials, persist context, spawn subagents, and run continuously against production systems are a different threat model — and agentic identity is one of the PM's core interests. This panel names the gap explicitly.
  • What: A panel asking what a real security model for autonomous agents looks like, on the premise that agents are ready but the governance and trust infrastructure to run them at scale does not yet exist. (from abstract only)

items.title: Solve the Day 1 Challenge of Landing LLM Inference in Enterprise

items.title: Supercharging AI With Multi-Gigawatt AI Factories
items.text:

Gilad Shainer, Peter Salanki (CoreWeave), Omar Baldonado (Meta), Yuya Kawakami (SoftBank), Alexis Bjorlin (NVIDIA), Evan Burness (Microsoft) — Panel, Wednesday, March 18

  • Why: The strongest lineup in the program for operator war stories — Meta, Microsoft, CoreWeave, and SoftBank builders in one room on network scaling lessons at hyperscale.
