  • What: Defines a Workload Identifier as a URI that uniquely identifies a workload inside a specific trust domain, intended for embedding in credentials to drive authn, authz, and policy. (from abstract only)
  • How: Standardizes the identifier format so the same identity semantics hold across certificates, tokens, and policy engines from different vendors.
  • Where applicable: General; foundational for any federation or policy enforcement that spans trust domains.

items.title: Workload Identity in a Multi System Environment (WIMSE) Architecture — draft-ietf-wimse-arch
items.text:
IETF 123 (Madrid) digest Core pick Madrid · 19–25 July 2025

Slides Session recording Materials

  • Tier: Core
  • Why: This is the architectural anchor for standardizing how workloads get and use identity across multi-cloud, multi-tenant, multi-service deployments — the exact problem SPIFFE/SPIRE solved proprietarily. An IETF-stream architecture means the surrounding protocol drafts (below) have a shared frame, and implementations stop being per-vendor.
  • What: An architecture document defining how to convey workload identity and security-context information, where a workload is software running for a specific purpose, possibly across many instances. (from abstract only)
  • How: It scopes the problem and defines the component model that the credential, token, and authentication drafts plug into, rather than specifying wire formats itself.
  • Where applicable: Broadly applicable to any container-orchestration or microservice estate; vendor-neutral by design. This is the document to read first before the rest of the WIMSE set.
path: Workload Identity in a Multi System Environment (WIMSE) Architecture — draft-ietf-wimse-arch

items.title: A Border Gateway Protocol 4 (BGP-4)
items.text:
IETF 124 (Montreal) — Standards digest Core pick Montreal · 1–7 November 2025

Draft Materials

Yakov Rekhter (independent), Tony Li (HPE), Susan Hares (Huawei), John Scudder, Ed. (HPE) — IDR WG document

  • Why: The once-in-a-generation rewrite of the BGP base specification — the document every BGP implementation will eventually be coded and tested against.
  • What: draft-ietf-idr-bgp4-rfc4271bis-03 obsoletes RFC 4271 along with RFC 6286, 6608, 8212, and 9687, and subsumes the core of RFC 7606 (treat-as-withdraw error handling) into the base. Consolidation, not new machinery: restructured per-message and per-attribute error handling, the send-hold timer, typed NLRI parsing rules, an explicit route-resolvability condition in the decision process, and a roadmap distinguishing the "core extensions" (RFC 4760 multiprotocol, RFC 8654 extended messages) from the wider extension ecosystem.
  • How: Full re-edit of RFC 4271 with a version-by-version change appendix and GitHub issue tracking; IDR milestone targets submission to the IESG as an Internet Standard by May 2027.
  • Where applicable: All BGP implementations globally. Mature WG document in active revision; read it as the consolidation of two decades of errata and error-handling practice into one standard.

items.title: BGP best path next-hop selection enhancements
items.text:
IETF 124 (Montreal) — Standards digest Core pick Montreal · 1–7 November 2025

Draft Slides Session recording Materials

Olivier Vroonen, Stéphane Litkowski (Cisco)

  • Why: BGP's resolvability and cost rules assume the NEXT_HOP is the actual forwarding endpoint. GRE/MPLS/SR-MPLS/SRv6 tunnels break that assumption, producing real blackholes and wrong picks — shown with concrete examples of a VRF route dropped because no transport tunnel exists to the best path's next hop, and a delay-optimized (colored) path chosen by lowest IGP metric.
  • What: Standardizes behavior vendors already implement: introduces the concept of a "forwarding address" (e.g., the tunnel endpoint) with a "forwarding context" (tunnel type and characteristics, resolution constraints such as which table to look up in); requires resolvability checks against the forwarding address, not just NEXT_HOP; makes costs from different contexts comparable via a preference notion (like RIB preference); and requires BGP to re-evaluate best paths whenever underlying reachability or cost changes (tracking).
  • How: Builds on the partial fixes already in RFC 9012 (tunnel encapsulation) and RFC 9252 (SRv6) but addresses both resolvability and path suboptimality generically, not just for one encapsulation.
  • Where applicable: Any tunnel-based BGP deployment, including SRv6 DC underlays — broadly applicable. Early individual draft (-00); value is mostly standardization of existing vendor behavior for interoperability.
path: BGP best path next-hop selection enhancements

items.title: BGP Flow Specification Extension for Feedback Binding
items.text:
IETF 124 (Montreal) — Standards digest Adjacent pick Montreal · 1–7 November 2025

Draft Slides Session recording Materials

Yong Cui (Tsinghua University), Yujia Gao, Lei Zhang (Zhongguancun Laboratory) — individual draft

  • Why: FlowSpec is one-way control today: "rule delivered ≠ rule effective." DDoS scrubbing rules fail silently on local ACL conflicts, unresolved redirect next-hops, inactive rules, or vendor gaps — and the operator has no standard way to see which nodes actually enforced the mitigation. This touches the network-security interest directly, as closed-loop visibility for a security mechanism.
  • What: A FlowSpec extension carrying a Feedback Action as a Generic Transitive Extended Community: a Feedback Identifier (FID), a window exponent (WINC) defining the periodic reporting interval as 2^n seconds, an event flag, and a scope selector (global / inter-AS / intra-AS) — propagated across AS boundaries unchanged.
  • How: Routers report rule lifecycle state (Received → Install → Active → Effective, or Inactive/Removed/Error) and data-plane hit statistics keyed by the FID, exported via a companion mechanism (BMP or a telemetry framework). The DDoS use case: a controller pushes scrubbing redirects and detects in real time which nodes failed to activate them. Signaling only in this draft; export is future work.
  • Where applicable: FlowSpec-based DDoS mitigation and traffic steering across enterprise–carrier boundaries. Early academic individual draft (-00) explicitly seeking requirements confirmation and interest; the concept (closed-loop control for FlowSpec) is more mature than the draft.
path: BGP Flow Specification Extension for Feedback Binding

items.title: BGP Next Hop Dependent Characteristics Attribute
items.text:
IETF 124 (Montreal) — Standards digest Core pick Montreal · 1–7 November 2025

Draft Slides Session recording Materials

John Scudder (Juniper) presenting the split of draft-ietf-idr-entropy-label

  • Why: NHC is the base container for per-next-hop forwarding-plane signaling in BGP — three other WG drafts (next-next-hop-nodes, iFIT capabilities, generic metric) now define their own NHC characteristics on top of it. The session resolves a two-year stall that was blocking them.
  • What: The NHC attribute — a transitive BGP attribute, extensible via TLVs, that conveys characteristics of the routes advertised in the UPDATE that carries it (unlike RFC 5492 capabilities). News at IETF 124: the parked draft-ietf-idr-entropy-label (WGLC'd November 2023, stuck "waiting for implementation") was split into draft-ietf-idr-nhc (the attribute plus a BGP Identifier characteristic) and draft-ietf-idr-elc (the Entropy Label Characteristic) — "nothing added or taken away."
  • How: Two implementations of NHC exist; the split (chairs' consensus call, no objections) separates the twice-implemented base from ELC, which still awaits a second implementation, and unblocks the registry the dependent drafts need. Next steps: update the implementation report, reconfirm WGLC, publish.
  • Where applicable: Any BGP deployment signaling datapath capabilities of next hops (entropy labels, GLB tuples, iFIT, metrics). Mature WG item now moving to publication; the plumbing beneath the NNHN/GLB work above.
path: BGP Next Hop Dependent Characteristics Attribute

items.title: BGP Next-next Hop Nodes
items.text:
IETF 124 (Montreal) — Standards digest Core pick Montreal · 1–7 November 2025

Draft Slides Session recording Materials

Kevin Wang, Jeff Haas, Changwang Lin, Jeff Tantsura (Juniper)

  • Why: AI/ML Clos fabrics carry high-throughput, low-entropy flows that random ECMP hashing cannot keep drop-free; local remedies (dynamic load balancing) can't see remote-link congestion. This draft is the BGP standardization of the topology discovery that Global Load Balancing (GLB) needs.
  • What: The NNHN characteristic for the NHC attribute, letting a leaf learn <next-hop, next-next-hop> tuples per route. Presented with GLB test results: on a 3-stage Clos with 100G links, a 90G flow that drops without GLB runs drop-free with it.
  • How: The key insight is that Clos symmetry means only next-hop and next-next-hop link congestion matters — congestion beyond that is absorbed by symmetric GLB at higher tiers — so a non-link-state protocol like BGP suffices for GLB topology discovery. BGP carries next-next-hop BGP IDs in a new NHC TLV; each spine broadcasts link quality to direct neighbors (sub-millisecond, via the companion UDP router-info protocol draft-zzhang-rtgwg-router-info's Neighbor Path Information TLV), and each leaf combines the two-hop link qualities to steer load. Works for 3-stage, 5-stage, and general Clos.
  • Where applicable: IP/IPv6-routed BGP Clos fabrics — i.e., modern AI back-end networks. WG draft (draft-ietf-idr-next-next-hop-nodes-00) at first presentation: early on the WG track, but with working multi-party test evidence. The single most directly relevant AI-fabric item in the program.

items.title: BMP v4: Extended TLV Support for BGP Monitoring Protocol (BMP)
items.text:
IETF 124 (Montreal) — Standards digest Adjacent pick Montreal · 1–7 November 2025

Draft Slides Session recording Materials

Paolo Lucente (NTT Data), Yunan Gu (Huawei) — GROW WG document

  • Why: BMP is how BGP is observed; Route Monitoring, Stats Reports, and Peer Down messages lack TLV extensibility, which blocks richer per-message telemetry — and the FlowSpec-feedback work below explicitly wants to export over BMP.
  • What: Updates RFC 7854 to support optional TLVs on all BMP message types, bumps the protocol version for backward compatibility, defines essential TLVs, and adds an Enterprise (E) bit allowing per-vendor type values.
  • How: WG-document mid-flight: post-E-bit-merge wording fixes pending, Stats messages need a container TLV to hold other optional TLVs, and an open question on merging draft-younsi-grow-bmp-snts.
  • Where applicable: BGP monitoring collectors and vendor telemetry stacks; broadly applicable operational plumbing rather than a research item.
path: BMP v4: Extended TLV Support for BGP Monitoring Protocol (BMP)

items.title: Credit-based Flow Control Based on RSVP for RDMA transmission in WAN
items.text:
IETF 124 (Montreal) — Standards digest Core pick Montreal · 1–7 November 2025

Draft Session recording Materials

Jiayuan Hu, Zehua Hu, Tanxin Pi, Yongqing Zhu (China Telecom)

  • Why: The other half of lossless WAN RDMA: instead of notify-and-reroute, backpressure — credit-based flow control (the InfiniBand model) extended across the WAN for cross-AIDC training with elephant flows and extreme concurrency.
  • What: A credit-based flow control mechanism for RDMA traffic in SRv6 tunnels over the WAN, carried by an extended RSVP, aiming to provide high-throughput, zero-packet-loss transmission guarantees (from abstract only).
  • How: Introduces credit grants into RSVP signaling so that senders transmit only against granted credits, giving precise per-flow traffic control across SRv6 tunnels rather than drop-based or ECN-based response.
  • Where applicable: Cross-data-center AI training over SRv6 WAN — a China Telecom carrier scenario. Very early: an individual draft whose current revision (-01, September 2025) has actually expired on Datatracker without a replacement, so momentum is uncertain; treat as a design signal, not a trajectory, and watch whether it is revived or folded into the broader FANTEL work.
path: Credit-based Flow Control Based on RSVP for RDMA transmission in WAN

items.title: Enhanced Encapsulating Security Payload (EESP)
items.text:
IETF 124 (Montreal) — Standards digest Core pick Montreal · 1–7 November 2025

Draft Slides Session recording Materials

Steffen Klassert, Antony Antony (secunet), Christian Hopps (LabN Consulting) — IPSECME WG document

  • Why: ESP has no version field and cannot evolve transparently; everything must be IKEv2-negotiated and is invisible to intermediaries. Meanwhile high-speed deployments need an inner-flow identifier for ECMP, CPU pinning, and QoS, and selective exposure of inner headers for middleboxes. This is the network-security wire-format change of the meeting.
  • What: EESP is a modernized ESP on a new IP protocol number: a Base Header (version, options length, 16-bit Session ID, SPI) that middleboxes can parse; a Peer Header (full 64-bit sequence number, IV) private to the peers; the ESP trailer eliminated (Next Header/Pad Length moved into a Payload Info Header); IPv6-style TLV options for future extension; and a Crypt Offset option to expose leading bytes of the inner packet for middlebox/telemetry use — covering the PSP (VNI/crypt-offset) use case, anti-replay subspaces, and shared-SA proposals in one mechanism.
  • How: The Session ID doubles as a Sub SA ID selecting independent 64-bit anti-replay sequence-number spaces (per core, path, or QoS class), each with keys derived via KDF, creatable "on the fly" in the data plane — including hardware offload deriving per-packet sub-SA keys. Combined-mode (AEAD) algorithms only; replay-disable is negotiated (useful in DCs where upper layers handle replay); an optimized packet format elides the Payload Info Header in IPv4/IPv6 tunnel mode. Negotiable via IKEv2 but portable to other keying protocols; Linux XFRM implementation status is tracked in the draft.
  • Where applicable: High-throughput IPsec — datacenter interconnects and large VPN fabrics where per-flow ECMP/QoS under encryption matters. WG document at -04, active; watch for the protocol-number allocation and PSP alignment.

items.title: EVPN Multi-Active Multihoming
items.text:
IETF 124 (Montreal) — Standards digest Core pick Montreal · 1–7 November 2025

Draft Slides Session recording Materials

Jeffrey Zhang, Changwang Lin, Jorge Rabadan (individual draft, BESS)

  • Why: EVPN offers All-Active or Single-Active multihoming today; operators want a hybrid — a subset of PEs active and load-balanced, the rest standing by for fast failover, without full active-active fanout.
  • What: Multi-Active mode for a multihomed Ethernet Segment: PEs with higher configured preference operate All-Active (ingress PEs load-balance to them); non-preferred PEs stay Single-Active/inactive and take over on failure of the preferred set.
  • How: Preference is signaled in the DF Election Extended Community (in ES routes); preferred PEs signal P=1/B=0 in the L2-Attribute Extended Community (in Ethernet A-D per-EVI routes) so ingress PEs load-balance to them, while non-preferred PEs signal P=0 and are excluded from DF candidacy via the AC-Influenced DF Election Capability. All PEs (including non-preferred) keep signaling All-Active in the ESI label Extended Community for backward compatibility. Strict-mode (only equal-top-preference PEs active) and loose-mode (M preferred PEs, possibly different values) variants are defined. Only the MHES's own PEs need to understand the mode; other PEs act on the P/B bits as usual.
  • Where applicable: EVPN multihoming deployments in DC access and DCI. Early individual draft (-00) seeking comments; authors believe there is no backward-compatibility issue and are asking the WG to scrutinize that claim.

items.title: Fast Network Notifications Problem Statement
items.text:
IETF 124 (Montreal) — Standards digest Core pick Montreal · 1–7 November 2025

Draft Slides Session recording Materials

Jie Dong (Huawei), Mike McBride (Futurewei), François Clad (Cisco), Zhaohui (Jeffrey) Zhang (Juniper), with contributors from China Telecom, China Mobile, China Unicom, Tencent, Telefónica, and Turkcell

  • Why: AI training/inference and large-scale cloud services need the network to adapt faster than today's feedback loops allow. This is the anchor problem statement for the whole FANTEL (Fast Notifications for TE and Load Balancing) cluster in RTGWG, carried forward from the IETF 123 BoF with unusual breadth of operator/vendor co-authorship.
  • What: A structured problem statement defining what fast network notifications must carry, who must receive them, and how they get delivered — the requirements frame every other fast-notification draft at this meeting builds against.
  • How: Tabulates four gaps in current mechanisms: (1) hop-by-hop control-plane distribution and round-trip end-to-end signaling (ECN) are too slow; (2) binary/threshold feedback is too coarse for precise adjustment; (3) decisions are made from a local view, yielding sub-optimal rerouting; (4) naive wide distribution churns the control plane. Proposes an information model (event type, location, fine-grained metrics such as utilization, queue length, delay, jitter, loss, plus path and flow 5-tuple identification), a recipient model (adjacent/non-adjacent routers, ingress nodes, end hosts, controllers/PCE/NMS), and delivery modes (unicast, multicast, hop-by-hop, scoped flooding) with subscription to suppress overhead.
  • Where applicable: General IP fabrics — use cases span intra-DC AI/ML, cross-DC training and inference, CDN/DC interconnect, and cloud-edge. Early-stage at the meeting (individual draft -01), but companion drafts now cite it on the WG track as draft-ietf-rtgwg-net-notif-ps, so adoption momentum is real.

items.title: Fast Notification for tunnel-based lossless RDMA transmission in WAN
items.text:
IETF 124 (Montreal) — Standards digest Core pick Montreal · 1–7 November 2025

Draft Session recording Materials

Zehua Hu, Yongqing Zhu, Jiayuan Hu, Tanxin Pi (China Telecom)

  • Why: Cross-AIDC LLM training and inference push RDMA through SRv6/GRE/VXLAN/MPLS tunnels over the WAN; a small number of losses collapses effective throughput, and neither ECN (end-to-end, long RTTs) nor PFC (link-local, DC-only) works there.
  • What: A concrete Fast Network Notification (FANN) protocol: transit (P) nodes detecting failure, congestion, or state change send structured notifications to the ingress PE, which reroutes to backup paths, rebalances across available paths, and/or throttles the affected traffic and notifies the sender and controller.
  • How: Defines a new ICMPv6 message — Code distinguishes event vs. recovery, a Hop Limit bounds propagation scope, Event Type covers link failure, congestion, performance degradation, microburst, signal degradation, and queue buildup (with sub-types, e.g., congestion severity tiers), a microsecond timestamp, the originating node's IPv6 address, and a 32-bit bitmap selecting fixed-length metadata fields (ingress/egress port IDs, link utilization, loss, latency, jitter, queue and buffer occupancy, flow 5-tuple, and a path ID carried as an SRv6 SID list or MPLS label stack). An identical structure can ride over UDP on a well-known port where ICMPv6 is filtered. Security: RFC 4443 rate limiting, length validation, and origination only from control-plane interfaces.
  • Where applicable: Carrier inter-DC WANs carrying tunnelled RDMA (China Telecom is the driving operator — this is operator-specific in origin, general in technique). Individual draft at -03; the protocol encoding is draft-stage and the FANN umbrella has competing notification proposals (ARN etc.) it must converge with.
path: Fast Notification for tunnel-based lossless RDMA transmission in WAN

items.title: JSON Web Proof
items.text:
IETF 124 (Montreal) — Standards digest Core pick Montreal · 1–7 November 2025

Draft Slides Session recording Materials

Mike Jones, David Waite — JOSE WG document

  • Why: The JOSE-side container for credentials using newer selective-disclosure and unlinkability algorithms (BBS-style) — the path beyond JWS/SD-JWT for zero-knowledge-ish verifiable credentials.
  • What: JWP: a JWS-like container that integrity-protects multiple payloads in one message, with a presentation form supporting selective disclosure of individual payloads, additional proof computation, and a Presentation Header to prevent replay. JPT (JSON Proof Token) constrains payloads to claims, targeting SD-JWT's problem domains with newer algorithms.
  • How: At IETF 124 the work added a "subclaim" syntax — based on CBOR Pointer (no negative array indexing, no indexing into serialized CBOR), chosen over JSON Path, SD-JWT VC metadata paths, and OID4VP's DCQL for remote-safety, simplicity, and CBOR-readiness — so a presentation can disclose just ["address","country"] or an is_over_18 predicate instead of a whole claim. Motivated by common feedback from two independent digital-credential prototypes. Other open items: aligning JWP's algorithm/header registries with JWK/CWK (which don't know about them — possibly by reusing the JWS/COSE algorithm registries), BLS key representation (compressed/ZCash style per IANA early review), and JSON/CBOR example parity that has already uncovered spec bugs.
  • Where applicable: Verifiable credentials and digital wallets. WG document in active revision; the subclaim decision is the one to track.

items.title: Kademlia-directed ID-based Routing Architecture (KIRA)
items.text:
IETF 124 (Montreal) — Standards digest Wildcard pick Montreal · 1–7 November 2025

Draft Session recording Materials

Roland Bless (Karlsruhe Institute of Technology) — individual draft, intended Experimental

  • Why: A genuinely different routing architecture rather than an increment: zero-touch, ID-based control-plane routing that scales to hundreds of thousands of nodes with no hierarchy and no manual configuration. Not deployable tomorrow, but the clearest signal in the program of where autonomic-networking research is heading — and a notable data point in the "control planes shouldn't depend on the data plane they're configuring" argument.
  • What: A two-tier architecture. The Routing Tier runs R²/Kad — a recursive Kademlia over self-assigned, topologically independent 112-bit NodeIDs with the XOR metric: k-bucket routing tables that grow O(log n), source routing between overlay hops, Proximity Neighbor Selection preferring short paths, overhearing of transit messages, periodic path probing, and loop-free operation even during convergence. The Forwarding Tier uses PathIDs (hashes of path-segment NodeID sequences) as label-like forwarding state, encapsulated over SRv6, IPv6-in-IPv6, or GRE — reusing existing IPv6 forwarding hardware. Add-ons include a built-in DHT for name resolution and the KeLLy topology discovery service; a domain concept provides administrative grouping; an end-system mode supports non-routing participants.
  • How: The explicit trade is path stretch for tiny routing tables and extreme resilience — the design goal is to never lose control-plane connectivity to a reachable device, accepting stretched paths as the price. Failure recovery is error-triggered rediscovery with NotViaList exclusion of failed links, not flooding.
  • Where applicable: Control-plane and management networks, autonomic networking, disaster-resilient infrastructure — explicitly not a data-plane replacement. Long-running individual draft (-06) with academic grounding; read it as architecture research with a reference protocol spec, not a deployment candidate.

items.title: More Accurate Explicit Congestion Notification (AccECN) Feedback in TCP
items.text:
IETF 124 (Montreal) — Standards digest Core pick Montreal · 1–7 November 2025

Draft Session recording Materials

Bob Briscoe (Independent), Mirja Kühlewind (Ericsson), Richard Scheffenegger (NetApp) — TCPM

  • Why: RFC 3168 ECN feedback allows one congestion signal per RTT; DCTCP, L4S, and ConEx need per-marking counts. This changes the TCP wire protocol itself — and it is now finished: published as RFC 9768 (Proposed Standard, April 2026).
  • What: AccECN replaces Classic ECN feedback: the receiver continually feeds back a count of CE-marked packets using the three TCP header flags (the former NS bit renamed AE, plus overloaded CWR/ECE) as a 3-bit ACE counter, negotiated in the three-way handshake with careful backward compatibility. An optional AccECN TCP Option (two alternative field orders, never on the SYN) supplements this with 24-bit byte counters per ECN codepoint.
  • How: Two-part design — the essential header counter works even where middleboxes strip options; the option adds byte-accuracy and ACK-loss resilience. The receiver acts as a "generic (mechanistic) reflector" so future sender behaviors deploy unilaterally. It also feeds back the IP-ECN value received on the SYN/SYN/ACK, letting endpoints detect middleboxes that mangle the ECN/ToS field instead of blindly disabling ECN. Normative compliance requirements cover TCP proxies, normalizers, ACK filters, and offload engines.
  • Where applicable: All TCP — public Internet and private networks including data centers; explicitly the enabler for DCTCP-style and L4S congestion control. Broadly applicable; as an RFC this is now implementation/deployment news rather than work-in-progress.
path: More Accurate Explicit Congestion Notification (AccECN) Feedback in TCP

items.title: OAuth 2.0 Delegated Authorization
items.text:
IETF 124 (Montreal) — Standards digest Core pick Montreal · 1–7 November 2025

Draft Slides Session recording Materials

Ruochen Li, Haiguang Wang, Chunchi Peter Liu, Tieyan Li (Huawei) — individual draft

  • Why: Down-scoping in OAuth today requires token exchange (RFC 8693) round-trips through the authorization server; this draft proposes client-local delegation with key-bound token chains — relevant to service chains and to how agentic clients might delegate constrained authority without AS involvement at each step.
  • What: Delegation Tokens (DTs) issued by the AS and bound to the client's key; the client locally issues Delegated Access Tokens (DATs) bound to a delegate's key. Only DATs are accepted at resource servers — DTs are never used as access tokens. The RS validates the ordered token chain, the restrictions imposed at each delegation step, and a DPoP proof signed by the key bound to the leaf token.
  • How: A digitally signature-linked chain analogous to PKI certificates; the explicit contrast with RFC 8693: no external STS involved, subordinate tokens tightly linked to their superior, delegation can occur at any node along the invocation chain including third-party intermediaries. Supports Rich Authorization Request details, encrypted (JWE) DTs, and sign-then-encrypt DATs; future work covers multi-layer delegation and multiple DTs per request.
  • Where applicable: Service-to-service and delegation chains. Early individual draft from Huawei, seeking feedback. Note: the slides the agenda links to this slot actually cover a different draft (Nick Watson/Google's refresh-token and authorization-expiration parameters, also seeking adoption); the Delegated Authorization deck was presented under the OAuth 2.1 slot — the write-up above uses that deck.

items.title: OAuth SPIFFE Client Authentication
items.text:
IETF 124 (Montreal) — Standards digest Core pick Montreal · 1–7 November 2025

Draft Slides Session recording Materials

Stian Thorgersen, Scott Rose, Pieter Kasselman, Arndt Schwenkschuster (individual draft, OAuth WG venue discussion)

  • Why: Sits exactly at the intersection of workload identity and OAuth: workloads acting as OAuth clients today authenticate with manually provisioned, long-lived client secrets; this profiles OAuth client auth to consume SPIFFE SVIDs instead.
  • What: Profiles RFC 7521/7523 so OAuth clients authenticate to authorization servers using JWT-SVIDs or X.509-SVIDs — no client secrets — with trust established via SPIFFE Bundle Endpoints (JWKS) for key distribution, and discussion of RFC 8705 (mTLS) handling for X509-SVIDs.
  • How: The draft explains precisely why vanilla RFC 7523 doesn't fit: its requirement that the assertion subject equal the client_id, and SPIFFE's subject-as-authority key-discovery model (spiffe:// URIs vs. https:// metadata). Evidence of real momentum: Keycloak 26.4 shipped a preview implementation, multiple community authenticators exist, and SPIFFE is already in production at Uber, Netflix, ByteDance, Google, and others. Open questions for the WG: venue, SPIFFE-ID vs. client-ID semantics, and registration/trust-establishment requirements.
  • Where applicable: Any environment where SPIFFE/SPIRE infrastructure and OAuth coexist — which is most enterprise service meshes. Early individual draft, but with shipping implementation evidence rather than slideware.

items.title: Proposal for Updates to Guidance on Packet Reordering
items.text:
IETF 124 (Montreal) — Standards digest Adjacent pick Montreal · 1–7 November 2025

Draft Session recording Materials

Greg White (CableLabs), Ingemar Johansson (Ericsson), Dibakar Das (Intel), Chris Box

  • Why: Several link-technology standards mandate in-order L2 delivery and implement resequencing buffers that add delay — exactly the machinery that defeats packet-spraying multipath in modern fabrics. Modern TCP and QUIC tolerate reordering far better than the L2 standards bodies assume.
  • What: Informational guidance for layer-2 standards organizations: IETF transport protocols do not require guaranteed in-order delivery, so the resequencing requirement can be relaxed where it causes net performance degradation (from abstract only).
  • How: Cites the modern TCP/QUIC features that improve out-of-order tolerance as the basis for updating the guidance L2 standards cite.
  • Where applicable: Link-technology standards (link aggregation, L2 transport) — general technique, not org-specific. Maturity signal worth noting: since the meeting, the individual draft was adopted by INTAREA and replaced by WG document draft-ietf-intarea-reordering, so consensus is forming.
path: Proposal for Updates to Guidance on Packet Reordering

items.title: Scheduling Network Resources for Machine Learning Clusters
items.text:
IETF 124 (Montreal) — Standards digest Core pick Montreal · 1–7 November 2025

Draft Slides Session recording Materials

Kompella (individual draft, rtgwg)

  • Why: Everything else at this meeting reacts to congestion; this draft argues the AI network should be scheduled like compute — a provocative reframe from "detect and signal" to "reserve in advance," with real implications for how TE and schedulers integrate.
  • What: A framework proposing that network resources (bandwidth, buffers, queues) be estimated, allocated, and deployed alongside compute for training/inference jobs, with contingency paths — citing SLURM and NVIDIA's KAI Scheduler as the compute-side model and the FANTEL/@Scale/OCP discussions as context.
  • How: Scheduling happens at compute-placement time (job size/type imply communication needs) and again when a communication phase starts (CCL API invocations reveal exact endpoints and mode — broadcast, scatter, gather, all-reduce). Uses multipath TE (MPTE) with resource reservation for unicast CCL primitives and multicast TE (MCTE, companion draft-kompella-teas-mcte) for multicast primitives. A key argument: reservation state means transit nodes know the sources, so congestion/event signaling can be sent to the right places (ingresses), and reserved alternates give fast recovery — proactive and reactive mechanisms compose.
  • Where applicable: Intra-DC backend networks (multipathing mandatory, unicast + multicast required), inter-DC DCI for distributed training, and metro/WAN edge inference. Early position/framework draft; broadly applicable to anyone running scheduled AI workloads, hypercaler and carrier alike.
path: Scheduling Network Resources for Machine Learning Clusters

items.title: SCONE TCP Option
items.text:
IETF 124 (Montreal) — Standards digest Wildcard pick Montreal · 1–7 November 2025

Draft Slides Session recording Materials

Wesley Eddy, Matt Joras (Meta) — individual draft in TCPM

  • Why: A different direction of network→endpoint signaling than FANTEL: instead of telling the ingress to reroute, middleboxes tell endpoints their rate limits. Interesting precisely because it parallels the AI-fabric notification philosophy (network signals, endpoints adapt) in an entirely different problem space — and shows the SCONE WG's charter spilling beyond QUIC.
  • What: A TCP option that network elements can insert or modify to give endpoints throughput guidance — motivated by rate-limiting of ABR video in mobile networks, where knowing the limit lets the player pick a compliant rendition instead of oscillating through losses.
  • How: Explicitly modeled on MSS clamping — an on-path element rewrites an option the downstream stack can act on; the same network elements being built for QUIC SCONE (a new QUIC packet type carrying rate-limit encodings middleboxes can read and set) would handle the TCP option. Many details open: application interfaces, interaction with other TCP options, send timing, insertion rules.
  • Where applicable: Rate-limited access networks (mobile) with adaptive video; the rate-signaling mechanism itself is general. Very early individual draft (-00) gauging whether TCPM wants this at all — a "watch the question, not the draft" item.

items.title: SD-JWT-based Verifiable Digital Credentials (SD-JWT VC)
items.text:
IETF 124 (Montreal) — Standards digest Core pick Montreal · 1–7 November 2025

Draft Slides Session recording Materials

Oliver Terbu (MATTR), Daniel Fett (Authlete), Brian Campbell (Ping Identity) — OAuth WG document

  • Why: The leading JSON format for selectively disclosable verifiable credentials (the format behind most government/wallet pilots); this session shows it converging to working-group last call.
  • What: Data formats plus validation and processing rules for verifiable credentials with JSON payloads, with and without selective disclosure, built on SD-JWT and the JWT extensibility model; defines issuer signature mechanisms (web-based metadata via .well-known/JWKs, inline x5c) and Type Metadata (claim schemas, rendering/display metadata).
  • How: The -11/-12 churn is stabilization: vct#integrity added to the non-disclosable claim list, Status List tokens must be JWTs, lang→locale, JSON schema removed from Type Metadata, x5c required in the protected header, sd=always/sd=never recommended to avoid ambiguity, and the relationship to Key Binding (SD-JWT+KB) clarified. The slides close with "WGLC?"
  • Where applicable: Digital credential ecosystems — government IDs, enterprise credentials, wallets. WG document on the cusp of last call; if your identity roadmap touches credentials at all, this is the format to build against.

items.title: Selective Disclosure CBOR Web Tokens (SD-CWT)
items.text:
IETF 124 (Montreal) — Standards digest Adjacent pick Montreal · 1–7 November 2025

Draft Slides Session recording Materials

M. Prorock, O. Steele, H. Birkholz, R. Mahy, M. Jones — SPICE WG document

  • Why: The CBOR/COSE twin of SD-JWT: selective disclosure for constrained devices and CBOR-native credential ecosystems. Watching it mature tells you where the JSON and CBOR credential formats will converge or diverge.
  • What: A data-minimization technique for CBOR Web Tokens, inspired by SD-JWT but realigned with COSE and CWT structure; at -05 with no major normative changes in the last cycle.
  • How: Recent tightening: AEAD guidance (no authentication tags under 16 bytes), corrected COSE key examples, explicit rules for verifier handling of unknown claims, sorted CBOR map keys for test vectors. Open issues are CBOR-specific hygiene: encoding restrictions (forbid indeterminate length, max nesting depth 16, bstr-encoded map keys), tagged map keys, decoy-digest examples — two issues gated on early IANA registration. About 2.5 implementations (Rust, JavaScript, Python) heading into interop testing.
  • Where applicable: Constrained-device and COSE-based credential ecosystems; WG document in the interop phase — steady, unglamorous, on track.

items.title: The OAuth 2.1 Authorization Framework
items.text:
IETF 124 (Montreal) — Standards digest Core pick Montreal · 1–7 November 2025

Draft Slides Session recording Materials

Dick Hardt (Hellō), Aaron Parecki, Ed. (Okta), Torsten Lodderstedt (SPRIND) — OAuth WG document

  • Why: The consolidated successor to RFC 6749/6750 — every OAuth product roadmaps against it, and the WG milestone targets IESG submission in December 2026.
  • What: A single standards-track specification replacing OAuth 2.0 and Bearer Token Usage, folding in OAuth for Native Apps (RFC 8252), Browser-Based Apps (RFC 10017), and the Security BCP (RFC 9700), and removing features found insecure: the implicit grant is gone, PKCE is required for the authorization-code flow, the redirect URI must be sent in token requests, sender-constrained tokens (DPoP, mTLS) are recommended over bare bearers, and refresh-token/client-credential behavior is specified in the base.
  • How: Consolidation and normative merge of the existing document set, with an explicit "Differences from OAuth 2.0" section enumerating the removals so implementers can plan migrations.
  • Where applicable: Every OAuth implementation, full stop. WG document at -17 — late-stage, expect the interesting discussion to be migration timing and 2.0-mode compatibility, not design.

items.title: Transaction Tokens
items.text:
IETF 124 (Montreal) — Standards digest Core pick Montreal · 1–7 November 2025

Draft Slides Session recording Materials

Atul Tulshibagwale, George Fletcher, Pieter Kasselman — OAuth WG document, post-WGLC

  • Why: The OAuth-side complement to WIMSE: maintaining immutable user identity, workload identity, and authorization context across a call chain inside a trust domain, enabling down-scoping at the edge and finer-grained authorization per hop.
  • What: Txn-Tokens — tokens internal to a trust boundary that carry subject, context, and authorization details through a multi-service call chain, shared across workloads processing the request.
  • How: Processing post-WGLC feedback: the purp claim became scope, the Txn-Token HTTP header is registered with an empty type in the HTTP fields registry, and an internal flow diagram was added. Open issues: request-context validation and replacement-token semantics (replacement process, lifetime extension, whether tctx can be modified). Implementations exist: Keycloak and Tokenetes (CNCF sandbox).
  • Where applicable: Microservice/API call chains within a single trusted domain. Mature WG document close to publication.

items.title: Updates to OAuth 2.0 JSON Web Token (JWT) Client Authentication and Assertion-Based Authorization Grants
items.text:
IETF 124 (Montreal) — Standards digest Core pick Montreal · 1–7 November 2025

Draft Materials

Michael B. Jones (Self-Issued Consulting), Brian Campbell (Ping Identity), Chuck Mortimore (Disney), Filip Skokan (Okta) — OAuth WG, in the RFC Editor queue

  • Why: Fixes a real, published vulnerability — "audience injection" attacks (Hosseyni, Küsters, Würtele, University of Stuttgart), found during security analysis of OpenID Federation — affecting private_key_jwt-style client authentication across OAuth/OIDC.
  • What: Updates RFC 7521, 7522, 7523, and 9126: for client authentication, the JWT aud claim MUST be the authorization server's issuer identifier as its sole value — the token endpoint URL is no longer an acceptable audience — and the AS MUST reject JWTs that don't comply. Authorization grants may still use either issuer identifier or token endpoint URL. SAML assertions for client authentication are deprecated; a new explicit type client-authentication+jwt SHOULD be used as a compliance signal.
  • How: Root cause: metadata-derived endpoint URLs used as audience values could be accepted at a different endpoint, enabling cross-endpoint token injection. The fix is deliberately asymmetric in rollout — updated clients interoperate with old servers, but not vice versa — so clients should move first; the draft documents this explicitly in its operational considerations.
  • Where applicable: Every AS and client doing JWT client authentication or assertion grants. Mature: IETF last-call reviews complete, IESG consensus recorded, sitting in the RFC Editor queue. Plan the migration now.
path: Updates to OAuth 2.0 JSON Web Token (JWT) Client Authentication and Assertion-Based Authorization Grants

items.title: WIMSE Applicability for AI Agents
items.text:
IETF 124 (Montreal) — Standards digest Core pick Montreal · 1–7 November 2025

Slides Session recording Materials

Yuan Ni, Chunchi Peter Liu (Huawei) — draft-ni-wimse-ai-agent-identity

  • Why: Agentic identity made explicit in a standards body: AI agents blur network boundaries, exhibit unpredictable access patterns, arrive over-privileged, and escape accountability — "no identity → no access control → no accountability."
  • What: Applies the WIMSE architecture to AI agents: an identity server issues agent credentials via an identity proxy with attestation evidence, with requirements for bootstrapping-independent trustworthy identities, automated credential management, minimal-privilege access tokens, and explicit workflows.
  • How: The core proposal is a dual-identity credential — the agent's identity bound to its owner's (a user or an organization admin) as the input to access control — instantiated through a credential-request / user-confirmation-and-signature flow. Open questions include counter-signing design choices, credential-format extensions, whether hardware roots of trust in user devices should anchor the process, and initial trust establishment between identity server and proxy. Positioned against CHEQ's per-task double-confirmation tokens: this is per-identity credentials instead.
  • Where applicable: Any trust domain hosting agent workloads (API agents, MCP-style clients). Huawei-driven individual contribution asking to become a WIMSE WG item — early, but agentic identity is moving from blog posts to standards requirements here.

items.title: WIMSE Architecture
items.text:
IETF 124 (Montreal) — Standards digest Core pick Montreal · 1–7 November 2025

Slides Session recording Materials

WIMSE WG presentation on draft-ietf-wimse-arch-06 (no Internet-Draft linked to the slides)

  • Why: WIMSE is the IETF's umbrella for workload identity — the standards track that SPIFFE-adjacent interests will land on. This presentation is the WG's open-issues snapshot.
  • What: Status of the architecture document after an interim: pending refactors of the service-to-service and identifier documents, terminology alignment, and an explicit list of topics to expand — security considerations, authorization, binding, key management, and attestation. The WG also refined its workload definition (PR#96): an independently addressable, executable software entity — microservices, containers, VMs, serverless functions — spanning fraction-of-a-second request handlers to multi-year database services and ML training jobs.
  • How: The architecture coordinates WIMSE's credential formats (WITs), protocols, and attestation work; the "topics to expand" list is effectively the WG's current risk register — authorization and binding are where the hard problems now sit.
  • Where applicable: Cloud-native service meshes broadly, not org-specific. WG work in progress; the interesting signal here is direction (authorization/key management next), not new mechanism.

items.title: Agent Operation Authorization
items.text:
IETF 125 (Shenzhen) digest Core pick Shenzhen · 14–20 March 2026

Draft Slides Session recording Materials

Dapeng Liu, Suresh Krishnan

  • Why: The sharpest articulation of OAuth's agent gap: OAuth grants broad permissions (scope=write), but prompt injection can steer an agent into malicious actions that are within the granted permission — permission ≠ behavior — and OAuth proves who the user is, not "agent X acting for user Y on task Z." This draft proposes binding behavioral policy plus delegation plus user-intent evidence into the access token.
  • What: The Agent Operation Authorization (AOA) framework: a structured, machine-readable agent_operation_proposal (a JWT, deliberately excluding the user's natural-language input), validated by the AS into an Agent Operation Authorization Token that cryptographically binds user + agent instance + operation policy constraints (e.g., amount ≤ 50, time == "Nov 11 night"), enforceable at runtime by agents and verifiers — resisting both prompt injection and hallucinated parsing of intent.
  • How: Tripartite binding via AS-signed evidence; trust model treats the LLM as untrusted, the agent runtime as trusted (signs requests), the AS as sole witness. Ecosystem fit: PAR, JWT, standard error codes; WIMSE workload identity for agent authentication; OPA/Rego for policy enforcement. Open-source implementation: Open Agent Auth (Alibaba), demoed at the IETF 125 hackathon.
  • Where applicable: Any autonomous-agent platform calling protected APIs. Early individual draft — the authors are explicitly seeking WG consensus on the problem and on the shift from scope-based to policy-based authorization. Whether or not this exact design wins, the problem statement is the one to align products against.

items.title: Agent-to-Agent (A2A) Profile for OAuth Transaction Tokens
items.text:
IETF 125 (Shenzhen) digest Core pick Shenzhen · 14–20 March 2026

Draft Slides Session recording Materials

Chunchi Peter Liu, Yuan Ni

  • Why: Agent-to-agent call chains are exposed to goal hijack, context poisoning, and privilege abuse (per OWASP's agentic-AI top 10). Transaction Tokens (draft-ietf-oauth-transaction-tokens, at -08) already propagate user/workload identity and authorization context across service chains; this profiles them for the agent case.
  • What: Extends Transaction Tokens from service-to-service to agent-to-agent, embedding A2A call-chain context — user and agent identity, authorization context, and A2A message structure (task_id, context_id, message_id, role, metadata) — as claims so identity and intent survive across distributed agent workloads.
  • How: Uses the Tx Token claim set: scope(purp) as immutable transaction purpose, tctx for immutable chain details, rctx for changeable environmental context; A2A message fields map into these. Open design questions flagged for the WG: whether scope derives from the A2A task_id or the external access token, and whether a new claim carries A2A context or rctx is reused. A merger with draft-oauth-transaction-tokens-for-agents is under discussion.
  • Where applicable: Trusted-domain multi-agent workflows. Early individual draft (-00/-02) — but Transaction Tokens themselves are mature, and this is one of the two live profiles competing to be the A2A identity mechanism; watch the consolidation.
path: Agent-to-Agent (A2A) Profile for OAuth Transaction Tokens

items.title: BGP Deterministic Path Forwarding (DPF)
items.text:
IETF 125 (Shenzhen) digest Core pick Shenzhen · 14–20 March 2026

Draft Slides Session recording Materials

Kevin Wang, Michal Styszynski, Wen Lin, Mahesh Subramaniam, Thomas Kampa, Diptanshu Singh (Juniper)

  • Why: Hop-by-hop EBGP gives every flow one best-effort service; AI/LLM flows, multi-tenant GPU-as-a-service SLAs, and PRP-style replication need path separation that plain IP fabrics don't offer. This is a lightweight traffic-engineering answer for IP fabrics.
  • What: Partitions a physical Clos fabric into multiple logical fabrics by "coloring" EBGP sessions and routes. Use cases shown: queue-pair pinning for ROCEv2 (pinning QPs to disjoint paths), per-tenant SLA separation for GPU-as-a-service, and fate-sharing avoidance (exception flows and PRP redundant flows mapped to different logical fabrics).
  • How: Each EBGP session carries a color community; a route is only accepted over a session of matching color (uncolored routes match any). A new SESSION-COLOR capability in the BGP OPEN negotiates color, in strict mode (early misconfiguration detection, session flaps on color change) or loose mode (no flap, late detection). Coloring modes: primary-only, primary+backup (AIGP makes backup劣 — backup paths carry AIGP so primary wins), primary+all-backups (the QPP mode), and all-colors ECMP with firewall-filter flow mapping.
  • Where applicable: Any EBGP Clos fabric (RFC 7938 style). Individual draft (-00) presented at IDR — early, no adoption signal yet; vendor-driven (Juniper) with concrete switch-level use cases.

items.title: BGP Link-State Extensions for BGP-only Networks
items.text:
IETF 125 (Shenzhen) digest Core pick Shenzhen · 14–20 March 2026

Draft Slides Session recording Materials

Ketan Talaulikar (independent), Aravind Babu MahendraBabu, Clarence Filsfils, Krishna Swamy (Cisco), Shawn Zandi (LinkedIn), Gaurav Dawra, Muhammad Durrani (Equinix)

  • Why: In BGP-only DC/AI fabrics, nodes have no visibility beyond direct neighbors — which blocks LFA/TI-LFA computation, remote protection, and controller TE. This draft is the enabler several other RTGWG/IDR drafts depend on, including the IPFRR-for-AI/ML draft below.
  • What: A WG draft (draft-ietf-idr-bgp-ls-bgp-only-fabric-04, adopted by IDR) that lets each BGP speaker advertise its local topology via existing BGP-LS NLRI types (Node, Link, Prefix), giving controllers a full underlay link-state and TE view in networks with no IGP.
  • How: Reuses existing BGP-LS descriptors and attribute TLVs (link bandwidth, SR adjacency SIDs, affinities, TE metric, SR prefix SIDs); adds one new BGP Route Type TLV in the Prefix Descriptor. Works via route-reflector distribution to controllers or a centralized BGP-LS collector; the base eBGP underlay is untouched.
  • Where applicable: BGP-only fabrics — DC/MSDN per RFC 7938 and emerging AI DC networks. The draft focuses on eBGP single-hop peering; other models not precluded. Implementations in progress; code-point allocation requested. Directly feeds draft-clad-rtgwg-ipfrr-aiml and efficient-remote-protection.
path: BGP Link-State Extensions for BGP-only Networks

items.title: Cryptographically Verifiable Actor Chains for OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange
items.text:
IETF 125 (Shenzhen) digest Core pick Shenzhen · 14–20 March 2026

Draft Session recording Materials

A Prasad, Ramki Krishnan, Diego Lopez (Telefónica), Srinivasa Addepalli (individual, SPICE WG)

  • Why: Multi-hop service-to-service and agentic workflows need delegation-path continuity: RFC 8693 allows nested act claims but prior actors are informational only — nothing today cryptographically proves the chain of token exchanges that produced a token. That's the auditability gap for agent-driven API access.
  • What: Six actor-chain profiles for RFC 8693 token exchange — Declared vs Verified, each in Full/Subset/Actor-Only disclosure variants — trading off visible chain-based authorization, cryptographic accountability, auditability, privacy, and long-running workflow support. sub, act, may_act semantics are preserved; plain RFC 8693 impersonation-shaped outputs remain valid but sit outside the profile family (from abstract only).
  • How: Profiling of token-exchange outputs such that the delegation path is preserved and validated across successive exchanges, with per-profile processing rules (from abstract only).
  • Where applicable: Same-domain and cross-domain delegation chains in service meshes and agentic workflows. Status caveat: presented in SPICE, but the individual draft (draft-mw-spice-actor-chain-05) has since expired and been replaced by draft-mw-oauth-actor-chain — the work is alive but moving to the OAuth WG; expect the successor document when tracking it.
path: Cryptographically Verifiable Actor Chains for OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange

items.title: Deprecating IPv6 Extension Headers on the Internet
items.text:
IETF 125 (Shenzhen) digest Core pick Shenzhen · 14–20 March 2026

Draft Session recording Materials

Tom Herbert (individual)

  • Why: Measurement shows packets carrying IPv6 extension headers are discarded at high rates across the public Internet, EHs enable DoS amplification and carry known vulnerabilities, and the loss rates deter anyone from deploying new EHs at all. For anyone operating both a limited domain (DC) and Internet-facing paths, this decides whether EH-based mechanisms (e.g., SRH) are ever viable outside the domain.
  • What: Recommends deprecating all IPv6 extension headers on the public Internet except ESP: relegate them to limited domains and discard EH-carrying packets at domain boundary routers — essentially formalizing what operators already do (from abstract only).
  • How: A recommendations document changing expectations about EH handling at domain boundaries rather than a wire-format change; motivated by discard-rate data, DoS vectors, and the chilling effect on new EH development.
  • Where applicable: Internet-facing IPv6 globally; the carve-out for limited domains is what keeps SRv6/segment-routing DC fabrics unaffected. Note maturity carefully: this is an individual draft that was never adopted by 6man and has expired on the datatracker — treat it as a provocative position statement shaping the EH debate, not emerging consensus.
path: Deprecating IPv6 Extension Headers on the Internet

items.title: DNS for AI Discovery
items.text:
IETF 125 (Shenzhen) digest Wildcard pick Shenzhen · 14–20 March 2026

Draft Materials

Jim Mozley, Nic Williams (Infoblox), Behcet Sarikaya, Roland Schott (Deutsche Telekom), Jeffrey Damick (Amazon)

  • Why: A quietly ambitious idea: use DNS — not a third-party registry — as the discovery substrate for AI agents. If agentic workloads standardize on DNS for finding each other, discovery becomes cacheable, deterministic, and organization-controlled, and the PM's agents stop depending on brokered directories.
  • What: DNS-AID publishes agents via SVCB records at the agent's own name (TargetName, ipv4/ipv6 hints, ALPN carrying agent protocols mcp/a2a alongside h2/h3, well-known URI for the agent card, a cap capability-descriptor locator plus cap-sha256 digest) and an organization-wide index at _index._agents.<domain>. Scope covers "known agent" and "known organization" discovery; cross-domain capability search is explicitly out of scope (derivable). No new RR types, opcodes, or response codes.
  • How: One SVCB query for the fast path; TLSA (DANE) records optionally authenticate the agent's TLS endpoint in permissive/preferred/strict postures with WebPKI fallback; DNSSEC-signed zones SHOULD; downgrade resistance via SVCB mandatory=. Security considerations are unusually honest: authentic records can still point at a malicious agent; cap-sha256 is integrity, not trust — trust judgments stay out of band. Experimental extensions (EDNS(0) discovery hints, zero-trust enroll-uri, domain-control validation) are fenced off in a future-work section.
  • Where applicable: Public and private networks, including agents hosted in provider domains. Individual draft (-02) — very early, and its fate in dnsop is uncertain — but this is the draft that makes "DNS as the agent directory" concrete, and it intersects directly with the A2A/MCP identity work above.

items.title: Encapsulating IPsec ESP in UDP for Load-balancing
items.text:
IETF 125 (Shenzhen) digest Core pick Shenzhen · 14–20 March 2026

Draft Slides Session recording Materials

Xiaohu Xu (China Mobile), Shraddha Hegde (HPE), Boris Pismenny (Nvidia), Dacheng Zhang, Liang Xia (Huawei), Mahendra Puttaswamy (HPE)

  • Why: ESP has no entropy, so IPsec tunnels hash onto one ECMP path / one LAG member and one CPU core (no RSS spread). For SD-WAN branch interconnects and, increasingly, cloud-provider encryption of DCI WAN traffic (financial/governmental clouds), this strands bandwidth and CPU.
  • What: A UDP encapsulation of ESP where the 16-bit UDP source port carries a per-flow entropy value, letting unmodified switches and routers load-balance IPsec traffic across ECMP/LAG, and letting x86 IPsec gateways RSS-distribute across cores. Alternative to running multiple parallel tunnels.
  • How: Standard UDP encapsulation with source-port-as-entropy; no changes required in transit switches or core routers. The slides state it is implemented by vendors (Juniper/HPE cited) and the draft (-15) is ready for WG adoption call.
  • Where applicable: Broadly applicable — enterprise SD-WAN, cloud DCI encryption, multi-core IPsec gateways. Mature individual draft on the edge of WG adoption; the closest to shipping of the security items here.
path: Encapsulating IPsec ESP in UDP for Load-balancing

items.title: EVPN Fast Notification and Handling for Multihoming
items.text:
IETF 125 (Shenzhen) digest Core pick Shenzhen · 14–20 March 2026

Draft Slides Session recording Materials

Jeffrey Zhang, Wen Lin (HPE), Changwang Lin (H3C)

  • Why: EVPN multihoming (DF election, local bias) assumes the Ethernet Segment type-4 route is withdrawn and processed quickly on link failure. BGP update propagation over TCP between routing engines isn't quick — delayed handling means traffic loss (DF down) or duplication (link-up local-bias lag). Per- BFD doesn't scale.
  • What: A UDP-based data-plane notification originated and processed in the forwarding plane of MH peers, (near-)instantly updating DF-election/local-bias state without waiting for the BGP control plane. Optionally also notifies all remote PEs (useful for single-active backup switchover and load-balancing rebalance), preferring multicast for the notification address unless the PE count is small.
  • How: UDP messages sent from the failing PE's forwarding plane to peers' forwarding planes, several sent back-to-back to compensate for UDP loss; fully independent of control-plane signaling, no EVPN protocol changes in the data plane, all local behavior — hence no interop issues.
  • Where applicable: EVPN multihoming deployments generally (All-Active and Single-Active). Individual draft, early — authors are collecting comments before an adoption request; complements time-synchronized DF election (RFC 9722).
path: EVPN Fast Notification and Handling for Multihoming

items.title: Fully Adaptive Routing Ethernet in Scale-Up Networks
items.text:
IETF 125 (Shenzhen) digest Core pick Shenzhen · 14–20 March 2026

Draft Slides Session recording Materials

Yongtao Yang (Centec), Yinben Xia, Weifeng Zhang (Tencent), Peilong Wang (Baidu), Yan Zhuang (Huawei), Xiaohu Xu (China Mobile), Zongying He (Broadcom), Nan Wang (Intel, Hygon), Jian Guo (Biren), Xiang Li (Enflame), et al.

  • Why: The same WECMP idea moved into the scale-up (GPU back-end) network, where MoE expert/tensor parallel traffic is low-entropy, bursty, and collision-prone across multi-plane topologies — and the GPU itself becomes a routing participant. This is where physical fabric design and GPU interconnect are converging (OCP ESUN, AMD UALoE, Broadcom SUE-T).
  • What: Extends FARE from switches to GPUs: each GPU has multiple 800G ports, at least one sub-port per scale-up plane, and performs per-flow or per-packet weighted load-balancing across planes using path-bandwidth feedback. New in -02: considerations for memory-semantic operations — weak ordering (full packet spray + GPU reorder buffers), strong ordering (in-order per QP), and partial ordering, selectable via the per-flow vs per-packet mode.
  • How: Per-flow mode needs ≥1 RDMA queue pair per sub-port per GPU pair and per-flow switch balancing (ordered delivery); per-packet mode needs a single QP per GPU pair and spraying across planes (disordered delivery). Switches do matching weighted balancing.
  • Where applicable: Ethernet-based scale-up networks specifically. A 64-GPU disaggregated SuperPod PoC over single-stage Clos is near completion; a 1024-GPU opto-electronic hybrid cascaded pod is under development. Co-authorship from GPU vendors (Intel, Hygon, Biren, Enflame) signals real hardware engagement, but this is early-stage (individual draft, -02).
path: Fully Adaptive Routing Ethernet in Scale-Up Networks

items.title: Fully Adaptive Routing Ethernet using BGP
items.text:
IETF 125 (Shenzhen) digest Core pick Shenzhen · 14–20 March 2026

Draft Slides Session recording Materials

Qingliang Zhang (H3C), Hang Wu (Ruijie), Yadong Liu, Yinben Xia (Tencent), Peilong Wang (Baidu), Xiaohu Xu (China Mobile), Shraddha Hegde (HPE), Keyur Patel (Arrcus), Zongying He (Broadcom), et al.

  • Why: Static ECMP in Clos fabrics breaks down for elephant-flow AI training traffic — collisions on equal-cost paths cost throughput exactly when a multi-thousand-GPU job is running. This is the most implementation-proven adaptive-routing item in the routing area.
  • What: FARE extends BGP so that each node advertises real-time path bandwidth in a path-bandwidth extended community; receivers compute weighted ECMP (WECMP) next-hops and rebalance per the live capacity of each spine path. New in -04: multihoming handling — when a prefix is multihomed to N leaf nodes, the advertised path bandwidth is divided by N (or the local link bandwidth multiplied by N) before taking the minimum, so weights stay honest.
  • How: Leaf takes min(local link bandwidth, advertised path bandwidth) as the route weight for weighted load-balancing; congestion or link-state changes propagate via ordinary BGP updates carrying the bandwidth community. The slides state the draft is ready for WG adoption call.
  • Where applicable: Broadly applicable to scale-out IP fabrics — implemented by at least 2 cloud providers (China Mobile Cloud, Baidu Cloud) and 5+ vendors, adapted to four mainstream merchant switch chips including Broadcom Tomahawk 5, Nvidia Spectrum-4, HiSilicon SD58XX, and Centec Arctic. Ethernet Clos fabrics only; not a WAN mechanism.
path: Fully Adaptive Routing Ethernet using BGP

items.title: IP Fast Reroute for AI/ML Fabrics
items.text:
IETF 125 (Shenzhen) digest Core pick Shenzhen · 14–20 March 2026

Draft Slides Session recording Materials

Francois Clad, Clarence Filsfils (Cisco), Roy Jiang, Dennis Cai

  • Why: AI backend networks lose huge compute value per millisecond of fabric failure; existing FRR (ECMP, LFA, TI-LFA) is CPU-activated and orders of magnitude too slow, plus it can't react to capacity/quality degradation (e.g., a failed bundle member or a down spine-to-super-spine path causing congestion rather than outage).
  • What: A requirements document for sub-100µs convergence in AI DC fabrics and DCI: it enumerates the limits of RFC 5714 mechanisms in large multi-tier Clos and BGP-only fabrics, and lays out what a replacement needs.
  • How: Four requirements: (1) hardware-accelerated protection activation using extended NPU capabilities without CPU intervention; (2) hardware-accelerated network notifications (the FANTEL discussion, draft-ietf-rtgwg-net-notif-ps, draft-camarillo-rtgwg-lsn); (3) complete topology visibility via BGP-LS in BGP-only fabrics (the draft above); (4) quality-aware remote protection — reacting to remote degradation by adjusting ECMP weights or using repair paths outside the ECMP set (solution sketched in draft-clad-rtgwg-efficient-remote-protection).
  • Where applicable: Scale-out AI backend networks (⅔-tier folded Clos, multi-plane/multi-rail, eBGP) and scale-across DCI; scale-up explicitly deferred. Requirements stage — individual draft seeking WG feedback; this is the umbrella over several companion solution drafts rather than a deployable mechanism itself.
path: IP Fast Reroute for AI/ML Fabrics

items.title: JSON Web Proof
items.text:
IETF 125 (Shenzhen) digest Adjacent pick Shenzhen · 14–20 March 2026

Draft Slides Session recording Materials

Mike Jones, David Waite (JOSE WG)

  • Why: Selective-disclosure credentials are moving from SD-JWT toward BBS-style ZK-friendly algorithms; JWP is the container that makes them usable in the JWT-shaped ecosystem the PM's identity stack already speaks.
  • What: A JWS-like container ("JSON Web Proof") that integrity-protects multiple payloads in one message and adds a presentation form supporting selective disclosure of individual payloads, plus a Presentation Header against replay. Recent -13 changes: proof_alg (separate from JOSE/COSE algorithm registries) in JWKs/COSE_Keys, and deterministic crypto operations in all examples.
  • How: Issuer proves over multiple payload slots; holder presents a subset with per-claim disclosure. Open work presented: JSON Proof Token subclaim support (selective disclosure within claims, e.g., address-country — proposed syntax aligns with SD-JWT VC metadata), BBS extensions (experimental, described separately), BBS blind signatures (holder-known messages), and per-verifier pseudonyms.
  • Where applicable: Digital-credential ecosystems (wallets, verifiable credentials) targeting unlinkability. WG draft, active; BBS-related pieces are explicitly less mature than the core.

items.title: ML-KEM Post-Quantum Key Agreement for TLS 1.3
items.text:
IETF 125 (Shenzhen) digest Adjacent pick Shenzhen · 14–20 March 2026

Draft Materials

Deirdre Connolly (Selkie Cryptography, TLS WG)

  • Why: The standalone post-quantum key agreement for TLS 1.3 is essentially done — this defines what PQ TLS looks like at the wire level for every product the PM ships.
  • What: Registers ML-KEM-512/768/1024 as TLS NamedGroups (0x0200–0x0202) for use in supported_groups/key_share, replacing (EC)DHE in the TLS 1.3 key schedule. Encapsulation keys run 800–1568 bytes with 768–1568-byte ciphertexts — the handshake-size implications every implementation will feel.
  • How: Client sends pk in KeyShareClientHello; server returns the ML-KEM ciphertext in KeyShareServerHello; the 32-byte shared secret feeds the key schedule. Server must run the FIPS 203 encapsulation-key check (abort illegal_parameter on failure); ciphertext reuse is forbidden; RNG hygiene is called out (encapsulation randomness discloses raw RNG output). Security considerations cite formal analyses that IND-CCA-secure KEM substitution preserves TLS 1.3 handshake security, and hybrid constructions (RFC 9954, RFC 10024) give compositional safety. Intended status is Informational; the registry entries are currently Recommended=N.
  • Where applicable: All TLS 1.3/DTLS 1.3 implementations. Maturity: WG draft at -11, submitted to IESG, in the RFC Editor queue with completed SECDIR/GenArt last-call reviews. Decisions remaining for implementers are deployment-level — standalone ML-KEM vs. PQ/T hybrids — not the spec itself.
path: ML-KEM Post-Quantum Key Agreement for TLS 1.3

items.title: OAuth SPIFFE Client Authentication
items.text:
IETF 125 (Shenzhen) digest Core pick Shenzhen · 14–20 March 2026

Draft Slides Session recording Materials

Stian Thorgersen, Scott Rose, Pieter Kasselman, Arndt Schwenkschuster

  • Why: This is the concrete SPIFFE↔OAuth bridge — exactly the workload-identity-meets-authorization intersection the PM owns. Workloads acting as OAuth clients today carry static client secrets in config files (the slides show Spring and JSON examples); this replaces them with automatically rotated SVIDs.
  • What: WG-adopted draft (draft-ietf-oauth-spiffe-client-auth) profiling RFC 7521/7523 so JWT-SVIDs serve as OAuth client-assertion credentials, X.509-SVIDs ride RFC 8705 mTLS client auth, and — new since IETF 124 — WIT-SVIDs (WIMSE workload identity tokens) fit the attestation-based client-auth draft, with key possession where applicable. New token_endpoint_auth_methods_supported values: spiffe_jwt, spiffe_x509, spiffe_wit.
  • How: The AS fetches SPIFFE trust bundles via the SPIFFE Bundle Endpoint (JWKS, RFC 7517) for SVID validation; trust establishment and client registration are prerequisites (enterprise environments typically require registration anyway). Works for 2-legged (client credentials) and 3-legged (auth code + PKCE) flows.
  • Where applicable: Any environment running SPIFFE/SPIRE or managed workload identity (Entra Workload ID, Google Managed Workload Identity; deployed at Uber, Netflix, ByteDance, etc.). Keycloak 26.4 ships a preview implementation; an MCP-OAuth client-auth demo exists. The strongest "adopt and implement soon" signal in the identity set.

items.title: One Signature Certificates
items.text:
IETF 125 (Shenzhen) digest Wildcard pick Shenzhen · 14–20 March 2026

Draft Slides Session recording Materials

Stefan Santesson, Russ Housley (LAMPS WG)

  • Why: A genuinely novel certificate profile: certificates that exist to validate exactly one signature, with the key destroyed immediately after — eliminating expiry and revocation complexity for long-lived document validation.
  • What: Per the slides: key pair generated, certificate issued, document signed, private key destroyed. The certificate never expires (notAfter = 99991231235959Z), never revokes (id-ce-noRevAvail), and is bound to the single signed document via a new signedDocumentBinding extension (dataTbsHash + hash algorithm + binding type), with binding-type variants for CAdES/XAdES/JWS/COSE that hash only the payload where the signing process covers certificate data.
  • How: Binding the certificate to the document hash makes the certificate meaningless for any other use; long-term validation reduces to verifying the signature against a certificate that can never be revoked or expire.
  • Where applicable: Long-lived signed documents (contracts, archival records) rather than TLS/workload identity. The LAMPS adoption call ended 2026-03-13 and the draft is being republished as a LAMPS WG document — a small but real shift in how PKI can work.

items.title: Requirements and Gap Analysis of Multicast in AI Data Centers
items.text:
IETF 125 (Shenzhen) digest Core pick Shenzhen · 14–20 March 2026

Draft Slides Session recording Materials

Junye Zhang, Weiqiang Cheng, Kefei Liu (China Mobile)

  • Why: MoE token dispatch (AlltoAll), AllReduce broadcast phases, model distribution, and checkpoint saving are all point-to-multipoint; unicast replication burns source GPU/NIC capacity and bandwidth. If network multicast could serve AIDCs, it would offload replication to switches — but no existing multicast tech fits.
  • What: A requirements-and-gap document. Requirements: interactivity (backward MP2P forwarding and ACK/congestion-feedback aggregation), reliability (lossless — RDMA throughput collapses to 0 at ~2% loss), dynamics (µs-scale member-set adaptation for MoE gating, no pre-defined groups), sparseness (e.g., 9 of 256 experts active in DeepSeekV3 — no BIER BitString bloat), and simplicity.
  • How: Gap analysis: PIM/MLDP convergence too slow and too complex; SR-P2MP needs global recalculation; BIER relatively good on dynamics/simplicity but BitString overhead hurts sparse membership; none handle MP2P feedback or losslessness. Conclusion: a new architecture or deep enhancement of existing multicast is needed for AIDCs.
  • Where applicable: AIDC scale-out fabrics. Individual gap-analysis draft (-00) seeking feedback — this is a problem statement that could charter new work rather than a solution; useful for the PM to anticipate where multicast requirements are heading.
path: Requirements and Gap Analysis of Multicast in AI Data Centers

items.title: Symmetry-Driven Asynchronous Forwarding with Fast Reroute for LEO Satellite Networks (SDAF)
items.text:
IETF 125 (Shenzhen) digest Wildcard pick Shenzhen · 14–20 March 2026

Draft Slides Session recording Materials

Shenshen Luan (Beihang University), Wenting Wei, Mingliang Ke (Xidian University), Dongxu Hou, Min Xiao (ZTE)

  • Why: Not the PM's domain — but a fresh routing idea: instead of fighting topology churn in LEO constellations, exploit the toroidal symmetry of Walker-Delta constellations to get microsecond convergence with almost no state. It's a reminder that geometric structure can replace protocol machinery.
  • What: SDAF performs failure-driven reverse-flow forwarding using only local link-state detection and a static Interface Symmetry Mapping Table — no control-plane convergence, no protocol extensions, no header changes. Compatible as-is with OSPFv3, IS-IS, MPLS.
  • How: On detecting a failed egress, a node tags packets by ingress port; when egress matches ingress (packet returning to its origin arc), it reverse-forwards along the ring's major arc to a Phase Transition Point, then resumes forward flow. Two policies — RF-CF (counter-facing detour first, best for intra-orbit failures) and RF-LF (lateral-facing first, best for inter-orbit) — scale from ring to torus. Simulation on a 16×16 torus: up to 17.5% packet-loss reduction vs. normal forwarding under link faults, RF-LF best. Real 5-router ring experiments with OSPFv3: total packet loss drops by ~3 orders of magnitude (e.g., 310 vs. 432,485 packets), microloop loss eliminated, black-hole loss near zero, latency/jitter comparable, peak congestion reduced from 3,000 to 2,000 Mbps.
  • Where applicable: LEO constellations with torus-like topology only, and only while the topology remains connected — a partitioned network needs higher-layer recovery. Individual draft (-00) seeking RTGWG feedback on whether the problem is even in scope. The evaluation is simulation plus a small physical testbed, not a production constellation.
path: Symmetry-Driven Asynchronous Forwarding with Fast Reroute for LEO Satellite Networks (SDAF)

items.title: The OAuth 2.1 Authorization Framework
items.text:
IETF 125 (Shenzhen) digest Core pick Shenzhen · 14–20 March 2026

Draft Slides Session recording Materials

Dick Hardt (Hellō), Aaron Parecki (Okta), Torsten Lodderstedt (SPRIND)

  • Why: OAuth 2.1 will be the baseline spec every identity product implements for the next decade. It obsoletes RFC 6749 and RFC 6750, folding a decade of security BCPs into one normative document — anything the PM ships that speaks OAuth will be measured against it.
  • What: A consolidation of RFC 6749 (core), RFC 8252 (native apps), RFC 9700 (security BCP), and RFC 10017 (browser-based apps) into a single framework, removing features found insecure in RFC 9700 — the TOC confirms removal of the implicit grant, changes to the redirect URI parameter in token requests, and deeply reworked security considerations including mix-up defenses via issuer identification and distinct redirect URIs, sender-constrained tokens (DPoP, mTLS) promoted to SHOULD, and extensive native/browser app guidance.
  • How: Same grant architecture (authorization code, refresh, client credentials, extension grants) with the insecure options deleted; supports both bearer and sender-constrained access tokens; explicitly HTTP-only.
  • Where applicable: Universal for OAuth implementations. Maturity is high: WG document at -17 with a WG milestone of submission to IESG by Dec 2026. (Note: the slides link attached to this agenda item actually presents a different OAuth draft — the Identity Assertion Authorization Grant — so use the draft text itself.)

items.title: Updates to OAuth 2.0 Security Best Current Practice
items.text:
IETF 125 (Shenzhen) digest Core pick Shenzhen · 14–20 March 2026

Draft Slides Session recording Materials

Tim Würtele, Pedram Hosseyni (University of Stuttgart), Kaixuan Luo (CUHK), Adonis Fung (Samsung Research America)

  • Why: This documents two new real-world attack classes found in production OAuth ecosystems — including agentic AI token vaults — with 20+ and 40+ affected vendors respectively. If the PM builds anything with connector marketplaces, integration platforms, or agent toolkits, these attack classes apply directly.
  • What: WG-adopted update to RFC 9700 covering: (1) audience injection attacks against client-authentication assertions, with attack mechanics and countermeasures (single audience value, issuer identifier, exact endpoint URI); (2) Cross-toolkit OAuth Account Takeover (COAT) — a malicious AS introduced via a connector/toolkit exploits mix-up defenses that don't work because issuer identifiers are unavailable, untrusted, or non-unique in practice (none of 20+ client vendors investigated applied issuer-based defenses); countermeasure: a client-assigned identifier for each toolkit, embedded in redirect_uri, matched at the client; (3) cross-user OAuth session fixation — platforms and AI token vaults introduce standalone auth sessions decoupled from the user-agent session, fixatable by sharing a request URL (Amazon Alexa, IFTTT, Microsoft Copilot, n8n, Perplexity, Manus, Bedrock AgentCore, Arcade.dev, Composio among 40+ affected); countermeasures are high-level (return to the origin where the original session lives; validate session binding), with concrete flows left to future profiling.
  • How: BCP-format security analysis with per-attack threat models, generalized deployment scenarios (integration platforms, agent token vaults), and immediately applicable client-side mitigations.
  • Where applicable: Every OAuth 2.0 deployment with multi-AS clients — especially connector/integration platforms and agentic token vaults. WG-adopted (-01); authors target WG last call after IETF 126.
path: Updates to OAuth 2.0 Security Best Current Practice

items.title: Use cases and Requirement for Flow Control Collaboration Across DCNs and WAN
items.text:
IETF 125 (Shenzhen) digest Core pick Shenzhen · 14–20 March 2026

Draft Slides Session recording Materials

Zhengxin Han, Ran Pang, Yi Yue, Jie Dong, Zheng Ruan, Quan Xiong (China Unicom)

  • Why: Distributed AI training and inference now span data centers over WAN, but PFC — the DCN lossless mechanism — fails badly in WANs: head-of-line blocking, congestion spreading, and deadlock under multipathing, with long RTTs amplifying everything. Extending lossless RDMA end-to-end across DCN+WAN requires the two flow-control regimes to interwork.
  • What: Use cases and requirements for co-deploying PFC inside DCNs with fine-grained flow control (fgfc) in the WAN: fgfc is a data-plane L3 backpressure mechanism (carried in ICMPv6 or UDP) operating at tenant/flow granularity, bounded to specific paths and slices, with ms-level response.
  • How: Edge gateways (R1/R5 in the examples) do bidirectional translation: DCN PFC pause → fgfc packet (priority, slice ID, pause time) upstream; WAN fgfc → standard PFC frame toward the DC. Requirements on edge nodes: PFC↔fgfc protocol conversion, port-level↔tenant/flow-level semantic mapping, policy coordination, slicing and HQoS support, buffer management. Supports both hop-by-hop and tunneled cross-hop WAN backpressure for legacy intermediate nodes.
  • Where applicable: DC-interconnect WANs carrying RDMA/AI traffic. Field trials reported over 200+km (Hangzhou–Jinhua storage/compute separation training) achieving >95% computational efficiency with RDMA lossless over the WAN — operator-specific (China Unicom) evidence but the mechanism is general. Individual requirements draft, seeking review.
path: Use cases and Requirement for Flow Control Collaboration Across DCNs and WAN

items.title: Use of Remote Attestation with Certification Signing Requests
items.text:
IETF 125 (Shenzhen) digest Core pick Shenzhen · 14–20 March 2026

Draft Slides Session recording Materials

M. Ounsworth, H. Tschofenig, H. Birkholz, M. Wiseman, N. Smith (LAMPS WG)

  • Why: CAs increasingly must verify policy compliance before issuance — e.g., that a CSR's private key lives in an HSM and is non-exportable. Today that's a zoo of proprietary attestation mechanisms.
