This standardizes carrying attestation evidence inside PKCS#10/CRMF, which matters for anyone automating certificate issuance for workloads and devices.
  • What: ASN.1 structures carrying attestation data in CSRs, supporting both standardized (RATS-family) and proprietary attestation formats. WG draft at -22/-23: a design team (formed to break an author stalemate over design options) did a deep editorial pass; the Attestation OID registry was removed in -23; two PRs remain open (one debating whether a "Hint" should become a full CMS Attribute — the authors lean toward dropping hints entirely; one revisiting ASN.1 choices).
  • How: Attestation evidence is generated, transmitted in the CSR, and verified by the CA as part of issuance policy (from abstract plus status slides; the precise ASN.1 details are still in flux per the open PRs).
  • Where applicable: Any PKI where issuance is gated on key-protection or environment properties — HSM-bound keys, device identity, workload certificates. Mature WG draft (years in progress, design-team-reviewed) — on the path to last call but not there yet.
path: Use of Remote Attestation with Certification Signing Requests

items.title: Using the Well-Known IPv6 Prefix to Represent Non-Global IPv4 Addresses
items.text:
IETF 125 (Shenzhen) digest Adjacent pick Shenzhen · 14–20 March 2026

Draft Slides Session recording Materials

Warren Kumari, Jen Linkova (v6ops WG)

  • Why: RFC 6052 currently forbids using 64:ff9b::/96 for RFC 1918 addresses and requires translators to drop such packets — which breaks IPv6-only nodes reaching IPv4-only services with private addresses, a daily pain in enterprise/SMB IPv6-only deployments.
  • What: A WG draft that updates RFC 6052 to relax the MUST NOT/MUST-drop: allow the Well-Known Prefix to represent non-globally-reachable IPv4 addresses and let translators process them. It keeps existing deployments safe: implementations keep default behavior, gain a config knob; administrators apply explicit drop policies where the old behavior was relied upon. The slides note the same restriction removal was proposed by Fred Baker in erratum eid5547 back in 2018, and discuss why the Network-Specific Prefix isn't always feasible.
  • How: A change to translation deployment guidance, not a new wire format — translate-or-not becomes an explicit policy question.
  • Where applicable: NAT64/DNS64-based IPv6-only enterprise and SMB networks. Mature: WG draft, WGLC requested at this meeting — close to done.
path: Using the Well-Known IPv6 Prefix to Represent Non-Global IPv4 Addresses

items.title: Workload Identifier Origin Hint for TLS ClientHello
items.text:
IETF 125 (Shenzhen) digest Core pick Shenzhen · 14–20 March 2026

Draft Slides Session recording Materials

Yaroslav Rosomakho, Jonathan Hoyland (individual, TLS WG)

  • Why: mTLS works well for workloads but there's no easy way to enable it on a shared endpoint — today you typically need a separate TLS server endpoint just to issue CertificateRequests. This extension lets a workload client signal mTLS capability and identity namespace in the ClientHello.
  • What: A TLS ClientHello extension carrying a list of workload identifier origins (URI scheme + trust domain, e.g., the spiffe:// scheme and trust-domain part of a SPIFFE ID). Presence of the extension tells the server the client (a) won't break on a CertificateRequest and (b) can present a certificate for one of the listed origins; the server uses the hint to decide whether client authentication is required and which policies/trust anchors apply.
  • How: An optional origin list in the extension; an empty list degenerates into a pure "request mTLS" flag. For privacy, the list can be carried in the Inner ClientHello under ECH with an empty outer list, hiding identifier information from on-path observers.
  • Where applicable: Machine-to-machine TLS deployments — SPIFFE/WIMSE-style workload identity, proxies, OT/IoT — not user-facing browsers. Early individual draft (-01) gauging TLS WG interest; complements SPIFFE client auth (OAuth layer) and the WIMSE effort.
path: Workload Identifier Origin Hint for TLS ClientHello

items.title: YANG Model for Border Gateway Protocol (BGP-4)
items.text:
IETF 125 (Shenzhen) digest Adjacent pick Shenzhen · 14–20 March 2026

Draft Materials

Mahesh Jethanandani, Keyur Patel (Arrcus), Susan Hares, Jeff Haas (HPE) — IDR WG

  • Why: A standard YANG model for BGP config/ops matters to anyone building automated DC or WAN fabrics — today every vendor's BGP schema differs. Once published, this becomes the north-star schema for BGP automation.
  • What: YANG data model for configuring and managing BGP — protocol, policy, and operational aspects including RIB — based on data center, carrier, and content provider requirements. The draft (presented at -19, now at -23) is modular: separate submodules for types, capabilities, common/neighbor state, multiprotocol AFI/SAFI, policy, RIB tables/attributes, and session security (key chains, TCP-AO), with IANA-maintained modules for capabilities, notification codes, AFI/SAFI types, and community types.
  • How: Standard NETCONF/RESTCONF data-model machinery layered on ietf-routing, ietf-routing-policy, ietf-key-chain, ietf-tcp, and BFD types.
  • Where applicable: BGP automation across DC, carrier, and enterprise; vendor-neutral intent for gNMI/NETCONF pipelines. Maturity: long-running WG draft (-23, updated the day before this digest), intended Proposed Standard, still clearing YANG validation errors — close to the end of a long road, not a finished RFC.
path: YANG Model for Border Gateway Protocol (BGP-4)

items.title: A RoCEv2 Flow-Level Load Balancing Method Based on the IPv6 Flow Label
items.text:
IETF 126 (Vienna) — for a networking, security, and identity PM digest Core pick Vienna · 18–24 July 2026

Draft Slides Session recording Materials

Jiayuan Hu (presenter), Jie Dong, Xia Gong.

  • Why: The classic RoCEv2 load-balancing flaw: many parallel RDMA sessions from one host share an identical 5-tuple, so ECMP hashes them all to one path — elephant flows, congestion, loss in AI/HPC clusters.
  • What: A 6man proposal to recover per-session entropy: the ingress network device parses the Queue Pair numbers (24-bit Source/Destination QP) from the RoCEv2 BTH/DETH headers, hashes them with the low 16 bits of each IPv6 address using CRC32, and writes the low 20 bits into the IPv6 Flow Label. Downstream devices then hash "5-tuple + Flow Label".
  • How: CRC32 with init 0xFFFFFFFF — deliberately hardware/ASIC-friendly; only the Flow Label field is modified, so firewalls and NAT behavior are untouched and hosts are fully transparent to the mechanism.
  • Where applicable: RoCEv2-over-IPv6 AI/HPC fabrics; requires ingress switch parsing capability. Early individual draft; the authors are asking for review, so expect evolution.
path: A RoCEv2 Flow-Level Load Balancing Method Based on the IPv6 Flow Label

items.title: Agent Authorization use cases and gap analysis
items.text:
IETF 126 (Vienna) — for a networking, security, and identity PM digest Core pick Vienna · 18–24 July 2026

Draft Slides Session recording Materials

Meiling Chen (China Mobile).

  • Why: The requirements document that justifies (and scopes) the OAuth WG's agent work — read it to understand why AIMS, PEDIGREE and delegate SD-JWT all exist.
  • What: Ten use cases across consumer, enterprise and security scenarios, each with authorization requirements and gaps: intent-to-permission mapping and interactive consent loops for personal assistants; scope explosion and missing conditional context in smart homes; the confused-deputy/agent-flagging problem when agents hit human-facing services (the "agent downloads 400 papers and gets the user's account banned" example); multi-hop delegation chains and group authorization for agent teams; and global/bulk revocation gaps (RFC 7009 revokes one token at a time — useless in an incident).
  • How: Gap analysis against RAR (too static), DPoP (fixed keys break agent migration), Transaction Tokens (internal-only), and CIMD (no agent metadata, no delegation traceability), each with proposed optimizations like attenuating agent tokens and parent_agent_id claims.
  • Where applicable: Vendor-neutral; informational individual draft -01 with biweekly open meetings — the input document for whatever OAuth extensions follow.
path: Agent Authorization use cases and gap analysis

items.title: AI Agent Authentication and Authorization
items.text:
IETF 126 (Vienna) — for a networking, security, and identity PM digest Core pick Vienna · 18–24 July 2026

Draft Slides Session recording Materials

Nick Steele (OpenAI), Aaron Parecki (Okta), Jeff Lombardo (AWS), Brian Campbell (Ping Identity), Yaroslav Rosomakho (Zscaler), Pieter Kasselman (Defakto Security).

  • Why: The strongest single framework document in the agent-identity land rush: deliberately anti-"invent a new AI protocol," it maps existing standards onto agent communications and surgically identifies what's missing. The author list (OpenAI, Okta, AWS) signals real platform intent.
  • What: An informational draft ("AIMS") covering the full stack: exactly one WIMSE identifier per agent (may be a SPIFFE ID); primary credentials as WIMSE WIC/WIT or SPIFFE SVIDs, secondary via OAuth token exchange and Transaction Tokens; authentication at transport (mTLS with workload X.509) or application layer (WIMSE proof tokens, RFC 9421 HTTP signatures over WIT); OAuth for delegated authorization including human-in-the-loop (noting CIBA doesn't fit mid-execution pauses); SSF/CAEP for continuous posture signals; policy and compliance explicitly out of scope.
  • How: Composition of existing specs with gaps named — the value is the map, not new mechanics.
  • Where applicable: Agent-to-LLM/tool/service/agent interactions generally. Requesting chairs consider WG adoption as a work item; expect it to become the umbrella the other agent drafts hang from.

items.title: Automated Certificate Management Environment (ACME) Remote Attestation Identifier and Challenge Type
items.text:
IETF 126 (Vienna) — for a networking, security, and identity PM digest Adjacent pick Vienna · 18–24 July 2026

Draft Session recording Materials

Peter Chunchi Liu (Huawei), Mike Ounsworth (Cryptic Forest Software), Michael Richardson (Sandelman Software Works), Ganesh Mallaya (AppViewX), Sven Rajala (Keyfactor).

  • Why: Where device attestation meets automated certificate issuance: enterprises increasingly want to issue client (and server) certificates only to devices that can prove their posture — measured boot, HSM-held keys, MDM registration — and ACME had no standardized way to ask.
  • What: A WG document (-03) defining a remote-attestation identifier type whose value is a property hint (measured-boot, hsm, …) rather than a real identifier, plus a remote-attest-01 challenge answered with a RATS Conceptual Message Wrapper (CMW) in any supported format (EAT, WebAuthn, TPM). The challenge object carries a freshnessNonce, an optional attestClaimsHint listing claims the server wants attested, and a verifierEncryptionCredential (JWK) so sensitive evidence can be JWE-encrypted in transit. The design supports both the RATS Passport model (attestation-result-01, mandatory to implement) and Background Check model (encrypted evidence), and is explicitly supplemental — the client still satisfies DNS-01/HTTP-01 for the identifiers that go into the certificate.
  • How: A pseudo-identifier plus challenge/response in the existing ACME order flow; verification and appraisal policy remain the CA's business.
  • Where applicable: Enterprise client certs, WiFi/EAP-TLS onboarding, BYOD S/MIME, code-signing keys in HSMs. Complementary to (broader than) the WebAuthn-based ACME Device Attestation extension; also worth reading alongside V-PEA below, which generalizes the same WHAT+environment idea.
path: Automated Certificate Management Environment (ACME) Remote Attestation Identifier and Challenge Type

items.title: BGP Link-State Extensions for BGP-only Networks
items.text:
IETF 126 (Vienna) — for a networking, security, and identity PM digest Core pick Vienna · 18–24 July 2026

Draft Slides Session recording Materials

Ketan Talaulikar, Aravind Babu MahendraBabu, Clarence Filsfils, Krishna Swamy (Cisco), Shawn Zandi (LinkedIn), Gaurav Dawra, Muhammad Durrani (Oracle).

  • Why: BGP-only fabrics (increasingly the default in AI/ML DCs) lose the topology visibility that link-state IGPs give to FRR and TE computation. This WG document supplies it — and its new use cases tie directly into the two AI-backend drafts above.
  • What: BGP-LS extensions (Protocol-ID 7) to advertise topology in BGP-only networks. Since IETF 125 it has added an IPFRR use case (LFA/TI-LFA/ERP in loss-sensitive AI Clos fabrics with strict convergence requirements) and SRv6 scenarios: unified SRv6 domain across DC frontend + WAN eliminating DCI gateway translation, and SR Policy computation for deterministic AI backend paths. Simplified procedures now reference RFC 9857/9514 directly.
  • How: Standard BGP-LS address-family advertisement of nodes/links from the BGP-only fabric, consumed by controllers or local PCEs for path computation.
  • Where applicable: Any BGP-only DC or WAN. Implemented in SONiC-FRR (merged FRR PR); IANA early allocation for the BGP Route Type TLV is done. Requesting WG review — mature and moving.
path: BGP Link-State Extensions for BGP-only Networks

items.title: Delegate SD-JWT
items.text:
IETF 126 (Vienna) — for a networking, security, and identity PM digest Core pick Vienna · 18–24 July 2026

Draft Slides Session recording Materials

Gareth Oliver (Google).

  • Why: Delegation of verifiable credentials with selective disclosure — the exact mechanism agentic payments need (user authorizes an agent to spend, merchant/bank sees only the delegated slice) and that plain SD-JWTs can't express.
  • What: An extension letting a Holder delegate to a Delegate Holder by making the Key Binding JWT itself an SD-JWT with its own disclosures and its own key binding: <issuer-jwt>~<disclosures>~~<kb-sd-jwt>~<disclosures>~<kb-jwt>. The whole design fits in that one line — the delegation is a holder-signed SD-JWT whose payload hashes and binds the issuer's original (sd_hash, cnf for the delegate's key).
  • How: Standard SD-JWT disclosure machinery at each layer; the verifier sees the issuer credential, the holder's delegation statement with narrowed/selective claims, and the delegate's proof of possession.
  • Where applicable: Agentic systems and digital-credential delegation (power-of-attorney and vehicle-registration examples given). Individual draft; open questions include a common delegation policy language (aud, exp-style) and where revocation status lists are hosted.

items.title: Enhanced ECMP for AI Cluster
items.text:
IETF 126 (Vienna) — for a networking, security, and identity PM digest Core pick Vienna · 18–24 July 2026

Draft Slides Session recording Materials

Weiqiang Cheng (China Mobile), Changwang Lin (New H3C Technologies).

  • Why: In AI training the flow count is small, so per-flow ECMP hash collisions are proportionally more damaging; per-packet ECMP balances perfectly but reorders — unacceptable for RDMA without reordering support.
  • What: Two complementary methods: (1) ingress-interface-group ECMP — group ingress interfaces and hash by in-group index so traffic from different ports lands on different ECMP egress ports; (2) egress-group ECMP — the egress leaf advertises a Group ID in a new BGP extended community (Router-ID + Group-ID, 6 bytes), and the ingress leaf maps flows to matching ECMP subgroups.
  • How: Purely control-plane/local hashing changes; no datapath encapsulation. Method 1 suits balanced GPU ingress traffic, method 2 suits balanced egress traffic.
  • Where applicable: Leaf-spine AI Clos. Individual draft -01 soliciting RTGWG feedback — with an explicit open question whether the BGP extended community should move to IDR. Overlaps in problem space with FARE and the flow-label draft but is a simpler, narrower fix.

items.title: EVPN First Hop Security
items.text:
IETF 126 (Vienna) — for a networking, security, and identity PM digest Core pick Vienna · 18–24 July 2026

Draft Slides Session recording Materials

Ali Sajassi, Lukas Krattiger, Krishna Ananthamurthy (Cisco), Jorge Rabadan (Nokia), Wen Lin (Juniper).

  • Why: First Hop Security functions (DHCP snooping, DAI, ND Inspection, Source Guard) depend on a local DHCP snoop binding database — which silently breaks in EVPN fabrics where hosts move and multi-home across PEs, causing legitimate traffic to be dropped or spoofed traffic to pass.
  • What: A WG-adopted BESS draft defining a new EVPN BGP route to distribute and synchronize DHCP snooping bindings (IPv4/IPv6-to-MAC, binding state, lease/create time) among all PEs in an EVI, covering host mobility, multi-homing, and distributed IRB.
  • How: Straightforward BGP route distribution with binding attributes; major technical issues are resolved and the authors consider the document ready for Working Group Last Call.
  • Where applicable: Any EVPN datacenter or campus fabric running FHS — broadly applicable, multi-vendor co-authored, and the most mature item in the DC-security space at this meeting.

items.title: Fully Adaptive Routing Ethernet in Multi-Plane Scale-Out Networks
items.text:
IETF 126 (Vienna) — for a networking, security, and identity PM digest Core pick Vienna · 18–24 July 2026

Draft Slides Session recording Materials

Yinben Xia, Weifeng Zhang (Tencent), Peilong Wang (Baidu), Haibo Wang (Huawei), and a large RNIC/switch author group (Broadcom, Intel, Ruijie, Yandex, China Mobile, GPU vendors).

  • Why: ~100K-GPU clusters are moving to multi-plane scale-out topologies (RNIC multi-homed across disjoint planes, no inter-plane links) — which pushes path selection into the NIC. Route scale is the blocker: 4 planes × 100K host routes ≈ 400K routes, impractical on an RNIC.
  • What: FARE-in-MPSON extends FARE-BGP from switches to RoCE NICs for multi-plane scale-out (complementing FARE-in-SUN for scale-up). It contributes two route-table suppression techniques: route aggregation with unreachability notification (zero-bandwidth community, or unreachable-prefix advertisement) and selective route filtering via Prefix ORF (RFC 5292), plus a transitive FIB-Suppress extended community so switches can omit RNIC host routes from FIB.
  • How: BGP sessions terminate on RNICs; the RNIC evaluates per-plane reachability and path bandwidth for weighted ECMP. Because collectives mean each GPU talks to a limited peer set, RNICs can request only needed host routes; on unreachability they install a host route from the aggregate's remaining next-hops.
  • Where applicable: Hyperscale multi-plane AI scale-out with RNIC-resident BGP — relies on predictable collective-communication peer sets. Version -00, very early, but the author list signals real industry intent.
path: Fully Adaptive Routing Ethernet in Multi-Plane Scale-Out Networks

items.title: Fully Adaptive Routing Ethernet using BGP
items.text:
IETF 126 (Vienna) — for a networking, security, and identity PM digest Core pick Vienna · 18–24 July 2026

Draft Slides Session recording Materials

Qingliang Zhang (H3C), with co-authors from Tencent, Baidu, China Mobile, Yandex, HPE, Arrcus, Broadcom, Ruijie, Centec, Huawei and IEIT SYSTEMS.

  • Why: AI training on 3–5 stage Clos fabrics needs non-blocking behavior; static per-flow ECMP collapses when a few large flows hash-collide onto one path. This is the most implementation-backed routing draft at the meeting.
  • What: FARE-BGP — a BGP extension (path-bandwidth extended community) that lets switches do weighted ECMP based on real residual path capacity rather than uniform hashing. Version -05 adds handling for multiple BGP sessions per switch pair (bandwidth computed at node granularity, not session granularity) and packet forwarding over tunnels (WECMP applies to tunneled packets with loopback endpoints). The authors state the draft is ready for a WG adoption call.
  • How: The prefix-originating node (e.g., leaf) attaches a maximum path-bandwidth value; each node computes path bandwidth = min(aggregate parallel-link bandwidth, advertised value) and either spreads the weight across ECMP paths or prunes the ECMP set so remaining links match the computed bandwidth.
  • Where applicable: BGP-only AI/DC fabrics. Implemented by at least two cloud providers (China Mobile Cloud, Baidu Cloud) and six vendors, and adapted to 6+ switch ASIC generations — Broadcom Tomahawk 5 (51.2T) and Tomahawk 6 (102.4T), Nvidia Spectrum-4, Huawei SD58XX, Centec Arctic, Clounix CLX86. Explicitly multi-vendor, not org-specific.
path: Fully Adaptive Routing Ethernet using BGP

items.title: GSE architecture for AIDC
items.text:
IETF 126 (Vienna) — for a networking, security, and identity PM digest Core pick Vienna · 18–24 July 2026

Draft Slides Session recording Materials

Rui Zhuang (China Mobile), Sandy Zhang (ZTE).

  • Why: A fundamentally different answer to AI-cluster congestion: instead of reactive ECN/PFC, schedule everything before sending. China Mobile/ZTE are fielding this, so it will surface in AIDC requirements even if it doesn't win in IETF.
  • What: Global Scheduling Ethernet: credit-based authorization (a sender must get a bandwidth grant from the receiver-side last hop before transmitting), packet aggregation into uniform-size segments for forwarding, improved ECMP that sprays packets while preserving receiver-side ordering, and interworking with PFC/ECN. The draft presents intra-PoD (GPU-to-GPU credit negotiation) and inter-PoD (Leaf-to-Super-Spine) scenarios, with port IDs advertised via BGP (draft-zhang-idr-portid-ec).
  • How: New Ethernet packet types carry a GSE header for uniform-size segments and for credit request/grant messages; switches recognize and forward GSE-framed traffic. PoDs from different vendors can interoperate by restoring original packets at the Core.
  • Where applicable: AI data centers. Implemented in prototype hardware/software with "early performance data [showing] significant gains over traditional RoCE" — no numbers published yet. China Mobile-driven; treat as one contender for the post-RoCE AIDC architecture rather than a settled standard.

items.title: IS-IS Support For The Power Conserving Path Placement Strategy (PCPPS)
items.text:
IETF 126 (Vienna) — for a networking, security, and identity PM digest Wildcard pick Vienna · 18–24 July 2026

Draft Session recording Materials

Colby Barth (Juniper), Tony Li, Vishnu Pavan Beeram, Ron Bonica (HPE).

  • Why: Not AI, not identity — but the signal that energy is entering the IGP standards track. PCPPS inverts usual traffic engineering: concentrate traffic onto a small set of links so the rest can be powered down until needed.
  • What: The IS-IS encoding for the power-state information that I-D.many-teas-power-steering's Power Conserving Path Placement Strategy needs distributed by an IGP. Notably, this individual draft has since been replaced by draft-ietf-lsr-pcpps with a call for WG adoption issued — i.e., LSR picked it up right after this meeting.
  • How: IGP advertisement of the information a PCPPS computation needs to know which resources can be safely idled. (Write-up from the abstract and datatracker status; no slides were available.)
  • Where applicable: WAN/operator networks where energy cost is a first-order routing input. Interesting tension with the AI-fabric work elsewhere in this digest, which wants maximum parallelism, not consolidation — expect the two objectives to collide in DC design discussions.
path: IS-IS Support For The Power Conserving Path Placement Strategy (PCPPS)

items.title: Merkle Tree Certificates
items.text:
IETF 126 (Vienna) — for a networking, security, and identity PM digest Core pick Vienna · 18–24 July 2026

Draft Session recording Materials

David Benjamin (Google), Devon O'Brien (Apple), Bas Westerbaan, Luke Valenta (Cloudflare), Filippo Valsorda (Geomys).

  • Why: The PKI arithmetic problem: post-quantum signatures are huge (ML-DSA-44: 2,420 bytes/sig; ML-DSA-65: 3,309) and certificate lifetimes are shrinking — two SCTs plus a leaf signature adds ~7,260–9,927 bytes of authentication overhead, and CT log storage scales with entry size and issuance rate. MTCs redesign the certificate to survive both trends.
  • What: A new X.509-adjacent certificate form where the CA certifies by logging: it appends TBSCertificate entries to append-only issuance logs, signs checkpoints and subtrees, and independent cosigners attest correct (optionally mirrored) operation. A certificate is the tbscert + a Merkle inclusion proof + cosignatures — log entries contain hashes instead of public keys and no signatures, so they don't scale with PQ key/sig size. An optional "landmark-relative" certificate eliminates signatures entirely for up-to-date relying parties, and "revoked ranges" let RPs bulk-discard long-expired log entries so monitoring infrastructure scales by retention policy, not log lifetime.
  • How: Uses a "subtree" Merkle primitive (inclusion and consistency proofs) so proofs stay small; ACME extensions (Section 9, the part presented in Vienna) define issuance; TLS use covers both standalone and landmark-relative forms.
  • Where applicable: Public web PKI first, but the mechanism is general. This is a WG document (PLANTS) now at -07 — the most mature PKI redesign on the IETF's table, with the browser/CDN ecosystem already at the table.

items.title: OAuth SPIFFE Client Authentication
items.text:
IETF 126 (Vienna) — for a networking, security, and identity PM digest Core pick Vienna · 18–24 July 2026

Draft Slides Session recording Materials

Stian Thorgersen, Scott Rose, Nancy Cam-Winget, Pieter Kasselman, Arndt Schwenkschuster.

  • Why: Workloads acting as OAuth clients today authenticate with static, long-lived client secrets — exactly the secret-sprawl problem SPIFFE/SPIRE exists to eliminate. This WG draft bridges the two worlds.
  • What: Profiles RFC 7521/7523, RFC 8705 (mTLS), and the attestation-based client-auth draft so JWT-SVIDs, X.509-SVIDs and WIT-SVIDs work as OAuth client credentials with no client secrets. Crucially it removes the "assertion subject == client_id" restriction of RFC 7521, since SPIFFE IDs are infrastructure-opinionated (spiffe://example.org/us-east-1/cluster-A/service-Z/instance-1) while OAuth client IDs are service-scoped and many workloads share one client.
  • How: The open problem is SPIFFE-ID → client-ID mapping, with three contending approaches: direct list, open-ended prefix wildcards, or path-segment wildcards — described as the last big remaining item.
  • Where applicable: Any shop running SPIRE/SPIFFE alongside an OAuth authorization server (the deck cites Entra, Google managed workload identity, Uber, Netflix, ByteDance deployments of SVIDs). WG document; blocked mainly on the WIT dependency (in WGLC) and mapping semantics.

items.title: PEDIGREE: Verifiable Delegation Identity for Agentic AI Systems
items.text:
IETF 126 (Vienna) — for a networking, security, and identity PM digest Core pick Vienna · 18–24 July 2026

Draft Slides Session recording Materials

Karthik Rampalli.

  • Why: The sharpest statement of the agentic-authorization failure mode: an orchestrator takes one human consent and spawns sub-agents that all inherit its ambient credentials — so a relying party cannot tell which agent acted, on whose authority, or within what limits. A bad charge can't be attributed.
  • What: A delegation-identity layer above workload credentials (WIT/WIC or X.509 SVID, unmodified). The SIT is a signed JWT (typ pedigree+jwt, EdDSA) with a parent chain, scopes, a Cedar-encoded mandate, an operator ceiling reference, consent chain and delegation depth. Its three claimed advances over AAuth and AIP: monotonic scope attenuation enforced at mint and verify (AAuth explicitly rejects attenuation), dual-layer authority enforcement (per-parent mandate AND operator ceiling — a single-layer guard fails when the orchestrator is compromised), and strict cryptographic re-verification of every parent SIT, catching parent-swap attacks that append-only token chains miss.
  • How: Relying parties evaluate three inputs — workload credential, SIT chain, local policy + operator ceiling — with Cedar static-analysis proofs of narrowing; revocation is bounded-staleness and fail-closed, explicitly not real-time.
  • Where applicable: Any multi-agent orchestration where sub-agents act under delegated human authority. Very early individual draft — the deck is candid that wire details still belong on the mailing list — but the three-tests framing (attribution, attenuation, enforcement) is the right vocabulary for this problem space.
path: PEDIGREE: Verifiable Delegation Identity for Agentic AI Systems

items.title: PFC PAUSE Frame Forwarded Transparently in Wide Area Networks
items.text:
IETF 126 (Vienna) — for a networking, security, and identity PM digest Core pick Vienna · 18–24 July 2026

Draft Slides Session recording Materials

Xiaoming He (China Telecom), Lijie Deng (China Telecom).

  • Why: AI and distributed-storage workloads now run RDMA across metro/wide-area links between data centers; the draft's argument is that AIDC interconnect needs lossless WAN transmission, and hop-by-hop PFC in the WAN is both costly and amplifies head-of-line blocking, deadlock and congestion diffusion.
  • What: China Telecom's proposal to carry PFC PAUSE frames transparently across the WAN: the egress PE validates the PFC frame (destination MAC must be 01-80-C2-00-00-01, source must be the directly-connected DC gateway port), encapsulates it in the DCI tunnel (SRv6, SR-MPLS, or VXLAN), and transit nodes forward it untouched; the ingress PE decapsulates, rewrites the source MAC to its own port, and delivers it to the source DC gateway. End-to-end flow control with zero PFC capability required in WAN nodes.
  • How: The price is buffering: the destination DC gateway must reserve Buffer > (R − T) × D per priority queue, where D is the PFC propagation delay across the WAN — the draft's key engineering constraint.
  • Where applicable: DCI/MAN interconnect of two AIDCs under one administrative intent. Individual draft -00; competing with the SRv6 approach below for the same problem.
path: PFC PAUSE Frame Forwarded Transparently in Wide Area Networks

items.title: Reverso for the QUIC protocol
items.text:
IETF 126 (Vienna) — for a networking, security, and identity PM digest Wildcard pick Vienna · 18–24 July 2026

Draft Slides Session recording Materials

Florentin Rochet (University of Namur).

  • Why: A genuinely surprising transport result: QUIC v1's wire layout — encrypted data potentially surrounded by encrypted control — makes contiguous zero-copy at the receiver impossible in a conforming implementation. This draft proposes a QUIC version that fixes it, and it's grounded in a published paper (ACM SIGCOMM CCR, Jan 2026).
  • What: vReverso changes three things from v1: a few more bytes in the short header (worst case 13 vs 5 — a stream ID and offset), a stream frame must be first in the packet, and frame element ordering is reversed on the wire. That's enough to drive data reassembly using decryption's hidden copy, so a receiver can expose a whole HTTP/3 data frame of arbitrary size in zero-copy.
  • How: Reversed frame ordering minimizes added header info (no need to locate where control begins), and a bidirectional buffer abstraction means the same code parses both v1 and vReverso. Loopback microbenchmarks show ~15.4 Gb/s for the prototype vs ~15.2 Gb/s QUIC v1 on comparable stacks — the author himself flags these numbers as "to be taken with a grain of salt."
  • Where applicable: Receiver-side throughput optimization for QUIC and derivatives (QMux is called out). Early individual draft with real maintenance-cost questions, but a rare case of wire-format research feeding directly into a standards venue.

items.title: SRv6 behavior extention for Flow Control in WAN
items.text:
IETF 126 (Vienna) — for a networking, security, and identity PM digest Core pick Vienna · 18–24 July 2026

Draft Slides Session recording Materials

Zhengxin Han (China Unicom, presenter), Zheng Ruan, Yao Liu, MengYao Han, Ying Liu (China Unicom/ZTE).

  • Why: The SRv6-flavored answer to the same lossless-WAN problem — with two advantages over transparent PFC: backpressure can traverse legacy non-PFC devices, and it can be scoped to per-tenant/slice queues instead of coarse port-level pausing. The SPRING list already reached consensus (June–July 2025) that a new SRv6 behavior is the preferred approach.
  • What: A new End.X.PFC behavior that flags PFC-capable interfaces along an SRv6 path. PFC frames are encapsulated into reverse SRv6 tunnels whose final segment is the End.X.PFC SID of the target upstream interface, delivering backpressure precisely to the right node even across non-PFC legacy transit devices.
  • How: Capability flooded via IGP (OSPF/IS-IS) and BGP-LS to a controller, which provisions reverse tunnels (E→C, C→A) before congestion; the data-plane pseudocode strips the outer IPv6/SRH on Ethernet next-header (143) and applies flow control when the PFC multicast MAC is seen.
  • Where applicable: Inter-DC RDMA over L2VPN/L3VPN SRv6 policies in mixed PFC/legacy infrastructure; multi-tenant isolation via NRP/slice queues. Draft -03, actively seeking operator co-review.
path: SRv6 behavior extention for Flow Control in WAN

items.title: SRv6 for Deterministic Path Placement in AI Backends
items.text:
IETF 126 (Vienna) — for a networking, security, and identity PM digest Core pick Vienna · 18–24 July 2026

Draft Slides Session recording Materials

Ahmed Abdelsalam (Cisco), on behalf of co-authors from Cisco, Microsoft, Oracle Cloud, IBM Cloud, NVIDIA and Arrcus.

  • Why: This is the hyperscaler reference design for AI backends — the draft the SRv6/srv6ops community is rallying around, and it is requesting WG adoption at this meeting.
  • What: Describes how SRv6 NEXT-CSID enables deterministic path placement: the NIC's transport stack encodes each path as an ordered segment list in the packet header, and the fabric forwards statelessly. It documents the MRC (Multipath Reliable Connection) design: packet spraying, ECN-based adaptive load balancing, out-of-order memory placement, selective retransmission, and packet trimming for incast — reaching 131,000 GPUs with only two tiers of switches (8×100Gb/s per host instead of 1×800Gb/s).
  • How: Switches carry no per-flow state, no resilient-ECMP hashing, no BGP convergence logic; the end host steers deterministically and can recover from failures within one RTT. Loopback SRv6 probes allow path probing without a peer.
  • Where applicable: Hyperscale production deployments (the deck cites OpenAI, Microsoft, and Oracle MRC+SRv6 deployments; rev04 adds Microsoft and Oracle as co-authors). Not directly transplantable to smaller estates, but it defines the pattern NICs and switches will be asked to support.
path: SRv6 for Deterministic Path Placement in AI Backends

items.title: TCP Packet Trimming Extension
items.text:
IETF 126 (Vienna) — for a networking, security, and identity PM digest Core pick Vienna · 18–24 July 2026

Draft Slides Session recording Materials

Flavius Mazilu, Valentin Bobaru, Costin Raiciu (University Politehnica of Bucharest).

  • Why: Modern datacenter switch silicon (Arista, Broadcom Tomahawk 5, Nvidia, Juniper are all cited) already supports packet trimming — discard payload, keep the header, mark it — but TCP has no way to consume the signal. This is the host-side counterpart to a shipping hardware feature, and it mirrors the trimming used in the MRC/SRv6 AI-backend design above.
  • What: A TCP extension: a "Trimming Permitted" option negotiated in the 3WHS; data packets then carry DSCP_TRIMMABLE; when a switch trims, the receiver gets the header (with DSCP_TRIMMED and updated IP checksum — TCP checksum is intentionally invalid) and returns a NACK option carrying the trimmed packet's sequence number. The sender treats the NACK as an explicit loss/congestion signal and enters fast recovery — deterministic loss recovery instead of SACK/RACK inference.
  • How: Optional two-queues-per-port scheme puts trimmed packets on a higher-priority queue so NACKs return quickly; NACKs could get their own DSCP (Ultra Ethernet's UET proposes DSCP_CONTROL for exactly this).
  • Where applicable: Data centers and controlled administrative domains only — explicitly not for the open Internet. Draft -00 with open questions (checksum handling, congestion-control response) posed to TCPM; watch whether the WG picks it up.

items.title: Verifiable Proof of Environment Attestation Profile
items.text:
IETF 126 (Vienna) — for a networking, security, and identity PM digest Wildcard pick Vienna · 18–24 July 2026

Draft Slides Session recording Materials

Michael Richardson (presenter), with R. Krishnan (JPMorgan Chase), N. Smith, D. Lopez (Telefonica), A. Prasad (Oracle), S. Addepalli (Aryaka), H. Birkholz (Fraunhofer SIT).

  • Why: Sovereignty and regulated-deployment requirements (RBI India, Korea's spatial-data act, GDPR) are demanding provable geographic residency — and nothing today cryptographically links a workload's identity, its execution integrity, and its location. This draft fuses them.
  • What: V-PEA (formerly the verifiable geofencing draft) is a profile of the RATS architecture (RFC 9334) that binds two hardware-rooted dimensions into one TPM-sealed Evidence object: WHAT (TPM provenance, platform/boot integrity, workload-agent binary digest) and WHERE (physical residency per GNSS/MNO/timing location sources, with Galileo OSNMA and multi-constellation cross-checks against spoofing added since IETF 125). Neither dimension can be forged or transplanted without invalidating the other, and the credential is issued only if both pass. The WHERE dimension supports transparent zero-knowledge proofs so an Attester can prove in-boundary compliance without disclosing coordinates. A WIMSE Integration appendix ties the Attestation Result to credential issuance.
  • How: Location sources produce signed claims; a TPM quote seal binds them to the platform's integrity Evidence; a Verifier appraises, and the result can be embedded in standard X.509 so downstream consumers never need to understand RATS. Running code exists (LF Edge AegisSovereignAI: TPM 2.0, SPIRE, Keylime, Plonky2 ZKP).
  • Where applicable: Regulated, sovereign, high-assurance deployments rather than general web workloads — but as hardware-rooted identity meets workload identity (see AIMS/OAuth-SPIFFE above), this is where attestation-gated credential issuance is heading. The draft was presented as a call for RATS WG adoption.
path: Verifiable Proof of Environment Attestation Profile

items.title: WIMSE Trust Domain Discovery
items.text:
IETF 126 (Vienna) — for a networking, security, and identity PM digest Core pick Vienna · 18–24 July 2026

Draft Slides Session recording Materials

Arndt Schwenkschuster, Yaroslav Rosomakho.

  • Why: WIMSE scopes identifiers to a trust domain but leaves how a relying party obtains that domain's trust anchors undefined — the exact gap SPIFFE fills with the Bundle Endpoint. In open environments with no prior relationship, that gap blocks any cross-org WIMSE deployment.
  • What: Defines the WIMSE Trust Bundle (JWKS-formatted, with use values distinguishing wimse-jwt and wimse-x509 signing material for both credential types) and a Trust Domain Metadata document at /.well-known/wimse-trust-domain (redirects allowed) that resolves a trust-domain name to its bundle endpoint.
  • How: A domain owner serves metadata and bundle publicly over HTTPS, mirroring the OIDC metadata/SPIFFE bundle patterns; private deployments can serve them privately or use .internal TLDs with different distribution.
  • Where applicable: Open federation-style workload identity. Individual draft asking "do we agree on the problem space?" — early, but it's the missing interoperability piece for the mature WIMSE credential docs.

items.title: WIMSE Workload Credentials
items.text:
IETF 126 (Vienna) — for a networking, security, and identity PM digest Core pick Vienna · 18–24 July 2026

Draft Slides Session recording Materials

Brian Campbell (Ping Identity), Joe Salowey (CyberArk), Arndt Schwenkschuster (Defakto Security), Yaron Sheffer (Intuit), Yaroslav Rosomakho (Zscaler).

  • Why: The credential layer of the workload-identity stack that OAuth-SPIFFE, the TLS hint, and the agent drafts all build on — and it was in Working Group Last Call at this meeting.
  • What: Defines the Workload Identity Token (WIT, a JWT) and Workload Identity Certificate (WIC, X.509) that bind a key to a workload's WIMSE identifier, usable across protocols; proof-of-possession mechanisms are deliberately out of scope and defined in companion documents.
  • How: Credential formats only — the separation of "what the credential is" from "how you prove possession" is the draft's main design contribution, letting the same credential work over mTLS, HTTP signatures, and proof tokens.
  • Where applicable: Any runtime in the WIMSE architecture, from basic single-service to multi-cloud multi-tenant. WG document past WGLC; the presentation indicated the road likely ends (i.e., publication) before the next meeting.

items.title: WIMSE Workload-to-Workload Authentication with HTTP Signatures
items.text:
IETF 126 (Vienna) — for a networking, security, and identity PM digest Adjacent pick Vienna · 18–24 July 2026

Draft Slides Session recording Materials

Joe Salowey (CyberArk), Yaron Sheffer (Intuit).

  • Why: The application-layer leg of WIMSE — authentication that survives the TLS-terminating proxies and load balancers that dominate real service topologies, which the PM's mesh/ingress world knows well.
  • What: WG draft -04 requesting WGLC. Two changes since -02: the audience indicator moved from a bespoke Wimse-Audience header to a wimse-aud HTTP Signatures parameter (still URI-shaped), letting a recipient confirm the signed message targets it; and a wimse-req-nonce parameter copies the request's random nonce into the signed response, closing a cut-and-paste attack where an on-path malicious proxy splices a valid response into the wrong request — RFC 9421 signs request and response but doesn't bind them.
  • How: RFC 9421 signatures over the Workload Identity Token and request components; response signing optional but recommended given the assumed-malicious-proxy threat model.
  • Where applicable: HTTP-based workload-to-workload traffic only (other protocols use other WIMSE proof mechanisms); needs updating of the draft's examples for the new parameters.
path: WIMSE Workload-to-Workload Authentication with HTTP Signatures

items.title: Workload Identifier Origin Hint for TLS ClientHello
items.text:
IETF 126 (Vienna) — for a networking, security, and identity PM digest Core pick Vienna · 18–24 July 2026

Draft Slides Session recording Materials

Yaroslav Rosomakho, Jonathan Hoyland.

  • Why: mTLS between workloads has an awkward bootstrap: a client can't know which cert/trust domain a server will accept, and servers can't enumerate acceptable trust domains — so deployments burn separate TLS endpoints. This fixes that with a small wire-format change.
  • What: A TLS ClientHello extension carrying one or more workload identifier origins (URI scheme + trust domain, drawn from the WIMSE identifier format). Presence of the extension signals the client won't choke on a CertificateRequest and can produce a certificate for a listed scope; the server uses the hint to decide whether client auth is required and which trust anchors apply.
  • How: An empty list is valid and degenerates into a "request mTLS" flag; for privacy, combine with ECH — empty list in the Outer ClientHello, real scopes in the Inner.
  • Where applicable: Cross-organization workload mTLS (the motivating case: a server with trust relationships with thousands of customer trust domains). Individual draft -02, with the authors asking whether there's appetite for an adoption call — this is the piece that makes WIMSE credentials usable in the TLS handshake.
path: Workload Identifier Origin Hint for TLS ClientHello

items.title: A First Look at Certificate Revocation Latency
items.text:
ACM IMC 2026 — for a Networking, Security, and Identity PM digest Core pick 16 October 2026

Abstract Paper

Authors: Nehal Fooda (University of Maryland), James Larisch (Cloudflare), John Schanck (Mozilla), Bruce Maggs (Duke University and Emerald Innovations), Tijay Chung (Virginia Tech), Dave Levin (University of Maryland)

  • Why: Revocation is the last line of defense after key compromise, and the entire chain has been measured except one leg: how long a CA takes to turn a revocation request into publicly downloadable revocation data. If you run incident response for key compromise, that leg determines your real remediation window.
  • What: The first study of CA-side revocation-data publication latency, covering six of the most popular CAs across both CRL and OCSP, plus end-to-end latency through to Mozilla Firefox's CRLite. Headline: CAs generally operate on tighter bounds than the CA/B Baseline Requirements strictly require, but some major CAs still show up to 24-hour delays from request to availability. (from abstract only)
  • How: A custom tool that requests revocations and polls/downloads the resulting revocation state, varying time of day, distribution mechanism (CRL vs OCSP), reason code, and other factors; separately measures end-to-end propagation into CRLite.
  • Where applicable: Web PKI broadly — relevant to incident-response playbooks (what "revoked" actually means hour-by-hour), and to CA/BR policy work. The CRLite end-to-end numbers are Firefox-specific.
path: A First Look at Certificate Revocation Latency

items.title: A System for Fast, Accurate, and Intuitive Querying of Large-Scale BGP Datasets
items.text:
ACM IMC 2026 — for a Networking, Security, and Identity PM digest Wildcard pick 16 October 2026

Abstract Paper

Authors: Thomas Holterbach, Thomas Alfroy (bgproutes.io), Abbas Mohsenpour (UCLouvain), Thomas Krenc (IIJ Research Laboratory), kc Claffy (CAIDA), Cristel Pelsser (UCLouvain)

  • Why: Not a paper about networking per se, but a strong signal of where infrastructure tooling is heading: LLM-synthesized code over purpose-built compressed data stores. The pipeline — measurement insight (BGP data is highly redundant and compressible) enabling a domain API that an LLM can drive — is a template worth stealing for any large operational dataset you own.
  • What: ChatBGP, a domain-specific chatbot that turns plain-English BGP questions into Python code running against a compressed BGP database, returning answers in seconds rather than the hours that MRT-archive analysis takes. Four contributions: a measurement study showing BGP data is highly redundant and compressible; a database scheme exploiting that redundancy for fast retrieval; an expressive API over the database; and a prompt-engineering scheme guiding ChatGPT to synthesize optimized, minimal-retrieval Python against that API. (from abstract only)
  • How: Redundancy-aware compression plus a query-shaped API, with the LLM constrained to synthesize code that retrieves only the data each query needs.
  • Where applicable: RIPE RIS / RouteViews-class BGP data; aimed at operators diagnosing connectivity issues, researchers, and students. Note the accuracy depends on LLM code synthesis — attractive for triage and exploration, but verify before acting on results in a production incident.
path: A System for Fast, Accurate, and Intuitive Querying of Large-Scale BGP Datasets

items.title: Calypso's Voyage: Charting Traceroute Paths to Submarine Cables
items.text:
ACM IMC 2026 — for a Networking, Security, and Identity PM digest Core pick 16 October 2026

Abstract Paper

Authors: Caleb Wang, Ying Zhang, Qianli Dong, Esteban Carisimo (Northwestern University), Ramakrishnan Durairajan (University of Oregon), Fabian Bustamante (Northwestern University)

  • Why: Submarine cables are the physical substrate of every intercontinental WAN and cloud-region interconnect. Knowing which cables a path actually rides — and which cables are disproportionately stressed — is foundational to reasoning about interconnect capacity, redundancy, and geopolitical/physical risk.
  • What: Calypso, a framework that maps traceroute paths to the specific submarine cables they traverse, plus Route Stress, a traceroute-derived metric estimating the relative importance of individual cables. Validated through expert validation, failure analysis, and regional case studies demonstrating SCN dependency discovery. (from abstract only)
  • How: Integrates cable ownership records, routing metadata, and geographic constraints to infer cable usage despite the opacity of the submarine cable network — handling complications like route virtualization and inland infrastructure before/after landing points.
  • Where applicable: Research and policy tool rather than an operational one; inference-based, so its accuracy is bounded by public ownership/routing data. Directly useful for WAN/interconnect planners assessing which cable systems their traffic depends on and for resilience studies.
path: Calypso's Voyage: Charting Traceroute Paths to Submarine Cables

items.title: Characterizing the Deployment of the STIR/SHAKEN Telephone Network PKI
items.text:
ACM IMC 2026 — for a Networking, Security, and Identity PM digest Adjacent pick 16 October 2026

Abstract Paper

Authors: Hamim Hamid, David Adei, Bradley Reaves (North Carolina State University)

  • Why: A rare natural experiment in federated identity infrastructure: a brand-new, industry-wide, federated PKI mandated and deployed in under two years. For anyone designing or operating federated trust frameworks (and thinking about PKI hygiene generally), the failure modes documented here are the canonical ones to design against.
  • What: A longitudinal study (Nov 2021–Feb 2026) of STIR/SHAKEN deployment from signaling data on 7.75 million calls collected by telephone honeypots. Rapid adoption, but pervasive standards non-compliance: providers signing calls with root keys, and originating calls with pre-signed attestations copied from unrelated calls. Practices and compliance are improving, but only at a modest pace. (from abstract only)
  • How: Longitudinal honeypot signaling-data analysis across standards compliance, CA practices, and provider call signatures/metadata.
  • Where applicable: US telephone network, mandate-specific context. The transferable content is the pattern — what a rushed federated PKI rollout actually looks like in practice — which generalizes to any federated trust ecosystem.
path: Characterizing the Deployment of the STIR/SHAKEN Telephone Network PKI

items.title: Eadem, Sed Aliter: Investigating the Instability of Browser Fingerprinting
items.text:
ACM IMC 2026 — for a Networking, Security, and Identity PM digest Wildcard pick 16 October 2026

Abstract Paper

Authors: Xu Lin, Jacob Anthony Eckfeldt (Washington State University), Shujiang Wu, Pengfei Sun (F5, Inc.), Jason Polakis (University of Illinois Chicago)

  • Why: Browser fingerprinting increasingly shows up as an authentication and fraud signal, so its actual stability matters to identity work. This paper subverts the community's established understanding: fingerprints are inherently unstable even when nothing about the device changes.
  • What: An in-depth analysis of fingerprints from users authenticating to high-value web services, revealing that prevalent attributes change even in stable execution environments (e.g., minor deviations in browsers' floating-point arithmetic or HTML element-size calculations) — a fundamental obstacle to fingerprinting's real-world effectiveness. It then proposes Predictive-FP, an adaptive strategy that uses historical population-wide information to anticipate unstable values and ignores ephemeral attributes, re-identifying ~51% more devices after 6 months than state of the art. A configurable privacy-preserving browser extension counteracts the technique on non-allowlisted sites. (from abstract only)
  • How: Longitudinal attribute-stability analysis over a production authentication dataset, followed by adaptive prediction modeling that separates stable-in-principle attributes from ephemeral ones.
  • Where applicable: Web services using device fingerprinting for auth or fraud. Dual-edged finding: it both improves fingerprint-based re-identification (a privacy risk the authors address) and tells you not to over-trust raw fingerprint stability in your own systems.
path: Eadem, Sed Aliter: Investigating the Instability of Browser Fingerprinting

items.title: EU Digital Sovereignty in Practice: A Technical Assessment of Digital Infrastructure Dependencies
items.text:
ACM IMC 2026 — for a Networking, Security, and Identity PM digest Adjacent pick 16 October 2026

Abstract Paper

Authors: Jürgen Brandl (TU Wien), Florian Holzbauer (IT:U), Aaron Kaplan (European Commission, DIGIT S.2), Johanna Ullrich (IT:U), Adrian Dabrowski (University of Applied Sciences Technikum Wien)

  • Why: Quantifies, for the first time systematically, how dependent EU institutions are on non-EU infrastructure. If your organization has EU regulatory exposure (NIS2, DORA) or sells into regulated EU sectors, this is a concrete dependency map of your customers' environment.
  • What: Empirical analysis of 1,988 domains across government, banking, media, and higher education in all 27 EU member states, across six sovereignty dimensions: nameservers, web hosting, external resources, certificate authorities, email, and SaaS. Only 61 domains (3%) show no detectable non-EU dependency. Key exposures: CDN/DDoS services, cloud-hosted email, office suites, and TLS certificates. A neat methodological detail: internal third-party SaaS deployments are detected via domain verification tokens. (from abstract only)
  • How: Collection of DNS records, TLS certificates, and HTTP responses; dependencies classified by criticality and EU/non-EU status, spanning infrastructure through application layer.
  • Where applicable: EU-regulated sectors specifically. The dependency categories (CDN, email, CA, SaaS) transfer well to any sovereignty/supply-chain assessment exercise; open dataset released for replication and monitoring.
path: EU Digital Sovereignty in Practice: A Technical Assessment of Digital Infrastructure Dependencies

items.title: Honey Configs: Measuring The Emerging Exploitation of Cloud IP Address Reuse
items.text:
ACM IMC 2026 — for a Networking, Security, and Identity PM digest Core pick 16 October 2026

Abstract Paper

Authors: Eric Pauley (Virginia Tech & Terrace Networks), Yohan Beugin (University of Wisconsin-Madison), Paul Barford (University of Wisconsin-Madison), Patrick Traynor (University of Florida), Patrick McDaniel (University of Wisconsin-Madison)

  • Why: The 2021 "cloud IP address reuse" vulnerability class (tenants pinning trust — allowlists, firewall rules, cert SANs — to public IPs that the provider will re-allocate to someone else) is directly relevant to anyone operating multi-cloud infrastructure. This is one of the few papers measuring both whether defenders fixed it and whether attackers are actually exploiting it.
  • What: A three-year longitudinal study of defender and attacker response. The headline findings are bad on both sides: 60% of originally-observed vulnerabilities were still present years after disclosure, and exploitation has increased 39x since the original disclosures. The active measurement surfaces a global, multi-cloud adversarial apparatus that identifies and exploits latent configurations — hosting malicious content, mal-issuing TLS certificates, and executing cookie-based attacks on target sites. (from abstract only)
  • How: Combines passive data (the DScope Internet telescope, certificate transparency logs) with a new active technique — honey configurations — deliberately deployed configurations that act as tripwires to directly measure exploitation rather than infer it.
  • Where applicable: Any organization using public cloud IPs with IP-bound trust relationships. Broadly applicable across major cloud providers; the attacker observations are from research vantage points, so treat specific attacker behaviors as a lower bound rather than a census.
path: Honey Configs: Measuring The Emerging Exploitation of Cloud IP Address Reuse

items.title: Lightscope: Turning Production Machines into Telescopes and Honeypots
items.text:
ACM IMC 2026 — for a Networking, Security, and Identity PM digest Wildcard pick 16 October 2026

Abstract Paper

Authors: Eric Kapitanski, Jelena Mirkovic (USC Information Sciences Institute)

  • Why: A genuinely new vantage point for Internet security measurement. The insight — attackers avoid known dark-space sensors and behave differently toward production endpoints — means your own production fleet is an underused sensor, and this work proves it quantitatively.
  • What: LightScope, a lightweight application that unifies passive Layer-4 observation with selective proxying to a remote Layer-7 honeypot, running on unused ports of production servers. Two months of data from 235 deployments shows scanner populations, port-targeting profiles, and post-login behaviors only partially visible from dark-space telescopes and honeynets — including 64,686 scanners observed by LightScope and no other vantage point. (from abstract only)
  • How: Embeds measurement on production hosts themselves, using a subset of unused ports; selective L7 proxying to a remote honeypot captures post-exploit behavior without putting production at risk.
  • Where applicable: Any production fleet with unused ports — broadly applicable technique, not org-specific. Worth understanding even if you never deploy it, because it changes how you interpret coverage gaps in your own threat telemetry.
path: Lightscope: Turning Production Machines into Telescopes and Honeypots

items.title: Mind the Gap: Policy vs Reality in Post-Quantum TLS Deployment
items.text:
ACM IMC 2026 — for a Networking, Security, and Identity PM digest Core pick 16 October 2026

Abstract Paper

Authors: Nimesha Wickramasinghe (UNSW), Frank Li (Georgia Tech), Sanjay Jha (UNSW), Arash Shaghaghi (UNSW)

  • Why: If you own or influence TLS-terminated services, the PQC migration is now an operational question, not a planning exercise. This paper tells you where the Internet actually is versus where government roadmaps say it should be — useful both for your own rollout sequencing and for evaluating vendor readiness claims.
  • What: Three measurement rounds (July 2025–March 2026) covering one million public HTTPS endpoints, with over two billion TLS 1.3 handshakes from 11 distributed vantage points. Key findings: every observed post-quantum negotiation converged on the same hybrid — X25519MLKEM768 — but there is no verified deployment of post-quantum signature algorithms for authentication; hybrid adoption is concentrated in managed infrastructure providers; country/sector deployment does not track published transition timelines; and — counter to earlier experimental studies — hybrid key exchange showed no meaningful latency penalty in Internet settings. (from abstract only)
  • How: Large-scale active TLS handshake measurement characterizing cryptographic negotiation behavior, cross-referenced against endpoint attribution (provider, country, sector) and against a survey of published PQC transition policies.
  • Where applicable: Public-facing HTTPS broadly. The latency finding is calibrated to Internet RTT regimes — it does not tell you the handshake cost inside a datacenter fabric, so don't extrapolate it to internal service-to-service TLS.
path: Mind the Gap: Policy vs Reality in Post-Quantum TLS Deployment

items.title: namefill: Synthesizing DNS Naming Conventions
items.text:
ACM IMC 2026 — for a Networking, Security, and Identity PM digest Adjacent pick 16 October 2026

Abstract Paper

Authors: Joel Sommers (Colgate University), Calvin Kranig, Wei-Shiang Wung, Paul Barford (University of Wisconsin-Madison), Mark Crovella (Boston University), Eric Pauley (Virginia Tech & Terrace Networks)

  • Why: DNS naming conventions leak infrastructure topology and operational structure — this work makes them machine-usable both for asset discovery and for auditing your own records. For anyone who cares about IPAM hygiene or infrastructure enumeration, this is a genuinely new tool capability.
  • What: namefill uses programming by example to synthesize executable functions that summarize DNS naming conventions. Unlike regexes, the synthesized functions can generate predicted FQDNs, enabling active probing for undiscovered names and systematic auditing of existing records. Applied to 1.2 billion PTR records: 313K distinct conventions across 254K domains, covering 67.7% of IP/FQDN pairs (complementary to geotoken-focused tools). Found 991 misconfigurations (43 verified with operators) and, as a discovery tool, surfaced 194M previously unrecorded forward DNS names from 2.76M training names — a 70× expansion. (from abstract only)
  • How: Programming-by-example synthesis over PTR records; validation against CAIDA's ITDK dataset; systematic anomaly detection using the synthesized functions; active enumeration queries for discovery.
  • Where applicable: General technique — researchers and operators auditing reverse DNS or discovering infrastructure. Note the dual-use nature: the same discovery capability that finds your misconfigurations finds your unrecorded hosts.

items.title: Replicability: Challenging the Myth of Randomness Patterns in Encrypted Traffic
items.text:
ACM IMC 2026 — for a Networking, Security, and Identity PM digest Wildcard pick 16 October 2026

Abstract Paper

Authors: Timofey Shpakov (ETH Zürich), Martin Burkhart (armasuisse Science and Technology), Laurent Vanbever (ETH Zürich)

  • Why: A methodological correction with real consequences: several recent studies (most prominently the often-cited ET-BERT) claim encrypted traffic exhibits detectable randomness deficiencies usable for application classification. If those evidentiary foundations are artifacts, a chunk of the encrypted-traffic-classification literature — and vendor claims built on it — rests on sand.
  • What: A systematic replication of the randomness experiments, re-implemented with the NIST Statistical Test Suite on encrypted traffic generated under controlled conditions. The reported statistical signals do not provide sufficient evidence of non-randomness beyond what statistical hypothesis testing and finite-sample effects would produce. Observed test failures and discriminative patterns are consistent with methodological artifacts: improper aggregation, p-value misinterpretation, and train/test information leakage. (from abstract only)
  • How: Controlled-condition re-implementation of prior experiments, examining the evidentiary step — the claim that detectable patterns exist in ciphertext — rather than the downstream classifiers.
  • Where applicable: Anyone evaluating encrypted-traffic classification research or products, or building on randomness-based classification themselves. The authors are careful to scope the critique: it says nothing about methods exploiting metadata, packet sizes, timing, or other side channels.
path: Replicability: Challenging the Myth of Randomness Patterns in Encrypted Traffic

items.title: RScope: Unveiling Global ROV Deployments and Dependencies in the Post-ROV Era
items.text:
ACM IMC 2026 — for a Networking, Security, and Identity PM digest Core pick 16 October 2026

Abstract Paper

Authors: Weitong Li, Yongzhe Xu (Virginia Tech), Mingwei Zhang, Vasileios Giotsas (Cloudflare), Taejoong Chung (Virginia Tech)

  • Why: RPKI/ROV is the routing-security mechanism the industry is standardizing on, and this paper answers the question every operator should ask before relying on it: who is actually filtering, versus who merely looks protected because their upstream does? Promoted from Adjacent: empirical routing-security deployment data is core to network-security work.
  • What: RScope maps ROV deployment and dependencies across 21,827 ASes. Findings: 1,127 ASes actively deploy ROV themselves; 1,815 rely purely on upstream filtering, and 69.6% of those "protected" ASes remain vulnerable to local hijacks. Leverage is starkly concentrated: enabling ROV in the top 100 ASes protects 27.6% of networks, while disabling it in Tier-1s exposes 23.8% to hijacks. Operationally notable: router enforcement lags ROA updates by 37 minutes on average. (from abstract only)
  • How: Dynamically manipulates Route Origin Authorizations from controlled publication points to isolate the effect of individual Relying Party (RP) servers — selectively invalidating prefixes for specific RPs and probing resulting connectivity changes — which sidesteps the classic confound between local ROV adoption and upstream filtering.
  • Where applicable: Global BGP routing. The framework requires controlled ROA publication points (research-grade setup, tools and data open-sourced), but the findings — which ASes actually filter, where RP fragility lies — are directly consumable by anyone planning RPKI rollout or assessing hijack exposure.
path: RScope: Unveiling Global ROV Deployments and Dependencies in the Post-ROV Era

items.title: Securing the Missing Link: Encrypted Recursive-to-Authoritative DNS in the Wild
items.text:
ACM IMC 2026 — for a Networking, Security, and Identity PM digest Adjacent pick 16 October 2026

Abstract Paper

Authors: Yevheniya Nosyk, Simon Fernandez, Andrzej Duda, Maciej Korczyński (KOR Labs / Univ. Grenoble Alpes, CNRS, Grenoble INP, LIG)

  • Why: The recursive-to-authoritative hop is the last unencrypted DNS link, and it is the one state censors have demonstratively used for traffic analysis and response injection. RFC 9539 (opportunistic ADoT/ADoQ) is the mechanism intended to close it — this paper tells you how much of the Internet actually speaks it.
  • What: A measurement of RFC 9539 deployment covering both recursive resolvers and authoritative nameservers. Bottom line: fewer than 1% of registered domains (3.1M) support authoritative DoT or DoQ, with one provider accounting for the vast majority of those deployments. (from abstract only)
  • How: Probing resolvers and authoritative nameservers for opportunistic DNS-over-TLS / DNS-over-QUIC support per the RFC 9539 mechanism.
  • Where applicable: DNS operators weighing authoritative-side encryption; also useful context for standards bodies tracking adoption. The near-absence of deployment means privacy-sensitive resolvers currently get almost no recursive-to-authoritative confidentiality in practice.
path: Securing the Missing Link: Encrypted Recursive-to-Authoritative DNS in the Wild

items.title: Split Alignment: Diffusing SPF Vulnerabilities With DMARC
items.text:
ACM IMC 2026 — for a Networking, Security, and Identity PM digest Adjacent pick 16 October 2026

Abstract Paper Recording

Authors: Muhammad Hamza, Eric Pauley, Taejoong Chung (Virginia Tech), Mattijs Jonker, Raffaele Sommese (University of Twente), Simon Fernandez, Olivier Hureau (Univ. Grenoble Alpes, CNRS, Grenoble INP, LIG)

Video

  • Why: Authentication protocols don't compose safely — SPF weaknesses, when layered with DMARC's organizational context, can enable organization-wide spoofing. This is a good study of how layered auth protocols amplify each other's flaws, with a deployable fix.
  • What: A comprehensive empirical analysis finding 528k vulnerable SPF policies which, paired with DMARC, enable spoofing of 79k domain hierarchies. The proposed mitigation, Split Alignment, is a configurational technique that protects established sending domains from all SPF failures anywhere in their hierarchy. The validation methodology also surfaced critical DMARC authentication-flow bugs in four major email services (disclosed). (from abstract only)
  • How: Large-scale dataset analysis of layered email-auth policies; the mitigation is pure configuration — no protocol change — validated with a reproducible security-and-deliverability test methodology.
  • Where applicable: Any organization that sends email at scale and uses SPF/DMARC. Broadly applicable since it is a domain-owner-side configuration technique; the disclosed service bugs show some receivers may mis-handle the configuration, so roll out with the deliverability validation in mind.
path: Split Alignment: Diffusing SPF Vulnerabilities With DMARC

items.title: Taming DNS Responses: A Measurement Study of Response Size and Its Impact
items.text:
ACM IMC 2026 — for a Networking, Security, and Identity PM digest Adjacent pick 16 October 2026

Abstract Paper

Authors: Zihan Li, Wenhao Wu, Zhaohua Wang, Yu Tian, Chuan Gao, Qinxin Li, Yiming Xia, Zhenyu Li (Chinese Academy of Sciences)

  • Why: DNS is increasingly a carrier for structured metadata and service-discovery data, and that growth directly feeds UDP amplification risk. If you operate resolvers or reason about DDoS surface, the global response-size picture matters.
  • What: A year-long measurement of response-size behavior across roughly one million open resolvers. Findings: resolver-enforced UDP response-size limits cluster around a small set of common values; configuration changes at major public resolvers propagate across the ecosystem; and regional differences in limits create uneven amplification risk, exposing limits of existing static and upstream-based defenses. Proposes Adaptive Response Scaling (ARS), a lightweight dynamic response-control mechanism claimed to reduce amplification by over 70% while preserving DNS functionality. (from abstract only)
  • How: Longitudinal measurement of resolver response-size limits across the open-resolver population, plus analysis of how major-resolver configuration changes propagate.
  • Where applicable: DNS operators and public resolvers broadly. ARS is a proposal evaluated by the authors, not a deployed standard — the measurement findings are solid ground, the mitigation is directionally promising.
path: Taming DNS Responses: A Measurement Study of Response Size and Its Impact

items.title: The Disputed Internet: Quantifying Fragmentation in the IPv6 Internet
items.text:
ACM IMC 2026 — for a Networking, Security, and Identity PM digest Adjacent pick 16 October 2026

Abstract Paper

Authors: Vivian Band (University of Glasgow), Romain Fontugne (IIJ Research Laboratory)

  • Why: As your dual-stack footprint grows, IPv6 reachability is not a clean mirror of IPv4 — peering disputes (the Cogent–Hurricane Electric case being the exemplar) fragment the IPv6 topology. Anyone running IPv6-only or IPv6-preferred infrastructure should understand this failure mode.
  • What: Quantifies IPv6 fragmentation via BGP-measured reachability differences between large transit providers, and uses forward DNS data to estimate the impact on popular website reachability. Findings: IPv6 fragmentation is substantial relative to the unified IPv4 topology, is worsening over time, and an increasing number of popular sites are partially reachable in IPv6. IPv4 fallback currently masks the user-facing impact. (from abstract only)
  • How: BGP-based reachability comparison across large transits in both protocols, plus forward-DNS-based estimation of popular-site impact.
  • Where applicable: Global Internet; most relevant if you operate or depend on IPv6-heavy paths. The mitigating reality today is happy-eyeballs-style fallback, so treat this as a structural risk to monitor rather than a current outage driver.
path: The Disputed Internet: Quantifying Fragmentation in the IPv6 Internet

items.title: Waiting at the front door: Continuous monitoring of latency in the host network stack
items.text:
ACM IMC 2026 — for a Networking, Security, and Identity PM digest Core pick 16 October 2026

Abstract Paper

Authors: Simon Sundberg, Anna Brunstrom (Karlstad University), Simone Ferlin-Reiter (Red Hat and Karlstad University), Jesper Dangaard Brouer (Cloudflare), Toke Høiland-Jørgensen (Red Hat)

  • Why: Once network paths drop into sub-millisecond territory — RDMA-era fabrics, co-located services — the host itself (NIC–CPU interconnect, kernel network stack, scheduling) becomes a first-order latency source. This is the paper at the intersection of your Linux datapath-internals interest and production reality, with authors from Red Hat and Cloudflare. Promoted from Adjacent: kernel-stack latency instrumentation in a production CDN is squarely core.
  • What: netstacklat, a monitoring tool that continuously captures latency at multiple points in the host network path, from the earliest parts of the Linux kernel network stack through to the application's read. Evaluated across 144 HTTP workload variations (Nginx and Apache), with monitoring overhead inflating tail latency by no more than ~6%, versus >100% for previous monitoring solutions. Includes initial findings from deployment in Cloudflare's global CDN. (from abstract only)
  • How: Lightweight instrumentation at several points along the host network path, designed for continuous production use rather than one-off tracing; testbed evaluation for overhead characterization plus real deployment experience.
  • Where applicable: Linux hosts running latency-sensitive services. The deployment context is Cloudflare's CDN, but the technique is general Linux tooling — applicable to any production fleet where you need to attribute latency between NIC, kernel, and application.
path: Waiting at the front door: Continuous monitoring of latency in the host network stack

items.title: When BGP Goes MAD: Multi-Scale Anomaly Detection in Internet Routing
items.text:
ACM IMC 2026 — for a Networking, Security, and Identity PM digest Adjacent pick 16 October 2026

Abstract Paper

Authors: Justin Loye, Romain Fontugne (IIJ Research Laboratory), Esteban Bautista (Univ. Littoral Cote d'Opale, LISIC)

  • Why: Outage and route-leak detection that operators could actually run — near real-time, unsupervised, and without large training datasets — has been a persistent gap. This is a credible attempt to close it.
  • What: MADBGP, an anomaly-detection pipeline combining (i) a temporal-graph modeling of the AS-level Internet, (ii) QuickRIB, a scalable tool for generating temporal graphs from public BGP data, and (iii) an extension of the MAD temporal-graph anomaly-detection method to weighted graphs, applied to real BGP anomalies for the first time. On ten major BGP events (outages and route leaks at different scales), it reportedly significantly outperforms IODA's BGP results. (from abstract only)
  • How: Unsupervised, multi-scale detection over a temporal graph representation of the AS-level Internet built from public BGP feeds, operating near real-time.
  • Where applicable: Network operators and researchers monitoring global routing health; consumes public BGP data, so no special vantage required. The outperformance claim is relative to IODA's BGP stream on selected events — validate on your own telemetry before operational reliance.
path: When BGP Goes MAD: Multi-Scale Anomaly Detection in Internet Routing

  • How: Unknown; at that scale this is necessarily automation and policy engineering around massive tables — the deck has the architecture.
  • Where applicable: The 26M figure signals a very large content/anycast or transit platform, so the scale is org-specific; the tooling and automation patterns partially transfer.
path: Transforming BGP operations to serve the best prefix out of 26 million

KubeCon + CloudNativeCon Europe 2025 (London) digest Wildcard pick London · 1–4 April 2025

  • Why: A genuine crossover between cloud-native tooling and physical hardware testing — using Kubernetes-native CI (Tekton) to drive real firmware flashing, booting, and hardware interfaces (CAN bus, serial, video) rather than simulating them. Not a fit for the PM's networking/identity focus directly, but a "cloud-native reaches into physical hardware" pattern worth having on the radar.
  • What: Jumpstarter, an open-source project connecting a software factory (CI/CD) to physical hardware, automating firmware testing on real devices from within Kubernetes. (from abstract only)
  • How: Tekton Pipelines and GitLab drive device leasing and automation for tasks like firmware flashing and booting, interfacing through serial, CAN bus, audio, and video; Eclipse Che supports the dev/debug loop. (from abstract only)
  • Where applicable: Embedded/firmware development for hardware devices (developed with an automotive manufacturer); the pattern of "Kubernetes-native CI orchestrating physical device labs" generalizes beyond automotive to any hardware-in-the-loop testing need.

items.title: Beyond Classical Cryptography: Building Quantum-Resistant Cloud Native Infrastructure With SPIFFE
items.text:
KubeCon + CloudNativeCon Europe 2025 (London) digest Core pick London · 1–4 April 2025

Abstract Recording

Andrés Vega, M42 & Hugo Landau, Messier42 — Core

Video

  • Why: A concrete, working demonstration of post-quantum cryptography threaded through the exact identity/networking stack the PM tracks (SPIFFE/SPIRE, Cilium, Envoy) rather than a standards-committee abstraction — a preview of what PQ migration actually touches in a real cluster.
  • What: A live demo of end-to-end post-quantum cryptography in Kubernetes: PQC-enabled SPIRE issuing Kyber KEM / Dilithium3 X.509 certificates, quantum-resistant mTLS, and Cilium L7 policy enforcement over that identity. (from abstract only)
  • How: Deploys PQC-enabled SPIRE, Cilium, and Envoy together — Kyber for key exchange, Dilithium3 for certificate signatures — with Cilium network policies doing L7 filtering and Envoy handling inter-node mTLS with the PQ algorithms. (from abstract only)
  • Where applicable: General technique for any SPIFFE/SPIRE + Cilium/Envoy deployment; depends on NIST's 2024 PQC algorithm choices (ML-KEM/Kyber, ML-DSA/Dilithium) holding up, which is the same assumption the IETF PQ-migration work (see the ietf-122 digest) is built on.
path: Beyond Classical Cryptography: Building Quantum-Resistant Cloud Native Infrastructure With SPIFFE

items.title: CNCF Project Demos | BGP Beyond Loadbalancers with MetalLB and FRR-K8s

items.title: Debugging Envoy Tunnels: A Deep Dive
items.text:
KubeCon + CloudNativeCon Europe 2025 (London) digest Adjacent pick London · 1–4 April 2025

Carlos Sanchez & Alexandra Stoica, Adobe — Adjacent

  • Why: A practitioner's account of a specific, painful operational pattern — Envoy tunnels with mTLS connecting Kubernetes pods to on-prem/customer infrastructure — with real troubleshooting scenarios rather than a theoretical overview.

items.title: Encryption, Identities, and Everything in Between; Building Secure Kubernetes Networks

KubeCon + CloudNativeCon Europe 2025 (London) digest Core pick London · 1–4 April 2025
