items.title: Hands-on ASPA: Configuration and Lessons Learned
items.text:
LACNIC 45 — for the Networking PM digest Core pick 28 May 2026

Slides Recording

Carlos Martínez (LACNIC), Guillermo Cicileo (LACNIC)

VideoPDF

  • Why: ASPA is the next deployment wave in routing security — LACNIC's own member-assembly report lists ASPA object support as its 2026 RPKI roadmap item, and the NRO's 2026 RPKI program explicitly aims to deploy ASPA — and this hands-on session connects directly to the hijack case above.
  • What: A fundamentals-plus-practice session on ASPA (Autonomous System Provider Authorization, IETF sidrops drafts): a new RPKI object in which an ASN cryptographically declares its authorized upstream providers (an AS0 ASPA declares "no providers," e.g., Tier-1s or route-server-only clients). It detects forged-AS-path/origin hijacks and mitigates global route-leak propagation, reusing the existing RPKI architecture (validators, repositories, rpki-rtr) without adding router-side cryptography.
  • How: ASPA formalizes valley-free routing: for each adjacent AS pair in an AS_PATH, the validator checks the customer's attestation — P (declared provider), nP (AS exists in the attestation but this neighbor is not a provider → lateral/customer hop), nA (no attestation published) — enabling both upstream and downstream path verification.
  • Where applicable: Any operator already running RPKI can adopt ASPA on the same infrastructure; benefits scale with ecosystem-wide adoption, which is still early (IETF draft stage). Pairs with the case study: RPKI origin validation alone would not have stopped the AS28001 impersonation; path verification is the missing half.
path: Hands-on ASPA: Configuration and Lessons Learned

items.title: Impacts of LLM Traffic on Peering Strategies
items.text:
LACNIC 45 — for the Networking PM digest Core pick 28 May 2026

Slides Recording

Tomás Lynch (AS20473 — presents from his own network's experience)

VideoPDF

  • Why: GPU/LLM clusters create a new traffic-profile class that changes both DC fabric architecture and external interconnect economics — directly relevant to the PM's DC fabric and DC/WAN interconnect work, and a rare first-person operator account rather than a projection.
  • What: How LLM traffic actually lands on a network. GPU clusters are built as two fabrics: a converged frontend leaf-spine (north-south inference and dataset-ingestion traffic, usually oversubscribed, 100GE/400GE at the edge) and a non-blocking backend leaf-spine (east-west training only), plus high-performance storage. The two LLM traffic classes behave oppositely: inference is low-volume, constant, bidirectional, geographically dispersed ("looks like traditional traffic" → latency-driven peering via IXPs and PNIs); dataset ingestion is massive, bursty, mostly inbound, concentrated — and it drives the 95th-percentile transit bill (→ cost-driven strategy: rate-limit/schedule ingestion with customers, raise minimum commitments, add/rebalance transit, direct connects to GPU customers). GPU frontend traffic itself breaks the classic compute sinusoid: spiky outbound vs near-constant inbound.
  • How: 24-hour traffic-graph comparisons of GPU vs traditional compute frontend patterns from the presenter's own network, then derived peering tactics per traffic class. Side observations: ingestion bursts can trip DDoS-detection thresholds (validate them), and mixed flow sizes make congestion management critical.
  • Where applicable: Operators serving GPU/AI customers and DC providers designing frontend/backend fabric separation. The traffic-profile taxonomy generalizes; the numbers are one operator's network, so scale-dependence should be assumed.
path: Impacts of LLM Traffic on Peering Strategies

items.title: IP Geolocation Update
items.text:
LACNIC 45 — for the Networking PM digest Wildcard pick 28 May 2026

Slides Recording

Lee Howard (presenting the IAB workshop report)

VideoPDF

  • Why: The IAB just ran a dedicated workshop because IP geolocation is breaking under CGNAT, satellite networks, and privacy proxies — and the remediation path runs through RPKI-signed geofeeds (RFC 9632), tying into the routing-PKI world the PM already follows.
  • What: A report on the IAB's December 2025 IP Geolocation Workshop (30 accepted submissions, 67 participants): why geolocation is used (CDN/edge selection, content licensing, fraud, compliance), current mechanisms (RFC 8805 CSV geofeeds plus RFC 9632 RPKI-based discovery and authentication), and the gaps: no ontology for what a location claim even means (user vs. egress vs. infrastructure vs. jurisdiction); >95% accuracy at country level but sharp degradation at city/coordinate level; CGNAT/mobile/satellite mapping users to gateway locations; "digital sinkholes"; stale data persisting after IPv4 block transfers; no feedback loop for ISPs to correct third-party databases; and privacy tension (IP-as-PII, VPN/proxy interactions).
  • How: Workshop-report format — use cases, current mechanisms, gaps, and future directions (richer geofeed expressiveness; new mechanisms that don't rely on implicit signals, e.g., authenticated and consent-based HTTP headers) — intended to seed future IETF/IRTF work.
  • Where applicable: Anyone whose services, compliance, or CDN/edge logic depend on IP geolocation, and operators who should be publishing accurate geofeeds. This is direction-setting standardization content, not deployable tech today.

items.title: LightScope: Turning Unused Production Ports into Global Network Telescopes and Honeypots
items.text:
LACNIC 45 — for the Networking PM digest Adjacent pick 28 May 2026

Slides Recording

Eric Kapitanski (USC Information Sciences Institute; advisor Jelena Mirkovic)

VideoPDF

  • Why: A genuinely new measurement vantage point for the network-security side of the PM's portfolio: as IPv4 dark space shrinks, this turns closed ports on live production hosts into telescope/honeypot sensors, with evidence it sees attackers that dark-space telescopes and honeynets miss entirely.
  • What: A lightweight sensor (median 7.5% of one core / 191 MB RAM; 295+ nodes) deployed across 27 domains and 243 internet-reachable endpoints (UCSD 57, Internet2 46, SDSC 35, Nebraska 28, Amazon 15, plus DFN, SURF, Verizon, Deutsche Telekom and others). It answers TCP SYN attempts to unused ports on in-use IPs — addresses attackers already know about — forwarding sessions to an ISI honeypot with the adopter's IP anonymized (IRB-approved). Findings: scanning behavior clusters by Jaccard similarity of port sets (broad multi-domain scanners vs targeted single-domain scanning); LightScope observes scanner IPs exclusive to any passive telescope or residential honeynet, and exclusivity increases down the attack funnel (scanners → attackers that log in and run commands). Cross-check against commercial intel: of 13,667 IPs that logged into honeypot ports and ran commands, GreyNoise classed 74% as malicious and AbuseIPDB recommended blocking 58%.
  • How: Agent on production hosts captures connection attempts to unused ports; analysis quantifies per-endpoint visibility and overlap with telescopes/honeynets using exclusivity and Jaccard metrics.
  • Where applicable: Research and CSIRT measurement programs; any network can adopt the sensor. Limitations: TCP SYN only, no UDP or backscatter, deliberately capped resource use. The broader implication matters to anyone reasoning from telescope data alone: dark-space-only visibility is increasingly incomplete.
path: LightScope: Turning Unused Production Ports into Global Network Telescopes and Honeypots

items.title: Routing under siege: how traffic engineering decisions facilitate prefix hijackings
items.text:
LACNIC 45 — for the Networking PM digest Core pick 28 May 2026

Slides Recording

Renan Paredes Barreto (Universidade Federal do Rio Grande — FURG; slides also credit Leandro Bertholdo and Pedro Marcos)

VideoPDF

  • Why: Controlled, real-Internet experiments that quantify how operators' own traffic engineering choices change hijack exposure — turning received wisdom ("prepends are harmless") into measured numbers with direct configuration implications.
  • What: Using the PEERING testbed (real BGP announcements from five PoPs: Amsterdam, UFMG, Seoul, Johannesburg, and a Northeast-US site), the authors ran type-0 hijack experiments in controlled windows (Nov 2024–Feb 2025) against 127,421 responsive data-plane targets across 45,462 ASes, measuring both control-plane reach (RIS Live monitors) and data-plane impact (ping responses). Key results: increasing AS-path prepends by the victim increases hijack impact; ASes can be significantly impacted even without prepending; more-specific-prefix hijacks affect even well-connected ASes with fairly uniform impact; and impact varies materially by PoP/location.
  • How: Victim and hijacker announce the same prefix from different PEERING sites; impact percentage = monitors/hosts selecting the hijacker's path vs. the victim's; each iteration varies TE technique (prepend count, prefix length, selective announcements), AS locations, and connectivity.
  • Where applicable: Any operator using prepends or managing announcement granularity — the practical lesson (heavy prepending measurably increases sub-prefix hijack exposure) is broadly applicable. Constraints: IPv4 only, type-0 hijacks only, no ROAs created — findings are scenario-specific rather than universal.
path: Routing under siege: how traffic engineering decisions facilitate prefix hijackings

items.title: The annoying Noisy BGP Speakers
items.text:
LACNIC 45 — for the Networking PM digest Adjacent pick 28 May 2026

Slides Recording

Alejandro Acosta and Elisa Peirano (both LACNIC, per slide contact addresses)

VideoPDF

  • Why: Quantifies BGP update noise with a simple, reproducible per-ASN metric — useful for NOC hygiene, route-server operations, and for grounding "BGP churn" conversations with peers in data.
  • What: Processing 2.2M+ BGP messages from RRC24 (Montevideo) and RRC15 (São Paulo), covering 86,398 ASNs and ~1.44M IPv4/IPv6 prefixes: the mean noise index is ~1,547 updates per announced prefix versus a median of 234 — noise is heavily concentrated in a small set of participants; IPv6 is measurably noisier than IPv4; and most of the noisiest ASNs belong to organizations outside the LAC region. Causes cited: software bugs, misconfigurations (notably missing update-source), and hardware/DoS-induced session instability. Mitigations: route filtering, correct update-source, prefix limits on peers, dampening, and moderate timer tuning.
  • How: A per-ASN noise factor (updates per announced prefix) following the SIDN Labs "Noisy Neighbours" methodology (CNSM 2025), computed with Python (mrtparser, pandas, numpy) against NRO delegated-extended files for country mapping.
  • Where applicable: IXP/route-server operators and any NOG doing BGP hygiene; methodology is reproducible from public collectors. Country-level conclusions are vantage-point-specific (two LAC collectors).

items.title: The Internet ASN graph
items.text:
LACNIC 45 — for the Networking PM digest Adjacent pick 28 May 2026

Slides Recording

Claudio Risso (Universidad de la República, Uruguay), Carlos Martínez (LACNIC)

VideoPDF

  • Why: A framework for building structural models of the Internet's AS-level graph — relevant to the PM's BGP-internals interest for policy simulation (RPKI/ASPA/ROA scenarios), topology reasoning, and understanding measurement vantage-point bias.
  • What: A methodology plus first results: reconstruct the AS-level graph from a full month of MRT data (24 RIPE RIS + 4 RouteViews collectors, April 2025). Raw graph: ~86,400 ASes / ~750,000 edges, 36.8% degree-1 leaves, mean degree 16.6 — Internet transit is only ~0.02% as dense as a full mesh. After reducing to the transit-only graph (84,497 nodes / 389,442 adjacencies) and homeomorphic reduction, the "backbone" is a 2-connected component of ~29,923 nodes, with dense cliques of 31 and 35 ASes (disconnecting one member of the 35-clique requires 34 simultaneous failures). The work also classifies node lifecycles (stable, born, dying, flapping, sporadic, reborn) and explicitly studies the probe-distribution problem: how many and which collectors are needed to reconstruct the topology.
  • How: All ASPATHs from MRT full + update dumps parsed with BGPStream; each ASPATH hop becomes an edge; bogons and prepends discarded; then combinatorial-optimization analysis (biconnected components, articulation points, n-connectivity) to identify core structure.
  • Where applicable: Routing-policy simulation, topology research, and data-informed peering/deployment decisions. Built from public collector data with the usual vantage-point bias; the probe-placement question is open, which itself matters for anyone consuming collector-derived "Internet views."

items.title: Towards detecting DoS attacks in the server's NIC
items.text:
LACNIC 45 — for the Networking PM digest Core pick 28 May 2026

Slides Recording

Adrián Lara (Universidad de Costa Rica), Juan Felipe Botero (Universidad de Antioquia)

VideoPDF

  • Why: Sits at the intersection of two of the PM's core interests — network security and datapath internals — by moving DoS detection off CPUs and IDS appliances into the server's NIC dataplane, with an eBPF/XDP variant that is broadly deployable.
  • What: Research on embedding ML-based DoS detection in SmartNICs to eliminate the two classic IDS deployment problems: traffic duplication (mirroring) and bottlenecks. Measured results on a Netronome SmartNIC show the ML model adds only a slight shift to the detection-delay distribution with low dispersion — inference at line rate with near-negligible overhead. A companion case applies the same idea with XDP + eBPF and model quantization (16/8/4/2-bit): all quantized models show median inference latency around 0.2 μs.
  • How: Strict role split — the CPU/control plane manages global policy, model updates and exceptions; the SmartNIC dataplane does per-packet feature extraction, filtering and inference. Simple models (decision trees) are compiled into P4 match-action tables (each branch becomes a table entry over feature ranges); quantization fits models into NIC memory; the NIC exports features so the CPU can (re)train. Malicious traffic is dropped before it reaches the OS.
  • Where applicable: Host-granularity DoS defense and edge microsegmentation. The P4 path requires programmable SmartNICs (demonstrated on Netronome); the eBPF/XDP variant runs on ordinary Linux hosts. Research-stage, but the architecture and quantization findings transfer directly.
path: Towards detecting DoS attacks in the server's NIC

items.title: Towards the Age of IPv6-Only
items.text:
LACNIC 45 — for the Networking PM digest Wildcard pick 28 May 2026

Slides (PDF) Slides (PDF) Recording

Speakers not listed on the program item; the LACNIC 45 tutorial overview identifies José Cotúa and Alejandro Acosta (LACNIC tutorial team)

VideoPDF 1PDF 2

  • Why: IPv6-mostly (RFC 8925) is quietly becoming the pragmatic end-state for campus, enterprise, and access networks — the PM may not be tracking it, and this tutorial carries real configurations and an OS-support matrix that de-risk a decision they will likely face.
  • What: A hands-on tutorial on IPv6-only and IPv6-mostly operation: NAT64/DNS64 mechanics and header translation; 464XLAT for IPv4 literals, legacy IPv4-socket software, and broken dual-stack servers; and the IPv6-mostly model (RFC 8925 §1.2) where one segment simultaneously serves IPv6-only, dual-stack, and IPv4-only hosts — hosts that request DHCPv4 option 108 simply do not get an IPv4 address. Claimed benefits: >⅔ savings in IPv4 addresses, less NAT, and a simpler network than dual stack. Companion decks cover an IPv6-only recursive DNS resolver behind NAT64, RFC 8950 (extended-nexthop encoding for routing IPv4 packets over IPv6-only links), and DHCPv6 prefix delegation.
  • How: DHCP option 108 signaling (client requests it; a configured server offers an IPv4 lease of "none for 30 minutes"; the client aborts and retries later), with host-side CLAT — native on Android 12+, iOS 15+, and macOS 12.0.1+ (CLAT activates on seeing the PREF64 router-advertisement option); Windows 11 support in recent releases; Linux via the clatd script or NetworkManager 1.52+.
  • Where applicable: Enterprise/campus/access networks with NAT64 in place and IPv4 pool pressure; DC relevance is narrower but real (RFC 8950 for IPv6-only fabrics). The OS-support matrix is the gating constraint — older client fleets simply keep dual stack on the same segment, which is precisely what the model is designed to allow.

items.title: What Is My RPKI Validator Doing Right Now?
items.text:
LACNIC 45 — for the Networking PM digest Adjacent pick 28 May 2026

Slides Recording

Santiago Aggio (CONICET BB / UTN-FRBB, Argentina)

VideoPDF

  • Why: RPKI validators are quietly becoming production-critical infrastructure for anyone doing ROV — this gives a concrete measurement plus an ops playbook for running and monitoring them, which the PM can treat as a case study in operating a PKI at scale.
  • What: An operator-oriented examination of relying-party software (FORT, Routinator 3000, rpki-client, StayRTR, rpki-prover) and the synchronization layer: RRDP (RFC 8182) vs rsync, where RRDP's snapshot/delta model substantially reduces data transferred per validation cycle (one publication point shows ~4,425 RRDP vs ~135 rsync fetches). Includes measured sync latencies from 20 RIPE Atlas probes in Argentina showing that the geographic location of publication points influences synchronization times, and notes 26 active IETF drafts in the RPKI space (publication-server BCP, ERIK sync protocol, decentralized repository architecture).
  • How: Routinator's Prometheus exporter + Grafana for VRP and session metrics; validator metrics pages; RIPE Atlas ping/traceroute to publication points. Operational recommendations: size the validator VM (memory, tmpfs, CPU); run more than one validator implementation for redundancy; use different IPv4/IPv6 source addresses toward repositories (to survive DDoS filtering); run DNS resolvers with parallel resolution; monitor both sides of the validator (RRDP/rsync toward publication points, RTR toward routers); consider RTRTR as an RTR proxy for mid/large operators.
  • Where applicable: Any operator running RPKI ROV — broadly applicable and immediately adoptable. The latency measurements are Argentina-specific; the practices are general.
path: What Is My RPKI Validator Doing Right Now?

items.title: A Network Tomography Approach to Imputing OD Traffic in an IP/MPLS Network
items.text:
LACNIC 46 digest Adjacent pick 22 October 2026

Slides Recording

Claudio Risso (Universidad de la República – FING), Carlos Martínez (LACNIC), Pablo Cuello (ANTEL)

VideoPDF

  • Why: Origin-destination traffic matrices drive capacity planning, what-if/failure analysis, anomaly detection, and interconnect optimization — and per-LSP statistics in IP/MPLS networks are unreliable precisely because they are not standardized.
  • What: A network-tomography method that infers OD traffic by combining LSP statistics with trusted physical-interface counters. Production validation on ANTEL's international network (May 2025: 31 nodes, 930 tunnels, 128 directed links, 5-minute samples): 47,430 model parameters fit against 261,248 measurements (~5.5:1) via positivity-constrained least squares that exploit the daily traffic profile's temporal correlation. The top 25 LSPs (2.69% of tunnels) carried 60% of traffic; solving sequentially from the heaviest LSPs first stabilizes the initialization-sensitive iterative fit. The "blackbox" mode is technology-independent (native IP, MPLS, Segment Routing) and works even where LSP statistics are absent.
  • How: Linear model Y = AX where A holds ECMP-aware routing fractions per link/tunnel, plus a piecewise-linear daily-profile constraint matrix B; constrained least squares; the toy example makes the underdetermination explicit (34 link measurements vs 132 OD unknowns).
  • Where applicable: Validated on ANTEL's production network — org-specific data — but the method generalizes to any IP/MPLS backbone with interface counters and known topology. Transient failures/restorations are explicitly out of scope, and results are approximations of an inherently underdetermined problem.
path: A Network Tomography Approach to Imputing OD Traffic in an IP/MPLS Network

items.title: Between the Law and the Protocol: An Overview of Blocking Orders on the Brazilian Internet
items.text:
LACNIC 46 digest Adjacent pick 22 October 2026

Slides Recording

Pedro de Botelho Marcos, with Thiago Ayub and Vinícius Anselmo (NIC.br, per slides)

VideoPDF

  • Why: Court-ordered blocking has become a routine operator workload with measurable collateral damage — relevant both operationally and to any DNS/security product with filtering features.
  • What: Brazil is estimated to have blocking orders covering roughly 135,000 Internet resources. One ISP received 733 orders between December 2022 and October 2026 (period growth: 16 → 150 → 295 → 272). Motivators: piracy, cybercrime, fake news. The mechanics are walked through end-to-end: ISP-resolver blocking vs public resolvers vs the registry sinkhole, IP/TCP-SYN interception at the AS border; and the evasions: VPNs, domain re-registration, IP changes. Collateral effects: shared-IP hosting takes down unrelated domains, indefinite IP blocks strand addresses as infringers move, and secret orders leave users unable to distinguish blocking from outages.
  • How: Measurement over a single ISP's order corpus plus public data; the presenters explicitly do not question the validity of the orders themselves. Caveat from the slides: no guarantee all ISPs received the same order set.
  • Where applicable: Brazil-specific dataset, but the overblocking mechanics and evasion patterns generalize to any jurisdiction with blocking regimes. A companion LACNIC/MARYVA study elsewhere in the program ("Site Blocking in Latin America and the Caribbean") covers 18 countries and finds reactive blocking now dominant, with dynamic IP lists and growing ISP obligations trending region-wide.
path: Between the Law and the Protocol: An Overview of Blocking Orders on the Brazilian Internet

items.title: Beyond RPKI Origin Validation: How to Close the Route Leak Gap with ASPA, Today.
items.text:
LACNIC 46 digest Core pick 22 October 2026

Slides Recording

Sthefany Conceição Duquini (UFMS); slides co-credit Antonio Marcos Moreiras (NIC.br)

VideoPDF

  • Why: ROV is now treated as done; route leaks are the unsolved residue because origin validation says nothing about path. This talk gives the actual deployment state of ASPA and a go/no-go framework, not just theory.
  • What: How ASPA works (an object lists an AS's authorized transit providers; upstream/downstream algorithms verify adjacent AS_PATH pairs via up-ramp/down-ramp counting, catching valley violations), current adoption (3.66% of routed ASNs globally — 3,249 of 88,714 per Hurricane Electric, Oct 14 2026; 195 LACNIC ASNs publishing, 156 of them in Brazil), tooling (Krill ≥0.14.0, Routinator ≥0.13 with ASPA enabled explicitly or objects silently ignored, FORT 1.7.0 experimental, RTR v2 required), and router support (OpenBGPD and BIRD available now; Juniper in Junos 26.1; Huawei NetEngine 8000; FRR not yet; MikroTik waiting on RFCs; Cisco testing in IOS XR). Includes a real misconfiguration case: AS945's ASPA omitted a genuine provider (AS61138), turning legitimate routes ASPA-Invalid.
  • How: Publish an ASPA listing only real transit providers — never peers or transparent IXP route servers; use {AS0} for ASes with no providers (e.g., tier-1s); the recommended posture is observe first, enforce later. Validation checks what you published, not what you intended.
  • Where applicable: Any AS that has finished ROA/ROV. IXPs are the best early testbed (route servers on BIRD/OpenBGPD reach many members at once). In the LAC region, publication is available hosted via MiLACNIC or delegated via Krill. Missing providers in your ASPA is the main operational risk.
path: Beyond RPKI Origin Validation: How to Close the Route Leak Gap with ASPA, Today.

items.title: Beyond the Radio Link: Routing Dynamics in LEO Satellite Networks
items.text:
LACNIC 46 digest Wildcard pick 22 October 2026

Slides Recording

Katarina Stefanović

VideoPDF

  • Why: LEO constellations are becoming a standard connectivity tier (the Venezuela keynote's emergency D2D roaming is the same trend), and routing over continuously changing topologies is a genuinely different routing problem — one the PM would not otherwise encounter in a routing-security-heavy program.
  • What: No abstract was published and no source text was available, so this entry reflects the title only: by its title, the talk addresses routing dynamics beyond the radio link in LEO satellite networks. (from abstract only — title and materials only)
  • How: Not determinable from the program text; slides and video are published.
  • Where applicable: Unknown until reviewed; flagged as a wildcard because the subject sits outside the program's routing-security mainstream while signaling where interconnect is heading.

items.title: BGP in 2026: Threats, Incidents, and Solutions
items.text:
LACNIC 46 digest Core pick 22 October 2026

Slides (PPTX) Slides (PDF) Recording

Erika Vega Valenzuela, Álvaro Retana, Guillermo Cicileo

VideoPPTXPDF

  • Why: The best single map of the current BGP threat and mitigation landscape, grounded in regional incident data rather than vendor framing. Directly in the PM's routing-security and BGP-internals lane.
  • What: A structured tutorial mapping each threat class to its mitigations — origin hijack → ROA/ROV; AS_PATH manipulation → ASPA (with BGPsec still undeployed); route leaks → filters, BGP Roles/OTC, ASPA; session abuse → GTSM, TCP-AO, max-prefix; volumetric DDoS → RTBH, BLACKHOLE community, Flowspec — plus real incident data for LAC and a monthly Argentina table for Jan–Oct 2026 (route misoriginations ranging 0–6 per month, bogon announcements 2–8, route leaks 0).
  • How: Threat/example/mitigation blocks sourced from RFC 4272, RFC 7454, SIDROPS, GROW, and MANRS; concrete config patterns for bogon prefix-lists and AS-path ACLs; a discussion of why static bogon lists go stale (today's bogon is tomorrow's IANA allocation); IRR vs RPKI as the two external sources for validating received announcements.
  • Where applicable: Broadly applicable to any BGP operator; the incident tables are LAC/Argentina-specific public-monitoring data. Ends with a practical adoption roadmap from information hygiene to path protection.
path: BGP in 2026: Threats, Incidents, and Solutions

items.title: Bypassing CGNAT. You Don’t Need PBR, and I Can Prove It!
items.text:
LACNIC 46 digest Adjacent pick 22 October 2026

Slides Recording

Douglas Fernando Fischer (NZM — network consultancy for ISPs)

VideoPDF

  • Why: A sharp, transferable edge-design pattern: steering CGNAT vs public-IP subscribers at a BNG without policy-based routing.
  • What: The argument, walked through topology by topology, that PBR for CGNAT steering becomes unmanageable ("cancerígeno") as BNGs and CGNAT nodes multiply — and that doubling BNG hardware per subscriber type is the resource-infinite fantasy. The alternative: per-subscriber-type VRFs on a single BNG — the CGNAT VRF holds a default route to the CGNAT, the public-IP VRF defaults to the border router — i.e., source classification by VRF membership instead of per-flow policy matching. Bonus: VRFs as quarantine zones for infected CPEs.
  • How: Logical-topology evolution from pre-CGNAT BNG designs, deliberately presented without CLI so the concepts transfer across vendors.
  • Where applicable: ISP BNG/CGNAT environments with MPLS/VRF capability; a general technique, no hardware dependency stated. Most valuable to access networks with multiple BNGs and CGNAT nodes.
path: Bypassing CGNAT. You Don’t Need PBR, and I Can Prove It!

items.title: From Classic L3VPN to EVPN: Mastering Type 5 Routes on the Backbone
items.text:
LACNIC 46 digest Core pick 22 October 2026

Slides Recording

Samuel Emanuel Urbano Tomassoni, Fernando Neiverth

VideoPDF

  • Why: This is the talk in the program squarely inside physical datacenter/campus fabric design — eliminating the centralized-L3-gateway tromboning problem in a leaf-spine EVPN-VXLAN fabric.
  • What: A migration from an edge running EVPN-VXLAN as "dumb" L2 transport with IRB gateways concentrated on a heavy core router, to distributed anycast gateways extended to the leaf/edge switches using EVPN Type 5 (IP prefix) routes. Reported control-plane effect on their network: the bgp.evpn table dropped from 141,156 routes (Type-2 host routes) to 276 summarized Type-5 advertisements — over 99% reduction. Spines act as route reflectors, removing full-mesh iBGP.
  • How: First-hop routing at the network edge via distributed anycast IRB on the leaves; Type-5 IP-prefix advertisements associated with BGP communities for granular inter-VRF traffic control; the EVPN control plane is decoupled from transport, so the underlay can move from VXLAN to SR-MPLS or SRv6 without refactoring edge configurations; BUM and management traffic confined to the edge.
  • Where applicable: Leaf-spine datacenter and campus fabrics with routing-capable (EVPN Type-5 capable) edge switches. The before/after route counts are from the presenters' own network — org-specific — but the design pattern and the Type-2-to-Type-5 summarization argument are general.
path: From Classic L3VPN to EVPN: Mastering Type 5 Routes on the Backbone

LACNIC 46 digest Wildcard pick 22 October 2026

Slides (PPTX) Slides (PDF) Recording

Luiz Cosme Puppin Magalhaes

VideoPPTXPDF

items.title: Going IPv6-Only: From Myths to Modern Network Realities
items.text:
LACNIC 46 digest Adjacent pick 22 October 2026

Slides Recording

Jen Linkova (Google)

VideoPDF

  • Why: The clearest statement of the "IPv6-only is becoming the default for high-performing networks" argument, from one of the most experienced IPv6-only operators — and it comes with a deep hands-on companion track elsewhere in the program.
  • What: Myth-busting (IPv6 is not "IPv4 with longer addresses," and the transition is not indefinitely deferrable), transition-technology realities in complex enterprise networks, and OS behavior with IPv4 fully disabled. Note: the published deck for this talk is largely charts (APNIC regional adoption stats; an addressing-efficiency example where a /19 was downsized to a /22, saving ~7K addresses). The concrete war stories live in the same speaker's tutorial in this program ("Hacia la transición definitiva de redes IPv6 Only"): Neighbor Discovery state-machine failures and unidirectional connectivity from broken multicast/ND filtering, ICMPv6 filtering breaking PMTUD, NAT64 MTU pitfalls (some vendors default NAT64 MTU to 1280; fragment-extension headers dropped by ACLs), IPv6 IPSec without UDP encapsulation, and AP/switch binding tables silently blocking the N+1 address of multi-address IPv6 hosts. The tutorial also covers DHCP option 108 via DHCP-Relay, 464XLAT with Jool on OpenWrt, DHCPv6-PD, and RFC 8950 (IPv4 routes with IPv6 next-hops) tested on MikroTik RouterOS v7.
  • How: Systematic troubleshooting discipline (verify/reproduce → localize/isolate → one-variable controlled changes) applied to IPv6 specifics, with pcap-level ND case studies.
  • Where applicable: Enterprise, campus, and access networks moving toward IPv6-only or IPv6-mostly; techniques are general, not Google-specific.
path: Going IPv6-Only: From Myths to Modern Network Realities

items.title: IPv6-Mostly on Campus
items.text:
LACNIC 46 digest Adjacent pick 22 October 2026

Slides Recording

Henri Alves de Godoy (UNICAMP)

VideoPDF

  • Why: Measured, published evidence of what DHCP Option 108, PREF64, and CLAT actually do on a production campus — rare empirical data for anyone planning IPv6-mostly rollouts.
  • What: A pilot on the FCA-Unicamp campus Wi-Fi (2,524 undergraduates). Findings: Option 108 (RFC 8925) does not prevent or disable IPv4 — the client decides; PREF64 (RFC 8781) is necessary but not sufficient; automatic CLAT activation is strongly associated with the absence of native IPv4. macOS/iOS/Android have native CLAT; Linux needs clatd or maturing NetworkManager support; Windows 11 began rolling out CLAT in September 2026. Dual-stack devices still send traffic toward PREF64/NAT64 (DNS64, Happy Eyeballs effects). Net effect: IPv4 DHCP pool pressure drops, and residual IPv4 dependency becomes visible and measurable — consistent with draft-ietf-v6ops-6mops (v10, Sep 2026).
  • How: Standard tooling — radvd, Kea DHCPv4, BIND, Jool NAT64 (--pool6 64:ff9b::/96) — plus Python measurement scripts the authors published for download.
  • Where applicable: Campus/enterprise managed networks; the methodology and scripts are replicable anywhere. Framed as "map where IPv4 is still needed" rather than "eliminate IPv4."

items.title: Keynote Presentation: Lessons in Digital Resilience: Multistakeholder Response and Connectivity Recovery in Venezuela Following the 2026 Earthquakes
items.text:
LACNIC 46 digest Adjacent pick 22 October 2026

Slides Recording

Alejandra Stolk Ganteaume (Internet Society Venezuela; Head of Networks and Connectivity, Universidad de Los Andes)

VideoPDF

  • Why: A postmortem of physical-layer, national-scale infrastructure failure and recovery — exactly the class of hard-won lesson operator programs exist to surface.
  • What: The 24 June 2026 earthquakes (a holiday, coinciding with a World Cup match at 18:00; alert at 18:04:31) produced simultaneous physical shear exceeding theoretical redundancy models for La Guaira's coastal infrastructure; NASA estimated 800+ collapsed buildings. Digitel's Direct-to-Device satellite roaming went from zero usage to peak within 5 days (Ookla measurements, 24 Jun–5 Jul). Around 77 emergency community networks were deployed by ISOC Venezuela and partners across isolated, rural, health, and education sites; the SAC submarine cable was cut and repaired; ISPs physically rescued fiber to reconnect communities.
  • How: The architectural lessons: deploy CDN nodes directly at the local IXP (nap.ve) to keep traffic in-country and avoid tromboning via Miami; treat decentralized switching as the resilience model; and coordinate in three layers — institutional (regulator, universities, ISOC, LACNIC), field (UN agencies, NGOs, community leaders), and specialized (TSF, satellite providers).
  • Where applicable: Venezuela-specific event, but the design lessons (IXP-localized traffic, edge caching, D2D as an emergency tier, converting emergency networks into self-sustaining community networks) transfer to resilience planning anywhere. Next step proposed: a regional technical emergency group for digital resilience.

items.title: Latency-Based BGP Route Selection – An Intelligent Failover Engine Optimized with Supervised Learning
items.text:
LACNIC 46 digest Core pick 22 October 2026

Slides Recording

Ernesto Sánchez (Universidad Católica de Salta, Argentina), Henri Alves de Godoy (Universidade Estadual de Campinas, Brasil)

VideoPDF

  • Why: Performance-aware routing is entering BGP via the IETF (a draft adding a NETWORK_LATENCY TLV to AIGP); this is a concrete, honestly-reported prototype of latency-triggered failover plus ML-based policy tuning.
  • What: A failover engine that scores peer/DNS/jitter metrics (weights 0.27/0.50/0.23, packet loss as a severity multiplier), switching providers when the max DNS score exceeds 1.10 sustained over consecutive cycles and returning below 0.80 — rules designed to filter noise (trend, coefficient of variation, p95 deviation, z-score acceleration). Supervised learning over ~62 features and 50,000 simulated cycles (~26 days, 98.7% "normal" class): XGBoost ranks feature importance (DNS dominates at ~30% gain), logistic regression yields interpretable weights, both suggesting DNS should carry ~0.76–0.79 vs the current 0.50. Results: recall 0.95–0.97, precision 0.65–0.72, ROC-AUC ≈0.999, stratified 5-fold cross-validation. The authors are explicit that the dataset is synthetic (Ornstein-Uhlenbeck background noise, Poisson episode starts) calibrated to real measurements, and recommend validating against months of real history.
  • How: Containerlab dual-provider ISP topology with DNS nodes, TimescaleDB metric store, Python capture/feature pipeline; the ML calibrates the existing deterministic scoring function rather than replacing it — that is the transferable idea.
  • Where applicable: Dual-transit ISPs and enterprises; lab-validated only, not production-proven. Recall-heavy/precision-light tuning means false positives are the operational cost to watch.
path: Latency-Based BGP Route Selection – An Intelligent Failover Engine Optimized with Supervised Learning

items.title: Mission Accomplished? The 2026 KSK Rollover Story
items.text:
LACNIC 46 digest Adjacent pick 22 October 2026

Slides

Carlos Martínez (LACNIC), Nicolás Antoniello (ICANN)

PDF

  • Why: The Internet's largest trust-anchor key rotation executed 11 October 2026 — and the talk's core message is a per-instance verification checklist, not a victory lap. A good template for any large-scale key-rollover program, including workload-identity trust roots.
  • What: KSK-2024 (key tag 38696 / 0x9728) has signed the root DNSKEY set since 11 Oct 2026 14:00 UTC, after 21 months of prepublication (published Jan 2025, RFC 5011 acceptance Feb 2025). KSK-2017 stays published but non-signing until revocation (11 Jan 2027) and retirement (22 Mar 2027). Telemetry reading: RFC 8145 _ta- anchor-tagging queries (one capture showed ~38,989 unique source IPs still announcing only the old anchor) are a risk signal, not a census of failures — the 2018 lessons hold: forwarders mask the origin, signaling does not prove validating, and few reports do not prove absence of failures. "Completed" does not mean "all systems verified."
  • How: Per-instance verification: 38696 present as accepted (not pending) in the effective trust-anchor state (rndc managed-keys status, rndc secroots), state persistence across restarts/replicas/containers/standbys and forwarding paths, and functional tests (valid root SOA with the AD bit; SERVFAIL on a known-broken domain; +cdflag as diagnostic only).
  • Where applicable: Anyone operating DNSSEC-validating resolvers — especially forwarders and replicated/containerized deployments where RFC 5011 state can be lost on restart. Fully general.

items.title: Monitoring to Mitigate Micro-Outages in MikroTik-Based ISP Topologies Using Natural Language
items.text:
LACNIC 46 digest Wildcard pick 22 October 2026

Slides Recording

Joaquin Tadeo Riedmaier, Santiago Agustín Zualet (Universidad Nacional de Misiones, Argentina)

VideoPDF

  • Why: The clearest example at this meeting of LLMs entering network operations — and it is designed privacy-first, which is the pattern most likely to survive contact with real enterprises.
  • What: An on-prem monitoring stack for MikroTik-based small ISPs: syslog push plus RouterOS v7 REST pull (interface traffic/errors, CPU/RAM, connection tracking, ARP, PPPoE/RADIUS sessions) through Django/Python/PostgreSQL, with noise filtering (37 cyclic log lines collapsed into one event row), threshold alerts via Telegram, and a locally hosted LLM answering natural-language questions via text-to-SQL over flattened read-only views with RAG-anchored responses (grounding goal ≥95%). Projected effect: critical-event diagnosis from ~90 minutes to ~18. Everything stays inside the ISP (framed against Argentine data-protection law 25.326); an external-API extension exists only as an anonymized option.
  • How: Flattened schema (fewer JOINs → fewer hallucinations), a SELECT-only database user so the model cannot modify anything, and cross-signal correlation of L2/L3 metrics, conntrack, RADIUS sessions, and syslog. The LLM runs on 32 GB of RAM locally.
  • Where applicable: Built for the 1,500+ small ISP/cooperative context in Argentina, but the architecture — a read-only natural-language query layer over normalized telemetry — transfers to any environment. The time-savings figure is a projection; the slides explicitly label the flagship correlation scenario as illustrative, not measured.

items.title: NTPv5 and Updated Time Security: What Changes for Network Operators
items.text:
LACNIC 46 digest Core pick 22 October 2026

Slides Recording

Antonio Marcos Moreiras (NIC.br)

VideoPDF

  • Why: Time is a load-bearing security dependency — RPKI ROA validity windows, TLS certificates, Kerberos' 5-minute skew, log forensics; NDSS 2016 showed a few days of clock shift suffices to attack RPKI. And time rides on routing: ~2M NTP servers use a single upstream, and the 14,153 ASes hosting those upstreams publish no ROAs (IMC 2025), so a prefix hijack could set the time.
  • What: NTS (RFC 8915) is deployable now (chrony ≥4.0, ntpd-rs; Ubuntu 25.10+ ships chrony with NTS by default) — yet 374 of 583 NTS servers are misconfigured (blocked TCP 4460, size filters dropping NTS packets on UDP 123). NTPv5 (draft 09, last call end-2026): client-server only, explicit timescale (UTC/TAI/UT1/smeared) and era fields, client cookies replacing request timestamps, 120-bit reference IDs. The 2035–2038 wall: leap seconds end by 2035, NTP era 0 ends 7 Feb 2036, 32-bit time_t overflows 19 Jan 2038 — equipment in service today will still be running. Plus NTP Pool research: ~10 well-weighted servers could capture most countries' time traffic (NDSS 2026), and some pool servers scan clients' IPv6 addresses (CCS 2026); Khronos (RFC 9523) and Roughtime as complements.
  • How: NTS = TLS 1.3 key exchange on TCP 4460 with stateless cookies. Concrete checklist: allow 4460, review UDP 123 size filters, NTS on clients and servers with auto-renewed certificates, 4 or more identified independent sources by name, ROAs (and eventually ASPA) for your time servers; test NTPv5 in the lab within 12–24 months and inventory devices that will live past 2036.
  • Where applicable: Any operator of time infrastructure or of anything time-dependent (PKI, RPKI, Kerberos, SIEM). Fully general, with an IETF document-status table (RFCs 8915, 9523, 9769, 10030; drafts for NTPv5, NTS pools, Roughtime, NTS4PTP).
path: NTPv5 and Updated Time Security: What Changes for Network Operators

items.title: RPKI in Action: Updates and Routing Security
items.text:
LACNIC 46 digest Core pick 22 October 2026

Slides (PPTX) Slides (PDF) Recording

Gerardo Rada, Jorge Cano, Carlos Martínez (LACNIC)

VideoPPTXPDF

  • Why: LACNIC's open-source RPKI stack — FORT validator plus the Barry and Rapport test tools — is production tooling anyone can adopt, and the session also covers ASPA and delegated-CA enablement in MiLACNIC.
  • What: FORT 1.7.0 (July 2026): experimental ASPA support, OpenSSL 4, recommended for production; FORT 2.0 targeted for December 1 with 51 improvements and a more modular architecture. Barry ("the eccentric cousin of FORT") generates valid and invalid RPKI test repositories for validator testing and research. Rapport is an automated test suite for validators — roughly 20 categories and 350 tests (e.g., aspa-profile, rfc6481, rfc6487, router connectivity), extensible to any validator — which replaced the manual smoke-testing that used to accompany every FORT code change. The session also runs interactive route-hijack scenarios and hands-on ASPA configuration, with ASPA and the delegated RPKI model now available through MiLACNIC.
  • How: The validator flow shown explicitly: fetch RPKI repositories → local cache → cryptographic validation → serve to routers; Barry scenarios define TA/CA/ROA objects with controlled parameters (validity windows, IP extensions) to build arbitrary test cases.
  • Where applicable: Any operator running or evaluating an RPKI validator, and any team building RPKI/ASPA tooling — all three tools are open source with public repositories.

items.title: The BGP Analyst's Notebook: 17 Years In
items.text:
LACNIC 46 digest Core pick 22 October 2026

Slides (PPTX) Slides (PDF) Recording

Doug Madory (Head of Internet Analysis, Infoblox)

VideoPPTXPDF

  • Why: Seventeen years of documented routing incidents from the analyst who published most of them — the right lens for separating durable trends (RPKI uptake) from headline noise, and for threat-modeling and monitoring product direction.
  • What: A retrospective in two buckets. Geopolitical: Egypt 2011 as the start of the shutdown era; Iran's 2026 shutdowns described as the most impactful in history (BGP routes stayed up while the country went offline via GFW-like filtering, nightly curfews, a national internet, and 2026 allowlisting); the Kherson switchover to Russian transit; the ALBA-1 submarine cable. Attacks: the first documented BGP MITM hijacks (Belarusian ASes, Feb 2013, targets including Visa, Mastercard, and foreign ministries); the coordinated Bitcanal (AS197426) takedown; and the IPv4 leasing / residential-proxy economy — Ukraine's routed footprint shrank 18.5% post-invasion as providers leased IPv4 for revenue, only for it to be abused by proxy networks (per Krebs). Also: China's ROA coverage jumped from 4% to 81% since April 2026, lifting the APNIC region from 55% to 77%.
  • How: His methodology: reconstruct the hidden per-AS routing-table state over time from merged BGP views rather than individual announcements, and analyze events by scope, duration, and context.
  • Where applicable: Global internet measurement; not a deployment talk but a high-signal framing of what changed, what hasn't (path validation), and what's coming (ASPA as the next question after ROV).
path: The BGP Analyst's Notebook: 17 Years In

items.text:
MORE-IP 2026 — Operator digest Core pick 29 May 2026

  • Why: For anyone who cares about BGP/datapath internals and the long, slow IPv6 transition, this is one of the sharpest technical titles on the program. The question it names — can we carry IPv4 reachability with IPv6-only transport in the core, so the core stops speaking IPv4 entirely — is one of the few genuinely structural changes still available to the internet without a flag day.
  • What: The title indicates a proposal or evaluation of running the core network IPv6-only: advertising IPv4 prefixes while using IPv6 next-hop addresses (the mechanism standardised in RFC 8950), eliminating the need for IPv4 addresses on core-facing interfaces and shrinking the core's IPv4 configuration surface. No abstract was published, so the exact contribution — measurement of current adoption, an operator how-to, or a transition proposal — cannot be confirmed. (from abstract only; no description published)
  • How: Presumably by combining extended-nexthop BGP encoding (IPv4 NLRI, IPv6 next hop) with v6-only core links, so IPv4 survives only as payload/edge reachability. Fiebig's group is known for large-scale BGP measurement, so expect deployment data or adoption obstacles rather than a purely theoretical argument.
  • Where applicable: Transit providers, IXs, and large DC/WAN interconnect operators — exactly the environments this event's audience runs. The main constraints are real-world ones: hardware/daemon support for extended nexthops on all core routers, and the operational discipline to keep v4 out once it's out. items.text:

  • Why: SCION is the most serious sustained attempt at a clean-slate, security-first internet architecture that has reached actual deployment discussions, and it speaks directly to the PM's network-security and interdomain-routing interests. Having its chief architect present at an operator event means the talk is aimed at people who run networks, not academics.
  • What: SCION (Scalability, Control, and Isolation on Next-Generation Networks) is a path-aware internetworking architecture: instead of letting BGP's path selection decide transit opaque to endpoints, receivers and senders hold visible, cryptographically authenticated path choices. The program publishes no description for this session, so the specific content (architecture overview vs. deployment status vs. operator onboarding) is unknown — but any of those would be valuable. (from abstract only; no description published)
  • How: SCION organizes the internet into Isolation Domains containing ASes, and lets endpoints select among authenticated AS-level path segments — enabling path failure isolation, protection against route hijacks, and control-plane attacks that today's BGP can't defend against. The Swiss financial sector has run SCION pilots over an exchange infrastructure, making this relevant to IX/peering operators like the host.
  • Where applicable: Interdomain/WAN transit and any environment with strict integrity or availability guarantees (finance, critical infrastructure). Not a DC-fabric or LAN technique — it's about the internet core and inter-AS paths. items.title: AI Backend: Deploying SRv6 uSID and SONiC for Deterministic Load Balancing
items.text:
NANOG 96 digest Core pick 2–4 February 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Pablo Camarillo — Cisco Systems; Rita Hui — Microsoft

VideoPDF

  • Why: The AI backend load-balancing problem is the defining fabric issue of this cycle: synchronized, bursty, low-entropy training flows destroy ECMP hash assumptions, and congestion/loss stalls GPU collectives. This is a production answer from one of the world's largest AI infrastructures, not a whitepaper.
  • What: Microsoft's deployment of SRv6 uSID strict source routing in the AI backend for deterministic, conflict-free traffic placement, implemented in SONiC. The deck grounds it in real cost data (Llama3 406B: 6k GPUs, 54 days, 419 unplanned interruptions; a single job crash loses 15-30 minutes of compute since the last checkpoint) and includes a taxonomy of every LB approach attempted — switch-based (flowlet, adaptive routing, packet spray) and NIC-based (oblivious spray, entropy recycling) — and why probabilistic entropy-value switching can't guarantee a new path.
  • How: GPU/NIC controls the full end-to-end path by encoding a uSID list in the packet header; on congestion or failure the NIC swaps SIDs and the path changes immediately with no state propagation through the fabric. The backend runs as a statically provisioned fabric with static SIDs and static routes — no dynamic routing, avoiding the ~120,000 packets lost when an ECMP group updates after a link flap on a fully utilized 400G link. Also covers tenancy/slicing via SRv6 policy without DPU cycles, and the SONiC SRv6 ecosystem (uN/uDT functions, FRR, contributors incl. Microsoft, Alibaba, Broadcom, Nvidia). The Alibaba eCore SRv6 DCI design is shown as the scale-across analog.
  • Where applicable: Microsoft-scale AI backends on SONiC whiteboxes; requires SRv6-capable NICs/DPUs and merchant silicon (Broadcom/G400-class). The "deterministic path placement" idea is also feeding UEC standardization, so the architecture is transferable even where the exact stack is not. Co-presented by Cisco's SRv6 lead — expect enthusiasm — but the operational data and failure math are the substance.
path: AI Backend: Deploying SRv6 uSID and SONiC for Deterministic Load Balancing

items.title: Automation for Operations -- T-Mobile Journey
items.text:
NANOG 96 digest Adjacent pick 2–4 February 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Issa Abu Eid, Udaya Tadikonda — T-Mobile USA

VideoPDF

  • Why: A Tier-1 operator's account of moving from manual workflows to automation-first operations, with the guardrail design spelled out — the "how do we make automated actions safe" question is where most automation programs actually fail, and this addresses it head-on.
  • What: Reactive and proactive automation categories: alert correlation/deduplication and auto-created tickets with SLA clocks starting at detection, multi-signal service-aware outage detection with impact identification before customers notice, guarded break/fix (explicitly not automating ambiguous failures or one-off fixes; every automated action gated by redundancy-aware checks, capacity validation, audit trail, and rollback), pre/post-change validation with policy-driven rollback evaluation, continuous compliance/drift/EOL-EOS monitoring, and capacity early-warning with trend analysis. A maturity model — Visibility → Intelligence → Enablement — with the honest sequencing rule that automation cannot succeed without reliable state and that early efforts must focus on visibility, not action. AI is framed as an assistive layer on top of strong automation foundations, not a replacement for operator judgment.
  • How: Automation treated as production software; one deliverable described is a centralized internal platform used by 1,300+ engineers with incident correlation across multi-vendor networks.
  • Where applicable: T-Mobile US Tier-1 scale (org-specific tooling and metrics), but the guardrail taxonomy, the "explicitly not automated" list, and the visibility-first phasing are directly transferable patterns for any operations organization, including much smaller ones.

items.title: BGP in 2025
items.text:
NANOG 96 digest Adjacent pick 2–4 February 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Geoff Huston — APNIC

VideoPDF

  • Why: The annual ground truth on DFZ health — directly relevant to FIB sizing, deaggregation trends, and (this year) a genuinely new datapoint: the IPv4 routing table and the advertised address span are now moving in opposite directions.
  • What: IPv4 FIB passed 1M entries for all peers, yet the advertised address span shrank by 11M /32s during 2025 (3.1B advertised vs 580M unadvertised, +10M) — IPv4 use declining in access networks (notably the US) while cloud use still grows. Biggest movers: China Mobile (+13,382 prefixes), Amazon (+14,004), AT&T (−2,605, echoing its consolidation described in the Ukraine talk), IPXO broker growth visible. Amazon's super-aggregate games through the year (+4.3M, −15.8M, +15.1M address swings). IPv6: ~20k entries/year (~10%) growth with 45% of prefixes being /48s; 2,096 new IPv6 advertisers vs 956 departing. Projections: best 5-year fit still polynomial for IPv4 but a 3-year linear fit is competing; IPv6 growth model highly uncertain.
  • How: Longitudinal analysis across Route-Views/RIPE RIS peers; churn (updates/withdrawals) notably stable — the IPv4 network is "surprisingly stable" with withdrawals flat for ~15 years.
  • Where applicable: Universal for capacity planning and RIB/FIB trend work. The headline nuance — prefix count growing while address span shrinks — matters for anyone modeling router table growth or arguing about IPv4 scarcity.

items.title: Decentralizing Software Defined Networking: The Hidden Complexities of SDN & What We Can Do About Them
items.text:
NANOG 96 digest Core pick 2–4 February 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Alexander Krentsel — Google / UC Berkeley

VideoPDF

  • Why: A rare quantified indictment of centralized SDN: at Google, >50% of large outages are root-caused to the control plane itself — the dedicated controller infrastructure, control-plane network, instrumentation services, and fallback protocols that SDN drags in. For anyone building WAN control systems, this is the architecture conversation to have.
  • What: Decentralized SDN (dSDN): run the operator's SDN control program as a container on every router instead of on external servers. Each node floods its local state (topology, link capacities, demand), each node independently computes all paths with the operator's TE algorithm, and traffic follows strict source routes programmed at the ingress. This removes central/regional controller jobs, dedicated servers, the control-plane network, instrumentation services, and traditional fallback protocols from the critical path while keeping SDN's benefits (operator-defined code, global-view TE, consensus-free path selection) and restoring fate-sharing between control and data planes.
  • How: Enabled by three industry shifts: on-router third-party containers, standardized APIs (gRIBI, gNMI, OF/P4), and multi-core router CPUs. Source routing makes decentralization simple — historically infeasible in WANs due to path length in the header, now practical via hardware advances and a novel encoding (details in the paper). Evaluation: a production-grade implementation on real routers, fed live B4 topology and demand, replaying production failure events — convergence 120-150x faster than centralized SDN (faster propagation and programming outweigh slightly slower local computation) with markedly lower convergence impact on low-priority traffic.
  • Where applicable: Global WAN operators (Google B4-class). Requires vendor on-router container support and vendor-neutral programmatic APIs — realistic on modern platforms but a real dependency. Research-to-production direction from Berkeley NetSys + Google, not a deployable product; the simplification argument (fewer components on the critical path → fewer complex cascading outages) generalizes to any control-plane design review.
path: Decentralizing Software Defined Networking: The Hidden Complexities of SDN & What We Can Do About Them

items.title: End-system controlled, dynamic multihoming and multipath transport
items.text:
NANOG 96 digest Wildcard pick 2–4 February 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Saleem Bhatti — University of St Andrews, Scotland, UK.

VideoPDF

  • Why: Multipath today means MPTCP or waiting on QUIC multipath. This demonstrates generic, end-system-controlled multipath for any transport — with working code, real transatlantic tests, and no changes to routers, applications, DNS infrastructure beyond what exists, or routing. It is a genuinely different architectural bet worth knowing about even if you never deploy it.
  • What: ILNP (Identifier-Locator Network Protocol, RFCs 6740-6748) reuses IPv6 address syntax but splits semantics: the routing prefix acts as a mutable Locator while the remaining bits become a stable end-system Identifier — only end systems examine the Identifier bits, so IPv6 routers forward unchanged. Transport state is keyed on the Identifier (not the address), so a connection survives locator changes; dynamic multihoming and multipath are signaled end-to-end via ICMPv6 Locator Updates, no NAT, tunnels, or proxies.
  • How: A FreeBSD 14 implementation tested between IETF 124 in Montreal and St Andrews: dynamic 4-way multipath with TCP CUBIC over iperf3, and DASH video streaming over nginx + Firefox with 3-way multipath — using standard, unmodified applications and libraries. Supporting ecosystem exists: DNS NID/L64 records (RFC 6742) in BIND, Unbound, Knot; a Wireshark dissector (v4.6+); FreeBSD binaries published.
  • Where applicable: Research testbed; IPv6-only; requires ILNP-aware end-system stacks (FreeBSD today). No network-side prerequisites, which is the interesting inversion — the network stays dumb and the edge controls path selection. Position this as a direction signal for edge-controlled multipath rather than a deployable capability.
path: End-system controlled, dynamic multihoming and multipath transport

items.title: EVPN Interconnect Architecture for Resilient Multi-Domain Fabrics
items.text:
NANOG 96 digest Core pick 2–4 February 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Patrice Brissette — Cisco Systems

VideoPDF

  • Why: Multi-site EVPN over heterogeneous underlays (IPv4 WAN meeting IPv6 DC fabrics) is exactly the DC/WAN interconnect problem the PM owns. This is a coherent answer to the two failure modes that plague DCI overlays: control-plane stability during fabric isolation, and L2 loops across sites.
  • What: A hierarchical multi-site design where each fabric stays an independent EVPN domain and Border Gateways provide DCI: dual physical-IP VTEPs per BGW (one for the DC domain, one for the WAN domain) so tunnels are terminated and re-originated at the BGW — creating a clean scaling and policy boundary. Key mechanics: Inter-site ESI for all-active BGW multi-homing, DF/NDF election with local-bias BUM forwarding rules and explicit per-bridge egress filtering to prevent loops, Normalized-VNI translation to resolve overlapping VNIs between independently administered sites, downstream-assigned VNI option, host mobility via /32 advertisement re-origination, and step-by-step packet walks for L2 unicast, BUM, and L3 flows.
  • How: Failure-isolation walkthroughs for both WAN loss and DC loss show the alternate BGW-to-BGW path preserving host reachability; decoupling DC from WAN VTEP space means either side can change without re-coordinating.
  • Where applicable: Any multi-site EVPN/VXLAN program; not tied to specific silicon, though presented by Cisco's lead EVPN architect (and SONiC routing workgroup chair), so feature availability on non-Cisco gear (I-ESI, normalized VNI) should be verified. Concepts (re-origination boundary, VNI normalization, DF local-bias) transfer across vendors.
path: EVPN Interconnect Architecture for Resilient Multi-Domain Fabrics

items.title: Exodus of IPv4 from War-torn Ukraine
items.text:
NANOG 96 digest Adjacent pick 2–4 February 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Doug Madory — Kentik

VideoPDF

  • Why: A striking data story about IPv4 as a war-driven national commodity, with direct consequences for anyone reasoning about IP address markets, proxy abuse, and routing-table hygiene — it also explains several of the movers in this year's BGP table.
  • What: Four years of war produced a ~20% reduction in Ukraine's footprint in the global routing table. Ukrtelecom's AS6849 dropped from 4,728 to 1,377 /24s (−71%), with the space leased via brokers (IPXO) and re-originated by Amazon, Windstream, NTT, Lumen, Orange; sister ASN AS6877 vanished from the table entirely. Mariupol's Trinity (AS43554) space popped up under as many as 54 foreign ASes and was confirmed in use as residential-proxy infrastructure. The second act is AT&T's 2025 BGP housekeeping: AS7018 collapsed from 3,200+ IPv4 routes to 641 via super-aggregation and a new policy requiring customers to originate from their own ASN — which chased out the proxy services; the displaced prefixes scattered across ~150 new origins. Also covers AWS's Dec 2024 move to originating 1,000+ super-aggregates (IPv4 footprint 49M → 157M addresses, absorbing space from Volia and legacy ranges) and similar patterns in Iran (Hetzner as recipient).
  • How: Longitudinal BGP/WHOIS analysis; RIPE database version-diffing to document the "Russification" of registrations and subsequent purging of records; proxy-use confirmation via Krebs's investigation.
  • Where applicable: Global — this is analysis anyone can replicate with public data, and the lessons (origin-ASN policy as abuse defense, prefix-count consolidation, broker-mediated leasing risks) apply to any large origin AS.
path: Exodus of IPv4 from War-torn Ukraine

items.title: From Datacenter to AI Center, building the networks that build AI
items.text:
NANOG 96 digest Core pick 2–4 February 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Tyler Conrad — Arista Networks

VideoPDF

  • Why: The best single "orientation map" for engineers moving from general-compute DC design to AI backends. Vendor-presented, but dense with concrete numbers you can reuse in capacity planning, and refreshingly honest about failure rates.
  • What: A design guide across topology (single-box vs 2-tier vs 3-tier with GPU-count ceilings per form factor; rail-isolated vs rail-optimized vs fat-tree; multi-plane scaling by port-speed fan-out — 1x800G/2x400G/4x200G), subscription ratios (target 1:1 or better), optics economics, load balancing and congestion control (ECMP hashing vs RDMA-aware static hashing vs DLB vs packet spraying vs SRv6 steering), RoCEv2 mechanics (DCQCN, PFC victim flows, ECN/ECT tuning, a concrete QoS queue design with CNP in SP queues), and segmentation options from VLANs to VRFs to SRv6 uSID.
  • How: Prescriptive with arithmetic: for a hypothetical 100k-GPU back-end, 257,904 links and 515,808 optics; at 2.3M-hour MTBF that is one optic failure roughly every 4.45 hours — about five per day. LPO optics (no DSP, DSP moved into switch silicon) claimed at ~0.5x power, ~0.7x cost, ~0.01x latency. Includes a common-failure checklist (QoS mismatch, dirty fiber, FEC/autoneg mismatch, MMU tuning) that mirrors what real AI-cluster escalations look like.
  • Where applicable: Greenfield AI back-end builds; the talk's own takeaway is that back-end reuse of existing gear is unlikely and power/heat is usually the first constraint. Arista perspective throughout, so silicon-specific framing (radix/speed tables) should be re-derived for other vendors.
path: From Datacenter to AI Center, building the networks that build AI

items.title: Improving Routing Security for Global Research and Education
items.text:
NANOG 96 digest Adjacent pick 2–4 February 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

steven wallace — Internet2.edu (with CAIDA, per ROOTBEER/NSF CICI)

VideoPDF

  • Why: R&E networks deterministically prefer R&E routes over commodity, which makes their route leaks high-impact (US scientific traffic transiting unintended international paths). Beyond the R&E story, this is a template for measuring local-pref policies you cannot see in public BGP views.
  • What: A measurement system that announces the same prefix from two origins — one via an R&E path (Internet2), one via commodity transit — with varying AS-path prepends, then pings responsive hosts to infer which route each of ~2,600 R&E ASes actually chose. June 2025 results: 80.8% of prefixes/75.3% of ASes always used the R&E route regardless of prepending; 7% always commodity; ~9% switch by AS-path length (implying equal local-pref). Real 2024 incidents documented: a South American R&E network leaking commercial routes (traffic rerouted through South America) and a Middle East member leaking R&E routes to a commercial provider (cloud return traffic transiting the Middle East, some members withdrawing specifics defensively).
  • How: Building on this, the ROOTBEER project is constructing an operational routing-security observatory at Internet2 — leak detection between R&E and commodity, a stakeholder dashboard, and a move toward an actively maintained public route filter on all peers, shareable by other R&E transit networks.
  • Where applicable: R&E-specific topology (route-preference policy), and public BGP visibility is thin here (only 27 of 2,659 R&E ASes provide RouteViews/RIS views). The dual-origin measurement technique, though, transfers to any policy-visibility problem, and the public-filter approach is a model for any community network with trusted transit.
path: Improving Routing Security for Global Research and Education

items.title: IP Geofeeds: Trust, Accuracy, and Abuse
items.text:
NANOG 96 digest Wildcard pick 2–4 February 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Calvin Ardi — IPinfo (with Oliver Gasser, William Leung)

VideoPDF

  • Why: Self-published IP geolocation (RFC 8805) is now consumed by every major geolocation provider and feeds compliance decisions (gambling law, content geo-blocking) — and this is the first large-scale measurement of whether geofeeds are true, plus documentation of active adversarial abuse of the format. Not a typical PM search topic, but the findings are broadly useful.
  • What: Validation via two methods: RTT multilateration from a ~1,300-probe global network (27.7M RTTs covering 205k IPv4 / 74.5k IPv6 prefixes) and GPS ground truth from mobile devices. Results: country-level consistency 92% (96.6% IPv4, 79.6% IPv6), but city-level only 79.6% for infrastructure measurements (median error a startling 759 km) and just 29.9% on mobile networks — the gap between infrastructure location and actual user location. Top mismatch sources: CDNs, tier-1s, VPNs, cellular, IP leasing. Adversarial geofeeds are real and quantified: one maps ~101k IPv6 prefixes to 249 countries and ~80k cities (including Antarctica and North Korea); 17 of 20 popular VPN providers had exit traffic in a different country than claimed; public guides exist for crafting metadata to manipulate geolocation databases.
  • How: Proposals to fix the ecosystem: format updates (validity periods/TTL, standardized location identifiers such as H3), validation and feedback mechanisms (geofeed-validator, OpenGeoFeed), and public/private hosting options — with an IAB workshop and possible future IETF WG.
  • Where applicable: Anyone publishing geofeeds (the companion best-practices talk gives authoring guidance) or consuming geolocation for compliance/security. The mobile-network city-level number is the one to remember when someone proposes city-level geo-enforcement.
path: IP Geofeeds: Trust, Accuracy, and Abuse

items.title: Keynote: AI Data Center Networking: Lessons from Meta's Evolution
items.text:
NANOG 96 digest Core pick 2–4 February 2026

Abstract Recording

Omar Baldonado — Meta

Video

  • Why: Meta operates some of the largest AI clusters in the world and, unusually for a hyperscaler, shares openly (FBOSS, TorchComms, OCP). A cross-generation retrospective on AI fabric design from the person who runs Meta's global DC networks is the highest-signal keynote on the program for physical DC networking.
  • What: A retrospective through successive AI network deployments — what each iteration taught and where false starts occurred — framed as a stack: PyTorch/framework behavior shapes xPU selection, accelerator traffic patterns drive topology choices, NIC capabilities enable or constrain operations. Also covers network automation at scale, density constraints (power, cooling, space), telemetry for AI workloads, and managing rapid technology transitions without destabilizing production, with gigawatt-scale clusters on the roadmap.
  • How: Lessons-learned format across production generations rather than a single architecture pitch; the value is in the cascade framing (framework → hardware → topology → operations) and the operational truths behind open-sourced artifacts like FBOSS and TorchComms.
  • Where applicable: Explicitly Meta-scale — multi-gigawatt buildouts, custom switch OS, OCP hardware. The layer-interaction reasoning transfers to anyone designing AI clusters, but the specific density and automation numbers are org-specific (from abstract only; the NANOG content page could not be retrieved and no slides were published in the source material).
path: Keynote: AI Data Center Networking: Lessons from Meta's Evolution

items.title: Keynote: Beyond the Chip: The Unprecedented Infrastructure Demands of AI and HPC
items.text:
NANOG 96 digest Core pick 2–4 February 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Bill Conrades, Chris Stewart, Michael Balasko — AHEAD

VideoPDF

  • Why: The most concrete "facility-to-fabric" framing of AI datacenter buildouts at this meeting. For anyone whose remit includes physical DC design, this maps how power and cooling constraints now dictate network architecture choices — the limiting factors are no longer transistors but power delivery, cooling, and system-level architecture.
  • What: A structured survey of AI/HPC infrastructure: rack density evolution from air-cooled (<10-15kW) through hybrid/liquid (30-80kW+) to liquid-everything (100-150kW+); a cooling technology ladder (perimeter CRAC → containment → rear-door heat exchange → direct-to-chip → immersion) with capacity bands per technology; and the networking backbone — AI backend (East/West, 1:1 oversubscription) vs frontend (North/South) reference architecture, rail-optimized topology for AllReduce collectives, and a useful comparative table of Ethernet variants (standard ECMP → enhanced ECMP+advanced LB → scheduled packet-spraying/VOQ → Ultra Ethernet) with honest cluster-size and losslessness trade-offs.
  • How: Built around AHEAD's own 10MW specialized integration facility case study (permitting timelines, hybrid air + facility-water cooling, D2C and RDHx plans) plus a Gartner impact radar for timing investments (DLC and AI Ethernet fabrics rated "act now"; in-package microfluidics, HVDC, 800V distribution on longer horizons). Includes physical-layer detail: MPO/xPC/breakout planning, 800G still riding 100G SerDes with 200G SerDes emerging, DC bus bar and ORv3/MGX rack standards.
  • Where applicable: Broadly applicable planning guidance for AI-era facilities, though presented by a systems integrator (with Cisco-credited diagrams and NVIDIA NVL72 examples), so expect consultative framing rather than an operator postmortem. The cooling-capacity numbers and Ethernet-variant table transfer to any AI DC program.
path: Keynote: Beyond the Chip: The Unprecedented Infrastructure Demands of AI and HPC

items.title: Lightning Talk: Seeing Through the RDMA Fog: Monitoring RoCEv2 with sFlow
items.text:
NANOG 96 digest Core pick 2–4 February 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Peter Phaal — InMon Corp.

VideoPDF

  • Why: AI/RDMA clusters create a genuine blind spot: kernel bypass means tcpdump, wireshark, and even eBPF-based host agents see nothing. For a PM who tracks both lossless fabrics and host-based observability (eBPF), this is the counterpoint — some visibility has to come from the switch ASIC.
  • What: A demonstration, on SDSC's Expanse production cluster (93k cores, 208 GPUs, 100G hybrid fat-tree), of sFlow-based RoCEv2 monitoring: RDMA I/O operations decoded from sampled packet headers (opcode, queue pair, PSN, DMA length, virtual address), ECN/CNP congestion-message rates, RoCE ack-credit tracking, per-link queue depth and transit delay, and — critically — immediate notification of every dropped packet with where/why/who.
  • How: Standard sFlow agents in leaf/spine switches stream sampled headers and counters over the out-of-band management network (no interference with RoCE); three lines of SONiC config enable it (sflow collector, sflow drop-monitor-limit 50, sflow enable), similar on Arista/Cisco/Dell/NVIDIA. sflowtool + tshark decode the InfiniBand transport headers from samples; new extensions add per-sample transit delay/queue depth and per-discard reports (reason-coded, e.g. dst_net_unknown). Ultra Ethernet is just another header format for the pipeline — no agent change needed.
  • Where applicable: Broadly applicable — this is a standard switch feature, not new silicon, and the technique covers exactly the visibility gap that host tooling cannot. Drop-notification support requires current releases (202511 SONiC for drop-monitor). The one honest caveat: sampling-based, so it complements rather than replaces per-flow precision.
path: Lightning Talk: Seeing Through the RDMA Fog: Monitoring RoCEv2 with sFlow

items.title: Lightning Talk: You Don't Need The DNS Root Server System
items.text:
NANOG 96 digest Wildcard pick 2–4 February 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Wes Hardaker — Google (with Geoff Huston, Warren Kumari, Jim Reed)

VideoPDF

  • Why: A DNS root server operator standing up at NANOG to ask you to stop sending him traffic is the most memorable pitch on the program, and it's technically sound: your resolver can hold the entire signed root zone locally (RFC 7706/8806). Root query load grew ~40% in two years to 130B queries/day — for data resolvers could already have.
  • What: The case for LocalRoot: fetch the ~1.5MB signed root zone 2-3x/day from IANA/CDN sources, serve it locally. Security improves (DNSSEC validation of unmodified data, ZONEMD integrity), robustness improves (multiple sources and protocols; survives a 24h+ DDoS of the root system), privacy improves (no queries to root at all), and performance improves (root RTT = 0, ~1.5-2.4MB/day of bandwidth).
  • How: Trivial deployment paths shown for the three major resolvers: Knot Resolver's prefill module, BIND type mirror, Unbound auth-zone with the IANA root-zone URL and prefetch. AXFR adoption to B-Root already visible and growing. Active IETF drafts (draft-wkumari-dnsop-localroot-bcp, publication-point and transfer-scheme drafts) aim to standardize and default this in 2026.
  • Where applicable: Any recursive-resolver operator, from enterprise to ISP; no client-side changes. The one cultural hurdle is accepting that the root system becomes an emergency backup rather than the bootstrap queried every time — exactly the inversion the talk argues for.
path: Lightning Talk: You Don't Need The DNS Root Server System

items.title: Multipath Traffic Engineering for WAN & AIDC
items.text:
NANOG 96 digest Core pick 2–4 February 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Zhaohui (Jeffrey) Zhang — HPE (with Kireeti Kompella)

VideoPDF

  • Why: Challenges a 25-year-old either/or — you could have ECMP load balancing or fine-grained TE with bandwidth control, not both. Kompella (co-author of the original MPLS TE RFCs) proposing a unified construct for both WAN and AI datacenters is a notable architectural signal, and the IETF drafts are live.
  • What: MPTE programs an optimally weighted load-balancing DAG (MPTED) across the network: a single construct with per-junction split ratios replaces the many parallel LSPs that conventional TE needs to fill fat pipes (their example: 1600 Gbps R1→R12 needs four LSP constructs conventionally, one MPTED with 25/25/50/50 splits under MPTE). Link failure adjusts junction ratios without reshaping the DAG; multiple ingresses and multiple egresses (multi-egress load spreading, not multicast) are supported with far less state than per-path tunnels.
  • How: Junction state = incoming bandwidth + previous-hops + next-hops with weighted load shares; signaling via RSVP-TE (prototype), with BGP/PCEP/programmable-API (gRPC, YANG-backed) prototypes underway. Contextualized against the existing toolkit (auto-bandwidth, container LSPs/TE++, cBPS AI/ML bandwidth prediction, tactical TE), and connected to the new IETF RTGWG conversation on ML network scheduling (draft-kompella-rtgwg-mlnwsched) — reserving and isolating network resources per inference/training task, since TE only makes sense in an ML cluster when it is split among multiple tenants/tasks.
  • Where applicable: WAN/MAN/DCI and multi-tenant AI clusters; assumes MPLS or IP-tunnel data planes and a controller/computer to originate MPTEDs. IETF draft-stage — conceptual architecture now, not shipping broadly. HPE/Juniper-heritage perspective.
path: Multipath Traffic Engineering for WAN & AIDC

items.title: Redefining Netflix BGP architecture
items.text:
NANOG 96 digest Core pick 2–4 February 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Fred Cuiller — Cisco; Elise Vennegues — Netflix

VideoPDF

  • Why: A large, real BGP architecture migration with the validation methodology, defect discovery, and phased cutover shown — the parts that usually get omitted. Netflix's edge is 400+ PoPs, 19,000+ OCAs, ~175 countries, 20,000+ eBGP sessions to 2,800+ ASNs; moving that off iBGP full-mesh is a serious operational story.
  • What: Replacement of iBGP full mesh between Edge Switches and Provider Edge routers with a route-reflector hierarchy built on Cisco IOS XRv9000 UCS M7 appliances (chosen over traditional routers and VNFs on integrated TPM, CoPP, operational simplicity). RRs placed in six global sites; production scale runs to 37M IPv4 paths / 300+ clients in North America, 20M paths / 250+ clients in EMEA. Interesting appliance-selection comparison table (router vs VNF vs appliance across scale, CoPP, security, cost).
