  • How: Early Field Trial with the vendor caught real defects before deployment (early-release memory leak, BGP process rlimit misassignment, duplicated LLDP entries on Mellanox NICs); one miss escaped lab — telemetry YANG path performance at scale with sub-60s polling, discovered only in pre-production, reinforcing that production churn/scale is unique. Migration: phased per-device (staging RR peering with pilot prefixes → release prefixes to RR → per-device depref-then-pref-up → remove mesh), driven by internal tooling with a per-device migration tag; telemetry dashboards track CPU/memory, session counts, and received paths per address family. BMP activation is the stated next step.
  • Where applicable: The Cisco appliance choice is Netflix/Cisco-specific, but the RR placement reasoning, EFT-style validation discipline, phased-migration mechanics, and telemetry checklist transfer to any iBGP-mesh-to-RR program at hundreds-of-PoPs scale.

items.title: Removing Barriers to RPKI Adoption
items.text:
NANOG 96 digest Adjacent pick 2–4 February 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Cecilia Testart — Georgia Institute of Technology

VideoPDF

  • Why: ROA coverage passed 50% but adoption is uneven, and this is a rigorous answer to why: it identifies planning complexity — not awareness — as the choke point, with numbers on where the remaining headroom is.
  • What: Combines 13 semi-structured operator interviews with BGP/WHOIS/delegation/RIR data analysis, framed by a technology-adoption model (RPKI is in the late-majority phase). Four barrier areas: IP resource management (years of poor recordkeeping), awareness/training, RPKI software, and monitoring/incident tooling. The core contribution is a systematic ROA-planning framework — who can issue, which more-specifics are routed, which delegations/other orgs are involved — made concrete via ru-RPKI-ready, a platform characterizing unrouted space: 47% of IPv4 and 71% of IPv6 prefixes not in RPKI could be covered with minimal technical effort, and if just ten organizations acted, global coverage would rise 7% (IPv4) and 19% (IPv6).
  • How: Worked examples show a single /20 requiring 7 ROAs across 7 origin ASNs and two organizations — the realistic complexity that scares operators off. RIRs are identified as pivotal actors across all four barrier areas.
  • Where applicable: Most actionable for small/mid-size operators and RIR outreach programs; the planning framework and tool are directly usable for anyone with messy, inherited address space.

items.title: RoVista+: Mapping Real ROV Deployments, Dependencies, and Delays
items.text:
NANOG 96 digest Core pick 2–4 February 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Tijay Chung — Virginia Tech

VideoPDF

  • Why: "Do you filter RPKI-invalids?" has always been hard to answer honestly — prior methods couldn't tell local enforcement from an upstream doing it for you. This work separates the two, and the findings about RP (relying-party) concentration are a systemic-risk result every operator should see.
  • What: A measurement framework that runs its own ASN and its own RPKI publication points, serving different test ROAs to specific relying parties, then probing the Internet to see who drops the route. Results across 21,827 measured ASes: 1,127 self-deploy ROV while 1,815 ASes rely entirely on upstream filtering — and 69.6% of those "protected" ASes remain vulnerable to local hijacks. 52% of ROV-deploying ASes depend on exactly one RP server (only 14% use multiple RPs in different ASNs, contra RFC 7115). Router enforcement lags ROA updates by ~37 minutes (60-120 minutes end-to-end). Simulation: ROV in the top 100 ASes protects 27.6% of networks; disabling it in Tier-1s exposes 23.8% to hijacks. ~74% of top-5,000 ASes self-deploy; smaller networks overwhelmingly depend on upstreams.
  • How: Dynamic publication points + controlled test-ROA-to-specific-RP delivery + Internet-wide ping/traceroute scanning. Timing-based inference distinguishes upstream filtering (downstreams drop in synchronized clusters when the upstream filters) from self-deployment (independent drop times due to unaligned RTR polling) — validated against Comcast (private RP, synchronized), Cloudflare (public RP, varied), and NTT (both patterns).
  • Where applicable: The tooling and datasets are open-sourced, and the operational lessons are immediate for everyone: diversify your RPs across ASNs, and understand your ROV posture may be inherited rather than enforced. The methodology (selectively invalidating to one RP at a time) also generalizes to AS-path exploration. Research-grade but production-relevant.
path: RoVista+: Mapping Real ROV Deployments, Dependencies, and Delays

items.title: Shaping the Future of BGP Observability: BMP Evolution at IETF
items.text:
NANOG 96 digest Core pick 2–4 February 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Narasimha Prasad S — Cisco (with Paolo Lucente, NTT DATA; Thomas Graf, Swisscom)

VideoPDF

  • Why: BMP is quietly becoming the vendor-neutral BGP telemetry substrate, and its IETF evolution this cycle is substantial. If the PM's world includes BGP monitoring pipelines (and the Netflix talk explicitly names BMP activation as next), this is the standards map.
  • What: A structured tour of the foundational RFCs (7854 Adj-RIB-In, 9069 Loc-RIB, 8671 Adj-RIB-Out — including the useful correction that pre-policy Adj-RIB-Out is not the Loc-RIB) and then the active drafts: BMPv4 TLV-ization making all message types extensible; Path Marking, which exports the best-path decision outcome per path with reason codes (finally answering "why wasn't this path installed" without memorizing the 13-step selection process); structured timestamps separating trigger time from export time; Generic Event Notification for non-route events; Route Event Logging for alerting on policy discards and validation failures; Snapshots for mid-stream collector sync and time-binned archives; ~20 new statistics types; and a YANG model for managing what gets exported.
  • How: Performance drafts attack BMP's high-scale cost — Route Monitoring Aggregation across peers, Common Updates across RIB-views (up to 4x), and Multi-Peer headers — claiming up to n-fold reduction in router/collector CPU and message volume. Security: TCP-AO as the RFC 7854 IPsec alternative, plus early BMP-over-QUIC (multi-streaming + TLS) and BMP-for-RPKI-monitoring proposals.
  • Where applicable: Standards-track and vendor-agnostic; directly relevant to anyone building or buying BGP observability. Implementation timing varies by draft status (some are WG documents, some proposed work) — the talk's own closing point is that operator use cases should drive which drafts advance.
path: Shaping the Future of BGP Observability: BMP Evolution at IETF

items.title: The BGP Clock and the BGP Observatory: Hunting Stuck Routes​
items.text:
NANOG 96 digest Wildcard pick 2–4 February 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Kemal Sanjta — Cisco ThousandEyes

VideoPDF

  • Why: BGP zombies — routes that persist in RIBs long after withdrawal because a router lost the UPDATE — happen hundreds of times a day on the public Internet and quietly direct traffic onto dead or congested links. Prior work showed withdrawn-and-RPKI-invalid prefixes persisting for months; this is the follow-up operational tool, and it's free.
  • What: The BGP Clock: a continuously running beacon that advertises a fresh prefix every 10 minutes and withdraws it, encoding time in the prefix itself (IPv6 2a0d:3dc1:NNNN::/48, N = 10-minute index since Jan 1, recycled yearly; IPv4 147.189.(216+N).0/24, N = hour mod 8, recycled every 8 hours — details retrievable via whois). Anyone can check their own RIBs for stale entries. On top of it, the Stuck Route Observatory: a free, no-login web tool where you search by AS and see whether stuck routes are present in your paths, plus a heuristic guess at whether the failure to propagate a withdrawal is yours or an upstream's. RFC 9687 is the new standards attempt at reducing impact — the presenters explicitly ask operators to request vendor support for it.
  • How: Beacon advertise/withdraw cycles correlated against RIPE RIS, RouteViews, and Cisco's near-real-time monitors. Honest limitations: direct visibility covers ~1,500 ASNs (~1% of all), extended to >50% via customer-cone inference; IXP route servers can misattribute blame; intra-AS inconsistency (only some routers in a large AS holding the stuck route — found cases with just 5% of a Tier-1's downstreams seeing it) makes root-causing genuinely hard, with BMP named as the partial future fix.
  • Where applicable: Universal — any operator can check their AS in the Observatory today and grep their RIBs for the clock prefixes tonight. The measurement-visibility limits mean absence of evidence isn't evidence of absence, but it's the best available Internet-scale stuck-route diagnostic.
path: The BGP Clock and the BGP Observatory: Hunting Stuck Routes​

items.title: 50 Years of Networking
items.text:
NANOG 97 digest Wildcard pick 1–3 June 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Geoff Huston – APNIC

VideoPDF

  • Why: Not a technique talk — a direction-of-field argument from one of the Internet's longest-running observers, and the argument lands squarely on questions this PM cares about (openness, centralization, what the AI build-out means).
  • What: Why Ethernet won (open, cheap, simple, self-operating, and — crucially — an invariant frame format that preserved capital across 50 years of speed and medium changes); IP as "large-scale Ethernet" pushing complexity to the edge. Then the uncomfortable present: name-based service delivery has replaced hop-by-hop address networking, the Internet's "core" is now private CDN feeder systems, and transit is dead. The alternate tomorrow: if Moore's Law stalls, the AI build-out looks like a return to centralized, expensive, specialized compute — and Huston's real warning is the resurgence of closed, black-box platforms whose applications deliberately avoid standard open technologies, making open standards the endangered species.
  • How: Historical analysis and argument; no mechanism to evaluate.
  • Where applicable: Speculative and big-picture, but a useful stress test for any strategy that assumes the next 50 years look like the last 50.

items.title: Channelmania! – future proof your DWDM network topology while keeping it flexible for 1.6T
items.text:
NANOG 97 digest Core pick 1–3 June 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Thomas Weible – Flexoptix

VideoPDF

  • Why: With IPoDWDM, IP engineers inherit the spectrum-planning problem that used to belong to the transport team, and the shift from narrow-grid channel-count thinking to wide-grid superchannels changes topology and filter decisions that lock in for a hardware generation.
  • What: An argument that as per-channel bandwidth grows (400G/800G/1.6T coherent superchannels), 400GHz COTS muxes future-proof the C-band (12×400GHz vs 96×50GHz) while remaining backward-compatible with legacy 50GHz services. Includes a compact coherent-detection primer (DP-QAM16, 425Gbps at 53.125GBd, phase- and polarization-diversity balanced receivers), the grid math (1.6T DP-QAM16 needs ~300GHz channel bandwidth), DIY superchannels via low-cost PLC 1x4 splitters feeding regular 50GHz mux/demux, and a market snapshot (800G ZR+ in DD/OSFP, 12.8T liquid-cooled XPO approaching).
  • How: Think in THz/GHz rather than nm and channel numbers; make a frequency plan per span; exploit the fact that coherent receivers are "blind" to foreign wavelengths to build filterless/colorless topologies — at the acknowledged cost of flexibility, which wide-grid filters win back.
  • Where applicable: For anyone planning or refreshing DWDM plant, especially IP engineers newly owning transport decisions. Caveat: this is Flexoptix research content and the 400GHz-COTS recommendation aligns with their product line — the physics and tradeoffs are general, the shopping advice is vendor-flavored.
path: Channelmania! – future proof your DWDM network topology while keeping it flexible for 1.6T

items.title: Crafting Network Configurations at Meta
items.text:
NANOG 97 digest Adjacent pick 1–3 June 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Santiago Alfonso Munoz Rodriguez – Meta

VideoPDF

  • Why: How a hyperscaler generates config for thousands of multi-vendor backbone devices daily is a useful reference point for anyone designing (or buying) network automation — and the compiler framing is genuinely clarifying.
  • What: Meta's stack — FBNet object store, Skynet Thrift API, Jinja2 config generation — extended with Skypath, a minimal query DSL embedded directly in templates ({$ Router[name={dev}]/asn $}), which turns templates into self-contained specifications that engineers can reason about close to plain CLI. The multi-vendor layer is a "Confpiler": vendor-agnostic IR (OpenConfig-like), frontend authoring/analysis, backend IR→vendor-YANG schema translation separated from serialization — so delivery protocol (CLI for humans, NETCONF/gNMI for machines) can switch on the fly, and the multi-vendor network is operated as if single-vendor.
  • How: Lazy-evaluating interpreter preprocesses templates; compile-time static blueprint with runtime-rendered dynamic values (a Java bytecode analogy); versioned packages pin code commits so rollback knows which implementation to return to.
  • Where applicable: Meta-scale backbone with daily change volume. The stated lessons temper transfer: "our ability to be declarative can only be as good as our database models," there's a limited budget for tooling change, and "abstraction only makes sense when behavior is portable." Concepts transfer; the surrounding systems are the hard part.

items.title: Designing Cloud Workloads For LEO Satellite Internet Users
items.text:
NANOG 97 digest Wildcard pick 1–3 June 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Sid Mathur – Fastah Inc.

VideoPDF

  • Why: LEO connectivity is quietly becoming a real user population, and it breaks assumptions (stable egress, stable IP geo, predictable RTT) that most cloud architecture takes for granted.
  • What: A mental model and design-pattern set for LEO-served users: traffic lands at ~200 (Starlink) / 300+ planned (Amazon LEO) ground gateways mapped to IX/PoPs; static users behave like fixed broadband, while in-motion users (aviation, maritime) change egress mid-session — the talk traces one flight's IP geolocation through Qatar, Kuwait, Jordan, Bulgaria, Hungary, Germany, and France, with all the GDPR/jurisdiction questions that implies. Amazon LEO B2B rides AWS Direct Connect, so once traffic lands it's ordinary VPC traffic; new multicloud interconnects (AWS Interconnect Multicloud, GCP Cross-cloud Interconnect) enable cross-cloud failover patterns.
  • How: Three patterns — pin static low-latency users to the nearest region with PNI for predictable RTT; build in-motion users as multi-region active-active with stateless services and HTTP/3 tolerance for TLS/TCP resets; use cross-cloud interconnects for "too expensive to fail" B2B workloads. Decision inputs: user-population geography, data sovereignty, egress cost, latency budget, failover topology.
  • Where applicable: Teams building applications for LEO user populations; the interconnect specifics are AWS/GCP-specific. Key takeaway: the routing path is the only truly different part.
path: Designing Cloud Workloads For LEO Satellite Internet Users

items.title: From Metrics to Investigation: How Agentic SRE Could Change Network Operations
items.text:
NANOG 97 digest Adjacent pick 1–3 June 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Mohibul Mahmud, Shamir Abdul Aziz, Karthik Srinivas Muthuramakrishnan – Microsoft

VideoPDF

  • Why: A working — not aspirational — agentic investigation system for network incidents, with an honest list of what still doesn't work; for anyone thinking about agentic identity and trust boundaries, this is the ground truth from an early deployment.
  • What: An LLM-driven investigation agent on Azure (Claude Opus-based, configurable) that handles the unknown-failure case runbooks can't: hop-by-hop topology discovery, protocol-level diagnostics across BGP, IKE Phase ½, and ExpressRoute, and a production case where it detected a blackhole route from a deallocated firewall in under 35 seconds. Four scenarios covered: live NL troubleshooting, scheduled monitoring with alert integration, topology discovery from minimal input, hybrid-connectivity analysis.
  • How: LLM reasoning + structured tools (Azure CLI, Resource Graph, Network Watcher) + operator-authored skills written in Markdown + governance (RBAC, isolated compute, safety hooks, human approval). The stated non-negotiables: read-only as the enterprise default, human approval required before any write action, and on-prem coverage only via telemetry forwarding to Log Analytics.
  • Where applicable: Demoed on Azure, but the pattern (reasoning layer + read-only tools + knowledge base + safety harness) is explicitly presented as generic. Azure-centric in tooling; the write-action approval gate is the identity/trust boundary worth watching as these systems mature.
path: From Metrics to Investigation: How Agentic SRE Could Change Network Operations

items.title: Gray failures in AI Fabric
items.text:
NANOG 97 digest Core pick 1–3 June 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Navtej Singh – Clockwork

VideoPDF

  • Why: AI training turned the DC fabric from boring plumbing into the throughput ceiling, and the failures operators now burn hours on are invisible to standard tooling — the motivating example is a GPU cloud that spent 19 hours hunting a slow training job caused by a hot transceiver whose FEC corrections had been climbing for days while the link stayed up.
  • What: A working taxonomy of gray failures in AI fabrics — optic degradation via rising FEC corrections, intermittent CRC below thresholds, asymmetric paths, ECMP hash polarization landing collectives on hot links, PFC headroom exhaustion, sub-poll-interval microbursts — plus three fully worked scenarios (ECMP polarization, optic degradation, PFC cascade) showing what each telemetry layer sees and what it misses.
  • How: Three time-aligned layers: host (NCCL kernel timing, RDMA QP stats, per-rank step time), edge (PFC pause counters, queue depth, per-packet HW timestamps), fabric (gNMI/INT streaming, buffer occupancy, FEC). The proposed gap-closers are sub-microsecond PTP clock sync (software-only, no special silicon) plus an out-of-band probe mesh (<1% of link capacity, separate QoS class) for one-way delay and per-path attribution; histograms over gauges; alert on p99.9 percentile drift; the SLO becomes p99.9 collective step time.
  • Where applicable: Aimed at RoCEv2/lossless GPU-training fabrics and deliberately vendor-agnostic (IEEE 1588, OpenConfig/gNMI, INT/P4, NCCL profiler, DCGM, Linux RDMA counters). The speaker works for a vendor (Clockwork), but the scenario walkthroughs and tool references are open and portable. Cardinality discipline is flagged as the main scaling constraint.

items.title: Lessons From Scaling BPF To Detect RDMA Device Drivers Bugs In Real Time
items.text:
NANOG 97 digest Core pick 1–3 June 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Prankur Gupta – Meta Platforms, Inc

VideoPDF

  • Why: RDMA driver bugs are a top cause of AI training failures at Meta — 10–20% of daily AI job crashes are RDMA-associated (not network-related), wasting 32k+ GPU hours over six months — and the RDMA control path is famously opaque to existing observability. This sits squarely at the intersection of eBPF and lossless-fabric operations.
  • What: RDMATracer, an eBPF-based tool that detects RDMA device driver bugs in real time by tracing kernel state mismatches across the ibverbs control path. In production it cuts diagnosis from 10+ minutes to seconds, auto-classifies issues, and was used to triage a black-box vendor driver bug (a dma_resv_wait_timeout overflow in ib_umem_dmabuf_map_pages on a newly deployed NIC driver).
  • How: fentry/fexit BPF probes on kernel functions along ibverbs ioctl paths (fexit measured at ~72% of kretprobe overhead); static analysis to prune call paths (skip reads, pure-kernel internals, cleanup/refcount functions; per-vendor focus); a ~256KB ring buffer (~8k records) exports error context to userspace; per-CPU counter maps track invocation/error/errno counts. Periodically captures "good" traces and compares against failing ones to find the bifurcation point. Measured tax: p50 88.7% lower, p99 98.9% lower bpf_tax; no impact on workflow QPS.
  • Where applicable: Built for Meta's Linux/RDMA GPU training fleet (vendor-specific driver paths baked into the pruning rules), but the engineering pattern — probe-point selection via static analysis, fexit over kretprobe, ring-buffer error-context export, good-trace diffing — transfers to any operator doing eBPF-based kernel-state tracing. Directly relevant to anyone running RoCE fabrics for training.
path: Lessons From Scaling BPF To Detect RDMA Device Drivers Bugs In Real Time

items.title: Migrating From Bespoke Hardware To An Open Load Balancing For Kubernetes
items.text:
NANOG 97 digest Core pick 1–3 June 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Sergey Kolobov, Marcin Wojciechowski (Arista Networks, per slides)

VideoPDF

  • Why: Replacing a 6.4Tbps proprietary stateless L4 load balancer with MetalLB in BGP mode is exactly the BGP-native Kubernetes ingress pattern many teams are evaluating, and the talk's core contribution is the network-side fix for ECMP's nastiest gotcha: widespread connection resets when the backend set changes.
  • What: A full migration story: a 4-node MetalLB cluster (dual E5-2650 v4, 20Gbps LACP per node) sustains 6–10k RPS and 30k+ established connections, and benchmarked identically to the hardware appliance (~80 vs ~79.6 req/sec, same latency, 100% 200s over 100k requests). The key technique is pre-provisioning resilient ECMP groups on the ToR (ip hardware fib ecmp resilience <IP>/32 capacity 16 redundancy 2) — fixed modulo duplication of next-hops so only flows hashing to the failed next-hop remap, instead of all flows rehashing.
  • How: MetalLB/FRR mode with BFD for sub-second failover; kube-proxy conntrack headroom (32k/core → nf_conntrack_max of 1,572,864); NIC ring buffer tuning (512→8192) against microburst RX drops; ingress nodes spread evenly across racks; ArgoCD GitOps; vtysh inside the speaker pod for BGP/BFD debugging. Also candid costs: strict port exposure replaced the "widely open" old model, adding a release-review step for developers.
  • Where applicable: The resilient-ECMP fix is switch-ASIC specific (Arista syntax shown; other vendors have analogues) — verify your ToR supports it before adopting. Otherwise broadly applicable to bare-metal Kubernetes with a BGP-capable fabric. The stated next steps (Cilium BGP vs MetalLB consolidation — noting Cilium lacks native BFD — eBPF CNI migration, IPv6 dual-stack) are a useful roadmap of where K8s edge networking is heading.
path: Migrating From Bespoke Hardware To An Open Load Balancing For Kubernetes

items.title: Monitoring 2,800 BGP Sessions using BMP Protocol
items.text:
NANOG 97 digest Core pick 1–3 June 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Pavel Odintsov – FastNetMon Inc (production network: Gcore)

VideoPDF

  • Why: Per-peer, route-level BGP visibility at scale is something SNMP, gNMI, and periodic full-table dumps each demonstrably fail to deliver — and this talk backs the claim with numbers rather than assertion.
  • What: Benchmarks on a ~1.04M-route table: GoBGP text dump 2.0GB/73s; JSON 543MB/75s; gRPC/protobuf 25.5–27.5s; binary NLRI 15–15.5s; Rotonda (Rust, NLnet Labs) 9.6s JSON with 6.5x lower peak memory than GoBGP. Then the case for BMP (RFC 7854): per-peer exports across pre-policy, post-policy, and Loc-RIB stages, plus per-session stats (policy-rejected prefixes, duplicate advertisements, loop-invalidated updates, adj-rib-in/loc-rib counts). Production numbers: 2,728 peers and 68.9M routes re-emitted as a 9.8GB BMP dump in ~318s.
  • How: BMP stations configured on Nokia, Juniper, Cisco XR, and Arista (config snippets shown for all four); Rotonda used as BMP collector and re-emitter, so downstream consumers get one initial full-table dump plus incremental updates instead of repeated snapshots. A Netomics fork addresses Rotonda's memory wall (112GB at 80M routes) with gzip, JSON streaming, TLS, and BMP output.
  • Where applicable: Multi-vendor networks of meaningful scale (Gcore: 210+ PoPs, 4 routing platforms, 194M routes). Open-source tooling throughout (GoBGP, Rotonda, benchmark code published). Explicitly complements rather than replaces SNMP/gNMI for session-level health and hardware counters.
path: Monitoring 2,800 BGP Sessions using BMP Protocol

items.title: Network OS Upgrades at Hyperscale
items.text:
NANOG 97 digest Core pick 1–3 June 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Sujitha Sekar Rajan – Meta Platforms Inc

VideoPDF

  • Why: Upgrading NOS across tens of thousands of multi-vendor devices without either security exposure or production incidents is a recurring dilemma, and this talk ships the pipeline and two rare, detailed war stories.
  • What: Meta's vendor-agnostic 5-step upgrade process (vendor testing → planning → internal testing → canary → cardinality-gated rollout) with a Testbed-as-a-Service framework: tag-driven test selection on real lab hardware across all vendors and roles (50+ test cases for backbone edge alone), automated gating so no image reaches production without a full pass, progressive canary (lab metros → low-traffic → high-traffic), and cardinality rules (per-site/per-metro/global limits, freeze periods, independent role pipelines). War story 1: a vendor code refactor truncated version numbers from 64-bit to 32-bit, desyncing RIB and FIB silently under route churn (~9 days to failure at 5k updates/sec) after ~⅓ of the fleet was upgraded — only a reboot clears corrupted forwarding state, drain does not. War story 2: a re-timer DFE re-tuning bug on one vendor's odd-numbered 100GE ports produced persistent framing errors after link flaps while the interface showed up, requiring three-vendor coordination to isolate.
  • How: Layered defensive pipeline; automated drain→reboot→undrain remediation; permanent forwarding-discard detectors promoted from incident tooling; shift to maintenance releases; sustained route-churn/FIB-consistency checks added to qualification after story 1.
  • Where applicable: Explicitly Meta-scale (tens of thousands of devices, 3 hardware vendors, 5+ roles, up to 1.5M-prefix tables), but the pipeline design and lessons — real hardware not emulation, vendor labs can't reproduce production-scale churn, keep the detector you built during the incident — transfer to any multi-vendor operator.

items.title: Paraglider: Streamlining Cloud Networking
items.text:
NANOG 97 digest Adjacent pick 1–3 June 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Sarah McClure – UC Berkeley (LF Networking project with Google, Microsoft, IBM)

VideoPDF

  • Why: A research-to-production attempt to fix the core pain of cloud networking — low-level, vendor-specific primitives — with a high-level connectivity abstraction; relevant context for anyone working on cloud-native networking intent models.
  • What: Evolved from Berkeley's NSDI'22 "Invisinets" into an LF project with cloud-provider contributors. The model: basic reachability is provisioned for you; connectivity is expressed as permit lists on resources (default-off), with tags naming/grouping resources across clouds. The demo makes the value concrete: connecting three VMs across Azure and GCP auto-generated 3 NSGs, 4 subnets, 3 VNets + 1 VPC, 3 peerings, 2 VPN gateways, a cloud router, and a VPN tunnel.
  • How: A glide CLI (create/attach resources, tag them, add permit rules) driving an orchestrator with per-cloud plugins (Azure, GCP, IBM; AWS in roadmap); the controller provisions peerings, VPN tunnels, and BGP underneath; supports Kubernetes clusters and private endpoints; permit lists auto-update as tag membership changes.
  • Where applicable: Multicloud operators, especially greenfield. Honest open problems stated: brownfield compatibility and deployment validation still in progress, private IP-space management across clouds, "the cloud is a moving, obscured target," and cloud customers are entrenched in existing APIs. Simplicity is an explicit compromise (boilerplate with escape hatches).

items.title: Show Me Your PRs
items.text:
NANOG 97 digest Core pick 1–3 June 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

steve ulrich – nexthop.ai

VideoPDF

  • Why: For a PM whose core work includes physical DC networking, the open-NOS question is a portfolio-level bet, and this is one of the few operator-perspective (not vendor-marketing) assessments of what a durable SONiC ecosystem actually requires.
  • What: A pragmatic map of where open NOS works today — greenfield L3 leaf/spine DC, AI/GPU cluster fabrics (with PFC and new hashing capabilities), campus refresh — and where it doesn't yet: the Internet edge (open NOSes lack high-scale ACL support even where the silicon, e.g. a Q3D ASIC with DFZ-scale FIB, could support it) and legacy SP core. Plus a security-compliance argument (patch out-of-support hardware yourself, Linux-LTS analogy), a sovereign-infrastructure/supply-chain angle, a sustainability warning (durable open source isn't free; "maintenance taxes" must be paid across the community), and a due-diligence checklist.
  • How: The actionable core: before buying, target platforms that can run an open NOS later, require an open-NOS offramp, verify SAI/driver status, and — the title — ask vendors to show their PRs: verifiable upstream contributions, TSC presence, bootloader availability, and the ability to build your own images.
  • Where applicable: Not org-specific; a strategy talk for any operator. Honest limitations stated: legacy-platform transitions are mostly unrealistic (no SAI pathway), secure/measured boot adds twists, and current roadmap leverage is concentrated in a handful of large operators. Explicitly not a vendor pitch, though the speaker's affiliation is worth noting.

items.title: The Hidden Costs of SSH at Scale (Remote Presentation)
items.text:
NANOG 97 digest Adjacent pick 1–3 June 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Brett Lykins – Amazon

VideoPDF

  • Why: SSH is the default automation transport, and this talk quantifies — with open-source benchmarks — what its 10–15 round-trip handshake actually costs across a WAN, then gives an adoptable fix that requires no device changes.
  • What: Measured with tc netem at 150ms RTT: SSH PTY (Netmiko-style) takes 2,565ms before/around 5 commands vs 151ms for batched HTTPS — 17x. An edge proxy (SSH local at 1–2ms, HTTPS over the WAN) reaches 5.3x on new connections and 14.7x with reuse; a transparent tunnel (SSH on both ends, HTTPS only on the WAN segment) gets 12.7x with zero code changes to existing Ansible/Nornir. At 100k devices with 100 parallel lanes: 42.8 minutes down to 8.1.
  • How: NAAS (Netmiko-as-a-Service) — a lightweight proxy co-located with devices, deployable via docker compose, 100+ platforms; device SSH keys never cross the WAN; treat it like a bastion (hardening, rotation, session logging). Migration path: tunnel first (no changes), proxy second, native HTTPS (eAPI/NX-API/RESTCONF) where supported. Decision framework included: <5ms RTT don't bother; 5–30ms measure first.
  • Where applicable: Any WAN-distributed automation estate. Broadly applicable, no vendor dependence, benchmark and tool code open source (github.com/lykinsbd/clibench, /naas).
path: The Hidden Costs of SSH at Scale (Remote Presentation)

items.title: The Kimwolf Aftershock: Residential Proxy Botnets One Year Later
items.text:
NANOG 97 digest Core pick 1–3 June 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Craig Labovitz – Nokia; Chinni Tadivaka (joint Comcast Threat Research Lab / Nokia ERT research)

VideoPDF

  • Why: Residential-proxy-driven DDoS is now a backbone-scale security problem — attacks saturating transit and POP links, not just enterprise targets — and this is the rare talk with a year of longitudinal data on what disruption actually achieved.
  • What: The follow-up to NANOG 94's warning: law-enforcement and provider takedowns measurably cut US outbound DDoS, but Kimwolf metastasized into 21+ successor botnets ("ResHydra") reusing the same ADB-based residential exploits; daily active DDoS botnet endpoints climbed from ~1M (summer 2025) to 8M+ (2026), aggregate capacity in the hundreds of Tbps, with 100+ Tbps rated as a potential threat to most national networks. The economics: 75% of res-proxy attacks originate from US or Brazilian homes; the multi-billion-dollar proxy market is now funded largely by AI scraping demand; and gigabit symmetric broadband keeps raising upstream capacity.
  • How: Measurement via large-scale crawling, a botnet security range, licensed third-party data, and collaborating ISPs/hosting providers. The concrete remedy demonstrated: one LATAM ISP enabling C2-blocking ACLs on May 7, 2026 saw an immediate multi-Tbps drop in outbound DDoS — infrastructure reliability genuinely equals disrupting botnet C2 in your network.
  • Where applicable: Most relevant to ISPs/backbones and anyone operating consumer-facing access networks. Research artifacts are published (github.com/deepfield/public-research). The C2-disruption remedy is real but constrained by accuracy, policy, and legal concerns — which is exactly why NA adoption lags.
path: The Kimwolf Aftershock: Residential Proxy Botnets One Year Later

items.title: Towards a Non-Binary View of IPv6 Adoption
items.text:
NANOG 97 digest Wildcard pick 1–3 June 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Sulyab Thottungal Valapu – University of Southern California / Information Sciences Institute (with John Heidemann)

VideoPDF

  • Why: Not about any of the PM's core areas, but the results reframe a long-running debate with measurement: IPv6 adoption isn't binary, and the "how much" numbers are surprising.
  • What: Client-side: 9 months of flow data from 5 dual-stacked LA residences shows daily IPv6 fraction varies enormously (a single application can swing a site between an 11% day and a 91% day), with per-site medians diverging widely. Server-side: a browser-based crawl (dependencies resolved to arbitrary depth) of the Tranco top 100k finds only 12% fully IPv6-loadable — 42% have v6 enabled but 30% of the total still require IPv4 to fully load; fixing the top 5% of popular v4-only resources would fix over 25% of partial sites. Cloud-side: same-tenant paired comparisons (Wilcoxon) show deployment mechanics dominate — CloudFront's automatic v6 hit 71% while S3's opt-in dualstack-URL requirement yields 0.4%; Azure Front Door shows 100% is possible with no opt-out.
  • How: Passive flow capture (no payload) for clients; OpenWPM crawl with link-clicking for servers; n×n tenant-pair grid to separate cloud support from tenant choice.
  • Where applicable: The cloud recommendations (deploy v6 transparently rather than opt-in) are actionable for any platform provider; the client/server figures are bounded by US broadband and top-100k methodology but the non-binary framing generalizes.
path: Towards a Non-Binary View of IPv6 Adoption

items.title: Vendor Independent Network Segmentation
items.text:
NANOG 97 digest Core pick 1–3 June 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Brian Jemes – University of Idaho

VideoPDF

  • Why: Network segmentation designs usually collapse under vendor churn or rule-count growth; this is a concrete, numbers-backed architecture that survived six major vendor changes in 20 years — directly relevant to the PM's network-security interest.
  • What: Subnet-level segmentation at the University of Idaho: 425 policy-enforced subnets (110 service-consumer, 190 service-provider, 120 behind the border), 230 router-ACL interfaces, 195 NGFW-interfaces carrying 840 rules, 10 router VRFs, 6 firewall virtual instances. The key policy insight is that provider subnets get "standalone" O(n) policies (inbound default-deny exposing only the services offered, outbound default-allow) referenced by subnet groups, avoiding O(n²) mesh rules.
  • How: Consumers sorted into subnets via RADIUS-assigned VLANs (802.1X/MAB) from IdP user/device groups; dedicated VRF per consumer group with router ACLs blocking east-west; per-group virtual NGFWs; uRPF on every subnet; L2 ACLs for same-subnet traffic. Hard-won lessons: VRF-lite doesn't scale past ~3 VRFs, PBR isn't operationally scalable, DHCP relay in firewalls silently drops at enterprise scale, aggregate the address plan by type before geography, and use hub-spoke virtual cloud architecture because clouds aren't structured for subnet segmentation.
  • Where applicable: Mid-size enterprise (12k students, ~70k WiFi endpoints, ~800 switches) but the pattern is deliberately vendor-independent and generalizes. The tradeoff is explicit: middleboxes in all internal traffic flows complicate intranet routing and troubleshooting; app-layer authn/authz is out of scope.

items.title: Versioned Services for Network Automation
items.text:
NANOG 97 digest Adjacent pick 1–3 June 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

James Henderson – Ductus

VideoPDF

  • Why: Automation systems are usually written as if the standards they implement never change; this offers a clean, adoptable pattern for managing service intent across time — with EVPN as the running example.
  • What: A pattern combining named service types, semantic versions, and managed features — where a feature is a flag with metadata (introduced-in, standard-in, when-disabled fallback behavior, conflicts-with) rather than a bare code switch — plus cascading (hierarchical) types that control which features a service may use. Versioned packages pin each service version to an exact code commit, so rollbacks know which implementation to return to, and individual features can migrate independently across services (the talk shows a mid-migration state where one customer's RT is migrated and another's RD is not).
  • How: Semantic versioning for services (major = breaking contract change, minor = golden-config update with new feature, patch = code fix); the type carries classification, the version carries which flags apply.
  • Where applicable: General technique for any golden-config/automation platform, org-agnostic despite the EVPN examples. Also argued (briefly) as a prerequisite for safe AI agents in network ops — reversibility and transparency — which pairs naturally with the agentic sessions below.

items.title: What's New at the IETF
items.text:
NANOG 97 digest Adjacent pick 1–3 June 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Yingzhen Qu – Futurewei Technologies; Yaroslav Rosomakho – Zscaler

VideoPDF

  • Why: Standards-watch with an unusually dense set of identity-relevant items for this program: the wimse WG (Workload Identity in Multi-System Environments) adopted its Workload Identifier draft and split service-to-service credentials and authentication mechanisms into separate drafts; the OAuth WG adopted OAuth SPIFFE Client Authentication and published RFC 9901 (selective disclosure for JWTs); plus ECH RFCs (9848/9849), ML-KEM/SLH-DSA identifiers for X.509, and the new "plants" WG on Merkle Tree Certificates for post-quantum PKI.
  • What: A survey of IETF/IRTF/IAB structure and active work across areas — routing (BGP-4 4271bis, ASPA verification, RPKI-to-router 8210bis), QUIC multipath and MoQT, DELEG for DNS, NEMOPS-derived service abstractions (ONSEN BoF), and agentic coordination work (CATALIST).
  • How: Overview format; the useful artifact is the map of where each effort sits and which drafts are newly adopted vs published.
  • Where applicable: Broad relevance; for this PM, the wimse, OAuth-SPIFFE, and post-quantum PKI threads are the take-homes for workload/agentic identity planning.

items.title: A Blueprint for Securing Networks for AI : From Architecture to Operations
items.text:
NANOG 98 digest Core pick 19–21 October 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Saju Salahudeen – NOKIA, Reda Laichi – NOKIA

VideoPDF

  • Why: The only talk focused specifically on securing AI backend fabrics, where RDMA bypasses the host stack — forcing enforcement down to the switch and DPU. Core to the PM's network-security + AI-fabric overlap.
  • What: A Day 0/½ framework. Day 0: SZTP (RFC 8572, ownership vouchers, IDevID on TPM) over insecure ZTP, secure/measured boot chains. Day 1: TLS for syslog/gRPC/RADIUS/NTP, gRPC RPC restriction via gNSI Authz (allow gNMI Subscribe, deny gNMI Set), AAA hardening, per-tenant VRFs on switches plus per-flow DPU policy pushed per job, backend default-deny ACLs (RoCEv2 UDP 4791 within same job/tenant only), DDoS tiers (edge scrubbing/Flowspec/RTBH, API-key rate limits for inference, PFC watchdog and per-tenant QoS against pause storms, CoPP). Day 2: monitoring shifts from packet inspection to streaming telemetry (sFlow, INT) plus behavioral baselining, because DPI/host IDS don't scale to 400G/800G and RDMA traffic is invisible to host-based tools.
  • How: Anchored in the OpenAI/Hugging Face incident (agents exploited a third-party artifactory via exposed HF credentials) and in a public multi-vendor reference lab (github.com/srlinuxamericas/n98-ai-security).
  • Where applicable: Vendor session (Nokia principal engineers) with framework flavor, but the techniques are multi-vendor and the lab is public; applies to any shared GPU fabric where kernel-bypass transports defeat host-based controls.
path: A Blueprint for Securing Networks for AI : From Architecture to Operations

items.title: A Journey of Accelerating and Offloading OVS with a DPU
items.text:
NANOG 98 digest Core pick 19–21 October 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Abdullah Sevincer – Crusoe, Alex Bortok – NVIDIA

VideoPDF

  • Why: A numbers-backed production account of moving SDN (OVS/OVN) from host kernel to hardware to DPU — datapath internals with real benchmarks, at AI-cloud scale. Squarely the PM's cloud-native/datapath interest.
  • What: Three stages: kernel OVS (connection rates topping out in the low thousands/sec, instability growing with load); hardware-accelerated OVS datapath on the host (order-of-magnitude higher connection rate, near-zero failures, but host CPU cores and memory reserved away from customer VMs); then offloading the OVS/OVN control plane itself onto BlueField-3 DPUs, freeing 100% of host CPU — with the lesson that DPU cores aren't host cores, so right-sizing thread count beat adding more.
  • How: Slow-path mechanics explained cleanly: PMD threads busy-polling pinned cores instead of IRQ→softirq→netlink upcalls; steering rules programmed by DMA'd descriptor queues the NIC drains itself instead of per-flow netlink/TC calls; per-core parallel connection tracking instead of shared kernel conntrack locks; VF representors programming the eSwitch. Benchmarks via Keysight CyPerf (HTTP over Geneve: overlay, stateful NAT patterns). OVN programs both Geneve east-west and north-south for customer VPCs.
  • Where applicable: Crusoe's AI factory (BlueField-3/OVS-DOCA on every node) — co-presented with NVIDIA, so expect product framing; the performance mechanisms and tradeoffs apply to any OVS/OVN fleet, with numbers specific to their hardware and workloads.
path: A Journey of Accelerating and Offloading OVS with a DPU

items.title: AI Training Parallelism, From a Network Engineer's Point of View
items.text:
NANOG 98 digest Core pick 19–21 October 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Adel Iazzag – NVIDIA

VideoPDF

  • Why: The best "why does my AI fabric traffic look like this" explainer on the program — parallelism strategy maps directly onto flow patterns, incast, and fabric design decisions. Presented as vendor-neutral from four years of building/running AI fabrics.
  • What: A tour of the four parallelism types with their wire signatures: data parallelism (few very large AllReduce gradient flows per step, sawtooth uplink utilization); pipeline parallelism (point-to-point stage handoffs, latency-sensitive, util graphs look fine while the job waits); tensor parallelism (constant small AllReduce every layer that must stay in scale-up — if you can see it on the fabric, placement is wrong); MoE (AllToAll, many flows, uneven by destination, worst-case incast). Real jobs stack all of these on the same wires.
  • How: NCCL picks ring vs tree algorithms based on topology and message size (256 GPUs: 510 ring steps vs 16 tree steps); design guidance: rail-optimized (NIC k to leaf k), 1:1 subscription, lossless with congestion control tested for many-to-one, and ECMP alone is not enough — packet or flowlet spraying needed.
  • Where applicable: General technique for anyone building or operating AI backend Ethernet fabrics; the "test the collective, not the parallelism" and "give the scheduler the topology" instincts transfer regardless of vendor.
path: AI Training Parallelism, From a Network Engineer's Point of View

items.title: ASPA la vista.. Route leaks
items.text:
NANOG 98 digest Adjacent pick 19–21 October 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Alastair Strachan – RIPE NCC

VideoPDF

  • Why: ASPA is the next RPKI deployment wave after ROV, and this carries the operational guidance plus fresh uptake numbers — useful context for the routing-security work the PM is already doing.
  • What: A clear primer on ASPA objects (signed provider-AS lists) with the upstream/downstream path-validation algorithms and the complementary-coverage matrix (ROA for misorigination, ASPA for leaks and partial path spoofing, BGPsec for path spoofing). Signing uptake as of Aug 2026: 2.2% of registered ASNs worldwide (RIPE region 4.6%; Czech Republic leads at 10.9%); hosted signing UIs now live across all RIRs (Krill July 2025, RIPE NCC Nov 2025, ARIN Jan 2026, APNIC June 2026).
  • How: Same validator/RTR deployment model as ROV; operational guidance: include all providers (including backups not visible in AS paths), include non-transparent IXP route servers or they register as valleys, reject (don't de-prefer) invalids, and start with logging-only.
  • Where applicable: General, but early — router validation support is incomplete ("talk to your vendor"). Mostly educational for a routing-security veteran, but the uptake data and signing checklist are current.

items.title: Auto-bandwidth for Segment Routing
items.text:
NANOG 98 digest Adjacent pick 19–21 October 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Dmytro Shypovalov – Vegvisir Systems

VideoPDF

  • Why: The missing RSVP-TE auto-bandwidth equivalent for SR is a real ISP pain; this is a working, open-source, standards-based design with honest production caveats.
  • What: The problem: SR LSPs are stateless and most routers can't advertise per-LSP traffic rate (RFC 8733/RFC 9857 exist but require router-side sampling). The solution: an external bandwidth sampler (open source: github.com/Vegvisir-Systems/srte-sampler) collects SR LSP counters via gNMI and advertises the traffic rate to the PCE as a BGP-LS type-5 route with bandwidth TLV; the PCE recomputes segment lists and pushes via BGP-SRTE. Works today with IOS-XR, JunOS, EOS. PCE redundancy needs no state sync (distinct SRTE distinguishers, like route reflectors); total PCE failure falls back to IGP shortest path. The critique is self-aware: this merely replicates RSVP-TE auto-bandwidth; the better future design has the PCE query raw counters from existing telemetry (Telegraf/VictoriaMetrics) for a centralized traffic-matrix view, burst reaction, and analytics.
  • How: Feedback loop: router counters → sampler → BGP-LS to PCE → updated segment list (BGP-SRTE preferred; PCEP explicitly discouraged). Mesh templates plus ACTN (RFC 8453) sketch the intent-based layer above it.
  • Where applicable: Multi-vendor ISP SR-MPLS/SRv6 WANs; the author is candid about what "production-ready" requires (deterministic sampling, cross-controller identical results).

items.title: BGP Role model: tracking the adoption of RFC 9234
items.text:
NANOG 98 digest Core pick 19–21 October 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Bryton Herdes – Cloudflare, Iliana Xygkou – Georgia Institute of Technology

VideoPDF

  • Why: RFC 9234 (BGP Roles + OTC) is the session-level route-leak defense that complements ASPA's AS-level attestations — and this is a measurement of who's actually setting OTC, and who is actively stripping it.
  • What: Roles encode business relationships per BGP session; OTC is attached automatically on sideways/downward propagation and leaks get rejected. The measurement (using Cloudflare's direct peering to attribute OTC setters with certainty) shows adoption growing but limited, with IX route servers setting the good example. The experiment — announcing OTC to all peers — found 15 OTC-stripping ASes including two Tier-1s; 33.1% of unique IPv4 and 17% of IPv6 AS_PATHs lacked OTC where expected. Arelion (AS1299) promptly fixed after outreach; GTT (AS3257) continues stripping. Plus a proposed RFC 9234 improvement (draft-herdes-idr-otc-rs-verification: RS as apex setting OTC) and an implementation support matrix (Junos/FRR/BIRD/OpenBGPD yes today; IOS XR 26.4.1 and EOS 4.37 coming; SR OS, Huawei, GoBGP no).
  • How: Session-level roles vs ASPA's AS-level granularity (mixed relationships exist); receiver-side compensation for missing OTC; role configs require a BGP session reset (new OPEN).
  • Where applicable: Every eBGP operator — deployment is cheap, has already started, and the stripping measurements make the case that partial adoption still leaks.
path: BGP Role model: tracking the adoption of RFC 9234

items.title: Botnet.cl - Live Botnet Monitoring and BGP Feed
items.text:
NANOG 98 digest Adjacent pick 19–21 October 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Rodrigo Peña – Bitred Group SpA

VideoPDF

  • Why: A ten-minute lightning talk, but a live example of AI-assisted security operations with community distribution — 115 ISPs subscribed in two months.
  • What: A protocol emulator (with AI-assisted recovery of C2 protocols) registers and heartbeats into botnet C2 servers, logging commands; ADB sinks capture Android malware acquisition paths. Observations become a BGP feed: 25 confirmed C2 IPs across 25 botnet families, distributed as IPv4 /32 routes tagged with the BLACKHOLE-style community 65535:666, origin ASN, and botnet-family metadata.
  • How: Emulation-first intelligence gathering (no need to run real bots at scale), then per-C2-IP blackhole announcements that member ISPs apply themselves.
  • Where applicable: Chile-origin effort but the pattern — a shared, metadata-rich blackhole feed — is general; the talk is thin on method detail (from slides only).
path: Botnet.cl - Live Botnet Monitoring and BGP Feed

items.title: Building a Network Troubleshooting Agent: Architecture, Tools, Guardrails, and Lessons Learned
items.text:
NANOG 98 digest Core pick 19–21 October 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Karthik Srinivas Muthuramakrishnan – Microsoft

VideoPDF

  • Why: Agentic network ops is arriving, and the hard problems are authorization and evidence control, not model choice — the design here (scoped approvals, fail-closed authority) maps directly onto the PM's workload/agentic-identity expertise.
  • What: An agent architecture that keeps reasoning, policy, and execution strictly separate: "the model proposes, trusted code decides what can execute." Four pillars: a model-agnostic harness (playbook version, tool schemas, target, and policy budget held constant while model and tool sequence vary — making runs comparable); guardrails (policy checks before any request reaches the adapter: tool allowlist, rate/concurrency, equivalent-call loop limits, failure thresholds, session budget with kill switch); audit (ordered observable events, not private model reasoning — one session artifact answers six operational questions); and memory (verified history reorders safe reads earlier but never authorizes; compatibility keys include device identity, software and playbook versions).
  • How: Approval binds one exact action — approver identity, target router, action name, arguments digest, expiry — and fails closed on wrong target, changed arguments, or expiry. Typed, staged reads per versioned playbook (e.g. bgp-neighbor-down 1.0.0) keep deterministic operations deterministic.
  • Where applicable: Demonstrated in a virtual router environment at Microsoft; the pattern generalizes to any organization exposing network capabilities to LLM agents, and the approval-grant model is essentially scoped, short-lived credentials — familiar territory for anyone thinking about workload identity for agents.
path: Building a Network Troubleshooting Agent: Architecture, Tools, Guardrails, and Lessons Learned

items.title: Digital coherent optics - Deployment and operation
items.text:
NANOG 98 digest Core pick 19–21 October 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Philip Bedard – Cisco

VideoPDF

  • Why: Coherent pluggables (400ZR/800ZR) are how router-to-router DCI is collapsing the transponder layer — the PM's DC/WAN interconnect interest. Standards-heavy and operational rather than a pitch.
  • What: Deployment patterns (unamplified single-channel dark fiber, amplified P2P DWDM, multi-degree ROADM) plus the management story: CMIS AppSel application codes (240 codes in CMIS 5.3+, 128 modes on one 800G-ZR optic), CMIS 0x51h interface-code descriptors that finally expose the optical parameters needed for alien-wave handling, C-CMIS 1.5 (Sept 2026) standardizing coherent performance registers, T-API for the photonic domain, and the OpenConfig operational-mode wart (non-standard numeric IDs like "5003"). Also notes the org convergence: cost savings are driving IP and optical teams to merge.
  • How: A working standards matrix across OIF 400ZR/800ZR, OpenZR+ vs 400ZR+, and 100G-ZR (reach/FEC/modulation/power), SFF-8024 host/media IDs, and a model-driven path from pluggable manifest → IP controller → multi-layer controller using IETF/OpenConfig pluggable and impairment-topology drafts.
  • Where applicable: Any operator interconnecting routers over dark fiber or DWDM; vendor-presented (Cisco TME) but the content is standards-first. 1.6T coherent standards work is underway — worth tracking for interconnect planning.
path: Digital coherent optics - Deployment and operation

items.title: Enforcing the First AS in BGP AS_PATHs
items.text:
NANOG 98 digest Core pick 19–21 October 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Bryton Herdes – Cloudflare

VideoPDF

  • Why: The hijack class neither ROV nor ASPA catches — stripping/padding enough of the path that the origin and provider attestations look fine — and the fix is a single, existing config knob. Ten minutes, immediately actionable.
  • What: Forged AS_PATHs where the adjacent peer's AS doesn't match the first AS in the path defeat both ROV and ASPA. An active test (advertised a prefix with a forged first AS, e.g. as-path-prepend 402542 ahead of localAS 13335) found half of Tier-1 networks not enforcing First AS. Vendor defaults are the culprit: JunOS/JunOS EVO, Nokia SR OS, Extreme SLX-OS, RouterOS, and BIRD ship with enforcement OFF by default; Cisco IOS XE/XR, Arista EOS, Huawei, OpenBGPD, and FRR ship ON.
  • How: Reject routes where peerAS != firstAS on eBGP neighbors, with documented exceptions (transparent IX route servers, iBGP, deliberate anycast probe cases). Per-implementation config knobs are listed in the deck.
  • Where applicable: Universal — any eBGP edge; check your configs, especially if your vendor defaults insecurely.
path: Enforcing the First AS in BGP ASPATHs

items.title: False Immunity: long prefixes that bypass ROV
items.text:
NANOG 98 digest Core pick 19–21 October 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Bryton Herdes – Cloudflare

VideoPDF

  • Why: ROV deployment creates false confidence — this talk demonstrates two concrete bypass classes with live tests against tier-1 networks. Routing security at its most operational.
  • What: (1) Long-prefix "TE" announcements: at least two tier-1s (Lumen AS3356 for IPv4, Zayo AS6461) accept RPKI-invalid >/24 and >/48 prefixes, apparently filtering on IRR only — enabling the demonstrated 1.1.1.1/32 hijack accepted via AS8452/AS3356. Tested by advertising purposely invalid /32 and /128s to peers one-by-one and checking reachability from looking glasses. (2) RTBH: blackhole routes are generally exempt from RPKI filtering (IRR-based, long by nature, RFC 7999 community), creating a hijack vector that took a Tier-1. Proposed fixes: loose ROV restricted strictly to RFC 7999 BLACKHOLE routes, or a dedicated RPKI Discard Origin Authorization object (draft-spaghetti-grow-rpki-doa); vendor feature requests (Cisco IOSXR-I-1742, Juniper ROUTSP-I-71, Arista RFE 1964539) are pending.
  • How: Active measurement from Cloudflare's peering position, plus the tension spelled out: RFC 9319 minimal ROAs (maxLength) vs long-prefix TE, and the forged-origin-hijack tradeoff of maxLength=32 ROAs.
  • Where applicable: Every ROV-validating network (check whether you exempt long prefixes or blackhole routes) and every prefix owner publishing ROAs. Test method is limited by Cloudflare's relationship types with the tested ASes, as the speaker notes.
path: False Immunity: long prefixes that bypass ROV

items.title: Interplanetary Internet Architecture, Addressing, and Routing
items.text:
NANOG 98 digest Wildcard pick 19–21 October 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Wesley Eddy – Aalyria

VideoPDF

  • Why: IP to the Moon and Mars is actually standardizing (IETF TIPTOP working group), and the design constraints — extreme delay, scheduled connectivity, disconnection — produce routing and addressing ideas you won't see anywhere else.
  • What: An architecture for IP-based networks spanning Earth and Lunar/Mars domains (draft-ietf-tiptop-ip-architecture). Surprisingly, modern IP stacks mostly work at lunar delays — the IETF 124 hackathon ran Discord, Slack, Apple Messages, YouTube, and web browsing at lunar RTTs, and simulated pings to Voyager distances; QUIC's tunability is a key enabler. Addressing is genuinely contested: IPv6, blocks per planet, one RIR or many, aggregation encouraged, and "who defines the list of planets?" (mirrored in ARIN's TIPTOP policy draft ARIN-2026-1). Routing is "scheduling, scheduling, scheduling": PCE-like centralized computation of time-varying routes distributed to nodes well in advance, with inter-domain time-varying BGP as a someday problem; temporospatial SDN (Aalyria's Spacetime, grown from Loon's aerospace mesh code) is the current exemplar, plus Outernet Council federation interfaces for multi-operator systems.
  • How: Architecture summary plus active IETF/ARIN policy threads.
  • Where applicable: No near-term operational relevance, but the scheduled-intermittent-connectivity routing concepts echo terrestrial challenged networks — and the speaker's signoff ("hope to see you at SSNOG") tells you where the community thinks this goes.
path: Interplanetary Internet Architecture, Addressing, and Routing

items.title: Keynote: Global Infrastructure and Layer 3 Interconnection
items.text:
NANOG 98 digest Adjacent pick 19–21 October 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Paul Brodsky – TeleGeography

VideoPDF

  • Why: Market and topology context for the PM's DC/WAN interconnect interest: where subsea capacity, investment, and concentration risk are heading.
  • What: Bandwidth volumes still soar even as growth rates moderate (incremental annual demand keeps rising); hyperscalers (Google, Meta, Amazon, Microsoft) now dominate new cable investment, but carriers remain necessary partners in hard regulatory geographies — and hyperscaler cables will still swap/sell fiber pairs and IRUs. Resilience improves via landing-site and corridor diversity, though connectivity ≠ capacity (82% of the Middle East's used international capacity still terminates in Europe). The US is no longer the sole hub (largest routes: US–LatAm, Europe–ME, Asia–Europe; Miami as the LatAm hub, Marseille/London as Africa's). AI's subsea impact remains unclear — Anthropic's FCC filing says most AI workloads don't touch submarine cables, but dataset movement and spatial-temporal load shifting could turn networks into global compute load balancers. LEO is an access technology that complements, not replaces, subsea backbones (Starlink ~9M subs, large share of constellation capacity stranded at any moment; satellite traffic rides ground stations into Layer 3 interconnection).
  • How: TeleGeography's Transport Networks dataset — lease price trends, cable construction costs, ownership analysis.
  • Where applicable: Analyst overview, not an operator technique — useful context for interconnect, peering, and capacity planning decisions.
path: Keynote: Global Infrastructure and Layer 3 Interconnection

items.title: Keynote: Why Do We Have Self-Driving Cars, But Not Autonomous Networks?
items.text:
NANOG 98 digest Wildcard pick 19–21 October 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

John Evans – Independent

VideoPDF

  • Why: Ten years on from Kompella's self-driving-network framing, this asks the structural question: why did configuration automation and network control progress while operations stayed in the alert → ticket → operator loop? (from abstract only — page fetch failed; no slides in the source set)
  • What: The argument: networking treats autonomy as an observability-and-workflow problem built on existing systems — the natural first step for applying AI — whereas self-driving cars showed autonomy is a paradigm shift in architecture, signals, models, and control, not an AI feature bolted onto an existing vehicle.
  • How: Applies the control-system approach from self-driving cars and robotics to network operations: what's missing today, where autonomy can be deployed safely first, and a realistic path from assisted operations toward autonomous control.
  • Where applicable: Conceptual keynote, no results — directional, but a useful frame for anyone shaping network-automation strategy and deciding where copilots/agents genuinely change the operating model versus decorating it.
path: Keynote: Why Do We Have Self-Driving Cars, But Not Autonomous Networks?

items.title: Multi-Path Traffic Engineering Workshop
items.text:
NANOG 98 digest Adjacent pick 19–21 October 2026

Abstract

Vishnu Pavan Kumar Beeram – HPE, Zhaohui (Jeffrey) Zhang – HPE, Kireeti Kompella – Juniper Networks

  • Why: MPTE unifies multipath and TE for WAN and AIDC/DCI, and is feeding into ML network scheduling at the IETF — relevant to the PM's WAN/interconnect and AI-fabric interests.
  • What: One MPTE DAG construct carries what previously needed many LSPs: unequal-cost, weighted load balancing at every junction, multiple ingresses and egresses, minimal churn on link failure (junction ratios adjust, DAG shape stays), and much less state than per-path signaled tunnels. For ML clusters: non-multipath TE is called "a total non-starter," and MPTE becomes the vehicle for network scheduling — resource reservation, protection, and traffic isolation per AI job (draft-kompella-rtgwg-mlnwsched, new at RTGWG).
  • How: MPTED tunnel/junction state (incoming bandwidth, previous/next-hop sets with load shares), signaled via RSVP or BGP extensions; the workshop ran it hands-on in HPE/Juniper virtual environments (vMX/cRPD) for both WAN and AIDC scenarios.
  • Where applicable: Vendor workshop (HPE/Juniper, registration required) around IETF drafts (draft-kompella-teas-mpte and signaling companions) — standards-track and worth tracking even if you don't run the vendors' stacks; the AIDC framing presumes job-aware scheduling above the fabric.

items.title: One Control Plane Away: Are Cloud Providers Critical Infrastructure
items.text:
NANOG 98 digest Adjacent pick 19–21 October 2026

Abstract Slides

Krassimir Tzvetanov – Purdue University

PDF

  • Why: Quantifies the web's provider concentration properly — separating fronting, hosting, and DNS — with a method operators can reuse on their own dependency chains; resonates with post-Cloudflare-2025 resilience thinking.
  • What: A weekly measurement pipeline (since Aug 2026) over the Tranco top 10,000. Naive apex-A-to-ASN attribution undercounts CNAME-deployed CDNs by up to 2.4–2.7× (Akamai) and overcounts clouds by conflating hosting with fronting; the full layered pipeline finds Cloudflare fronts 29.4% of the top-1,000 but 46.3% of the top-10,000 (bigger properties diversify; 13% of strongly-fronted domains are multi-CDN), while the mid-tail single-homes. DNS is separately concentrated (Cloudflare 26.1%, Route 53 21.8%, only 13.7% self-hosted). Combining layers: 21.9% of live top-10k domains depend on Cloudflare for both DNS and delivery — one control-plane event from total unavailability — and 37.9% are double-dependent on some single organization. Tool and dataset to be released at publication.
  • How: Layered evidence (strongest wins): CNAME chains for apex and www, provider-published service ranges (e.g. AWS CLOUDFRONT vs EC2 tags), HTTP/TLS fingerprints, BGP origin data, with inter-layer disagreements retained rather than silently resolved.
  • Where applicable: The exposure-assessment recipe is general — run it against your own domains and dependency chains; the headline numbers are specific to the Tranco cohort.
path: One Control Plane Away: Are Cloud Providers Critical Infrastructure

items.title: Quantum-Safe Networking Starts With the Network You Already Have
items.text:
NANOG 98 digest Core pick 19–21 October 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Vincent Paul Celindro – Quantum Foundry

VideoPDF

  • Why: PQC migration framed for network operators, not cryptographers: keep the network, replace only the quantum-vulnerable public-key functions. Sits at the intersection of the PM's network-security and key-establishment/identity interests.
  • What: A migration model with three jobs: authentication (RSA/ECDSA → ML-DSA/SLH-DSA, FIPS 204/205), key establishment (DH/ECDH → ML-KEM, FIPS 203, typically hybrid ECDH+ML-KEM), and bulk protection (AES-256-GCM retained — Grover only trims margin and is hard to parallelize). Positioning: deploy PQC broadly, add QKD only where physics/topology/risk justify it. Roadmap: inventory crypto, prioritize by confidentiality lifetime (Harvest-Now-Decrypt-Later makes long-lived tunnels urgent), build crypto-agility, test vendor interop, in the context of EO 14412.
  • How: Built up from IKEv1/IKEv2 architecture — a recorded Phase 1 DH exchange can later unlock the entire captured IPsec session (Phase 2 keys and ESP), so hybrid ML-KEM in the handshake is what defuses HNDL. "Upgrade the handshake, not every packet."
  • Where applicable: General technique for any operator with long-lived confidential tunnels (IPsec VPNs, MACsec-adjacent planning); QKD is explicitly selective, not the default.
path: Quantum-Safe Networking Starts With the Network You Already Have

items.title: RNG: Flat Datacenter Networks at Scale
items.text:
NANOG 98 digest Core pick 19–21 October 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Ratul Mahajan – AWS

VideoPDF

  • Why: The most consequential physical DC topology talk of the meeting: Amazon claims the first production flat (non-tree) datacenter networks, solving the two problems — cabling and routing — that kept expander topologies academic for a decade. Directly in the PM's wheelhouse (topology, optics, cabling, routing).
  • What: RNG (Random Resilient network Graphs) replaces fat trees with quasi-random graphs for most workloads at Amazon, now the default for new fabrics. Headline results from the deck: 69% fewer switches, 40% less power, 27% lower cost (slides also give 9–45% fewer switches depending on config), with application flows performing as well as or better than fat trees and graceful degradation under failures rather than the outsized impact trees suffer from small cuts.
  • How: Three coupled inventions. ShuffleBox, a passive optical device that internally shuffles cables (e.g. 32×4×100G to 4×32×100G), giving random-graph connectivity with fat-tree-like cabling complexity. Spraypoint, a distributed routing protocol that exploits random-graph properties to find nearly all edge-disjoint paths via multi-level waypoints instead of shortest paths. Predictive models combining random-graph concentration properties with Spraypoint decorrelation, so oversubscription and path length are predictable at design time from topology parameters.
  • Where applicable: AWS production (research 2022 → two experimental fabrics torn down 2024 → production 2025 → default). Not retrofittable — it assumes a custom passive optical shuffle and a new routing protocol — but it is the strongest evidence yet that expander/flat fabrics are operationally viable, and it should reshape any next-gen DC topology roadmap.
path: RNG: Flat Datacenter Networks at Scale

items.title: Salvaged Silicon: Building an Open Network OS for a Switch the Industry Left for Dead
items.text:
NANOG 98 digest Adjacent pick 19–21 October 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Christopher Wright – EdgeNOS / NOSaic

VideoPDF

  • Why: A genuinely free-and-open NOS for EOL Broadcom-based switches — probing what "open networking" should have meant, and architecturally interesting: the kernel FIB is the source of truth.
  • What: EdgeNOS/NOSaic: a from-scratch NOS with no license or support contract, treating the box as an ordinary Linux router — routing daemons (FRR, static routes) program the kernel FIB, and a userspace agent (edged) mirrors it into the ASIC's tables; front ports are real netdevs so ip, ethtool, and tcpdump work unmodified; any daemon installing a kernel route gets hardware forwarding for free. Running on AS5610 (Trident+), AS4610 (Helix4), Arista 7050TX-64/SX2-72Q, Nexus 3172TQ; the Intel Fulcrum FM6000 currently forwards only by replaying a captured EOS boot trace. AI-assisted reverse engineering collapsed the register-bring-up problem (9 directions → 250+ actions → 115 live probes in one session).
  • How: No vendor SDK — hardware state reconstructed from dumps of a known-good install; hard-won lessons include: copy-to-CPU is internally a multicast replication (no replication engine, no copy), stale status registers masquerade as dead hardware, and every optic needs switch-side code. ONIE installable, Linux 6.1 maintained into 2027 with A/B slots and auto-rollback.
  • Where applicable: Hobbyist-origin but real; applies to the large category of abandoned Broadcom-era gear (~600 Broadcom device IDs). Not a supported production NOS today — its value is as a proof of the disaggregation model's unfinished half and a signal for open-NOS strategy.
path: Salvaged Silicon: Building an Open Network OS for a Switch the Industry Left for Dead

items.title: SRv6 and MRC for AI Data Centers
items.text:
NANOG 98 digest Core pick 19–21 October 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Michal Styszynski – Juniper Networks

VideoPDF

  • Why: The backend AI fabric problem this program circles repeatedly — making RoCEv2 survive at 100k+ GPU scale without PFC — approached via an emerging OCP spec (MRC). Core to the PM's RDMA/lossless-fabric interest. Vendor session, but grounded in a specification rather than a product pitch.
  • What: MRC (Multipath Reliable Connection) is modified RoCEv2 with reliability (SACK/NACK), packet trimming on congestion, packet spraying, and multiplanar fabric design — explicitly "no more PFC." Two transport flavors: IP-ECMP MRC (works with EVPN-VXLAN multitenancy, switch hashing) and SRv6 MRC (source-routed paths computed by a path orchestrator/fabric manager). Scale worked through an 8-plane design: ~131K GPUs, ~8K GPUs per pod, with optical shufflers breaking 2×800G into 8×200G plane links.
  • How: SRv6 uSID shift-to-left: the orchestrator computes congestion-avoiding healthy paths and encodes each as a uSID chain in the outer IPv6 destination address; the NIC encapsulates RoCEv2, each transit node executes shift-left, and the leaf decaps. RoCEv2 Entropy Values are mapped to SRv6 Path-IDs at the NIC, which rotates across them; on congestion the switch trims the packet to headers, the receiver NACKs with source PSN, and the sender changes EV/Path-ID. The BTH header gains RTX/TSETH fields and new opcodes (e.g. reliable probe 0xDE), per the OCP MRC 1.0 spec.
  • Where applicable: Requires MRC-capable NICs, AI Ethernet switches, and a path controller — an early, ecosystem-dependent stack. Multiplane designs assume no cross-plane links. Watch it as the OCP-specified alternative to PFC-based lossless fabrics; not something deployable on current commodity gear.
path: SRv6 and MRC for AI Data Centers

items.title: Stop using 100GBASE-LR4
items.text:
NANOG 98 digest Core pick 19–21 October 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Richard Steenbergen – Petabit Scale

VideoPDF

  • Why: A reference-grade optics talk aimed squarely at the interconnection world (IXP ports, peering cross-connects), which is still standardizing on a 2010 pre-FEC optic that hyperscalers abandoned within one product cycle of CWDM4 (2014). Cost, power, and physics — core PM territory.
  • What: A complete guide to 100G client optics generations: Gen 1 LR4 (4×25G NRZ, LAN-WDM grid, four cooled lasers with TECs, no host FEC — raw BER or nothing), Gen 2 CWDM4/4WDM (uncooled lasers, ±6.5nm grid, host RS-FEC worth ~5–6dB margin, roughly half the price, everything else identical), Gen 3 single-lambda (53GBd PAM4, one laser, DSP + mandatory KP4 FEC). The thesis: every LR4 datasheet claim, including reach, has since been beaten by cheaper optics; the interconnection ecosystem has paid the "TEC tax" for a decade out of habit because changing requires coordinating with a remote party.
  • How: Physics-driven walkthrough — chromatic dispersion penalty scales with baud², FEC (KR4/KP4 Reed-Solomon) has been baked into every 25G+ SerDes since ~2015 and is idle in the box, and pre-FEC BER is free early-warning telemetry (you can watch a link degrade for weeks before a real error).
  • Where applicable: Universal for 100G handoffs; no hardware change needed (FEC is already in the host ASIC). The friction is procedural — coordinating a different optic with peers/IXPs — not technical.

items.title: Understanding and optimising transceiver efficiency using internal metrics for improved power savings
items.text:
NANOG 98 digest Core pick 19–21 October 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Gerhard Stein – Flexoptix GmbH, Thomas Weible – Flexoptix

VideoPDF

  • Why: Optics power is a growing DC OpEx line; this is real measurement work on what transceiver telemetry (VDM/TEC current) can and cannot save you.
  • What: Bench results across 100G QSFP28, 400G coherent ZR, and 800G optics on Cisco/Juniper gear. The punchline inverts the thesis: laser and TEC are negligible power drawers — the MCU/DSP are the real consumers — so laser-temperature optimization (~200mW average gain from a 20K temperature drop) isn't worth chasing. The real saving is operational: shutting a port forces the optic into low-power mode at ~7–20× lower consumption. Switch behavior differs (Juniper supplies optic power even with no RX; Cisco's Nexus is smarter here), and VDM support is patchy — two of three switches tested expose DDM only, and the one CMIS VDM implementation bakes in a 50°C laser-temp assumption.
  • How: CMIS VDM parsing beyond DDM, TEC current and laser power via V×I, SFF-8636/CMIS power-class budgeting, plus a heat-transfer analysis (Nusselt/Prandtl/Reynolds) showing fan speed and case temperature dominate the thermal picture.
  • Where applicable: Any operator with >100G optics fleets; vendor-authored (Flexoptix sells programmable optics) but measurement-driven with named DUTs and honest caveats. Next steps teased: port-shutdown automation across SONiC/Mellanox, and water cooling.
path: Understanding and optimising transceiver efficiency using internal metrics for improved power savings

items.title: When BGP Graceful Restart Wasn't Graceful
items.text:
NANOG 98 digest Core pick 19–21 October 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Marian Rychtecky – NIX.CZ

VideoPDF

  • Why: The kind of hard-won postmortem NANOG exists for: a GR feature that lengthened an outage from "hidden" to two minutes, with packet captures, lab reproduction, and multiple vendor bugs unpacked.
  • What: During a firewall HA upgrade, BGP sessions re-established but carried zero prefixes for ~121s. Root causes found: (1) the router sent TCP RST on the new connection because the old session wasn't cleanly torn down — violating RFC 4724's "treat old session as terminated"; (2) the firewall's GR coupled IPv4 and IPv6, so IPv4 routes waited on a stuck IPv6 session's End-of-RIB (the suspicious ~120s was the default reconnect timer); (3) a parsing bug stored the IPv6 peer as 2001:db8:1: (missing ::2), so the OS couldn't find the VRF context and RST'd. Vendor fix lands in 8.0.1 (Aug 2026), not backported to supported 7.4/7.6 branches; workaround: set connect-timer 1.
  • How: Classic disciplined troubleshooting: EoR timing analysis, packet captures on both sides, a BIRD lab where impolite kills (kill -9) reproduced the RST window, two separate vendor tickets, and the operational mitigations (short connect timer, static routes with AD 255 during upgrades).
  • Where applicable: Anyone running BGP GR across dual-stack, multi-vendor HA pairs — the failure pattern (AFI-coupled GR state, TCP session cleanup on failover) is general even though the specific bugs are vendor-embedded.
path: When BGP Graceful Restart Wasn't Graceful

items.title: When the World Cup Moved to YouTube: 416 Gbps and the Limits of Local Delivery in Brazil
items.text:
NANOG 98 digest Wildcard pick 19–21 October 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Renato Ornelas – OpenX (Brazil)

VideoPDF

  • Why: Not the PM's usual beat, but a rare, complete dataset of an entire nation's traffic arriving over one CDN with no delivery infrastructure of its own — hard numbers on cache ceilings, PNI saturation, and event-driven capacity.
  • What: 34 match nights measured at OpenX (AS263444, 60+ downstream ASNs, 1–3M broadband subscribers): 18.4 PB of Google traffic; 416 Gbps peak; 12 PB above football-free baselines. At the peak, embedded cache pinned at its 79 Gbps ceiling and one PNI site saturated at 2×100G — so 40% of delivered traffic (165 of 409 Gbps) arrived over international transit from North America and Europe. Kickoff hour predicted peaks better than audience size (21.1M devices at 2pm Monday → 207 Gbps; 18.5M at 5pm Sunday → 391 Gbps). The half-time signature: Google sheds 128 Gbps in ten minutes while Meta jumps and Netflix stays flat — three CDNs moving three directions inside fifteen minutes.
  • How: Five-minute flow telemetry (Kentik) over 16-hour nightly windows, with a per-night appendix chart marking half-time, extra time, and shootouts.
  • Where applicable: Brazil-specific vantage (single-CDN delivery, one wholesale operator) — but the transferable lessons are explicit: size for the event not the busy hour; local-delivery ceilings are ones you don't control; and measure it yourself, because flow data at five-minute resolution showed everything.
path: When the World Cup Moved to YouTube: 416 Gbps and the Limits of Local Delivery in Brazil

items.title: Your Change Deserves a Dress Rehearsal: Digital Twins from Production State with Containerlab and OTG
items.text:
NANOG 98 digest Core pick 19–21 October 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Brad Tarno – The Walt Disney Company

VideoPDF

  • Why: The most directly adoptable tooling talk of the program: a self-service lab-as-a-service that builds disposable twins from what production actually runs, closing the "valid config is not a safe config" gap (their motivating change: one peer-reviewed line silently suppressed 36→1 routes).
