  • What: A walkthrough of a real Telstra outage in which the network apparently behaved as if the date were 2006. (from title only — no abstract published)
  • How: Unknown until the talk; expect an incident timeline, root-cause analysis, and the detection/remediation path. Netnod's involvement suggests a Swedish/IX perspective on a global event.
  • Where applicable: Broadly applicable — time-dependence is universal in routing, PKI, and control-plane security. The specific trigger may be Telstra-topology-specific, but the lessons on time sanity checks and blast-radius control transfer anywhere.
path: Telstra outage: The night a network decided the year was 2006

items.title: The Internet Change Clock
items.text:
Netnod Tech Meeting 2026 digest Wildcard pick 6 October 2026

Speakers: not listed in the program.

  • Why: A genuinely novel-sounding measurement concept — apparently a way of quantifying the rate of change of the Internet's structure or behavior over time. This is the kind of thing the PM wouldn't search for, but which can reframe how they think about measuring their own network's stability and churn.
  • What: Presentation of something called the "Internet Change Clock" — an instrument for tracking change in the Internet. (from title only; the actual metric, data source, and findings are unknown)
  • How: Unknown; plausibly built on BGP/route-collector time series measuring structural change over time, but this is inference from the name.
  • Where applicable: Unknown from the title; if the underlying data is public collector data, the approach may be reusable by anyone doing network trend analysis.

items.title: Understanding and optimising transceiver efficiency using internal metrics for improved power savings
items.text:
Netnod Tech Meeting 2026 digest Core pick 6 October 2026

Recording

Speakers: not listed in the program.

Video

  • Why: Transceiver power is becoming a first-order constraint in DC design (often a large fraction of a port's total power budget), and a talk about driving savings from internal transceiver metrics — not vendor datasheets — is exactly the operational, measurement-driven optics content the PM values.
  • What: A method for understanding and optimizing transceiver power efficiency using the transceivers' internal telemetry. (from title only)
  • How: Presumably reads internal metrics (per-lane power, DSP/CDR state, temperature) from pluggable optics and tunes operating points for power savings — plausible given the title, but unconfirmed.
  • Where applicable: Potentially broadly applicable since it works on standard pluggables; the savings and the specific metrics exposed depend on the transceiver vendors/generations tested, so note those constraints.
path: Understanding and optimising transceiver efficiency using internal metrics for improved power savings

items.title: Autonomous System Provider Authorisation
items.text:
NetUK3 (The Brewery) — for a networking/identity PM digest Core pick The Brewery · 7 July 2026

Abstract Recording

Ralph Smit (RIPE NCC)

Video

  • Why: The natural companion to the talk above: ASPA is the concrete next step in RPKI path validation, and this is the operator-facing how-to from the registry that runs hosted RPKI for most of Europe.
  • What: An introduction to ASPA objects — a relatively new RPKI object type signed by AS owners that declares an AS's authorised upstream providers, preventing route leaks, BGP path spoofing, and valley-free violations. Covers how to create ASPA objects (hosted RPKI at ARIN/RIPE NCC, or delegated CA software such as Krill) and the current state of uptake, including support in some software routers (from abstract only).
  • How: An AS signs an ASPA listing its providers; validators can then reject paths in which the AS appears to route via an unauthorised upstream — enforcing a signed, valley-free provider relationship.
  • Where applicable: Any AS owner; ASPA creation is available today through the mainstream hosted and delegated RPKI paths, so this is directly actionable rather than speculative. Expect a short talk (25 min) — intro-and-summary depth.

items.title: Data Centers in Space - The Big Picture
items.text:
NetUK3 (The Brewery) — for a networking/identity PM digest Wildcard pick The Brewery · 7 July 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Geoff Bennett (Nokia)

VideoPPTX

  • Why: Not a core interest, but a rigorous reality-check on the extreme extrapolation of the PM's daily constraints — space, power, water, permitting — from a respected industry explainer. If multi-gigawatt AI campuses are colliding with those limits on the ground, this is the "what if we simply left" scenario, with the failure modes taken seriously.
  • What: A critical assessment of orbital data centers: what problems the idea is actually trying to solve, the technologies that must be developed, the scale that would be required, and the unavoidable consequences — anchored in real signals: SpaceX's January FCC filing for up to one million "orbital data center" satellites, Google's Project Suncatcher suggesting viability as soon as 2027, and funded startups. The speaker explicitly asks which problems are simply insoluble, and what damage filling orbit this way inflicts (from abstract only).
  • How: Structured as problem-first analysis rather than hype: constraints (launch mass, radiation, thermal rejection, serviceability, debris) versus the terrestrial pain (power, water, land, community backlash) the idea claims to escape.
  • Where applicable: Strategic/forward-looking context rather than actionable practice — useful for anyone calibrating where compute placement could plausibly go over the next decade, and a well-informed sceptic's set of questions to hold vendor narratives against.
path: Data Centers in Space - The Big Picture

items.title: Data Signal-Based Distributed Fibre Optic Sensing
items.text:
NetUK3 (The Brewery) — for a networking/identity PM digest Core pick The Brewery · 7 July 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Jasmine Parkes (Comtek Network Systems and Bangor University)

VideoPPTX

  • Why: Physical fibre plant causes roughly a third of network outages, and conventional distributed fibre sensing (DAS) requires dedicated fibre pairs and extra lasers — capex that blocks most operators. This is the physical-infrastructure talk of the program.
  • What: A "Data-Driven Sensing" architecture from a joint R&D initiative (Bangor University's DSP Centre of Excellence, Sorrento, and Comtek Networks) in which the live, revenue-carrying data signal itself acts as the sensor. Validated to classify and localise fibre faults with ~98% claimed accuracy, with no extra fibre assets, no additional lasers, and no downtime — eliminating the standalone-DAS capital overhead. The talk closes with a research roadmap toward simultaneously monitoring physical infrastructure running alongside fibre routes.
  • How: DSP-based analysis of the active data signal's own impairments/reflections to detect, classify, and locate faults on the in-service fibre, instead of injecting a separate sensing signal on a dark pair.
  • Where applicable: Operators of backbone or critical leased routes without spare fibre to dedicate to sensing. This is R&D-stage output from an academic/industry collaboration, not a shipping product — treat it as a strong signal of where fibre monitoring is heading rather than something to procure this quarter.
path: Data Signal-Based Distributed Fibre Optic Sensing

items.title: Edge Network Evolution
items.text:
NetUK3 (The Brewery) — for a networking/identity PM digest Adjacent pick The Brewery · 7 July 2026

Abstract Recording

Ben Ryall, Ian Cleary (Meta)

Video

  • Why: A hyperscaler reshaping its edge topology for AI workloads changes the peering and traffic landscape for every operator downstream — directly relevant to DC/WAN interconnect thinking.
  • What: How Meta's edge infrastructure is evolving from traditional content delivery to AI-driven experiences, reshaping topology to balance efficiency and quality of experience while preserving direct 1:1 peering relationships for networks of all sizes, with optimisations intended to help operators defer or avoid capex (from abstract only; the event page adds nothing beyond it).
  • How: Architectural shifts at Meta's edge — the talk is short (10 min + Q&A) and the slides/recording will not be published, so this is attend-live-or-miss-it.
  • Where applicable: Meta-specific scale and workload mix; useful as directional input on how AI traffic changes edge/peering economics, not as a transferable design.

items.title: Evaluation of BGP Roles (RFC 9234) with the aid of an AI Assistant
items.text:
NetUK3 (The Brewery) — for a networking/identity PM digest Wildcard pick The Brewery · 7 July 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Dr Julian Lucek (HPE)

VideoPPTX

  • Why: The clearest signal in this program of where the network operations toolchain is heading — LLMs driving device configuration through MCP servers — demonstrated on a routing-security feature (RFC 9234 BGP Roles, itself a route-leak mitigation) by one of networking's best-known educators.
  • What: Three parts: benchmarking results showing a general-purpose reasoning LLM (Opus 4.7, per the event page summary) achieving solid scores across three tiers of a network certification exam track; a retrospective analysis of a real past network outage showing LLMs would have found the root cause significantly faster; and the main demo — an LLM driving a Junos MCP server to configure, test, and document BGP Roles from just a few, deliberately vague prompts, with the LLM filling in missing details in an intent-based manner and proving a substantial time-saver over manual work.
  • How: LLM + Model Context Protocol server pattern: the model discovers device capabilities and state through the MCP tool interface, plans the configuration, executes and validates it, and generates the documentation — the human supplies intent, not commands.
  • Where applicable: Junos-specific in the demo (Junos MCP server), and a single-operator workflow at demo scale — but the pattern (LLM agent over an MCP tool surface, applied to a security-relevant protocol feature) is the transferable idea, and directly relevant to how network engineering work changes in the near term.
path: Evaluation of BGP Roles (RFC 9234) with the aid of an AI Assistant

items.title: Everything is Fine and Our Automation Works Perfectly
items.text:
NetUK3 (The Brewery) — for a networking/identity PM digest Adjacent pick The Brewery · 7 July 2026

Abstract Recording

Stefan Funke (Inter.link)

Video

  • Why: A wry counterpoint to the automation track: automation is only as good as the data counterparties feed it (IRR records, RTBH fields, survey data), which ties directly back to the routing-security sessions.
  • What: Per the title and one-line abstract, an operator's account of what their "working perfectly" automation actually requires from others — updated IRR, RTBH fields, and survey compliance (from abstract only — the program text gives just the punchline).
  • How: Unknown from the abstract; expect a short lightning-format talk on the human/data prerequisites of inter-operator automation.
  • Where applicable: Peering and transport automation; content cannot be verified in advance from the thin abstract, so treat as a low-commitment slot filler between the LON2 and SCION talks.
path: Everything is Fine and Our Automation Works Perfectly

items.title: Hollow Core Fibre - Nothing is better than glass for guiding light
items.text:
NetUK3 (The Brewery) — for a networking/identity PM digest Core pick The Brewery · 7 July 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Steve Jones (Huber+Suhner)

VideoPPTX

  • Why: Hollow-core fibre is the first genuine step-change in transmission medium in decades — guidance through air rather than glass — and it is being positioned specifically for datacentre interconnect and AI compute-cluster links, which are core DC/WAN interconnect territory.
  • What: A technology primer on HCF: how it works, the performance benefits, the application space (the event page summary confirms explicit coverage of DCI and AI compute cluster usage), and — crucially — the constraints of deploying it into a market dominated by singlemode fibre and LC/APC connectors, including a proposed solution to the HCF-to-LC/APC interop conundrum.
  • How: Physics-level: light guided in an air core rather than solid glass, which changes latency, nonlinearity, and loss characteristics; the talk covers what that buys operationally and where the connector/splicing ecosystem still fights the installed SMF base.
  • Where applicable: DCI, low-latency backhaul, AI cluster interconnects. Vendor talk (Huber+Suhner, a connectivity supplier), but the abstract is about the technology category and its constraints rather than a product. The practical constraint — splicing, patching, and connector maturity against a singlemode-dominated plant — is the part that matters for anyone scoping an HCO deployment.
path: Hollow Core Fibre - Nothing is better than glass for guiding light

items.title: LON2 Network Refresh
items.text:
NetUK3 (The Brewery) — for a networking/identity PM digest Core pick The Brewery · 7 July 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Jan Kayser (LINX)

VideoPPTX

  • Why: The rarest commodity at an operator conference — a public postmortem-flavored account of refreshing a production fabric with live members on it. LINX ran the world's first disaggregated EVPN IXP LAN (2018) with hardware and software from different vendors, so their refresh story is a directly transferable lesson in multi-vendor fabric migration risk.
  • What: How LINX refreshed LON2, their second-biggest London LAN, while roughly a third of LINX membership remained connected — and the title's pointed "or was there?" promises the parts that went wrong, not just the happy path (from abstract only).
  • How: Per the abstract: an in-house, redundant dual-LAN design (LON1/LON2 since 2002, deliberately avoiding a single point of failure for UK connectivity), EVPN control plane on disaggregated hardware/software, migrated around end-of-life equipment. The talk is short (10 min + Q&A); expect the migration sequencing and failure detail rather than deep architecture.
  • Where applicable: The dual-LAN IXP resilience model is LINX-specific, but the underlying problem — refresh an EVPN fabric in place without evacuating tenants — is universal for anyone running a DC or exchange fabric. Watch for what the multi-vendor sourcing actually cost them operationally.

items.title: Rethinking Network Monitoring
items.text:
NetUK3 (The Brewery) — for a networking/identity PM digest Adjacent pick The Brewery · 7 July 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Mr David Flores

VideoPPTX

  • Why: Monitoring modernisation is the flip side of automation — every session on source-of-truth and automation at this event depends on telemetry you can actually act on.
  • What: A reframe of monitoring as observability: a modular open-source stack spanning collection, processing, storage, visualisation, and alerting, enriched with a network source of truth, correlating metrics/logs/flows, with event-driven automation and AI-assisted root cause analysis. The event page summary adds the honest trade-off framing: scale, operational overhead, and expertise costs of building your own stack, with modularity as the mitigation.
  • How: Pair telemetry with a source of truth so data becomes queryable and context-rich, then layer automation and AI-assisted RCA on top; the speaker positions this as a pilotable blueprint.
  • Where applicable: General technique, vendor-neutral (independent speaker), applicable to any size of network — though the "build vs buy" trade-offs the summary flags are the real decision content.

items.title: SCION: Secure Path-Aware Internet Routing for Critical Infrastructures
items.text:
NetUK3 (The Brewery) — for a networking/identity PM digest Core pick The Brewery · 7 July 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Kevin Meynell (SCION Association)

VideoPPTX

  • Why: SCION is the most mature "beyond BGP" routing architecture with real production deployment, and its trust model — cryptographic path validation with a standalone trust root rather than third-party CAs — sits right at the intersection of network security and the PM's identity/trust interests.
  • What: SCION as an answer to BGP's fundamental limitation that operators have little control over where traffic transits: high resilience to routing attacks, explicit path selection, fast failover, geofencing (with a post-quantum angle), and comparison against RPKI, MPLS, SD-WAN, Segment Routing, and BGPSEC. The event page adds that it is supported by several UK-based ISPs including BT and Colt, and is in production in Swiss financial services, healthcare, and power utilities, with a vendor-neutral IETF specification in progress.
  • How: A trust model built on logical groupings of networks ("trust domains"/ISDs) sharing a common jurisdiction and agreed trust policies, with a standalone trust root; traffic is exchanged only within a trust domain unless explicitly permitted, enabling sovereign networks and user/operator path selection.
  • Where applicable: Initially critical infrastructure and regulated sectors (finance, healthcare, energy, defence) that need provable path control; requires SCION-capable connectivity, which in the UK is emerging via BT and Colt. Not a drop-in for commodity Internet operations, but relevant to any strategy discussion about trustworthy interconnect for critical workloads.
path: SCION: Secure Path-Aware Internet Routing for Critical Infrastructures

items.title: Telecoms Inventory for GPON using Kuwaiba
items.text:
NetUK3 (The Brewery) — for a networking/identity PM digest Adjacent pick The Brewery · 7 July 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Corey Maltby (Solent University), Craig Gallen (Entimoss and Solent University)

VideoPPTX

  • Why: Physical/logical inventory is the unglamorous prerequisite for fibre operations; Kuwaiba is a credible open-source alternative to commercial telecoms inventory systems and this is a grounded evaluation of it, including failure modes.
  • What: An introduction to Kuwaiba (open-source telecoms inventory, originating in South America, modelling physical and logical network resources and services at significantly lower cost than commercial systems) via a student industrial consulting project: modelling a city-wide GPON network in Kuwaiba populated from UK UPRNs and OpenStreetMap GIS data. The event page summary adds discussion of the issues with populating the system from UK public GIS data sources, plus an offered demo.
  • How: GIS data import (UPRNs, OpenStreetMap) into Kuwaiba's resource model to design and document a citywide GPON deployment — testing how practical the tool and data pipeline are.
  • Where applicable: ISPs and service providers, especially UK altnets building fibre; the GIS-data-quality findings are UK-specific, but the Kuwaiba evaluation is relevant to any operator weighing open-source inventory.
path: Telecoms Inventory for GPON using Kuwaiba

items.title: The Network Automation Forum Framework: A vendor-neutral reference model for building automation at scale
items.text:
NetUK3 (The Brewery) — for a networking/identity PM digest Adjacent pick The Brewery · 7 July 2026

Abstract

Pete Crocker (OpsMill)

  • Why: A shared vocabulary and reference architecture for network automation is the missing layer that makes automation conversations between engineers, vendors, and consultants coherent — useful for anyone mapping their own automation estate.
  • What: A walkthrough of the Network Automation Forum's reference architecture, developed over a year by a multi-stakeholder community: why standardised language around network automation was needed and how to apply the framework both starting from scratch and retro-fitting it to what you already built (from abstract only).
  • How: A layered reference model (published at reference.networkautomation.forum) that names the components of an automation architecture so tooling choices can be positioned against it.
  • Where applicable: Broadly applicable — the framework is deliberately vendor-neutral even though the speaker is from OpsMill; it is a mapping tool, not a stack you deploy.
path: The Network Automation Forum Framework: A vendor-neutral reference model for building automation at scale

items.title: Understanding and optimising transceiver efficiency using internal metrics for improved power savings
items.text:
NetUK3 (The Brewery) — for a networking/identity PM digest Core pick The Brewery · 7 July 2026

Abstract Recording

Dr Gerhard Stein (Flexoptix)

Video

  • Why: Power per port is becoming a first-order datacenter constraint and transceivers are a large, controllable share of it. This is one of the few talks showing a concrete, measurable method for cutting optical power without performance loss.
  • What: A data-driven method using Versatile Diagnostics Monitoring (VDM) — internal transceiver telemetry available in modern >100G optics — to find operating conditions that minimise wattage. The event page summary confirms the analysis focuses on Thermoelectric Cooler (TEC) current and laser current, correlated against temperature and total power draw. The authors built software prototypes and analyse real-world VDM data to evaluate and visualise transceiver efficiency in Watts.
  • How: Correlation analysis of TEC/laser current against temperature (and cable length) to identify optimal operating points — essentially treating existing per-transceiver telemetry as a power-optimisation sensor rather than just a health alarm.
  • Where applicable: Broadly applicable to any operator of >100G optics — the metrics are standard transceiver telemetry, not vendor-proprietary, so the method is replicable with any VDM-capable fleet. Caveat: results are prototype-stage from a transceiver vendor, so treat the savings claims as directional until reproduced on your own hardware.
path: Understanding and optimising transceiver efficiency using internal metrics for improved power savings

items.title: When UK Traffic Takes an Unplanned Detour: Routing Security for the UK Peering Community
items.text:
NetUK3 (The Brewery) — for a networking/identity PM digest Core pick The Brewery · 7 July 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Ritesh Mukherjee (Nokia)

VideoPPTX

  • Why: Routing security is core network security, and this is the program's substantive treatment: it moves past RPKI-ROV checklists to the attack classes ROV cannot see, grounded in real incidents (the 2019 Swiss leak of 70,000 routes via China Telecom Frankfurt; the 2025 BGP hijack disrupting DNS root infrastructure; documented "stealthy" hijacks that pass all RPKI checks).
  • What: A practical, prioritised roadmap for UK peering networks: what LINX and LONAP route-server RPKI filtering already protects against; where bilateral (non-route-server) peers remain exposed; an introduction to ASPA, which all five RIRs have committed to supporting by end-2026; and the case for BMP as the missing observability layer that turns silently discarded invalid routes into active threat intelligence (from abstract only — the event page reproduces the abstract).
  • How: A layered defence model: ROV on route servers (deployed), ROV on bilateral sessions (gap), ASPA for path-manipulation and valley-free enforcement (emerging), BMP-driven route monitoring for anomalies invisible to both ROV and ASPA (observability gap).
  • Where applicable: Any network that peers. The framing is UK/LINX-specific but the ROV → ASPA → BMP maturity ladder is universally applicable, and the "quick wins this quarter" structure makes it actionable. Speaker is from Nokia, but the content is standards-based rather than product-based.
path: When UK Traffic Takes an Unplanned Detour: Routing Security for the UK Peering Community

items.title: Which in my switch? LPO, CPO, XPO optics. What are they, when to use
items.text:
NetUK3 (The Brewery) — for a networking/identity PM digest Core pick The Brewery · 7 July 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Dr Robert Friskney (Arista)

VideoPPTX

  • Why: Optics format choice is now a switch-architecture decision, not a line-item: LPO, CPO, and XPO change power, latency, port density, and the vendor lock-in surface of a fabric. Anyone planning 800G/1.6T generations needs this decision framework.
  • What: An explainer and decision guide: what linear-drive pluggable optics (LPO) are versus traditional DSP-based pluggables; how co-packaged optics (CPO) differs; the practical cost/latency/power trade-offs; which switch and routing use-cases LPO wins today and which it loses; how the answer shifts as port rates rise; and the future evolution toward CPO's density versus the alternative "extra-dense pluggable" (XPO) approach (from abstract only — the event page confirms it is a reprise of a well-received community talk at Net.Ldn with the Q&A topics folded in).
  • How: LPO removes the DSP for short-reach links (trading reach and interoperability margin for power and latency savings); CPO integrates optics into the switch package; XPO keeps pluggability while pushing density — the talk maps each onto switch/routing use-cases.
  • Where applicable: Short-reach in-fabric and backplane-adjacent links are the LPO sweet spot; CPO/XPO are next-generation switch design questions. Arista-led, so expect some roadmap framing from a switch vendor's perspective, but the material is a category primer, not a product pitch.
path: Which in my switch? LPO, CPO, XPO optics. What are they, when to use

items.title: Workshop: Open Source Data Management Platform - Infrahub
items.text:
NetUK3 (The Brewery) — for a networking/identity PM digest Adjacent pick The Brewery · 7 July 2026

Abstract

Alex Gittings (OpsMill), Pete Crocker (OpsMill)

  • Why: Source of truth is the foundation every other automation talk at this event assumes; this is a hands-on evaluation opportunity for the leading open-source SoT platform rather than a slide deck about it.
  • What: A two-hour hands-on workshop on Infrahub, an open-source infrastructure data-management platform combining Git-like version control on top of a graph database, with three pillars: flexible schema, native version control, and unified storage. Structured as two modules/labs: foundation and network source-of-truth setup (devices, IPAM, CSV/API imports), then config generation via GraphQL queries and Jinja2 templating, with a GraphQL lab using the built-in GraphiQL explorer.
  • How: Version-controlled graph data with a flexible schema as the SoT, queried via GraphQL, feeding Jinja2 templating for config generation and integration with existing automation tools.
  • Where applicable: Teams evaluating open-source SoT/IPAM options. Vendor-led (OpsMill builds Infrahub) but the format is working directly with the actual open-source product in a sandbox — a genuine evaluation, not a pitch.
path: Workshop: Open Source Data Management Platform - Infrahub

items.title: How to change the Internet itself?
items.text:
NLNOG Day 2026 digest Core pick Hilversum · 4 September 2026

Slides Recording

Job Snijders

VideoPDF

  • Why: Part retrospective on routing-security wins (Large Communities, RPKI ROV, ASPA design), part forward look at a genuinely new piece of RPKI infrastructure — Erik Synchronisation — from someone who ships RPKI validator code. The process lessons for effecting protocol change are a bonus for anyone who has to drive standards adoption.
  • What: Four case studies: how BGP Large Communities finally solved a problem IETF discussion had failed to close for 15+ years; how RPKI ROV deployment snowballed from the Netherlands; why ASPA deliberately unified IPv4/IPv6 upstream handling against academic objections; and why rsync and RRDP are both poor fits for RPKI repository distribution and what replaces them. The recurring thesis: minimum viable solutions, implementer preferences over academic elegance, and relentless evangelization.
  • How: Erik Synchronisation combines Merkle trees, content-addressable storage, and concurrency control to take the best of rsync (stateless, jump-to-latest, delta-only) and RRDP (pre-calculated static content over HTTP). The key differentiator: anyone can run an "Erik Relay" mirroring all global RPKI data, and clients can rotate between relays for robustness — solving the "you can't force the origin to sit behind a good CDN" problem of RRDP.
  • Where applicable: The RPKI/Erik material matters to every RPKI publisher and validator operator, and permissionless incremental deployment is the design goal. The case-study methodology (pick a problem, find who owns the solution space, build a PoC, teach it) is general. No org-specific constraints.
path: How to change the Internet itself?

items.title: Internet exchanges in space
items.text:
NLNOG Day 2026 digest Wildcard pick Hilversum · 4 September 2026

Slides Recording

Iljitsch van Beijnum

VideoPDF

  • Why: Genuinely novel — an ESA-commissioned study (STARS, prime SINTEF) on whether Internet exchanges can be built on LEO satellites using optical inter-satellite links, with real BGP simulation results. It stress-tests basic protocol assumptions (BGP convergence, layer-2 vs. layer-3 IX models) in an environment where topology changes at 7 km/s.
  • What: A feasibility analysis of IX-in-space: motivations (removing the ground bottleneck, cheaper/faster interconnection between LEO constellations like Starlink/OneWeb/Leo/IRIS², new use cases such as alliance-flexible diplomatic peering), hardware reality-check (a Tbps-class 32-port switch at ~€6,000/11 kg/1500 W plus an ARM route server, radiation-hardened), and the finding that satellites move slowly relative to each other, so handovers can be hours apart. SINTEF's BGP simulation showed ~180-second link-down detection; the speaker's FreeRangeRouting-in-Docker setup with tweaked timers plus BFD was "immediately much better." Follow-up proposals include embeddable "PIGS" (Programmable Internet Gateway Subsystems) modules for other satellites, paralleling NASA's Space BACN.
  • How: Optical ISLs (~100 Gbps laser links between satellites) replace fiber; BGP sessions are taken down proactively just before leaving communication range; and — the notable architectural conclusion — a mature space IX would almost certainly be layer-3, because a dozen-plus IX satellites each peered with many "peering satellites" would exhaust any sane layer-2 addressing plan. A live interactive demo was made available.
  • Where applicable: Currently a study/simulation, not a deployed system — early-stage and ESA/European-program specific. The BGP-over-dynamic-topology lessons (BFD, proactive session teardown, L3 vs. L2 peering economics) generalize to any highly-dynamic interconnect problem.

items.title: Kubernetes for Network Engineers
items.text:
NLNOG Day 2026 digest Adjacent pick Hilversum · 4 September 2026

Slides Recording

Egbert Verhage (NIT Solutions)

VideoPDF

  • Why: For the PM this is mostly foundational, but it is a well-structured, demo-driven (asciinema recordings) walkthrough of exactly the K8s networking primitives in their interest area — CNI choice, MetalLB and Cilium BGP announcements, IPAM (pod/service CIDRs, Whereabouts), and Multus/SR-IOV — useful as enablement/reference material for network teams they work with.
  • What: A bottom-up tour of Kubernetes networking aimed at network engineers: pods and their disposable IPs, Services (ClusterIP/LoadBalancer/NodePort), namespaces (explicitly not a network boundary), pod-CIDR vs. service-CIDR, flannel as a first CNI, then progressively more network-y builds: MetalLB for bare-metal LoadBalancer services, swapping to Cilium to announce pod pools and LoadBalancer IPs over BGP without node masquerade, and Multus to attach extra interfaces (e.g., macvlan) to pods. Brief pointers to KubeVirt, Rook, SR-IOV CNI, and Whereabouts IPAM.
  • How: Live demos via asciinema casts: deploy flannel, apply an IP pool with MetalLB, then configure ciliumbgpadvertisements.cilium.io CRDs to originate BGP for pod and service prefixes, and Multus for multi-interface pods.
  • Where applicable: Broadly applicable — vanilla kubeadm clusters, no specific vendor platform. Introductory level: for someone already working on Cilium/K8s networking daily this covers familiar ground, with the Cilium-BGP and Multus demos being the most transferable bits.

items.title: Lessons from 10 months of ASPA
items.text:
NLNOG Day 2026 digest Core pick Hilversum · 4 September 2026

Slides Recording

Tim Bruijnzeels (RIPE NCC)

VideoPDF

  • Why: Routing security is squarely in the PM's network-security scope, and this is the rare talk with actual deployment telemetry rather than aspiration. It gives a clean mental model of what ROA, ASPA, and BGPsec each do and don't protect against, plus real uptake numbers.
  • What: A status report on ASPA (AS Provider Authorization) ten months in: how ASPA objects work, the AS0 convention for transit-free networks, valley-free path validation from both ends of a path, and the deployment picture. Key data points: signing UIs landed across Krill, RIPE NCC, ARIN, and APNIC through 2025–2026; relative signing uptake as of 15 Aug 2026 is 2.2% of registered ASNs worldwide, 4.6% in the RIPE region, 6.1% in NL, and 10.9% in CZ. Validation is coming: supported in BIRD, OpenBGPd, and NIST-BGP-SR, with Cisco IOS-XR in test; YYCIX was the first to drop ASPA-invalid (2023).
  • How: ASPA objects are RPKI-signed by a customer AS listing its provider ASes; validators feed routers over RPKI-RTR (no router crypto), and routers evaluate plausible up-ramp/down-ramp paths. The talk shows working config: deny quick from ebgp avs invalid in OpenBGPd, and aspa_check_downstream() filters in BIRD 3.2.1+ as deployed in the RIPE meeting network. RIS-based path analysis toward AS0 networks shows how common invalids already are.
  • Where applicable: Any operator with an ASN. Actionable today: sign ASPAs (include all transits, maintain them), and plan to reject invalids — with the explicit warning that ASPA is a "sharp tool" and people will drop invalids. Not org-specific; the uptake figures are global/regional RIR statistics.

items.title: Networking without the Internet
items.text:
NLNOG Day 2026 digest Wildcard pick Hilversum · 4 September 2026

Slides Recording

Marlies Heijkoop

VideoPDF

  • Why: Not a technical deep dive and it says so upfront — but a thought-provoking look at a nationwide license-free LoRa mesh (Meshcore) that achieves near-countrywide coverage on cheap hardware, and a candid perspective piece on staying engaged with networking as a craft (from a founding architect at Gomibo/Belsimpel, speaking openly about burnout).
  • What: An accessible overview of the Dutch Meshcore network: companions (end devices, e.g., nrf52-based Heltec T114) and solar-powered repeaters (Heltec v4, SenseCAP), packet characteristics (tiny, text-only, no delivery guarantees — "the Two Generals have nothing like TCP sequence numbers"), and an honest assessment of the flooding model (worse than an Ethernet hub — even the sender hears its own frame back). Practical uses are deliberately modest: Home Assistant integration, out-of-band "is it my house or is it Ziggo" checks, and last-resort communication. The talk's real argument: play with networks for fun to keep the flame burning.
  • How: LoRa modulation giving long range at very low power and terrible SNR, with repeaters re-broadcasting everything they hear (no spanning tree — counter-intuitively it works). Concrete recommendations: flash "Dutch Meshcore" firmware, buy a companion-plus-repeater pair rather than a standalone cyberdeck, and there's an NLNOG channel on the mesh.
  • Where applicable: Hobbyist/community infrastructure in the Netherlands specifically (Meshcore firmware variant, national radio settings), not production tooling — the speaker explicitly says you won't need this for monitoring prod. Worth it as a working example of an extreme-constraint mesh network and its emergent behavior.

items.title: The Art of Making Vendors Agree: Lessons from Interoperability Testing
items.text:
NLNOG Day 2026 digest Core pick Hilversum · 4 September 2026

Slides Recording

Patrick Prangl (Arista)

VideoPDF

  • Why: Directly relevant to running multi-vendor DC fabrics. It explains how EANTC's Berlin interop event works, what actually failed when vendors met, and what the 2026 test scope says about where DC/SP technology is heading (EVPN-VXLAN, SR-MPLS/SRv6, and a brand-new AI/UEC testbed).
  • What: An operator-usable guide to reading the EANTC interoperability report — plus concrete failure examples from the 2026 event, including malformed IS-IS TLV 222 (MT routing, RFC 5120) that led to corrupted LSPs, missing SRv6 Capability TLV 25 breaking backup-path calculation, and TI-LFA initially steering SRv6 routes to DROP. Also useful maturity signals: OISM (overlay multicast) control planes converge but data planes diverge; NOS-only vendor participation is shrinking.
  • How: Multi-vendor test beds (EVPN-VXLAN, EVPN-SR, MPLS-SR, SRv6, SDN/PCEP) run over two weeks with EANTC-validated results; the report only includes successful tests, and config/image details are reported to EANTC but not published. The talk walks through how ambiguous RFC language ("SHOULD", reserved bits) turns into real interop bugs.
  • Where applicable: The EANTC report and methodology are vendor-neutral and freely usable by anyone doing DC fabric procurement or PoCs. Speaker is an Arista systems engineering lead, so the framing leans toward a participant's perspective, but the content is the test event, not a product pitch. Explicit caveat from the speaker: passing interop tests does not replace your own PoC.
path: The Art of Making Vendors Agree: Lessons from Interoperability Testing

items.title: The Hitchhiker's Guide to IPv6: Don't Panic… We've Only Got 30 Minutes
items.text:
NLNOG Day 2026 digest Adjacent pick Hilversum · 4 September 2026

Slides Recording

Nicole Wajer (Cisco)

VideoPDF

  • Why: Practical IPv6 operational hardening in the trenches — the kind of small failure modes (ACLs, neighbor discovery, wireless RA handling) that bite during dual-stack or IPv6-only rollouts. Relevant background for anyone running DC edge or enterprise access alongside the fabric.
  • What: A war-story tour of IPv6 gotchas: IPv6 ACLs have implicit permits for ND-NS/ND-NA (so "tightening" an ACL can still break or unexpectedly pass neighbor discovery); a GUA-loss case caused by SSID jumping and stale neighbor cache; and a case where Windows + Cisco Secure Client stopped receiving unsolicited RAs, killing IPv6 after ~15 minutes until a bug fix shipped. Closes with an IPv4-to-IPv6-only migration path slide.
  • How: Diagnosis via neighbor-cache state machines, RA/RS behavior on interface bounce, and Wireshark captures — emphasizing that IPv6 failure modes are control-plane (ND/RA) rather than the IPv4-style ARP debugging people reach for.
  • Where applicable: General dual-stack/enterprise-wireless advice, not org-specific. Speaker is a Cisco evangelist and the war stories involve Cisco gear and Cisco Secure Client specifically, so some fixes are vendor-fix rather than technique; the diagnostic approach transfers anywhere.
path: The Hitchhiker's Guide to IPv6: Don't Panic… We've Only Got 30 Minutes

items.title: VPP eVPN Controlplane
items.text:
NLNOG Day 2026 digest Core pick Hilversum · 4 September 2026

Slides Recording

Pim van Pelt (IPng)

VideoPDF

  • Why: The most substantive talk for anyone working on DC/WAN fabric software. It demonstrates that a fully open-source, commodity-hardware eVPN fabric — DPDK/VPP dataplane plus BIRD control plane — can run a real production network (IPng operates AS8298 with 22 VPP/BIRD routers and ~2,200 BGP adjacencies), not just a lab.
  • What: A complete open-source eVPN stack: an eVPN management/control plane for VPP, a custom vppevpn protocol for BIRD, and a management plane (vpp-evpn / epvnd daemon) that orchestrates eVPN services across Mellanox BlueField DPUs at scale targets of O(100) routers, O(1,000) L3 subnets, and O(10,000) P2MP L2 segments.
  • How: VPP provides the building blocks (bridge domains, BVIs, VXLAN tunnels, split-horizon groups, learn/flood disabled on tunnels); BIRD speaks BGP eVPN NLRI (MAC/IP/IMET routes, RD/RT, RFC 5512 encapsulation ext-communities for VXLAN) against route reflectors, and the new vppevpn protocol reconciles VPP state with BIRD every N seconds — creating tunnels from IMETs, programming L2FIB from MAC routes. A per-DPU daemon adds a healthchecker (CARP/HSRP-style multicast IPv6 probes), gRPC endpoint, and Prometheus metrics; the whole thing interoperates with Arista EOS, Juniper, Cisco, and Centec VTEPs.
  • Where applicable: Broadly adoptable — all components are open source (VPP 26.06+, BIRD 2.19 with a patch) and the demo includes multi-vendor VTEPs, so it's not an island. Performance claims (100Mpps+/100Gbps+ per node on commodity x86) are IPng's own production numbers, and the scale figures are IPng-specific, but the architecture transfers to any operator willing to run DPUs as eVPN PE devices.

items.title: A deep-dive into NLNOGs tools
items.text:
nog.fi meeting 2026.06 — talk digest digest Core pick 16–17 June 2026

Abstract Recording

Nick Bouwhuis (NLNOG)

Video

  • Why: Free, community-maintained, vendor-neutral tooling that operator teams can adopt immediately — the highest transferability-per-effort item on the program.
  • What: A tour of NLNOG's operator tools — the RING (shared shell access across member networks) and IRRexplorer (IRR/RPKI cross-checking), among others — what each is useful for, and the maintenance challenges of running community infrastructure. (from abstract only)
  • How: RING members contribute a node and in return get shell-level vantage points across other member networks for debugging from outside their own AS; IRRexplorer aggregates IRR and RPKI data to check consistency of route objects and ROAs.
  • Where applicable: Open to any operator willing to participate (contribute a node); no vendor dependency; broadly applicable across scales. The maintenance-challenges portion is useful for anyone considering similar shared tooling.

items.title: About localroot
items.text:
nog.fi meeting 2026.06 — talk digest digest Adjacent pick 16–17 June 2026

Abstract Recording

Roy Arends (ICANN)

Video

  • Why: Serving a local copy of the root zone in resolvers is a recurring resilience-vs-correctness debate; an unbiased treatment of both sides is rare and useful.
  • What: A 5-minute lightning talk laying out the pros and cons of locally hosting the root zone in your resolver. (from abstract only)
  • How: Short tradeoff discussion; details not in the abstract.
  • Where applicable: Recursive-resolver operators weighing elimination of root-server queries against staleness and consistency risks.

items.title: ASPA - RPKI BGP Path Verification
items.text:
nog.fi meeting 2026.06 — talk digest digest Core pick 16–17 June 2026

Abstract Recording

Tim Bruijnzeels (RIPE NCC)

Video

  • Why: RPKI today only validates route origin; ASPA is the next mechanism, validating AS paths and rejecting route leaks. Anyone responsible for BGP security needs to know where this stands operationally.
  • What: A walkthrough of the ASPA object type and its verification algorithm, how to sign provider authorizations in the RIPE NCC RPKI Dashboard, how validation behaves in practice, and real uptake and lessons learned so far. (from abstract only)
  • How: AS holders publish an ASPA object authorizing their upstream providers; validators use it to check received paths for customer→provider consistency, detecting and rejecting "valleys" — leaked paths — in addition to origin validation.
  • Where applicable: General BGP technique, not org-specific. Requires RPKI CA participation and validator support on receiving routers; protection only materializes as transit providers adopt it, which makes the uptake discussion the key operational caveat.

items.title: Digital Networks Act and fair share update
items.text:
nog.fi meeting 2026.06 — talk digest digest Adjacent pick 16–17 June 2026

Abstract Recording

Klaus Nieminen (Traficom)

Video

  • Why: EU regulation will reshape interconnection economics — directly relevant context for anyone whose products touch EU peering and transit markets.
  • What: A regulator's update on the EC's "complex voluntary conciliation" on fair share — the deck frames it as "From Fair Share to Ecosystem Cooperation: how the EC's DNA proposal plans to reshape IP interconnections" — with the outcome still undecided among the co-legislators.
  • How: Policy talk, not technical; explicitly tentative about where the discussions will end.
  • Where applicable: EU-operating networks, IXPs, and content delivery players. Finnish-regulator (Traficom) perspective on an EU-wide process still under debate.
path: Digital Networks Act and fair share update

items.title: Knowledge is the power - Network Automation beyond the vendor
items.text:
nog.fi meeting 2026.06 — talk digest digest Core pick 16–17 June 2026

Abstract Recording

Amin Hamidi Younessi (Reonel Oy)

Video

  • Why: Demonstrates that vendor-portable automation is achievable with plain Python and native APIs — a counterpoint to framework lock-in, relevant to anyone running mixed estates or setting automation strategy.
  • What: One Python skillset — querying live state, provisioning BGP peers, pushing wide config changes — applied across MikroTik RouterOS and Cisco IOS-XE via their native APIs, demonstrated on a real ISP/IXP lab built on EVE-NG. No Ansible, no heavy frameworks: HTTP, JSON, and a few dozen readable lines of Python. (from abstract only)
  • How: Direct API calls against each vendor's native interface, with the protocol (BGP) as the stable abstraction — "when you understand the protocol underneath, the vendor becomes just a detail."
  • Where applicable: General technique, but the demo is lab-based (EVE-NG) and covers exactly two vendors, so expect small adapters per platform. Most practical for small/mid-size operators; not a scale-out automation architecture.
path: Knowledge is the power - Network Automation beyond the vendor

items.title: Managing Cryptographic Transitions: Crypto‑Agility as an Enabler and a Challenge
items.text:
nog.fi meeting 2026.06 — talk digest digest Core pick 16–17 June 2026

Abstract Recording

Markus Rautell (VTT)

Video

  • Why: PQC migration will land squarely on identity and network-security infrastructure — passkey, token, and certificate stacks all need swappable primitives. This talk frames the architectural problem that precedes any migration plan.
  • What: A position talk: cryptographic primitives offer temporary rather than permanent protection, PQC transition timelines are external and time-critical, and system architectures are still widely designed so that cryptographic updates are risky, slow, and resource-intensive; crypto-agility is hard but the work must continue. (from abstract only)
  • How: Architectural/design discussion rather than a specific mechanism — the abstract offers no concrete technique.
  • Where applicable: Broadly applicable to any system with long-lived cryptographic dependencies (identity, DNSSEC, TLS, control-plane protocols). Conceptual rather than deployable — treat it as framing for migration planning, from a research organization's perspective.
path: Managing Cryptographic Transitions: Crypto‑Agility as an Enabler and a Challenge

items.title: NAF Framework
items.text:
nog.fi meeting 2026.06 — talk digest digest Adjacent pick 16–17 June 2026

Abstract Recording

Jaakko Rautanen

Video

  • Why: A shared vocabulary for network automation systems helps compare tools, architectures, and roadmaps — directly useful to a PM defining automation product strategy.
  • What: A 5-minute introduction to NAF, a community-driven effort that helps understand network automation systems by giving them shared vocabulary. (from abstract only)
  • How: Not detailed in the abstract — expect taxonomy and concepts rather than a runnable artifact.
  • Where applicable: Anyone building, buying, or comparing network automation. Early-stage community effort; judge maturity accordingly.

items.title: RFC8950 for a V4LESS(-AS) World: Diving into the magic of IPv4-with-IPv6 Next-Hops
items.text:
nog.fi meeting 2026.06 — talk digest digest Core pick 16–17 June 2026

Abstract Recording

Daniel Wagner (DE-CIX), Tobias Fiebig (TU Wien)

Video

  • Why: The most directly relevant fabric/interconnect talk on the program. Carrying IPv4 routes with IPv6 next-hops dissolves several standing design pains in both IXP peering LANs and large ECMP fabrics — exactly the DC/WAN interconnect territory this PM works in.
  • What: A working walkthrough of what IPv4-with-IPv6 next-hops (RFC 8950, which extends RFC 5549-style extended next-hop encoding to eBGP) enables: IXPs without IPv4 peering-LAN growth pain, seamless IPv4 routing at /32 granularity, IPv4-free transport links, a fully ARP-free infrastructure, and ECMP-enabled L3 underlays for 100G+ fabrics without LACP. Includes an open invitation to peer with V4LESS-AS (AS215250), their live RFC 8950 testbed at an internet exchange.
  • How: IPv4 NLRI is advertised over BGP sessions using IPv6 next-hops, so the entire L3 core — peering LANs, transport, fabric underlay — can be IPv6-only while still serving IPv4 destinations; with no IPv4 at L2/L3, ARP disappears and routed ECMP replaces LACP-bundled L2 links.
  • Where applicable: A standards-based technique, not vendor- or org-specific in principle. Constraints: every router on the path must support extended next-hop encoding, and the ARP-free/no-LACP benefits are easiest to realize in greenfield or single-administrator fabrics. The V4LESS-AS testbed (AS215250) is the concrete proof point.
path: RFC8950 for a V4LESS(-AS) World: Diving into the magic of IPv4-with-IPv6 Next-Hops

items.title: Root KSK Rollover 2026: An Operator's Readiness Checklist
items.text:
nog.fi meeting 2026.06 — talk digest digest Adjacent pick 16–17 June 2026

Abstract Recording

Roy Arends (ICANN)

Video

  • Why: October 2026 brings the first root KSK rollover since 2018; validating resolvers with badly managed trust anchors are the ones that break. This is a concrete, adoptable checklist — exactly the kind of ops content worth taking away.
  • What: A minutes-long readiness checklist for validating-resolver operators: verify resolvers use managed trust anchors, confirm the active root KSK, and inspect RFC 5011 state — with concrete commands and expected outputs for common resolver software, designed to slot into existing workflows. (from abstract only)
  • How: Relies on RFC 5011 automated trust-anchor updates (or RFC 9718 operation); the checklist catches hardcoded/static trust-anchor configurations before they break.
  • Where applicable: Any operator of validating recursive resolvers, regardless of scale. Should be routine if trust anchors are already managed correctly.
path: Root KSK Rollover 2026: An Operator's Readiness Checklist

items.title: The IRR Landscape and its Implications on Global Internet Traffic
items.text:
nog.fi meeting 2026.06 — talk digest digest Core pick 16–17 June 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Daniel Wagner (DE-CIX)

VideoPPTX

  • Why: Route-server prefix filters at IXPs are generated from IRR data; when AS-SETs are inconsistent or stale, traffic that should flow through the peering fabric doesn't. This is the data-quality counterpart to the ASPA talk, attacking the same trust gap from the legacy side.
  • What: Latest results from Wagner's RIPE Labs article series on the IRR landscape, including previously unreleased insights on AS-SET heterogeneity, IRR lookup ordering, and the measured traffic impact at a very large IXP, ending in a community call to action. (from abstract only)
  • How: Analysis of IRR database contents and route-server filter-generation behavior, correlated with observed traffic at a large IXP.
  • Where applicable: The measurement is DE-CIX-scale (org-specific), but the mechanism — filters generated from heterogeneous IRR data — applies to every IXP participant and most transit relationships. Direction of findings transfers; absolute numbers do not.
path: The IRR Landscape and its Implications on Global Internet Traffic

items.title: The No-Nonsense Approach to Build Infrastructure that Lasts
items.text:
nog.fi meeting 2026.06 — talk digest digest Core pick 16–17 June 2026

Abstract Recording

Tony O'Sullivan (RETN)

Video

  • Why: Physical-infrastructure resilience — cable cuts, geopolitical and climate shocks — is core WAN territory for this PM, and this is a hard-won experience report from a network that stayed online through events that took others down.
  • What: An experience talk (the deck is titled "Hardwired for Chaos") on how RETN (AS9002) has scaled a lean, 44-country network and kept it running "under fire, literally," challenging the industry to build infrastructure that is innovative, scalable, and sustainable.
  • How: The abstract gives principles rather than mechanism — expect lessons on physical/route diversity, lean operations, and surviving cable cuts rather than a technical deep dive.
  • Where applicable: RETN-specific scale and geography (pan-Eurasian footprint with distinct geopolitical exposure). The resilience lessons transfer; the specific operating model and cost base do not.
path: The No-Nonsense Approach to Build Infrastructure that Lasts

items.title: Veeam MCP server
items.text:
nog.fi meeting 2026.06 — talk digest digest Wildcard pick 16–17 June 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Janne Haatainen (Veeam)

VideoPPTX

  • Why: Not about networking at all, but a signal of where ops tooling is heading: local AI agents acting on infrastructure products through MCP — the same wave that will demand identity and authorization models for agents.
  • What: A quick, sponsored lightning talk introducing a Veeam MCP server that lets local AI interact with Veeam products (the materials reference a Claude-based setup).
  • How: An MCP server exposing product operations to a local LLM client — the pattern, not the product, is the takeaway.
  • Where applicable: Veeam estates specifically; flag it as a sponsor slot. The generalizable signal is the MCP-ification of infrastructure tooling, which sits interestingly next to questions of identity and authorization for AI agents.

items.title: (Why) GPUs are awful (to virtualize)
items.text:
nog.fi meeting 2026.06 — talk digest digest Adjacent pick 16–17 June 2026

Abstract Recording

Johannes Brummer

Video

  • Why: For anyone running networks for AI-era compute, knowing why GPUs are painful to virtualize (device assignment, passthrough, memory mapping) shapes what the fabric must support — SR-IOV/passthrough choices interact directly with RDMA fabrics.
  • What: Hands-on experience virtualizing different GPU types on multiple different hardware platforms, plus approaches to providing them to actually paying customers. (from abstract only)
  • How: Practical experience report; no methodology stated in the abstract.
  • Where applicable: Hosting/service providers offering GPU compute. Useful context for designing networks under GPU clusters, but it is a compute virtualization talk, not a networking one.

items.title: Achieving Wire-Latency Storage Systems by Exploiting Hardware ACKs (Juneberry)
items.text:
NSDI '25 digest Core pick 28–30 April 2025

Abstract Paper Slides Recording

  • Authors / tier: Qing Wang, Jiwu Shu, Jing Wang, Yuhao Zhang (Tsinghua University). Core.
VideoPDF

  • Why: Touches RDMA datapath internals directly: it questions whether storage requests need a full RPC round trip plus server-CPU involvement to commit, which is relevant to anyone designing lossless-fabric storage paths.
  • What: Juneberry gives storage requests a fast path that commits in a single round trip while bypassing the server CPU, with request execution happening asynchronously on the server afterward.
  • How: An "Ordered Queue" abstraction treats the NIC's hardware ACK as the commit signal while preserving linearizability; durability comes from landing requests in persistent memory. Built on commodity RDMA NICs and integrated into Memcached and PMemKV, with significantly lower latency than RPC under write-intensive workloads.
  • Where applicable: RDMA + persistent-memory storage deployments on commodity RNICs. General mechanism, but the durability story assumes PM availability.
path: Achieving Wire-Latency Storage Systems by Exploiting Hardware ACKs (Juneberry)

items.title: Efficient Direct-Connect Topologies for Collective Communications
items.text:
NSDI '25 digest Adjacent pick 28–30 April 2025

Abstract Paper Slides Recording

  • Authors / tier: Liangyu Zhao, Tapan Chugh, Arvind Krishnamurthy (University of Washington); Siddharth Pal, Jason Fantl, Prithwish Basu, Joud Khoury (Raytheon BBN); Weiyang Wang (MIT CSAIL). Adjacent.
VideoPDF

  • Why: Sits at the physical-topology/collective-communication boundary that increasingly drives ML cluster fabric design — relevant context for DC topology and interconnect decisions.
  • What: An algorithmic framework that jointly synthesizes direct-connect topologies and their communication schedules, then picks the topology/schedule best suited to a given workload's latency-vs-bandwidth profile and degree constraints.
  • How: Start from small optimal base topologies and schedules, then iteratively expand them to large sizes; a novel polynomial-time algorithm produces efficient collective schedules for well-known large-scale graph topologies. Validated on multiple testbeds plus large-scale simulation.
  • Where applicable: Degree-constrained direct-connect networks (e.g., optical/cabled interconnects without a central switch). General framework; most valuable where you control the physical topology.
path: Efficient Direct-Connect Topologies for Collective Communications

items.title: Efficient Multi-WAN Transport for 5G with OTTER
items.text:
NSDI '25 digest Adjacent pick 28–30 April 2025

Abstract Paper Slides Recording

  • Authors / tier: Mary Hogan (Oberlin College); Gerry Wan (Google); Yiming Qiu (University of Michigan); Sharad Agarwal, Ryan Beckett (Microsoft); Rachee Singh (Cornell); Paramvir Bahl (Microsoft). Adjacent.
VideoPDF

  • Why: WAN interconnect is core to the PM, and multi-WAN coordination for 5G is an operator-grade problem. The paper shows a way to stitch routes across multiple WANs using existing cloud primitives.
  • What: OTTER coordinates transport across multiple WANs to improve performance for 5G traffic, managing route identification and use across providers from one system.
  • How: Uses cloud-native components (VNet peering, VPN gateways, firewalls) configured so that VMs in one region can use a gateway in another and carry transit traffic, with scale-up/scale-out per component to span large geographies without per-component code changes; supports asymmetric paths. Reported >25 Gbps between VMs in their GCP topology.
  • Where applicable: Multi-cloud/multi-WAN operators; the prototype leans on specific cloud networking features, so it's somewhat provider-configuration-specific.
path: Efficient Multi-WAN Transport for 5G with OTTER

items.title: eTran: Extensible Kernel Transport with eBPF
items.text:
NSDI '25 digest Core pick 28–30 April 2025

Abstract Paper Slides Recording

  • Authors / tier: Zhongjie Chen (Tsinghua); Qingkai Meng (Nanjing University); ChonLam Lao (Harvard); Yifan Liu, Fengyuan Ren (Tsinghua); Minlan Yu (Harvard); Yang Zhou (UC Berkeley and UC Davis). Core.
VideoPDF

  • Why: New transport designs almost never reach the mainline kernel, and when they do it takes years. eTran is a credible answer to "how do we get customizable transports into production without forking the kernel" — directly relevant to anyone reasoning about datapath internals and congestion control.
  • What: A framework that makes kernel transport extensible: operators implement and customize transports (it ships DCTCP-style TCP and Homa) as eBPF rather than kernel patches, while keeping kernel-level safety and absorbing userspace-transport performance tricks.
  • How: Core transport ops run in the kernel via eBPF; packets reach a thin, untrusted userspace library through AF_XDP sockets, where they are reassembled into TCP flows or Homa RPCs. All packets traverse eBPF hooks, so monitoring, access control, and rate limiting are modular eBPF programs chained via bpf_tail_call. Reported up to ~7.5x lower P99 latency than Linux Homa on RPC workloads. Open source.
  • Where applicable: Datacenter Linux hosts (evaluated on kernel 6.6.0 with AF_XDP). General technique, but tied to a recent kernel and AF_XDP; synchronization support in eBPF is a noted limitation.
path: eTran: Extensible Kernel Transport with eBPF

items.title: Everything Matters in Programmable Packet Scheduling (PACKS)
items.text:
NSDI '25 digest Core pick 28–30 April 2025

Abstract Paper Slides Recording

  • Authors / tier: Albert Gran Alcoz (ETH Zürich); Balázs Vass (BME-TMIT); Pooria Namyar (USC); Behnaz Arzani (Microsoft Research); Gábor Rétvári (BME-TMIT); Laurent Vanbever (ETH Zürich). Core.
VideoPDF

  • Why: PIFO is the ideal programmable scheduler but can't be built at line rate in hardware. Prior approximations (SP-PIFO, AIFO) each capture only one of PIFO's two behaviors. This advances the "one scheduling abstraction on commodity switches" agenda that matters for anyone tuning FCT on Tofino-class hardware.
  • What: PACKS approximates PIFO while capturing both required behaviors — scheduling order and admission control — which prior schemes handled only separately.
  • How: Packets are tagged with ranks; PACKS uses a sliding window of recent ranks plus queue-occupancy to make admission decisions, and maps ranks across a small set of priority queues to minimize rank inversions. Reported: up to 7x and 15x fewer rank inversions than SP-PIFO and AIFO, up to 60% fewer drops vs SP-PIFO, and up to 33%/2.6x lower mean FCT for small flows under pFabric ranks.
  • Where applicable: Existing programmable switches; implemented in P4 and shown to run at line rate on Intel Tofino. General technique within the constraints of fixed-queue hardware.
path: Everything Matters in Programmable Packet Scheduling (PACKS)

items.title: From Address Blocks to Authorized Prefixes: Redesigning RPKI ROV with a Hierarchical Hashing Scheme
items.text:
NSDI '25 digest Core pick 28–30 April 2025

Abstract Paper Slides Recording

  • Authors / tier: Zedong Ni (CNIC, CAS / Southeast University); Yinbo Xu, Hui Zou, Yanbiao Li (CNIC, CAS / UCAS); Guang Cheng (Southeast University / Purple Mountain Labs); Gaogang Xie (CNIC, CAS / UCAS). Core.
VideoPDF

  • Why: RPKI Route Origin Validation is becoming table stakes for routing security, and its memory/lookup cost on routers is a practical adoption barrier. Directly relevant to the security-and-routing side of the PM's remit.
  • What: A redesign of ROV's validation data structure to make origin validation fast and memory-efficient, reframing the problem from address blocks to authorized prefixes.
  • How: A hierarchical hashing scheme for prefix-to-authorization lookup. (Specific performance numbers were not captured in this digest pass; confirm them from the paper.)
  • Where applicable: Router-side ROV implementations; broadly applicable to any operator deploying RPKI.
path: From Address Blocks to Authorized Prefixes: Redesigning RPKI ROV with a Hierarchical Hashing Scheme

items.title: Mitigating Scalability Walls of RDMA-based Container Networks
items.text:
NSDI '25 digest Core pick 28–30 April 2025

Abstract Paper Recording

  • Authors / tier: Wei Liu (Tsinghua and Alibaba Cloud); Kun Qian (Alibaba Cloud); Zhenhua Li (Tsinghua); Feng Qian (USC); Tianyin Xu (UIUC); Yunhao Liu (Tsinghua); Yu Guan, Shuhong Zhu, Hongfei Xu, Lanlan Xi, Chao Qin, Ennan Zhai (Alibaba Cloud). Core.
Video

  • Why: RDMA-offloaded container networks deliver big wins (the paper shows ~21 Gbps TCP rising to ~180 Gbps once forwarding and VXLAN move to the RNIC and RDMA carries packets), but performance collapses unexpectedly at the scale of millions of containers. Anyone betting on RNIC offload for container fabric needs to understand this ceiling.
  • What: The "scalability wall" is traced to the RNICs themselves — design/implementation defects that are invisible because RNIC internals are closed. They build ScalaCN, which infers the most likely causes despite that opacity and proactively reschedules NF offload.
  • How: Combinatorial causal testing reconstructs an approximate RNIC architecture and performance model from black-box behavior; ScalaCN then optimizes the network-function offload schedule against that model. On production workloads: ~1.4x end-to-end bandwidth and ~31% lower forwarding latency after resolving 82% of inferred causes. Issues were reported to and confirmed by vendors.
  • Where applicable: Production RDMA container networks at hyperscale; evaluation is on Alibaba's production RCN with NVIDIA ConnectX-6 RNICs, so specifics are vendor- and deployment-tied, but the causal-inference methodology for black-box NICs generalizes.
path: Mitigating Scalability Walls of RDMA-based Container Networks

items.title: Mutant: Learning Congestion Control from Existing Protocols via Online Reinforcement Learning
items.text:
NSDI '25 digest Adjacent pick 28–30 April 2025

Abstract Paper Recording

  • Authors / tier: Lorenzo Pappone (Saint Louis University); Alessio Sacco (Politecnico di Torino); Flavio Esposito (Saint Louis University). Adjacent.
Video

  • Why: Congestion control is core datapath territory; the "learn to switch among existing CCAs online" framing is a pragmatic middle ground between hand-tuned and clean-slate learned CC, worth watching as a design pattern.
  • What: An online-RL approach that adapts among existing congestion-control protocols rather than learning one from scratch. (Detailed mechanism and results not captured in this digest pass; confirm from the paper.)
  • Where applicable: General transport; treat performance claims as to-be-verified.
path: Mutant: Learning Congestion Control from Existing Protocols via Online Reinforcement Learning

items.title: NDD: A Decision Diagram for Network Verification
items.text:
NSDI '25 digest Adjacent pick 28–30 April 2025

Abstract Paper Slides Recording

  • Authors / tier: Zechun Li, Peng Zhang, Yichi Zhang (Xi'an Jiaotong University); Hongkun Yang (Google). Adjacent. Awarded Outstanding Paper.
VideoPDF

  • Why: Network verification underpins config-change safety and reachability analysis. BDDs have been the standard data structure for a decade; an Outstanding Paper that improves the substrate is worth tracking even if you consume verification rather than build it.
  • What: Network Decision Diagram (NDD), a data structure customized for verification that natively supports equivalence classes and beats BDD on memory and computation.
  • How: NDD wraps BDD in another decision-diagram layer — each NDD node represents a header field, and each edge is labeled with a BDD encoding that field's values. Because field-based matching is local, NDD sharply reduces BDD node counts and makes equivalence-class handling transparent to verifiers. Released as a library; existing verifiers (AP Verifier, APT) were ported to it.
  • Where applicable: General — a drop-in substrate for BDD-based verification tools.
path: NDD: A Decision Diagram for Network Verification

items.title: ONCache: A Cache-Based Low-Overhead Container Overlay Network
items.text:
NSDI '25 digest Core pick 28–30 April 2025

Abstract Paper Slides Recording

  • Authors / tier: Shengkai Lin, Shizhen Zhao, Peirui Cao, Xinchi Han (Shanghai Jiao Tong University); Quan Tian, Wenfeng Liu, Qi Wu, Donghai Han (Broadcom); Xinbing Wang (SJTU). Core.
VideoPDF

  • Why: Overlay networks (VXLAN/Geneve CNIs) are the default in Kubernetes but impose a per-packet tax versus bare metal. This is the exact tradeoff a cloud-native networking PM lives with, and the paper quantifies where the kernel datapath actually spends its time.
  • What: The authors profile the overlay datapath segment by segment, observe that most of the extra overhead recomputes the same results across packets of a flow, and cache those invariant results. The result reaches near-bare-metal throughput while keeping overlay flexibility and compatibility.
  • How: Three caches (egress, ingress, filter) hold the invariant per-flow results; implemented as four eBPF programs plus three eBPF maps and a small userspace component, in roughly 524 lines of eBPF C — far less than prior approaches like Slim or Falcon. Reported gains: ~12% TCP throughput and ~36% transaction-rate improvement (20%/34% for UDP), with reduced soft-interrupt CPU.
  • Where applicable: Broadly applicable to overlay CNIs; the prototype is shipped as an Antrea plugin (Broadcom is a co-author), so the cleanest integration path is Antrea/OVS-based fabrics. The technique itself is CNI-agnostic.
path: ONCache: A Cache-Based Low-Overhead Container Overlay Network

items.title: PreAcher: Secure and Practical Password Pre-Authentication by Content Delivery Networks
items.text:
NSDI '25 digest Core pick 28–30 April 2025

Abstract Paper Slides Recording

  • Authors / tier: Shihan Lin, Xiaowei Yang (Duke); Suting Chen, Aleksandar Kuzmanovic (Northwestern); Yunming Xiao (University of Michigan); Yanqi Gu (UC Irvine). Core.
VideoPDF

  • Why: Sits in the identity/authentication lane: it offloads password authentication to CDNs to absorb application-layer DoS against login interfaces, without ever revealing passwords to the CDN. A genuinely novel three-party auth architecture.
  • What: A system that inserts a third-party CDN into the password-auth path to pre-authenticate users and filter ADoS traffic before it reaches the origin, while preserving password secrecy and usability.
  • How: A three-party (client/CDN/server) protocol combining an Oblivious Pseudorandom Function (OPRF) with Locality-Sensitive Hashing (LSH). The client derives a secret key from the password via OPRF+LSH and interacts with the CDN rather than the server, so the CDN can validate login attempts without learning the password. Demonstrated against a commercial-CDN setup where login-interface ADoS slips past standard WAF/rate-limit protections.
  • Where applicable: Web services fronted by CDNs that want login-layer DoS protection; deployable unilaterally by a server operator. General architecture, though it changes the login flow and assumes CDN cooperation.
path: PreAcher: Secure and Practical Password Pre-Authentication by Content Delivery Networks

items.title: Pyrrha: Congestion-Root-Based Flow Control to Eliminate Head-of-Line Blocking in Datacenter
items.text:
NSDI '25 digest Adjacent pick 28–30 April 2025

Abstract Paper Slides Recording

  • Authors / tier: Kexin Liu, Zhaochen Zhang, Chang Liu, Yizhi Wang (Nanjing University); Vamsi Addanki, Stefan Schmid (TU Berlin); additional co-authors at Nanjing University and Huawei. Adjacent.
VideoPDF

  • Why: Head-of-line blocking in lossless DC fabrics (PFC and friends) is a recurring operational pain. Congestion-root-based flow control is a notable angle for anyone working on RDMA/lossless fabrics.
  • What: A flow-control scheme that targets the root of congestion rather than reacting hop-by-hop, aiming to eliminate HoL blocking. (Detailed mechanism not captured in this digest pass; confirm specifics from the paper.)
  • Where applicable: Lossless datacenter fabrics; involvement of Huawei co-authors suggests hardware-oriented validation. Treat as fabric-class research relevant to RDMA deployments.
path: Pyrrha: Congestion-Root-Based Flow Control to Eliminate Head-of-Line Blocking in Datacenter

items.title: Quicksand: Harnessing Stranded Datacenter Resources with Granular Computing
items.text:
NSDI '25 digest Wildcard pick 28–30 April 2025

Abstract Paper Slides Recording

  • Authors / tier: Zhenyuan Ruan, Kaiyan Fan, Adam Belay (MIT CSAIL); Shihang Li, Malte Schwarzkopf (Brown); Seo Jin Park (USC); Marcos K. Aguilera (VMware Research by Broadcom). Wildcard.
VideoPDF

  • Why: Stranded resources (memory/CPU that exist but can't be allocated) are a real efficiency drain in datacenters. The granular-computing angle is an emerging subfield a DC-infra PM wouldn't necessarily search for but should see.
  • What: A runtime that reclaims stranded datacenter resources by exposing computation at fine (granular) units that can be packed into otherwise-unusable capacity. (Detailed mechanism not captured in this digest pass; confirm from the paper.)
  • Where applicable: Datacenter resource scheduling; research-grade, but points at where utilization-efficiency work is heading.
