items.title: Securing Public Cloud Networks with Efficient Role-based Micro-Segmentation (ZTS)
items.text:
NSDI '25 digest Core pick 28–30 April 2025

Abstract Paper Slides Recording

  • Authors / tier: Sathiya Kumaran Mani, Kevin Hsieh (Microsoft); Santiago Segarra (Rice); Ranveer Chandra (Microsoft); Yajie Zhou (University of Maryland); Srikanth Kandula (Microsoft). Core.
VideoPDF

  • Why: Micro-segmentation is the canonical zero-trust control for limiting blast radius, but authoring precise policies at cloud scale is the perennial blocker. This sits squarely in network security and is grounded in real deployment.
  • What: ZTS (Zero Trust Segmentation) ingests large volumes of flow logs, infers endpoint roles, and generates micro-segmentation policies automatically, with continuous communication-graph generation and policy enforcement.
  • How: Role inference combines domain knowledge with communication patterns rather than relying on manual tagging (which breaks as pods migrate or scale). Evaluated against ground truth across 11 first- and third-party deployments; reported up to 21.5x more cost-efficient than Apache Flink for the stream-processing workload, with higher role-inference accuracy than prior algorithms.
  • Where applicable: Large public-cloud networks; built and evaluated inside Microsoft's environment, so the productized form is Azure-flavored, but the role-inference approach is general.
path: Securing Public Cloud Networks with Efficient Role-based Micro-Segmentation (ZTS)

items.title: Suppressing BGP Zombies with Route Status Transparency (RoST)
items.text:
NSDI '25 digest Core pick 28–30 April 2025

Abstract Paper Slides Recording

  • Authors / tier: Yosef Edery Anahory, Yossi Gilad (Hebrew University of Jerusalem); Jie Kong, Nicholas Scaglione, Justin Furuness, Amir Herzberg, Bing Wang (University of Connecticut); Hemi Leibowitz (College of Management Academic Studies). Core.
VideoPDF

  • Why: Withdrawal suppression ("zombie" routes that stay active after withdrawal) has been a known BGP weakness for over a decade, with real reliability and security consequences. This is the first systematic defense, relevant to anyone tracking inter-domain routing security alongside RPKI.
  • What: RoST lets an AS efficiently and securely verify whether a route has actually been withdrawn, defeating both misconfiguration-driven and adversarial withdrawal suppression.
  • How: A verification scheme that is compatible with BGP and composes with existing BGP security enhancements (rather than replacing them). The design targets efficient per-route status checks.
  • Where applicable: Inter-domain routing broadly; an incrementally deployable addition to BGP/RPKI-style security rather than a clean-slate redesign.
path: Suppressing BGP Zombies with Route Status Transparency (RoST)

items.title: The Benefits and Limitations of User Interrupts for Preemptive Userspace Scheduling
items.text:
NSDI '25 digest Wildcard pick 28–30 April 2025

Abstract Paper Slides Recording

  • Authors / tier: Linsong Guo, Danial Zuberi, Tal Garfinkel, Amy Ousterhout (UC San Diego). Wildcard.
VideoPDF

  • Why: A clear-eyed measurement study of a newer x86 hardware feature (user interrupts) for preemptive userspace scheduling — the kind of "here's what the new primitive actually buys you, and where it doesn't" result that informs datapath and dataplane-OS design.
  • What: An evaluation of user interrupts as a mechanism for preemptive scheduling in userspace, characterizing both the wins and the limits rather than pitching a single system.
  • Where applicable: Userspace network/dataplane stacks and low-latency runtimes on hardware that supports user interrupts. General, forward-looking.
path: The Benefits and Limitations of User Interrupts for Preemptive Userspace Scheduling

items.title: Towards Energy Efficient 5G vRAN Servers (RENC)
items.text:
NSDI '25 digest Wildcard pick 28–30 April 2025

Abstract Paper Recording

  • Authors / tier: Anuj Kalia (Microsoft); Nikita Lazarev (MIT); Leyang Xue (University of Edinburgh); Xenofon Foukas, Bozidar Radunovic (Microsoft); Francis Y. Yan (Microsoft Research and UIUC). Wildcard.
Video

  • Why: A surprising result at the intersection of real-time systems and power: you can claw back substantial CPU energy from vRAN servers despite hard sub-millisecond deadlines and black-box proprietary software. The eBPF-based slack-measurement trick is a clever pattern beyond RAN.
  • What: RENC saves energy by adjusting CPU frequency in response to sub-second cellular-load variation without missing real-time deadlines.
  • How: It establishes safe low-load intervals by coupling MAC-layer rate limiting to frequency changes; computes safe frequencies by measuring deadline slack in vRAN threads via Linux eBPF hooks (or minor binary rewriting of the closed vRAN binary); and handles control-driven load spikes (e.g., new-user attach). Reported up to 45% CPU power reduction (29% server-wide) on a state-of-the-art vRAN testbed.
  • Where applicable: vRAN/telco edge servers; the technique is specific to real-time-deadline workloads, but the "measure slack with eBPF, then undervolt/underclock safely" idea generalizes to other latency-critical services.

items.title: A Composable Emulation Framework for Whitebox Switches
items.text:
NSDI '26 — Network Papers Worth Your Time digest Adjacent pick 30 April 2026

Abstract Paper Slides Recording

Congcong Miao (Tencent), Xianneng Zou (Tencent and Tsinghua Shenzhen), Chuwen Zhang (Tsinghua), et al., with Ang Chen (University of Michigan)

VideoPDF

  • Why: As switches disaggregate into vendor-mixed modules (data plane, control plane, optics), monolithic firmware emulators stop matching reality — and config errors slip through to production. This is the first emulation framework built for that composed world.
  • What: "MirSwitch," a composable whitebox-switch emulation framework deployed in Tencent's production network; operators used it to troubleshoot 97.5% of 203 issues in a recent year, with 2.2x better forwarding-emulation performance.
  • How: An adaptor-centric design that stitches together diverse emulator modules for data plane, control plane, and peripherals (including optical components), reconciling differing interface contracts across modules so mixed-vendor compositions can be emulated faithfully before deployment.
  • Where applicable: Operators building disaggregated/whitebox switches from multiple vendors; the 97.5%-of-issues production statistic is unusually strong validation for an emulation paper.
path: A Composable Emulation Framework for Whitebox Switches

items.title: Bifrost: Alibaba's Next-Generation VPC Network with High-Performance Multipath Reliable Transport
items.text:
NSDI '26 — Network Papers Worth Your Time digest Core pick 30 April 2026

Abstract Paper Slides Recording

Zihao Fan (SJTU and Alibaba Cloud), Xing Li (Zhejiang University and Alibaba Cloud), Ye Yang, et al. (Alibaba Cloud), Rong Wen (Fudan and Alibaba Cloud), Shunmin Zhu (Alibaba Cloud), et al.

VideoPDF

  • Why: This is the logical endpoint of the "TCP in the guest can't survive cloud-network instability" argument: Alibaba moved reliable, multipath transport into the VPC overlay infrastructure itself, tail-latency problem included. An operational-systems paper with 26x-scale production evidence.
  • What: Next-gen VPC networking delivering reliable transport as an infrastructure service: up to 307x tail-latency reduction for Redis and 66x for Nginx, millisecond-level failure recovery, and O(100k) concurrent connections per SmartNIC.
  • How: RTT-aware multipath packet spraying across the underlay (bypasses failures, spreads elephant flows), in-place reordering in the guest for in-order delivery, delayed bitmap ACKs for end-to-end reliability, and reliability-state management engineered for SmartNIC deployment at scale.
  • Where applicable: Alibaba Cloud production (operational systems paper); requires SmartNIC-capable tunnel endpoints, so it presumes a cloud provider's level of control over the hypervisor/SmartNIC layer. The architecture — reliable multipath overlay as a tenant-transparent service — is the transferable idea.
path: Bifrost: Alibaba's Next-Generation VPC Network with High-Performance Multipath Reliable Transport

items.title: BURST: Seeking High-performance, Interoperability and Scalability in Soft-RDMA
items.text:
NSDI '26 — Network Papers Worth Your Time digest Core pick 30 April 2026

Abstract Paper Recording

Huijun Shen (Hunan University), Zelong Yue, Jian Yang, et al. (ByteDance), Xijin Yin, et al. (Hunan University)

Video

  • Why: Heterogeneous pods — commercial RNICs, plain Ethernet NICs, in-house hardware — are now the norm, and non-RNIC↔RNIC traffic keeps falling back to TCP. ByteDance attacks exactly the interoperability wall that limits RDMA estate scaling during LLM-infra buildouts.
  • What: A user-space software RDMA stack that runs unmodified Verbs applications on ordinary Ethernet NICs at 400G: 98.7% line-rate bandwidth, 3.2–6.3x kernel RXE throughput, LLM inference latency at 25.2% of TCP, and 12x faster connection setup than native RDMA CM.
  • How: Runs as an independent user-space process with full Verbs API compatibility; lock-free DPDK data plane for line-rate packet processing; Intel DSA offload to cut CPU cost; kernel-bypass connection manager.
  • Where applicable: Data centers with mixed NIC estates, especially where RNIC hardware can't be everywhere (storage-attached hosts, upgraded clusters). x86-specific today (DPDK + Intel DSA); ByteDance production-workload validation, academic authors.
path: BURST: Seeking High-performance, Interoperability and Scalability in Soft-RDMA

items.title: CCC: Re-architecting Delay-based Congestion Control in Datacenter Networks
items.text:
NSDI '26 — Network Papers Worth Your Time digest Core pick 30 April 2026

Abstract Paper Recording

Wanchun Jiang, et al. (Central South University), Danfeng Shan (Xi'an Jiaotong), Fengyuan Ren (Tsinghua), Jiawei Huang, Jianxin Wang (Central South)

Video

  • Why: TIMELY/SWIFT-style delay CC runs in production, but the paper's key insight — that even perfectly measured delay can yield incorrect congestion-information deduction under certain conditions — explains instability modes practitioners see and haven't had a framework for.
  • What: A re-architecture of delay-based CC that makes rate adjustments depend not just on congestion state but on trustworthiness of the deduction from delay signals. The resulting CCC matches INT-based CCs (HPCC, PowerTCP) using only delay — no INT headers, no special switch support — and beats DCQCN, TIMELY, and SWIFT.
  • How: Demarcates operating regions where delay-derived congestion info is untrustworthy (using congestion criteria plus system inertia), applies probing-style rate adjustment there, and applies analytical adjustment elsewhere to reach the target state while keeping the deduction trustworthy.
  • Where applicable: Standard datacenter fabrics — the whole point is needing nothing beyond RTT signals. Validated with DPDK testbeds and large-scale simulation. General technique, no hardware prerequisites; a serious competitor to deployable delay-based schemes like SWIFT.
path: CCC: Re-architecting Delay-based Congestion Control in Datacenter Networks

items.title: CrossCheck: Input Validation for WAN Control Systems
items.text:
NSDI '26 — Network Papers Worth Your Time digest Adjacent pick 30 April 2026

Abstract Paper Slides Recording

Alexander Krentsel (UC Berkeley and Google), Rishabh Iyer (UC Berkeley), Isaac Keslassy (Technion and UC Berkeley), Bharath Modhipalli (Google), Sylvia Ratnasamy (UC Berkeley and Google), Anees Shaikh, Rob Shakir (Google)

VideoPDF

  • Why: WAN outages increasingly trace to bad inputs to the SDN controller (telemetry bugs, corrupted state) rather than bad control logic. CrossCheck guards that interface — a class of failure most validation work ignores.
  • What: A shadow validation system for SDN-WAN controller inputs. Four weeks in a production WAN: it caught the single invalid-input incident that occurred with 0% false positives; simulation shows detection of demand perturbations as small as 5% at 100% accuracy, and zero false positives with up to 30% corrupted telemetry.
  • How: Cross-validates controller inputs (demands, topology, telemetry) against consistency constraints before they drive TE decisions, alerting operators pre-outage rather than post-mortem.
  • Where applicable: Google-scale WAN operator deployment; the pre-deployment shadow-mode evaluation pattern is what makes the 0%-FP claim credible. Concept transfers to any SDN-controlled WAN (or even large DCN controller) with telemetry-driven inputs.
path: CrossCheck: Input Validation for WAN Control Systems

items.title: DDoS Detection at the Scale of One Hundred Tbps
items.text:
NSDI '26 — Network Papers Worth Your Time digest Core pick 30 April 2026

Abstract Paper Recording

Yunming Xiao (CUHK Shenzhen and Tencent), Xijun Luo, et al. (Tencent), Heng Yu, Jiahao Cao (Tsinghua), Yan Chen (Northwestern), Congcong Miao (Tencent)

Video

  • Why: Existing programmable-device DDoS detectors top out around Tbps per box; cloud incumbents see ~100 Tbps aggregate. This is the production answer to two orders of magnitude more traffic — with the scaling lessons made explicit.
  • What: "Canopy," a DDoS detection system deployed in Tencent production that scales past 100 Tbps via distributed detection across many servers — dynamic load balancing that adapts to mice/elephant mixes, plus traffic compression at the programmable switch to shrink per-server workload.
  • How: Instead of naive flow-level load balancing across detection servers (which skews badly), Canopy dynamically rebalances under fluctuating traffic patterns, and pre-aggregates/compresses traffic in the switch offload stage before it reaches the servers.
  • Where applicable: Tencent-specific production deployment, but the architecture (switch-side compression + adaptive distribution over a detection-server fleet) generalizes to any large scrubbing/detection pipeline. Real-world attack mitigation in production validates it.
path: DDoS Detection at the Scale of One Hundred Tbps

items.title: Defending against Traffic Analysis Attacks with Flexible In-Network Obfuscation
items.text:
NSDI '26 — Network Papers Worth Your Time digest Adjacent pick 30 April 2026

Abstract Paper Slides Recording

Guorui Xie, Qing Li (Pengcheng Laboratory), Zhenning Shi (Tsinghua Shenzhen), Gianni Antichi (Politecnico di Milano), et al.

VideoPDF

  • Why: Encrypted-traffic side channels (packet sizes, timing) keep working through TLS 1.3 and QUIC; existing defenses trade too much bandwidth or need unrealistic coordination. This makes in-network defense cheap enough to consider.
  • What: "Securitas," an obfuscation framework that cuts traffic-analysis attack accuracy by up to 95.89% while consuming 42.69x less bandwidth than prior defenses; real-Internet tests show ~0.15s added web page load.
  • How: A learning-guided mix of packet fragmentation and insertion, chosen adaptively rather than via fixed padding rules; implemented across four data planes — Tofino switch, FPGA, eBPF, and BMv2 — which is unusual deployability evidence.
  • Where applicable: Any operator that can insert obfuscation on-path (switch, NIC, or eBPF host). The multi-dataplane implementation means the defense isn't tied to one vendor's silicon; evaluation includes real-world Internet paths, not just lab topologies.
path: Defending against Traffic Analysis Attacks with Flexible In-Network Obfuscation

items.title: Express Lane to Efficiency and Reliability: Multi-Dimensional Control in Meta’s Express Backbone Network
items.text:
NSDI '26 — Network Papers Worth Your Time digest Core pick 30 April 2026

Abstract Paper Recording

Faisal Iqbal, Vitaly Neganov, et al. (Meta), Aditya Akella (UT Austin), Ying Zhang (Meta)

Video

  • Why: Meta's EBB is one of the largest WANs on earth, and this is the follow-up evolution under AI-era traffic pressure — useful as a reference point for how far you can push a mature multi-plane SDN WAN design before adding new control dimensions.
  • What: An operational account of evolving EBB's control plane along two new dimensions beyond per-plane TE: Unequal Cost Multi-Path (UCMP) for cross-plane load balancing and Fast Re-Route (FRR) for rapid local failure detection/recovery — meeting AI-era efficiency and resiliency demands without fundamental architectural change.
  • How: UCMP extends control across planes so traffic can be split unevenly across parallel planes for utilization; FRR adds per-device, time-slice control for sub-second failure handling. Both are described with design, implementation, and production results.
  • Where applicable: Meta-specific production WAN, but the multi-dimensional control framing (global-across-planes + local-per-device + existing per-plane TE) is a clean conceptual model for any large multi-plane backbone. Real deployment experience, not simulation.
path: Express Lane to Efficiency and Reliability: Multi-Dimensional Control in Meta’s Express Backbone Network

items.title: Eywa: Automating Model-Based Testing using LLMs
items.text:
NSDI '26 — Network Papers Worth Your Time digest Wildcard pick 30 April 2026

Abstract Paper Slides Recording

Rajdeep Mondal, Rathin Singha, Todd Millstein, George Varghese (UCLA), Ryan Beckett, Siva Kesava Reddy Kakarla (Microsoft Research)

VideoPDF

  • Why: Model-based testing finds real protocol bugs but has always been gated on humans hand-writing RFC-conformant models — months of expert effort. Eywa removes that gate and immediately found 16 previously-undiscovered bugs in DNS/BGP/SMTP implementations. This is the clearest signal yet of LLMs changing core network-engineering practice (spec → model → tests), with results that survived review.
  • What: A protocol-testing framework that uses LLMs to automatically build models of intended protocol behavior from RFCs, blogs, and natural-language sources; case studies across DNS, BGP, and SMTP found 33 unique bugs, 16 novel despite extensive prior manual testing.
  • How: LLM-synthesized models are combined with mitigation for hallucinations and the inability to monolithically generate complex models (decomposition, validation against spec behavior), then fed into standard model-based test generation to drive high-coverage conformance testing of real implementations.
  • Where applicable: Protocol conformance testing broadly — DNS, BGP, and SMTP demonstrated; the approach is protocol-agnostic in principle where written specs exist. Artifact evaluated (available/functional/reproduced). If you own protocol conformance or interop testing, this is the paper to read this cycle.
path: Eywa: Automating Model-Based Testing using LLMs

items.title: From Bits to Tokens: Knowledge-Driven Generative Communication of Multimodal Data
items.text:
NSDI '26 — Network Papers Worth Your Time digest Wildcard pick 30 April 2026

Abstract Paper Recording

Xingyu Chen (UC San Diego), Zihao Feng (USC), Wuqiong Zhao (UCSD), Jianrong Ding (CUHK), Ke Sun (Michigan), Xinyu Zhang (UCSD)

Video

  • Why: Not your domain — and that's the point. This is the most complete systems argument yet that "the network should transmit task-relevant knowledge, not bits," backed by a working prototype rather than a position paper. It signals where edge/IoT/real-time communication research is going as foundation models meet the network stack.
  • What: Knowledge-Driven Communication (KDC): a framework transmitting semantic tokens rather than raw bitstreams. A full prototype achieves high downstream task accuracy with a fraction of the transmitted data and degrades gracefully under wireless loss, beating state-of-the-art codecs and learned baselines.
  • How: A task-aware transmitter uses multimodal foundation models to abstract source data into tokenized embeddings and prioritize semantically critical content (zero-shot, no task-specific retraining); the receiver reconstructs task-relevant information from pretrained knowledge bases plus incrementally updated context.
  • Where applicable: Wireless, lossy, bandwidth-constrained multimodal settings today (sensors, video analytics at the edge). Long-horizon relevance rather than near-term deployability for DC networking — but the tokens-not-bits framing will increasingly show up in adaptive video and agentic-traffic contexts.
path: From Bits to Tokens: Knowledge-Driven Generative Communication of Multimodal Data

items.title: HybridMesh: A Hardware-software Hybrid Approach for Accelerating Service Mesh Ingress
items.text:
NSDI '26 — Network Papers Worth Your Time digest Core pick 30 April 2026

Abstract Paper Slides Recording

Myoungsung You (University of Seoul), Jaehyun Nam (Dankook University), Minjae Seo (ETRI), Taejune Park (Chonnam National University), Seungwon Shin (KAIST)

VideoPDF

  • Why: The ingress gateway is the spot where service-mesh overhead is worst, and the paper quantifies it: up to 4x throughput loss from CPU-intensive traffic analysis plus a convoluted forwarding path. A clean answer to the "sidecar or no sidecar" debate's ingress half.
  • What: A hybrid ingress gateway that puts traffic analysis and routing on a SmartNIC, augmented by a lightweight CPU-side proxy for features that don't fit the hardware. 4.4x HTTP throughput over existing gateways; 2.3x cost-effectiveness and 2.8x power-efficiency versus software-only or hardware-only designs.
  • How: Split the gateway data path — SmartNIC handles per-packet analysis and forwarding; the CPU proxy retains flexible traffic-management features — so neither the fully-software nor fully-hardware extreme is forced.
  • Where applicable: Any Istio/Envoy-style service mesh with hardware offload available; research prototype (testbed evaluation, not production), so treat numbers as best-case. The hybrid split principle is the transferable part.
path: HybridMesh: A Hardware-software Hybrid Approach for Accelerating Service Mesh Ingress

items.title: In Link We Trust: BFT at the Speed of CFT using Switches
items.text:
NSDI '26 — Network Papers Worth Your Time digest Core pick 30 April 2026

Abstract Paper Slides Recording

Lior Zeno, Naama Ben-David, Mark Silberstein (Technion)

VideoPDF

  • Why: Byzantine fault tolerance has always cost a large multiple of CFT performance; this paper erases that penalty using properties of the modern DC network itself. A genuinely novel trust model — trusting the network fabric, not cryptography — that reframes what "trusted network" means in a DC.
  • What: SwitchBFT, a datacenter BFT consensus protocol matching the performance and fault tolerance of the fastest CFT protocols — attaining the speed of NOPaxos (an in-switch CFT) while tolerating Byzantine replicas.
  • How: Exploits packet source authentication to eliminate cryptographic-signature overhead in the fault-free path, and switch programmability to enforce agreement decisions and verify safety, all within tight switch resource budgets. Handles packet loss and switch-crash faults as design cases.
  • Where applicable: Data centers with programmable (Tofino-class) switches and source-authenticated links — the "trusted network" assumption is the constraint. For the identity-minded: this is an alternative to per-message cryptographic attestation, complementing rather than competing with workload-identity approaches like SPIFFE for different threat models.
path: In Link We Trust: BFT at the Speed of CFT using Switches

items.title: Iris: Expressive Traffic Analysis for the Modern Internet
items.text:
NSDI '26 — Network Papers Worth Your Time digest Adjacent pick 30 April 2026

Abstract Paper Slides Recording

Thea Rossman, Diana Qing, Gerry Wan, Zakir Durumeric (Stanford University)

VideoPDF

  • Why: Security/ops teams keep bolting one-off sniffers and Zeek scripts onto high-speed links; Iris asks what a framework for high-performance traffic analysis should look like and delivers one that composes hundreds of tasks on one box.
  • What: A compiler-based framework that turns user-defined filters, stream transformations, and computations written in Rust into an optimized pipeline — executing hundreds of concurrent analysis tasks at 100 Gbps+ on a single commodity server.
  • How: The compiler eliminates redundant logic across concurrent analysis tasks to produce one unified runtime minimizing aggregate work; users get connection- and application-layer semantics exposed as Rust types rather than a constrained DSL.
  • Where applicable: General monitoring/security-analysis infrastructure, not tied to specific hardware. Artifact evaluated (available/functional/reproduced), so teams could realistically pilot it against existing Zeek/Graylog-style pipelines.
path: Iris: Expressive Traffic Analysis for the Modern Internet

items.title: KRAKENGUARD: Towards Fine-Grained eBPF Isolation
items.text:
NSDI '26 — Network Papers Worth Your Time digest Core pick 30 April 2026

Abstract Paper Slides Recording

Jainil Patel (IIT Roorkee), Lucas Graeff Buhl-Nielsen (Quantco), Adrien Ghosn (Microsoft), Marios Kogias (Imperial College London)

VideoPDF

  • Why: eBPF's security model is the dirty secret of the ecosystem — CAP_BPF is all-or-nothing, which is untenable as multi-tenant eBPF/XDP programs from different parties land on the same host. This is a serious attack on exactly that gap.
  • What: A trusted user-space manager enforcing fine-grained, policy-driven constraints on eBPF bytecode at load time: restricting helper usage, memory/map access, and return values. It demonstrably blocks misuse in real-world programs, detects existing CVEs, and enables an XDP-as-a-Service use case where tenants' XDP programs run directly on the host interface without mutual interference.
  • How: Symbolic execution of program paths at load time to check compliance with policy; cross-program interference detection to make co-location on the same hook safe.
  • Where applicable: General Linux/eBPF environments — any platform running third-party or tenant-supplied eBPF. Load-time analysis (not runtime) so the cost is per-load; the trusted-manager design makes assumptions about who controls the host. Highly relevant to Cilium-style deployments where programs multiply across hooks.

items.title: Learning to Tune Optical WANs: A Field Deployment of Noise Models in Optical Networks
items.text:
NSDI '26 — Network Papers Worth Your Time digest Core pick 30 April 2026

Abstract Paper Slides Recording

Bhaskar Kataria, Howard Hua (Cornell), Andrea D'Amico (NEC Labs), Bill Owens (NYSERNet), Rachee Singh (Cornell)

VideoPDF

  • Why: Rare example of physical-layer optimization (amplifier gain tuning) actually deployed in a live ISP backbone with measured results — the kind of ground-truth that usually stays inside vendor tooling.
  • What: A Gaussian Noise model of a New York state ISP's optical backbone covering amplifiers, fiber spans, ROADM s, and transceivers; hyperparameter search over this model identifies amplifier gain settings that improve end-to-end SNR. In a live field deployment, the tuned settings achieved a 2 dB SNR improvement on a single wavelength.
  • How: Model the full optical chain to predict end-to-end SNR accurately, then treat the model as an opaque box and run ML-style hyperparameter search over amplifier configurations under practical network constraints.
  • Where applicable: Small/mid ISP optical backbones (NYSERNet-scale); the 2 dB single-wavelength result is modest but real. Techniques are broadly reusable for any operator that wants model-driven optical tuning instead of vendor-blessed defaults; not a hyperscale DWDM result.
path: Learning to Tune Optical WANs: A Field Deployment of Noise Models in Optical Networks

items.title: Matryoshka: Realizing Hyperscale Data Center Network Design for the AI Era
items.text:
NSDI '26 — Network Papers Worth Your Time digest Core pick 30 April 2026

Abstract Paper Slides Recording

Yan Cai, Jialong Li (Max Planck Institute for Informatics), Kutalmis Akpinar, Tianxiang Li, Hany Morsy, Jason Wilson, Sunil Khaunte (Meta), Yiting Xia (MPI), Ying Zhang (Meta), et al.

VideoPDF

  • Why: The gap this paper names — between logical DCN designs and the concrete switch configurations that realize them — is exactly the "last mile" problem anyone running multi-generation fabric automation knows. It's also the clearest public account yet of how a hyperscaler's DCN tooling strains under AI-cluster growth.
  • What: Meta's production DCN design system, operational for 6+ years, that compiles high-level design intent (physical connectivity, addressing, routing policy) into working switch configurations. It has guided the design of nearly 900 DCs across 18 distinct types, including Meta's latest 100K-GPU training supercluster.
  • How: Intent-based, model-driven compilation: DCN designs are expressed as machine-readable models and systematically compiled down to per-switch configs, so design, addressing, and routing evolve together and heterogeneous cluster types are treated as first-class variants rather than snowflakes.
  • Where applicable: Meta-specific production experience, but the architecture pattern (model-driven intent-to-config compilation for rapidly evolving, heterogeneous AI fabrics) generalizes to any operator building multi-generation DCNs. The 6-year production track record and ~900-DC scale make the claims firmly substantiated.
path: Matryoshka: Realizing Hyperscale Data Center Network Design for the AI Era

items.title: Offloading Cloud Network Services at Production Scale with SONiC DASH SmartSwitch
items.text:
NSDI '26 — Network Papers Worth Your Time digest Core pick 30 April 2026

Abstract Paper Slides Recording

Shaofeng Wu (CUHK and Microsoft Research Asia), Zhixiong Niu (MSRA), Riff Jiang, et al. (Microsoft), Hong Xu (CUHK) — Community Award Winner

VideoPDF

  • Why: A decade of Azure offload lessons distilled into an open, community-governed architecture — and a concrete datapoint that the DPU pool is collapsing back into the T1 switch itself. Directly relevant to where cloud-network offload roadmaps are heading.
  • What: SONiC DASH SmartSwitch, deployed at Azure production scale for stateful network services: 1.53 Tbps throughput, 19.2M CPS, 256M concurrent connections, ~1.8x power efficiency and ~2.7x space efficiency over the prior generation.
  • How: Three design lessons encoded: an immutable, hardware-friendly DASH pipeline programming model (vs. overly flexible models that block acceleration); a "uni-box" SmartSwitch converging NPU and DPU resources inside a single T1 switch (vs. appliance-style DPU pools); and community-driven P4 behavior specifications (vs. vendor SDKs).
  • Where applicable: Built on the open SONiC/DASH ecosystem rather than a proprietary fork, so this is the rare Microsoft-scale result a non-hyperscaler can actually build on. Requires SmartSwitch-class hardware (integrated NPU+DPU in the T1).
path: Offloading Cloud Network Services at Production Scale with SONiC DASH SmartSwitch

items.title: OpenOptics: Enabling Open Research and Implementation of Optical Data Center Networks
items.text:
NSDI '26 — Network Papers Worth Your Time digest Core pick 30 April 2026

Abstract Paper Slides Recording

Yiming Lei, Federico De Marchi (Max Planck Institute for Informatics), Jialong Li (Shenzhen University of Advanced Technology), Raj Joshi (Harvard), Shu-Ting Wang (UC San Diego), Xiaoqi Chen (Purdue), Balakrishnan Chandrasekaran (VU Amsterdam), Yiting Xia (MPI)

VideoPDF

  • Why: Optical DCNs have been stuck as closed, hardware-tied ecosystems — every research prototype is bespoke. This is the first serious open framework, and it lowers the cost of experimenting with circuit-switched fabrics to "Python script" level. If you track OCS-based DC designs, this is the platform to watch.
  • What: An open research/implementation framework that decouples optical DCN software from optical hardware. It implements six optical DCN architectures and seven routing schemes on a real testbed (108 ToRs) and achieves a 2 µs minimum optical circuit duration on commodity devices — a record for circuit-switched DCN granularity.
  • How: Three pieces: a time-flow table abstraction as the common hardware/software interface, a unified workflow + Python API for defining optical DCNs, and a backend that re-architects queue management around time-flow tables so packets are staged for rapidly reconfiguring circuits.
  • Where applicable: Broadly applicable to researchers and builders experimenting with optical/express-loop fabrics; requires programmable (P4-class) switches plus commodity optical hardware. Artifacts were evaluated and reproduced (available/functional/reproduced badges), so it is genuinely usable, not just described.
path: OpenOptics: Enabling Open Research and Implementation of Optical Data Center Networks

items.title: OSCAR: O(1)-Step Convergence and Readily-deployable Congestion Control
items.text:
NSDI '26 — Network Papers Worth Your Time digest Core pick 30 April 2026

Abstract Paper Slides Recording

Zhaochen Zhang, Feiyang Xue, Rui Ning (Nanjing University), Keqiang He (SJTU), Gianni Antichi (Politecnico di Milano & QMUL), et al. — Awarded Outstanding Paper

VideoPDF

  • Why: The outstanding-paper pick of the congestion-control cluster. It removes the main barrier to fast-converging CC (precise INT headers that commodity high-speed hardware can't parse) while keeping constant-time convergence.
  • What: The first CC achieving O(1)-step convergence — reaching fair share in constant time regardless of network conditions — without specialized network features. In large-scale simulations with realistic workloads it beats precise-INT-based CCs by 12–48% on average FCT and 40–74% on tail FCT.
  • How: Insight that delay and delay gradient carry precision comparable to INT; then three techniques: accurate low-overhead delay-gradient estimation, eliminating overreaction in MIMD updates, and coordinating independent control loops toward a single target.
  • Where applicable: Commodity datacenter hardware (no INT support needed); testbed evaluation under real-world noise plus large-scale simulation. Pairs naturally with CCC above — the two papers collectively argue delay signals can replace INT for the next generation of deployable DC CC.
path: OSCAR: O(1)-Step Convergence and Readily-deployable Congestion Control

items.title: SPLIDT: Partitioned Decision Trees for Scalable Stateful Inference at Line Rate
items.text:
NSDI '26 — Network Papers Worth Your Time digest Wildcard pick 30 April 2026

Abstract Paper Recording

Murayyiam Parvez (Purdue), Annus Zulfiqar (Michigan), Roman Beltiukov (UCSB), Shir Landau Feibish (University of Haifa), Walter Willinger (Northwestern), Arpit Gupta (UCSB), Muhammad Shahbaz (Michigan)

Video

  • Why: In-network ML keeps stalling on the same wall — hardware limits force tiny fixed feature sets per flow. SPLIDT's partitioning trick is a real mechanism (not an ML benchmark bump) for getting past that wall, and it generalizes to any stateful line-rate inference problem on switches and SmartNICs.
  • What: A system for deploying decision trees in the data plane that supports up to 5x more stateful features than prior approaches (NetBeacon, Leo) at the same low time-to-detection, scaling to millions of flows with ≤0.05% recirculation overhead.
  • How: Two ideas: group DT subtrees into partitions where each subtree gets its own feature set (instead of computing all features upfront for the whole tree), and use in-band recirculation as a control channel to reuse register/match-key resources across partitions at line rate. A training + design-space-exploration framework jointly optimizes feature allocation, partitioning, and depth.
  • Where applicable: Programmable switches and SmartNICs doing traffic classification, security monitoring, or in-network decisions. Artifact evaluated (available/functional/reproduced), so the partitioning approach is reproducible, not vendor-locked.
path: SPLIDT: Partitioned Decision Trees for Scalable Stateful Inference at Line Rate

items.title: Starfish: A Topology-Routing Co-Design for Small-Scale Data Centers
items.text:
NSDI '26 — Network Papers Worth Your Time digest Core pick 30 April 2026

Abstract Paper Slides Recording

Anchengcheng Zhou (Princeton), Vipul Harsh (Conviva), Sangeetha Abdu Jyothi (UC Irvine), Maria Apostolaki (Princeton), Brighten Godfrey (UIUC)

VideoPDF

  • Why: Almost all DC topology research targets hyperscalers, yet most real data centers run hundreds to a few thousand servers on leaf-spine with painful cost/oversubscription tradeoffs. This is a rare, rigorous design for that population — directly useful if your fleet is enterprise/colo-scale rather than 100K-GPU.
  • What: A topology-routing co-design (DRing topology + adaptive routing) that supports 56% more traffic than an equal-cost leaf-spine on real traces with the same equipment. The routing scheme also generalizes to expander topologies, where it yields 52% more traffic than leaf-spine — fixing expander designs' biggest deployment hurdle (no practical routing).
  • How: DRing spreads servers across all switches to raise per-server egress capacity and expose diverse near-shortest paths; routing exploits DRing's structural properties and adapts to traffic using standard hardware and protocols — no exotic switching required.
  • Where applicable: Small-to-mid data centers (hundreds–thousands of servers); uses standard equipment and protocols, making it unusually deployable for a topology paper. Artifact evaluated (available/functional/reproduced).
path: Starfish: A Topology-Routing Co-Design for Small-Scale Data Centers

items.title: SyncWise: Error-Aware Time Synchronization for Reconfigurable Data Center Networks
items.text:
NSDI '26 — Network Papers Worth Your Time digest Core pick 30 April 2026

Abstract Paper Slides Recording

Yiming Lei (MPI for Informatics), Jialong Li (Shenzhen University of Advanced Technology), Zhengqing Liu (Imperial College London), Raj Joshi (Harvard), Yiting Xia (MPI)

VideoPDF

  • Why: As reconfigurable DCNs (OCS-based) shrink circuit durations to microseconds/sub-microseconds, accurate time sync becomes the correctness backbone of the whole fabric — and this paper shows the problem was previously unformalized. A foundational gap-fill for the reconfigurable-fabric subfield.
  • What: The first time-synchronization protocol designed specifically for reconfigurable DCNs. It formalizes the RDCN sync problem, builds an RDCN-specific error model, and achieves provably optimal sync — sub-10 ns maximum sync error, well beyond what the most accurate traditional-DC protocols achieve.
  • How: Uses the RDCN error model (sources of error specific to dynamic optical circuits) to guide "wise" selection of sync parents — choosing the peers whose sync exchanges will be least corrupted by circuit reconfiguration dynamics.
  • Where applicable: Specific to OCS-based reconfigurable DCNs; prototyped on an Intel Tofino2 + OCS testbed with large-scale simulations backing the testbed numbers. Not relevant to static packet fabrics, but core reading for anyone evaluating express-loop/circuit-switched designs.
path: SyncWise: Error-Aware Time Synchronization for Reconfigurable Data Center Networks

items.title: ZooRoute: Enhancing Cloud-Scale Network Reliability via Candidate Path Provisioning and Overlay Proactive Rerouting
items.text:
NSDI '26 — Network Papers Worth Your Time digest Core pick 30 April 2026

Abstract Paper Slides Recording

Xiaoqing Sun (Alibaba Cloud), Xing Li (Zhejiang University and Alibaba Cloud), Xionglie Wei, et al. (Alibaba Cloud), Yang Xu (Fudan), Shunmin Zhu (Alibaba Cloud), et al.

VideoPDF

  • Why: Fast, deterministic failure recovery offered by the cloud provider instead of pushing HA plumbing onto tenants — an explicit product decision worth understanding. The mechanism is a clever use of an oft-ignored header field.
  • What: A tenant-transparent, underlay-agnostic failure-recovery service, deployed 26 months in Alibaba Cloud: cumulative outage time reduced 93.19%, and 98.21% of failures masked from tenant awareness.
  • How: Reroutes traffic by varying the outer source port on VXLAN encapsulation — different source ports hash to different underlay paths. Tunnel endpoints proactively probe a set of healthy source-port candidates per destination IP, guaranteeing one-shot deterministic reroute onto a known-good path. Engineering challenges addressed: hypervisor probing overhead, Tofino-gateway memory limits, and stateful middlebox disruption.
  • Where applicable: Planet-scale cloud overlays (Alibaba production, Tofino gateways). The source-port-as-path-selector trick is broadly reusable in any ECMP-overlay network; the full proactive-probing service assumes provider control of both tunnel endpoints.
path: ZooRoute: Enhancing Cloud-Scale Network Reliability via Candidate Path Provisioning and Overlay Proactive Rerouting

items.title: 6–12x Route Programming Acceleration in SONiC: A Collaborative Profiling and Optimization Journey
items.text:
OCP Global Summit 2026 — for a DC/Cloud-Native Networking & Identity PM digest Core pick 15 October 2026

Abstract Materials

Deepak Singhal (Microsoft), Amol Rawal (Nokia)

  • Why: Contributor-led SONiC internals with hard numbers (2K–4K routes/sec baseline → 6–12x), a reproducible benchmarking methodology, and upstreamed code — the archetype of a talk that reveals where an open-source project is actually heading.
  • What: A joint Microsoft–Nokia effort that built a Snappi-based benchmarking framework, profiled existing optimization proposals and their combinations across multiple hardware platforms, then contributed fresh optimizations: replacing Redis-based IPC with direct ZMQ communication, offloading synchronous recording from the hot path, and integrating tcmalloc into FRR daemons (from abstract only).
  • How: Measurement-first — the framework identifies which optimizations actually matter and how they interact, rather than merging proposals blindly; results were driven through SONiC Routing Working Group consensus with published HLDs across multiple sonic-net repositories.
  • Where applicable: SONiC on any supported platform (multi-platform profiling included); most relevant to fabrics pushing 1M+ route scale, e.g. large AI clusters with heavy ECMP.
path: 6–12x Route Programming Acceleration in SONiC: A Collaborative Profiling and Optimization Journey

items.title: Achieving AI Cluster Reliability at Scale: Lessons in Reducing Workload Interruptions
items.text:
OCP Global Summit 2026 — for a DC/Cloud-Native Networking & Identity PM digest Adjacent pick 15 October 2026

Abstract

Bob Wang (Meta), Ramachandra Reddy Kallam (Meta)

  • Why: Not a networking talk per se, but network events are one of the correlated signals — and the root-cause methodology (attributing every interruption across host, firmware, network, and workload telemetry) is reusable by anyone operating large fabrics.
  • What: A framework for diagnosing AI workload interruptions at 32K→100K+ GPU scale, built on root-cause classification via Perfetto time trees correlating host telemetry, firmware logs, network events, and workload signals; key contributors include NVLink failures, HBM fragmentation, thermal failures, silent data corruption (SDC), and firmware bugs (from abstract only).
  • How: Data-driven root-cause analysis feeds back into next-gen hardware requirements, including vendor decisions on error reporting, fault isolation, and resilience; the diagnostic framework is being offered to the broader OCP community.
  • Where applicable: Meta GBx00 clusters — org-specific failure data, but the methodology (correlated time-tree attribution) and the hardware-requirements feedback loop generalize well.
path: Achieving AI Cluster Reliability at Scale: Lessons in Reducing Workload Interruptions

items.title: An Introduction to Attesting Hitlessly Updatable Systems
items.text:
OCP Global Summit 2026 — for a DC/Cloud-Native Networking & Identity PM digest Core pick 15 October 2026

Abstract

Matt King (NVIDIA)

  • Why: A sharp conceptual contribution to the PM's identity/attestation interest: hitless firmware updates break the standard attestation model, because the platform can change between evidence production and relying-party use.
  • What: An analysis of what attestation must become for platforms that update firmware while tenant workloads run: conventional measurements of the TCB that has run are insufficient; the relying party must also assess whether future updates could compromise the properties it depends on (from abstract only).
  • How: Combine three evidence classes — current TCB measurements, the history of prior updates, and the policy governing future updates — so a relying party can make an informed decision about a system that changes while it runs.
  • Where applicable: General technique for any attested platform doing hitless updates (switches, NICs, BMCs, accelerators); an introductory/conceptual talk, but it defines the problem shape the DMTF/OCP attestation work will have to address. Pairs with the SPDM provisioning talk below.
path: An Introduction to Attesting Hitlessly Updatable Systems

items.title: Beyond Traditional BGP: Decoupling Route Distribution for Large-Scale AI Clusters at Alibaba
items.text:
OCP Global Summit 2026 — for a DC/Cloud-Native Networking & Identity PM digest Core pick 15 October 2026

Abstract

Eddie Ruan (Alibaba), Dennis Cai (Alibaba)

  • Why: Directly in the PM's BGP/datapath-internals interest: a concrete alternative to Microsoft's Fairwater host-SRv6 approach for AI-cluster routing scale, from a provider that can't mandate host-side changes — a real architectural debate with numbers attached.
  • What: An architectural decoupling of service route distribution from infrastructure route distribution: regular BGP continues to carry infrastructure routes within spine/leaf, while service routes are redistributed among leaf switches by multiple route reflectors, recursively resolved over the loopback of the anchoring leaf switch (from abstract only).
  • How: A "Group RR" concept coordinates multiple RRs to provide Graceful Restart capability and high availability for critical service prefixes, so service routes survive RR cluster outages; positioned explicitly against Fairwater's <1,000-route / 256-way-ECMP host-SRv6 model from OCP 2025.
  • Where applicable: Alibaba-specific architecture for multi-tenant clouds that cannot impose host changes — broadly applicable to any provider facing the same constraint; BGP-only, no host or silicon requirements.
path: Beyond Traditional BGP: Decoupling Route Distribution for Large-Scale AI Clusters at Alibaba

items.title: Clock-Aligned Telemetry for AI Clusters: From BMC to GPU to Fleet
items.text:
OCP Global Summit 2026 — for a DC/Cloud-Native Networking & Identity PM digest Wildcard pick 15 October 2026

Abstract Materials

Ahmad Byagowi (TBD), Lukas Landgraf (turbalance)

  • Why: The observability gap this addresses — many dashboards, no common evidence model — sits exactly at the junction of the PM's telemetry and Kubernetes/eBPF interests, and clock alignment as the basis for cross-machine trust is an idea worth stealing.
  • What: A lab-built reference architecture for clock-aligned AI telemetry: a source-bundle contract, live agents, a conservative benchmark ladder, a Redfish/BMC lane, and a lakehouse path that preserves provenance and never synthesizes unsupported metrics; links DCGM/NVML, host counters, Prometheus, Kubernetes, Redfish, eBPF/OTel evidence, and PTP/NTP clock state (from abstract only).
  • How: Per-datacenter ingestion without global shared state feeds one Iceberg layer over cold and fresh stores; a six-level benchmark ladder (metric to global baseline), auto-discovery, credential-gated agents, 1s freshness, and capability labels — PTP/NTP state as a first-class signal changes what cross-machine comparison can be trusted.
  • Where applicable: Prototyped on a heterogeneous lab fleet (not hyperscale production yet), with an open-source repo and a proposed OCP collaboration path — early-stage, which is exactly why it's a wildcard rather than core.
path: Clock-Aligned Telemetry for AI Clusters: From BMC to GPU to Fleet

items.title: Clustermapper: Deterministic path diagnosis for AI backend networks using SRv6
items.text:
OCP Global Summit 2026 — for a DC/Cloud-Native Networking & Identity PM digest Core pick 15 October 2026

Abstract Paper Materials

Ryder Lewis (OpenAI), Guohan Lu (OpenAI)

  • Why: Turns path diagnosis from statistical inference into ground truth — a genuinely clever use of SRv6 source routing, and the operational companion to the MRC spec from the same OpenAI team.
  • What: A path-diagnosis system for MRC/SRv6 AI backend networks: a lightweight agent on every node sends SRv6 source-routed self-probes through T0/T1 switch paths, producing a deterministic link-health map used to localize faults (NIC-T0 links, T0-T1 links, switch forwarding) and turn urgent link-failure incidents into scheduled maintenance (from abstract only; the linked arXiv paper — titled "Resilient AI Supercomputer Networking using MRC and SRv6", 18 pages, 22 figures — was not retrievable beyond its landing page).
  • How: SRv6 deterministic source routing pins each probe to an exact path, eliminating ECMP ambiguity and routing-convergence noise so failures localize to specific links even between training jobs; output feeds path-avoidance policy for MRC.
  • Where applicable: Requires SRv6 (and works best with MRC) in the backend network — OpenAI production, but the technique is general to any SRv6 fabric and notably valuable for small network teams operating huge clusters.
path: Clustermapper: Deterministic path diagnosis for AI backend networks using SRv6

items.title: Co-Designing AI Fabrics: Inside Google's Virgo Network and the Campus-as-a-Computer
items.text:
OCP Global Summit 2026 — for a DC/Cloud-Native Networking & Identity PM digest Core pick 15 October 2026

Abstract

Sunil Ahluwalia (Google), JK Lee (Google)

  • Why: One of the few public looks inside Google's AI fabric — the architectural shift from "data center as a set of servers" to campus-scale supercomputer is the defining physical-networking problem of this cycle, and Google is unusually specific here about the transport and telemetry mechanisms.
  • What: Virgo, a megascale multi-plane AI datacenter fabric running open-source SONiC, built for synchronized-burst ML traffic with a stated value proposition of predictable low latency and maximized "goodput" (from abstract only).
  • How: Open-source RDMA transport (Falcon), Congestion Signaling (CSIG), and High-Speed Telemetry (HST), on a multi-plane architecture over open standards and merchant hardware ecosystems.
  • Where applicable: Google-specific production design, but the constituent technologies (CSIG, HST, Falcon) are being pushed into SONiC/open ecosystems — see the Google SONiC CSIG/HST talk below, which is the deployable version of this story.
path: Co-Designing AI Fabrics: Inside Google's Virgo Network and the Campus-as-a-Computer

items.title: Enabling AI Networking @ Scale with Multi-path Reliable Connections (MRC)
items.text:
OCP Global Summit 2026 — for a DC/Cloud-Native Networking & Identity PM digest Core pick 15 October 2026

Abstract Materials

Guohan Lu (OpenAI), Eric Spada (Broadcom Inc.)

  • Why: MRC is now a ratified OCP specification co-authored by OpenAI and Broadcom — a concrete, open alternative for AI-fabric transport that a PM in this space will need to track against MetaRoCE and Falcon.
  • What: MRC combines multipath transport, adaptive load balancing, reliable delivery, and path-aware congestion management to keep utilization high and tail latency low in fabrics of hundreds of thousands of XPUs (from abstract only).
  • How: Multipath reliable connections at the transport layer with awareness of per-path congestion state; the OCP MRC 1.0 document is the spec itself, which the session walks through.
  • Where applicable: Designed for open Ethernet-based AI infrastructure broadly, not one operator's fabric; requires switch/NIC support for the MRC semantics (Broadcom involvement signals merchant-silicon intent).
path: Enabling AI Networking @ Scale with Multi-path Reliable Connections (MRC)

items.title: ESUN: Open Ethernet for the Scale-Up Era
items.text:
OCP Global Summit 2026 — for a DC/Cloud-Native Networking & Identity PM digest Core pick 15 October 2026

Pratik Marolia (Microsoft), Manoj Wadekar (Meta)

  • Why: Scale-up (in-rack/in-pod XPU interconnect) was the last proprietary holdout — NVLink territory. ESUN 1.0, ratified by OCP in March 2026 with 170+ contributors from 20+ organizations including NVIDIA itself, is the strongest signal yet that open Ethernet is expanding from scale-out into scale-up.
  • What: An operator-requirements specification for Ethernet-based scale-up networks: minimizing header/framing overhead designed for general internet traffic, and breaking single-vendor interconnect lock-in (from abstract only).
  • How: Cross-industry coalition (Meta, Microsoft, AMD, Arista, Broadcom, Cisco, Marvell, NVIDIA, OpenAI, Oracle) producing an OCP spec in months; the talk covers the what and the roadmap for future versions.
  • Where applicable: Industry-wide; it is a requirements/spec document, so its impact depends on silicon (Tomahawk-class and similar) implementing it — pair with the SUE-T and Tahan talks for the transport and hardware instantiations.
path: ESUN: Open Ethernet for the Scale-Up Era

items.title: From Fleet to Firmware: Bringing AI-Native Security to Open Hardware with Project Equilibrium presented by Google
items.text:
OCP Global Summit 2026 — for a DC/Cloud-Native Networking & Identity PM digest Wildcard pick 15 October 2026

Abstract

Andres Lagar-Cavilla (Google)

  • Why: AI turned on the systems that run AI — a genuinely novel direction: autonomous, continuous security for open-source firmware that outpaces what periodic audits and static scanning can do as frontier models accelerate vulnerability discovery.
  • What: Google's Project Equilibrium, an AI-native security architecture pairing live, repo-colocated threat models with autonomous pre-submit scanning and automated patching — catching deep bugs and cutting false positives before merge — plus a path to extend the workflow from fleets to bare-metal firmware via open security cookbooks (from abstract only).
  • How: Threat models live next to the code they describe; autonomous pre-submit analysis and patching run against the millions of lines of low-level code in OpenBMC, Caliptra, CXL, and NVMe.
  • Where applicable: Open-hardware ecosystem broadly (cookbooks are explicitly meant as a shared baseline); currently a Google internal capability being externalized, so treat maturity accordingly — but for anyone whose supply chain includes open firmware, this is where the field is heading.
path: From Fleet to Firmware: Bringing AI-Native Security to Open Hardware with Project Equilibrium presented by Google

items.title: Integrated Optics at Scale for AI Infrastructure: From 51.2T CPO Validation to Meta's 102.4T Integrated Optics Switch
items.text:
OCP Global Summit 2026 — for a DC/Cloud-Native Networking & Identity PM digest Core pick 15 October 2026

Abstract

Granthana Rangaswamy (Meta), Siamak Amiralizadeh (Meta), Xu Wang (Meta Platforms, Inc.)

  • Why: The strongest quantified case at this conference for integrated optics over pluggables — real power and reach numbers from a platform moving from 51.2T validation into a 102.4T product, at the exact 200G/lane inflection point where pluggables struggle.
  • What: A 1.5OU, 100% liquid-cooled, fanless blade with 64 optical ports via 16 four-port MMC interfaces and 16 ELSFP external-laser modules, delivering ~60% optics power reduction, ~30% system power reduction, and 500m reach versus pluggables (from abstract only).
  • How: Optical engines placed on (CPO) or near (NPO) the ASIC substrate, eliminating pluggables; decoupling the laser lifecycle from the ASIC via ELSFP external lasers; fanless liquid cooling to reduce fiber contamination risk.
  • Where applicable: Meta platform, but the power/reach trade-offs and the laser-decoupling architecture are broadly applicable to any operator weighing CPO/NPO at 102.4T; built on prior-generation 51.2T validation, so the numbers have production lineage.
path: Integrated Optics at Scale for AI Infrastructure: From 51.2T CPO Validation to Meta's 102.4T Integrated Optics Switch

items.title: Large-Scale Deployment of 800Gb/s Active Electrical Cables (AEC) in Meta Data Centers for AI Applications
items.text:
OCP Global Summit 2026 — for a DC/Cloud-Native Networking & Identity PM digest Core pick 15 October 2026

Abstract

Jingyu Yu (Meta), Abhijit Chakravarty (Meta)

  • Why: Cabling is a first-order cost/power lever in AI clusters and rarely gets a full methodology talk; this covers multi-vendor qualification to volume production, which is the hard part.
  • What: Meta's qualification, validation, and deployment methodology for 800 Gb/s AECs (112 Gb/s/lane) in large-scale GPU clusters, spanning component characterization, environmental reliability, multi-vendor interoperability, system-level traffic validation, and manufacturing readiness across multiple suppliers and production sites (from abstract only).
  • How: Lab plus in-cluster validation of link stability, packet integrity, latency, and firmware compatibility; the program resolved signal-integrity, manufacturing-consistency, and firmware-interoperability issues to reach multi-sourced volume adoption.
  • Where applicable: Meta AI clusters but the qualification framework is general; AECs apply to short-reach in-cluster interconnect (rack-to-rack distances), as a power- and cost-efficient alternative to optics and passive DAC at 800G.
path: Large-Scale Deployment of 800Gb/s Active Electrical Cables (AEC) in Meta Data Centers for AI Applications

items.title: Lessons learned from GW-scale AI deployments
items.text:
OCP Global Summit 2026 — for a DC/Cloud-Native Networking & Identity PM digest Core pick 15 October 2026

Abstract

Mark Filer (Oracle)

  • Why: An end-user case study with production statistics on one of the world's largest 800G 2xDR4 LPO deployments — exactly the real-numbers, real-failure-mode content this PM values over vendor demos.
  • What: Hard-won operational learnings from OCI's deployments supporting top AI customers at 10,000+ GPU scale, where single link flaps stall multi-million-dollar training jobs; includes production statistics on the LPO deployment and how the experience translates to 1.6T (from abstract only).
  • How: Operational discipline at "laws of large numbers" scale — treating per-link instability as the primary availability adversary, with forward-looking paths to uptime/resilience in massive distributed systems.
  • Where applicable: OCI-specific production data, but the failure-mode taxonomy and the 800G→1.6T extrapolation are relevant to any operator of GPU backbones; pairs naturally with the LPO talk above as the customer-side view.
path: Lessons learned from GW-scale AI deployments

items.title: Meta 102.4T Ethernet Switch
items.text:
OCP Global Summit 2026 — for a DC/Cloud-Native Networking & Identity PM digest Core pick 15 October 2026

Abstract

Rongchun Zhou (Meta), Reza Niazmand (Meta)

  • Why: The switch platform that much of Meta's next-gen AI fabric story runs on — a concrete OCP hardware contribution on the newest merchant silicon, directly in the PM's physical switching interest.
  • What: IceCube, a 102.4T non-blocking Ethernet switch on the Broadcom TH6C ASIC running FBOSS: 2OU form factor, 64× OSFP-RHS user ports, liquid-cooled; IecPack is an ORv3-HPRv1 rack integrating eight IceCube blades plus servicing equipment for versatile switch roles (from abstract only).
  • How: Standard OCP open-hardware contribution model — merchant silicon + open NOS + open rack; engineering focus is reliability, power efficiency, and NPI velocity.
  • Where applicable: Meta-specific platform but fully OCP-documented; requires TH6C-class silicon and liquid-cooled racks. Pair with the integrated-optics talk for where this platform line is heading optically.

items.title: MetaRoCE: Rethinking RDMA for the AI presented by Meta
items.text:
OCP Global Summit 2026 — for a DC/Cloud-Native Networking & Identity PM digest Core pick 15 October 2026

Abstract

Arvind Srinivasan (Meta), Sandeep Nagaraja (Meta), Balakrishnan Raman (AMD)

  • Why: A clean-sheet replacement for RoCEv2 from one of the largest GPU-fleet operators, now being opened as a spec — directly in the PM's lossless-fabrics/RDMA core interest and a candidate competitor/complement to MRC (below).
  • What: MetaRoCE, a multipath, out-of-order, receiver-driven RDMA transport that treats Ethernet as lossy by design rather than patching lossless fabrics with more tuning; Meta is publishing the specification for industry adoption (from abstract only).
  • How: All transport intelligence is pushed into the NIC; multipath and receiver-driven delivery replace PFC-style losslessness as the reliability model.
  • Why it matters for triage: Paired with MRC and SUE-T, this is the third open transport spec from a hyperscaler this cycle — the field's verdict that decade-old RoCEv2 is done at 10k+ GPU scale.
  • Where applicable: Meta production (tens of thousands of GPUs); AMD co-presenting suggests NIC-side implementation requirements — adoption depends on NIC vendor support, so watch the ecosystem response.
path: MetaRoCE: Rethinking RDMA for the AI presented by Meta

items.title: Mitigating AI Training Power Oscillations: Utility Requirements and In-Rack Power Filtering
items.text:
OCP Global Summit 2026 — for a DC/Cloud-Native Networking & Identity PM digest Wildcard pick 15 October 2026

Abstract

Bo Wen (Microsoft), Xianyong Feng (Microsoft)

  • Why: A surprising cross-domain result: synchronized GPU compute/communication phase transitions at cluster scale overlap with sensitive utility-grid frequency bands, creating forced-oscillation and impedance-stability risks — power design is becoming a networking-adjacent constraint on cluster architecture.
  • What: A framework connecting grid-side power-transient requirements (power-change and oscillation limits, ramp-rate expectations, synchronized monitoring from utility interconnect down to rack level) with practical in-rack mitigation, including PSU + CBU filtering concepts, frequency-sweep test methods, attenuation analysis, and verification results (from abstract only).
  • How: Rack-level buffering (PSU plus CBU) measurably reduces upstream power ripple; measurement and modeling align AI rack power design with utility requirements.
  • Where applicable: Relevant to any operator at multi-hundred-MW AI scale interacting with utilities; Microsoft-specific verification data, but the utility constraints are universal for large campuses.
path: Mitigating AI Training Power Oscillations: Utility Requirements and In-Rack Power Filtering

items.title: OCP Device Identity Provisioning over SPDM
items.text:
OCP Global Summit 2026 — for a DC/Cloud-Native Networking & Identity PM digest Core pick 15 October 2026

Abstract

Fabrizio Damato (AMD), Xiaoyu Ruan (Intel)

  • Why: Directly in the PM's workload-identity core interest at the hardware layer: operator/tenant-owned PKI enrollment for fleet devices, standardized over SPDM instead of per-vendor proprietary flows.
  • What: The OCP Device Identity Provisioning specification: an Attested CSR that cryptographically binds a newly generated device keypair to the device's attested identity and measured state, plus a keypair-discovery flow so enrollment authorities can enumerate the identity keys a device exposes (from abstract only).
  • How: Flows currently ride on SPDM vendor-defined messages for early deployment, while OCP drives the capability into DMTF SPDM (anticipated in SPDM 1.5); open-source RoTs such as Caliptra are expected to adopt it.
  • Where applicable: Broadly applicable — this is a standardization talk, not an operator case study; the constraint is that full benefit requires RoT/BIOS support (Caliptra adoption is the open-source path) and SPDM-capable devices.
path: OCP Device Identity Provisioning over SPDM

items.title: Open, Trusted, and Secure SONiC at Scale presented by Cisco
items.text:
OCP Global Summit 2026 — for a DC/Cloud-Native Networking & Identity PM digest Core pick 15 October 2026

Abstract

Will Eatherton (Cisco), Dina Papagiannaki (Microsoft)

  • Why: SONiC security posture is becoming an adoption gate as it moves into enterprise and AI infrastructure, and this lays out an end-to-end framework — FIPS, attestation, and eBPF-based live patching — that touches the PM's security and eBPF interests directly.
  • What: An end-to-end SONiC security framework spanning supply-chain integrity, verified software authenticity, secure build pipelines, FIPS-ready hardware with a platform root of trust, confidential networking (protecting data and network state), and Day-2 monitoring with integrated CVE intelligence (from abstract only).
  • How: eBPF-based runtime protections enable rapid mitigation and live patching without reboots — protect immediately, apply permanent patches in a planned window, revalidate; hardware/firmware/software integrity validated across the system lifecycle.
  • Where applicable: General SONiC security architecture rather than a single deployment; note this is a vendor-led expo-hall session, so expect framework-level content without deployment metrics — the eBPF live-patch workflow is the concrete piece to take away.
path: Open, Trusted, and Secure SONiC at Scale presented by Cisco

items.title: Operating Linear Pluggable Optics at Hyperscale: From Link Management to Production Reliability
items.text:
OCP Global Summit 2026 — for a DC/Cloud-Native Networking & Identity PM digest Core pick 15 October 2026

Abstract

Amin Yekani (Meta), Qing Wang (Meta)

  • Why: LPO removes the DSP and shifts equalization to the host ASIC — an architecture any PM evaluating power-vs-reliability in optical links must judge. This is one of the few talks with fleet-scale production data rather than lab claims.
  • What: Meta's operational experience with LPO across link management, link-health monitoring, and production results: a large-scale live-traffic deployment with tens of millions of accumulated link-hours, including failure-rate, signal-quality, power, and thermal measurements (from abstract only).
  • How: Host- and module-side signal conditioning maintained fleet-wide (since no DSP auto-adapts), plus multi-layer monitoring covering signal quality, error metrics, and early detection of lane-level degradation.
  • Where applicable: Explicitly framed as applicable to any DSP-free optical architecture; the operational framework (not just the modules) is the transferable artifact. Constrained by host-ASIC equalization capability — not a drop-in for any switch.
path: Operating Linear Pluggable Optics at Hyperscale: From Link Management to Production Reliability

items.title: Scale-across Networking: Panel discussion on routing and transport equipment implications
items.text:
OCP Global Summit 2026 — for a DC/Cloud-Native Networking & Identity PM digest Core pick 15 October 2026

Abstract Materials

Jeff Rahn (Meta), Yawei Yin (Microsoft), Xiguang - Henry Wu (Broadcom), Tad Hofmeister (Google)

  • Why: The PM's DC/WAN interconnect territory: with power and space capping single-site clusters, operators are extending AI fabrics across metro/regional distances to reach 0.5M–1M XPUs — a problem that diverges sharply from conventional cloud DCI.
  • What: A multi-operator panel (Meta, Microsoft, Google, Broadcom, with Arista referenced) on the scale-across use case: real-world rollout experience and the architectures being built for clusters beyond 100k XPUs, where propagation delay, higher oversubscription, and massive synchronized bursts change the equipment requirements (from abstract only).
  • How: Panel focuses on concrete technology implications: coherent pluggables (ZR/ZR+) to overcome fiber scarcity, deep packet buffering to absorb regional latency, wire-rate security, and advanced congestion control.
  • Where applicable: Multi-operator (not single-vendor) and forward-looking — panel format means less depth per topic, but it is the best cross-industry read on where AI DCI equipment requirements are heading. Pair with the Alibaba AI DCI/WAN TE talk for the deployment-level counterpart.
path: Scale-across Networking: Panel discussion on routing and transport equipment implications

items.title: Software-Assisted Congestion Signaling and Sub-Millisecond Telemetry in SONiC
items.text:
OCP Global Summit 2026 — for a DC/Cloud-Native Networking & Identity PM digest Core pick 15 October 2026

Abstract

Arpitha Raghunandan (Google), Shane Gao (Google)

  • Why: The deployable half of the Virgo story: how Google gets microsecond-scale telemetry and per-packet congestion signaling into SONiC — and, crucially, onto older ASICs that don't support it in hardware.
  • What: A SONiC architecture proven at Google scale with two components: HST (High-Speed Switch Telemetry) — lightweight digests and high-resolution traces enabling microsecond-scale per-device profiling — and CSIG (Software-Assisted Congestion Signaling), which updates packet signals with real-time switch state to give end hosts high-frequency per-packet telemetry (from abstract only).
  • How: Sub-millisecond runtime write-backs of per-port metrics via the HST framework, and reuse of unused match-action table resources in the ASIC pipeline to implement custom signal types the hardware doesn't natively support — enabling CSIG on existing networks with older silicon.
  • Where applicable: Google-proven but designed for upstream SONiC; the "software-assisted on older ASICs" angle makes this broadly applicable to brownfield fabrics, not just new AI builds.
path: Software-Assisted Congestion Signaling and Sub-Millisecond Telemetry in SONiC

items.title: Srv6 powered backbone networks
items.text:
OCP Global Summit 2026 — for a DC/Cloud-Native Networking & Identity PM digest Core pick 15 October 2026

Abstract

Jasmeet Bagga (Facebook), Andrey Golovanov (Meta)

  • Why: Meta WAN/backbone architecture is squarely in the PM's DC/WAN-interconnect core interest, and this is an unusually internals-heavy talk: SRv6 for traffic engineering, shallow-buffer switches for long-haul, and real SAI/FBOSS experience.
  • What: RBB (Regional Backbone), a newly designed inter-region connectivity network running in parallel to Meta's express backbone (EBB), motivated by the cost of replicating latency-sensitive core services into every region as region count grows (from abstract only).
  • How: Traffic-engineered SRv6 over shallow-buffer switches for long-haul backbone links — a counterintuitive choice the talk explains — with SRv6 SAI support and deployment experience on FBOSS OCP switches.
  • Where applicable: Meta-specific WAN, but the design pattern (parallel TE'd backbone with SRv6, shallow buffers for long-haul) and the SAI/SRv6 standardization feedback are broadly relevant to multi-region operators.

items.title: SUE-T - An Ethernet transport for Scale-Up Networking
items.text:
OCP Global Summit 2026 — for a DC/Cloud-Native Networking & Identity PM digest Core pick 15 October 2026

Abstract

Tom Emmons (Arista Networks), Karen Schramm (Broadcom)

  • Why: ESUN defines the network requirements; SUE-T defines what actually rides on it — the semantics of moving memory transactions between XPUs over Ethernet. This is the layer where scale-up Ethernet becomes a real RDMA-class competitor.
  • What: The Scale-up Ethernet Transport framework: low-latency, high-bandwidth connectivity where a SUE-T instance moves memory transactions between XPUs across rack/multi-rack clusters (from abstract only).
  • How: An Ethernet-based transport protocol suitable for deployment over ESUN-defined networks; the session walks the specification and how it meets scale-up's latency and bandwidth demands for next-gen XPU designs.
  • Where applicable: General technique (open spec, not operator-specific), but requires XPU and switch support for the transport; relevant to anyone evaluating open alternatives to proprietary scale-up fabrics.
path: SUE-T - An Ethernet transport for Scale-Up Networking

items.title: Tahan: An Open, Ethernet-Based Scale-Up Switch for Meta's MTIA Accelerators
items.text:
OCP Global Summit 2026 — for a DC/Cloud-Native Networking & Identity PM digest Core pick 15 October 2026

Abstract

Ashutosh Grewal (Meta), Vimal Vasudevan (Meta Platforms inc.)

  • Why: The best "show me the hardware" talk on scale-up Ethernet: a first-generation open scale-up switch with real numbers, and a rare case of one NOS (FBOSS) and one transport (RoCE) spanning both scale-out and scale-up.
  • What: Tahan, Meta's first scale-up switch for MTIA 300 accelerators: 6.4 Tbps per accelerator over 8× 800GbE passive copper links, 16 accelerators per liquid-cooled rack interconnected via 4 switches in a non-blocking topology, on merchant 25T/51.2 Tbps silicon running FBOSS (from abstract only).
  • How: Reuses the scale-out network's lossless RoCE transport (routed IPv6, PFC, AI-tuned QoS) on the scale-up fabric, eliminating separate software stacks and operational silos; next-gen targets 8 switches on 102.4 Tbps silicon, 72 accelerators per rack, adopting OCP ESUN as the dataplane.
  • Where applicable: Meta-specific (MTIA, FBOSS, in-rack passive copper reach), but the architecture pattern — unifying scale-up/scale-out under one Ethernet transport and NOS — is broadly instructive; note the passive-copper choice constrains it to in-rack distances.
path: Tahan: An Open, Ethernet-Based Scale-Up Switch for Meta's MTIA Accelerators

items.title: Traffic Engineering in AI DCI/WAN for AI Traffic
items.text:
OCP Global Summit 2026 — for a DC/Cloud-Native Networking & Identity PM digest Core pick 15 October 2026

Abstract

Yuanchao SU (Alibaba Cloud), Clarence Filsfils (Cisco)

  • Why: Geo-distributed AI training is now the driving WAN workload; this pairs the SRv6 inventor with a hyperscaler that has actually deployed it, covering both the problem framing and two real deployments.
  • What: The traffic-engineering problem and requirements for AI DCI/WAN connecting geographically distributed training data centers — how it was solved for legacy non-AI traffic, why that solution falls short for synchronized, elephant-heavy AI flows, and the AI-specific solution including the data and telemetry collection needed to drive it (from abstract only).
  • How: TE over the WAN for AI job traffic (presumably SRv6-based given the co-author); the abstract emphasizes required telemetry and two real deployment case studies rather than architecture alone.
  • Where applicable: Alibaba Cloud production deployments — org-specific specifics expected; the requirement analysis (bursty synchronized traffic over constrained DCI) generalizes to any multi-DC training operator. Pairs with the scale-across panel below.
path: Traffic Engineering in AI DCI/WAN for AI Traffic

items.title: Automating Root Cause Analysis in OVS/OVN-Based Deployments Using AI/ML
items.text:
Digest: Open vSwitch and OVN 2024 Fall Conference (Prague) digest Wildcard pick Prague · 20–21 November 2024

Abstract Slides Recording

Speakers: Gurpreet Singh, Red Hat, Inc.

VideoPDF

Why: A PM-to-PM talk that is thin on its own results but signals where vendor investment is going: closed-loop, ML-driven RCA for virtualized networking.

What: The problem statement is real and well-framed: OVS/OVN-level metrics are missing in shared virtualized environments, nothing correlates metrics to policies or resource allocation, and RCA is manual and slow. The proposed approach: Self-Organizing-Map-based anomaly detection (citing prior published work reporting 99% accuracy on real DC data, with acknowledged processing-time and scale challenges), a fault-injection sandbox (CPU/network/memory stress, Tx/Rx queue oversubscription) for pre-training models on simulated environments, OpenTelemetry-based collection, and closed-loop anomaly mitigation.

How: Architecture and prior work only — no results from the authors' own deployment in the available material.

Where applicable: OpenStack/OCP-style virtualized infrastructure; watch with skepticism, but the "train on injected faults in a sandbox before production" pattern is a credible approach to the data-scarcity problem in network ML.
path: Automating Root Cause Analysis in OVS/OVN-Based Deployments Using AI/ML

items.title: Composable Services in OVN
items.text:
Digest: Open vSwitch and OVN 2024 Fall Conference (Prague) digest Core pick Prague · 20–21 November 2024

Abstract Recording

Speakers: Mark Michelson, Red Hat, Inc. (from abstract only)

Video

Why: Reveals where the core OVN team is taking the project's architecture — the session type this digest is told to up-rank.

What: A new proposal to extract certain functionality from existing OVN logical datapaths and implement it as standalone specialized datapaths ("composable services"), giving administrators more clarity and power over packet processing, with ACLs, NATs, and load balancers called out as beneficiaries, plus possible future offerings.

How: Not detailed in the available material — this is a proposal-stage design talk rather than a shipped feature.

Where applicable: OVN project-level direction; anyone building products on OVN should track how ACL/NAT/LB semantics change under this model.

items.title: Current Challenges with OpenStack Ironic, SR-IOV, and OVN
items.text:
Digest: Open vSwitch and OVN 2024 Fall Conference (Prague) digest Adjacent pick Prague · 20–21 November 2024

Abstract Slides Recording

Speakers: Michal Nasiadka, Bartosz Bezak, StackHPC (from abstract only)

Video

Why: SR-IOV and bare-metal networking against OVN is an under-documented corner of the stack, told by an operator (StackHPC) rather than a vendor.

What: The ongoing problems implementing OpenStack Neutron ML2/OVN with Ironic/SR-IOV external ports: root causes, solutions under development and their upstream status (testing and reviews), plus temporary production workarounds.
