items.title: SCION Inter-Domain Routing
items.text:
SwiNOG #41 digest Core pick 28 April 2026

Slides Recording

Tilmann Zäschke - ETH Zürich

VideoPDF

  • Why: SCION has crossed from research architecture to regulated critical-infrastructure deployments (Swiss banking, payments, healthcare, power). For anyone whose remit covers inter-domain security and next-gen network identity/trust, this is the most concrete clean-slate architecture actually in production.
  • What: A 2026 status briefing by the ETH group. Trust model: Isolation Domains (ISDs) — groups of ASes with self-governed trust roots and no third-party CAs, ASes authenticated via X.509 certificates. Path-awareness: endpoints build end-to-end paths from beaconed segments and select among them (latency, bandwidth, geolocation — enabling geofencing and hijack prevention), with failover in ~RTT and concurrent multi-path use. Real deployments: SSFN (Secure Swiss Finance Network, ~300 finance institutions, governed by Swiss National Bank and SIX), SEPN (EFTPOS payments), HIN (healthcare), SSUN (planned all Swiss electricity market partners by 2030), SCIERA (research/education). Public network: 242 registered ASes, 98 publicly reachable, median 204 paths per destination (max 5,828); fastest path median 4 hops / 4.1 ms. Specs: data plane and control plane drafts are with the RFC editor (independent submission stream); reference implementation v0.15.0 adds NAT support; native SCION endhost apps expected to bring 100k+ native users by end of year; client libraries in Go, Rust, C, Java, Python, plus a Chromium plugin.
  • How: Control plane: beacon service propagates path segments, path servers store them, certificate service manages inter-AS keys. Data plane: packets carry the end-to-end path; border routers forward per-path. Deployment needs no changes to intra-AS infrastructure; legacy endpoints attach via SCION gateways (SIGs) translating IP ↔ SCION.
  • Where applicable: Inter-AS/critical-infrastructure connectivity — multi-ISP L2/L3 services with enforceable governance and path control. Not a DC fabric or general-Internet technology yet; the deployment footprint is heavily Swiss/European, and the ecosystem is still anchored on ETH tooling and Anapaya as the commercial vendor.

items.title: Shared Spectrum & MOFN
items.text:
SwiNOG #41 digest Core pick 28 April 2026

Slides Recording

Liam Taylor - EXA Infrastructure

VideoPDF

  • Why: The gap between buying individual wavelengths (low bandwidth, high cost/Gbit) and building your own DWDM line system (high complexity, staffing, licensing) is exactly where inter-DC and long-haul capacity buyers are stuck. Spectrum products are the current answer.
  • What: A taxonomy of photonic-layer sharing models with their operational trade-offs: Alien Waves (customer transponders directly on the vendor's mux — cheapest, but limited monitoring, fixed transmission modes, one cross-connect per wave), Managed Spectrum (customer-owned WSS add/drop, vendor-assigned channels — advanced monitoring, power policing, privacy, but changes need negotiation and require customer line-terminal equipment), and Unmanaged Spectrum (a spectral block assigned by the vendor, channels fully customer-managed — maximum flexibility, but demands the most expertise). Plus MOFN (Managed Optical Fiber Network): a provider-built dedicated fiber + DWDM system delivered as a managed service. Spectrum sizing depends on distance, fiber quality, ROADM count, amplification (Raman vs EDFA), and transponder generation (e.g., Nokia ICE6).
  • How: The vendor assigns and polices GHz-wide spectrum blocks in its photonic layer; the customer brings transponders and manages the optical/electrical layers above them.
  • Where applicable: Operators scaling WAN/inter-DC capacity without building their own line system; terrestrial and submarine (subsea may require ASE fill). Note this is an EXA Infrastructure talk and is largely a product-landscape explainer rather than a neutral engineering treatment — useful for the model taxonomy and the acceptance-criteria/change-process checklist it implies, not as vendor-independent advice.

items.title: The Network Automation Map: Navigate Your Journey with the NAF Automation Framework
items.text:
SwiNOG #41 digest Adjacent pick 28 April 2026

Slides Recording

Damien Garros - OpsMill

VideoPDF

  • Why: Most automation programs stall in ad-hoc scripts and tool-specific arguments. NAF offers a tool-agnostic shared vocabulary that teams can use to assess maturity and compare architectures — useful regardless of your stack.
  • What: The Network Automation Forum framework: seven functional building blocks — Intent, Collector, Observability, Executor, Orchestrator, Presentation, Infrastructure — each defined by purpose, MUST/SHOULD/MAY capabilities, and boundaries. Explicitly not a standard or reference architecture; a living community document. Tools map to multiple blocks and blocks to multiple tools (e.g., Infrahub = Intent + Presentation; SuzieQ/Kentik each span Collector → Observability → Presentation). A worked example rolls a new subnet out to 50 mixed-vendor NETCONF branches across 8 tools, including an automated drift-detect-and-remediate loop (Observability → Orchestrator → Executor → Collector → Observability).
  • How: Functional decomposition first, tools second; each block has clear inputs/outputs so responsibility boundaries and tool gaps become visible. Backed by community docs on GitHub and a solution-wizard app.
  • Where applicable: Any network automation program, any vendor mix — that is the point. No requirement to implement all blocks; start from your use case.
path: The Network Automation Map: Navigate Your Journey with the NAF Automation Framework

items.title: Toward Agentic Network Operations: What AI Can (and Can’t) Do
items.text:
SwiNOG #41 digest Wildcard pick 28 April 2026

Slides Recording

Tobias Bühler - netfabric.ai

VideoPDF

  • Why: Not one of your four core areas, but if agentic identity is on your radar, this is the ops-side mirror: a fact-driven talk (by an ETH Vanbever-group PhD, now NetFabric CTO) with real numbers on where agentic AI in networking actually stands — including the failure modes and the cost math most talks omit.
  • What: An honest positioning: most operators sit between awareness and experimentation; production use is blocked by hallucinations, privacy, unstable results, and cost. The concrete worked example is syslog: a ~100-device network produces millions of log lines/day; naive LLM ingestion costs ~$500k/year (100 tokens/log, 5M logs/day, $3/1M tokens) and overflows any context window. Their key mechanism: LL-generated parsers that compress 69M raw log lines into ~700 typed event types — and their deployment data shows new event types keep appearing even after a month (OS upgrades, maintenance days), so parser generation must be continuous. Documented pitfalls: overly specific parsers, overly general parsers, missing domain knowledge. Five enablers that measurably improved performance: in-context learning with clustering-selected diverse examples, injecting expert parsers for known parameters (e.g., MAC-address formats), guardrails/error checks, targeted system prompts, dedicated log-prefix handling. On agentic data access, a clean control-vs-flexibility framing: agent-written SQL queries (expressive, unsafe) vs targeted tool calls (safe, limited) — recommendation is to choose per LLM model, not one-size-fits-all.
  • How: Log abstraction layer first (parsers → events), then LLM reasoning over events rather than raw logs; the agent interacts with structured stores via either SQL or curated tool interfaces.
  • Where applicable: Brownfield multi-vendor environments; the numbers come from NetFabric's own deployments (vendor talk, but unusually candid about limitations). The parser-generation pattern itself — LLM + clustering + human correction — is directly stealable for any log-heavy system, networking or not.
path: Toward Agentic Network Operations: What AI Can (and Can’t) Do

items.title: Understanding and optimising transceiver power consumption using internal metrics
items.text:
SwiNOG #41 digest Core pick 28 April 2026

Slides Recording

Gerhard Stein - Flexoptix GmbH

VideoPDF

  • Why: Optics power is a growing slice of DC energy budgets, and the common assumptions (laser temperature tuning matters, TEC is a big draw) turn out to be wrong. This talk replaces folklore with measurements.
  • What: A measurement study of >100G transceivers (100G QSFP28, 400G coherent ZR, 800G QSFP-DD) in Cisco Nexus 93600CD-GX, C9500, and Juniper QFX5120, using Versatile Diagnostics Monitoring (VDM/CMIS) internals. Headline findings: laser and TEC power draw is negligible at any transceiver temperature (the 50 °C laser target makes no efficiency difference; a ~20 °C ambient delta moves only ~200 mW); the real energy consumers are the DSP/MCU. The single biggest lever is administrative: shutting a port forces the transceiver into low-power mode at 7–20× less energy. Also documents real power-per-speed trends (400G FR4 from 12 W → 9 W via DSP node shrink 16→7 nm; 1.6T OSFP 30 → 26 W).
  • How: Read VDM metrics (TEC current, laser temperature) alongside DDM; compute P_laser = V_fwd × I_laser and P_TEC = V_trc × I_TEC; measure per-state transceiver draw with a Flexbox research tool (their pytest/PyQt/matplotlib prototype); a "frozen transceiver" experiment with ice cubes validated the temperature insensitivity.
  • Where applicable: Any operator with >100G optics. Practically constrained: VDM support is patchy — Juniper QFX5120 (JunOS 25.2R1.9) and Cisco C9500 (IOS XE 17.14.1) expose DDM only; the Nexus 93600CD-GX (NX-OS 10.5.3(f)) supports CMIS VDM. Flexoptix is a vendor and the Flexbox is theirs, but the talk's findings (port shutdown as the dominant lever, DSP as the consumer) transfer to any environment.
path: Understanding and optimising transceiver power consumption using internal metrics

items.title: Automating Target Discovery in the gNMIc Operator
items.text:
SwiNOG #42 — Operator digest Core pick 21 October 2026

Slides

Daniel Schatzmann

PDF

  • Why: Streaming telemetry (gNMI) moving into Kubernetes, plus automatic synchronization with a source of truth — squarely in the PM's cloud-native networking and network-automation space. It's also a nice example of upstream-able operator work from a bachelor thesis at OST.
  • What: An extension to the gNMIc Operator (open-source, started 2026) that removes the last manual step in gNMI telemetry: keeping the monitored-target list current. Targets are synchronized from an external source of truth (NetBox in the demo), closing the gap where the monitoring stack and the inventory drift apart.
  • How: Two complementary mechanisms: periodic pull from NetBox via an export template, and event-driven push from NetBox via webhook — so inventory changes propagate to the collectors without human edits. The demo runs targets in Containerlab with a Prometheus/Grafana monitoring stack; the export template and webhook receiver have both been contributed as examples in the gNMIc Operator docs, and the mechanism is extensible to other sources of truth. (The work is a BSc thesis by Valentino Diller and Roman Weber at OST, supervised by Daniel Schatzmann.)
  • Where applicable: Any team running gNMI/gNMIc — the operator itself is upstream and open, and the NetBox integration patterns ship in its documentation. General technique, not org-specific.
path: Automating Target Discovery in the gNMIc Operator

items.title: Beyond RPKI Origin Validation, what do we gain with RFC9234 (BGP roles) and ASPA
items.text:
SwiNOG #42 — Operator digest Core pick 21 October 2026

Slides Recording

Claudio Jeker - RSSF (OpenBGPD lead developer, rpki-client co-maintainer)

VideoPDF

  • Why: BGP security is a core interest, and this is the rare talk that grounds the RFCs in real 2025–2026 incidents and gives a concrete, ordered deployment checklist. The Hetzner forged-origin hijack case alone is worth the read: it shows exactly where ROV stops protecting you.
  • What: An argument that ROV is necessary but insufficient — it does nothing against path leaks (Voxility/Lumen April 2025, Cloudflare January 2026, both with intact origins) and nothing against forged-origin hijacks — and that RFC 9234 (BGP roles + OTC) plus ASPA close those gaps. Includes a sharp section on ROA maxLength as an attack surface: a /16 with maxLength /24 authorizes an attacker to forge your origin for any unannounced more-specific.
  • How: RFC 9234 exchanges role information (provider/peer/customer/RS/RS-client) in the BGP OPEN, rejects role-mismatched sessions, and adds the transitive Only-To-Customer attribute so routes learned from providers/peers/RS are marked and rejected when re-exported upward — catching type 1–4 leaks at the source even with a broken export filter. ASPA publishes a signed provider list in the RPKI; routers check AS_PATHs for valley-free propagation, so even partial deployment rejects provably Invalid paths while leaving Unknown paths usable. The Hetzner case (162.55.80.0/24, forged AS_PATH ... 6204 62390 24940, ROV result "Valid") was later invalidated by AS24940's post-attack ASPA record, which doesn't authorize AS62390. Call to action: reject ROV invalids, publish minimal ROAs, configure roles/OTC, publish complete ASPA provider lists (including backup and DDoS-mitigation transit).
  • Where applicable: Any ISP, transit provider, or IXP route server; vendor support is the practical constraint — OpenBGPD/BIRD/FRR and (recently) JunOS 25.2R1 and MikroTik RouterOS 7.21 support RFC 9234; ASPA is available in OpenBGPD and BIRD now, with FRR/JunOS/XR planned or in field trial. Broadly applicable; publishing ROAs/ASPA works even before your routers validate.
path: Beyond RPKI Origin Validation, what do we gain with RFC9234 (BGP roles) and ASPA

items.title: From Connectivity to Cyber Resilience : Defense in Depth for the connected Enterprise
items.text:
SwiNOG #42 — Operator digest Adjacent pick 21 October 2026

Slides Recording

Yannick Gautier - NI ION NOKIA

VideoPDF

  • Why: PQC migration is a real, dated obligation for network security programs (harvest-now-decrypt-later), and the slides contain useful framing — cryptographic debt, discovery→assess→prioritize, migration timelines of 5–15+ years by organization size, and the argument that symmetric crypto survives quantum with larger keys while asymmetric is broken (Shor vs Grover).
  • What: Nokia's Quantum-Safe Networks pitch: layered, multi-technology key establishment (PQC ML-KEM/ML-DSA per FIPS 203–205, symmetric key infrastructure, optional QKD per ETSI GS 014) with centralized key management (1830 SMS), line-rate encryption at multiple layers, crypto-agility, and sovereignty over entropy. Interesting data point: the estimated qubits needed to break RSA-2048 dropped from ~1 billion (2012) to under 100,000 (2026) across three papers in twelve months.
  • How: Defense in depth across application/IP/MPLS/L2/physical layers with different key-establishment architectures (PQC-only via PKI, QKD+symmetric, hybrid PKI+PSK), coordinated key rotation, and certified entropy; ends with four telco monetization models for quantum-safe connectivity.
  • Where applicable: Enterprises and carriers with long-lived confidential data and regulated critical-infrastructure obligations. Caveat: the second half is a Nokia portfolio and services pitch (1830 optical line, SMS key management, QSN service models) — take the threat framing and migration methodology, discount the product push.
path: From Connectivity to Cyber Resilience : Defense in Depth for the connected Enterprise

items.title: From Lab to Production: The Hard Parts of Agentic NetOps
items.text:
SwiNOG #42 — Operator digest Core pick 21 October 2026

Slides Recording

Tobias Bühler - NetFabric

VideoPDF

  • Why: The follow-up to SwiNOG #41's agentic-AI-in-network-ops talk, now with real production deployment scars. For a PM thinking about agentic identity and AI safely operating production networks, this is the most concrete failure-mode catalog available — all drawn from Swiss ISP/MSP deployments on 1000+ devices.
  • What: The three hard problems of production agentic NetOps — correctness, security, and model/paradigm churn — with real failure cases and code-level fixes. The core thesis: rely on code wherever it matters, and run continuous evaluation, because prompt and skill changes alone do not reliably change agent behavior.
  • How: Correctness: agents analyzing firewall policies checked only the PREROUTING chain or the first 50 of 950 rules, ignored default-drop policies, and mis-evaluated subnet membership — fixed with a dedicated, multi-vendor firewall logic module in code (given rules and a flow, does it pass: yes/no). Security: agent-written SQL against a multi-tenant metrics DB is wrapped in guardrails that rewrite queries at the AST level to enforce tenant isolation, cap analyzed rows, block modifications, and reject oversized results before they blow the context window; CLI access is mediated by a grammar of available commands scraped from lab devices, categorized with operator approval, so production lookups only pass approved commands (a DMVPN troubleshooting example drops from ~25 blind failed commands to one-shot success). Evaluation: pitfalls include a TODO-list prompt change that tripled run time (3→10 min), synthetic test traces without production noise, and unit-style tests that don't predict long agentic investigations. Reported results: ticket root cause and proposed fix in 2–3 minutes in multiple deployments, early hardware-degradation detection, config-vs-source-of-truth drift detection.
  • Where applicable: Any operator considering AI agents on production networks. The patterns (guardrails in code, approved command grammars, eval harnesses fed by production incidents) are general; the specifics reflect NetFabric's own deployments and products.
path: From Lab to Production: The Hard Parts of Agentic NetOps

items.title: FRRouting Open Discussion
items.text:
SwiNOG #42 — Operator digest Adjacent pick 21 October 2026

Slides Recording

Martin Winter - NetDEF / FRRouting

VideoPDF

  • Why: Light on content by design (it was an interactive feedback session), but worth a note for a PM with BGP/datapath interests: it's a deliberately vendor-free channel to the maintainers of the open-source routing suite that underpins SONiC, white-box NOSes, and much of the leaf-spine world.
  • What: An experiment in format — no product pitch, just community Q&A on FRR's state (forked from Quagga 2017, ~30 maintainers, BGP/OSPF/IS-IS/LDP/BFD and more, 10.7.1 current) and what's missing for operator use cases.
  • How: Structured prompts (who uses it, who tried and stopped and why, what's missing), with NetDEF — which runs FRR's community CI and has three employees in Switzerland — explicitly inviting feature requests, bug reports, and contributions.
  • Where applicable: Relevant to anyone evaluating open-source control planes for routers, route servers, or container-networking BGP; the session itself is a one-off, but the contact channel is durable. Skippable if you weren't in the room.

items.title: Internet Domain Blocking: Current Legal Situation and Outlook on the Current Revision of the Telecommunications Act
items.text:
SwiNOG #42 — Operator digest Adjacent pick 21 October 2026

Slides Recording

Simon Schlauri - Ronzani Schlauri Attorneys

VideoPDF

  • Why: Not technical, but directly operationally relevant to any Swiss ISP: prosecutors are ordering access providers to block domains, and the talk documents the actual cases, the technical-refutation expert opinion, and the draft legislation. For a PM whose products sit on Swiss networks, this is where content-blocking obligations are heading.
  • What: A case history from 2025–2026: Vaud and Valais prosecutors ordered providers to "seize" domains (reinterpreted as blocking after the fact), imposed a CHF 6,000 fine on a non-compliant provider, and ordered blocking of a climate-activist group's URLs — even though the site was hosted in Switzerland and the prosecutor never asked the host to take it down. The Vaud Cantonal Court lifted that block in May 2026 but dodged the core legality question; a Federal Supreme Court appeal is pending.
  • How: Legal analysis plus a decisive technical contribution: a Switch expert opinion establishing that individual URLs cannot be blocked via DNS at all, and that the only practicable ISP measure is blocking an entire domain on their resolver — which over-blocks (all services under the domain, including email) and violates net neutrality. The proposed new Art. 6a Telecoms Act would mandate blocking of fraud-related second-level domains on fedpol notification — narrow, but still without judicial review or a hearing for site operators. The speaker's position: "delete, don't block" — go after the hosting source, and if blocking exists at all, only by statute with a court weighing interests.
  • Where applicable: Swiss access providers and anyone operating DNS resolvers there. Jurisdiction-specific, but the pattern — courts accepting "the other providers comply" as proof of feasibility — is a caution for operators everywhere.
path: Internet Domain Blocking: Current Legal Situation and Outlook on the Current Revision of the Telecommunications Act

items.title: Managing IP Allocation with an Open-Source DDI
items.text:
SwiNOG #42 — Operator digest Core pick 21 October 2026

Slides Recording

Marco Martinez - Swisscom

VideoPDF

  • Why: IPAM is an explicit core interest, and this is a practitioner's build report: no open-source DDI exists today, so the speaker assembled one from three proven components rather than building DNS/DHCP/IPAM from scratch.
  • What: A composable DDI built on Infrahub (IPAM/source of truth), Kea (DHCP), and PowerDNS (DNS), orchestrated by Event-Driven Ansible into a single event-driven configuration plane. The IPAM layer is authoritative: DNS entries and DHCP reservation pools are generated dynamically from the modeled dependencies in Infrahub.
  • How: An earlier attempt (a "configuration plane" over the three products with separate automation tooling) failed on consistency; the working design makes Infrahub the source of truth, and events from it drive Ansible workflows that apply only the defined properties to Kea and PowerDNS — which keep their production-grade secure configuration for everything else. Reconciliation is built in. The result and code are published (github.com/marcom4rtinez/ddi).
  • Where applicable: Environments priced out of commercial DDI (the stated motivation: cost, transparency, source of truth, moving out of silos). Honest limitations: HA and the "one vendor supports the whole stack" property of commercial DDI are what you give up; everything runs on containers/Linux and the integration complexity is higher than a monolithic product. Operator-specific in architecture choices, but the pattern (SoT generates DNS/DHCP, event-driven push, reconcile) is broadly reusable.
path: Managing IP Allocation with an Open-Source DDI

items.title: Networking for AI
items.text:
SwiNOG #42 — Operator digest Core pick 21 October 2026

Slides

Remi Locherer - Arista Networks

PDF

  • Why: AI training/inference clusters are the hardest physical datacenter networking problem of the moment, and this is a dense technical walkthrough of the fabric design decisions: lossless Ethernet, load balancing, topology, optics, and power. Directly in the PM's physical-DC wheelhouse (RoCE/lossless fabrics, optics, topology).
  • What: A structured treatment of why AI traffic breaks traditional DC design — few, large, long-lived, highly synchronized flows; bursts at 100% of link rate with no stat-muxing; a single loss or XPU failure halts the whole job — followed by concrete scale-out designs, congestion control, load balancing evolution, and the Ultra Ethernet / MRC trends, plus the optics and cooling consequences.
  • How: Covers RoCEv2 framing and why "converged Ethernet" means lossless Ethernet (PFC hop-by-hop on ingress, ECN end-to-end, DCQCN). Explains why ECMP fails on low-entropy XPU-to-XPU flows (collisions, out-of-order delivery on link flap) and the progression from RDMA-aware hashing to dynamic and cluster-aware load balancing. Compares fat-tree vs planar/rail topologies (flexibility vs fiber cost and 1:1 bandwidth), gives per-tier XPU-count design tables up to ~660k hosts on multi-planar 7060XE7 fabrics, and covers UET packet spraying, packet trimming (64B trimmed frames as fast congestion signals), and the OpenAI-led Multipath Reliable Connection (MRC) OCP transport spec. Finishes with the physical layer: LPO transceivers (≤8W vs 14-16W, ~50% power reduction, 9x lower latency), liquid cooling, and XPO extra-dense pluggable optics for 204.8T in 1OU.
  • Where applicable: AI backend/scale-out fabric design generally; the concepts (lossless forwarding, entropy, oversubscription, power-as-constraint) transfer to any DC operator. Note it is an Arista session and the design tables are Arista-platform-specific (7060X6/7800R4/7060XE7), but the vast majority of the content is protocol- and silicon-generic, not a disguised pitch.

items.title: On-prem LLM cluster for network and security analyses
items.text:
SwiNOG #42 — Operator digest Core pick 21 October 2026

Slides Recording

Mischa Diehm - narrowin

VideoPDF

  • Why: A reference architecture for running AI over network data entirely on-prem — and, unusually, it takes the identity and security model seriously (scoped agent credentials, RBAC, MCP authorization, audit trails linking user → tool call → device change), which maps directly onto the PM's workload and agentic identity interests. It also includes real small-cluster physical networking detail.
  • What: A four-layer sovereign stack: interaction (chat/web/API + a planning agent), AI (open-weight models — GLM, Qwen, Nemotron, DeepSeek — on a local GPU cluster served by vLLM behind an OpenAI-compatible API), integration (MCP servers exposing purpose-built tools plus skills, not raw data), and context (topology, configs, syslog, CMDB/IPAM, ticketing, or a single device via SSH/REST/SNMP). Evaluated on a multi-vendor IT/OT Containerlab lab network and agent-driven assessments of production data from real networks.
  • How: Hardware is 4× NVIDIA DGX Spark (512 GB pooled memory for weights/KV cache when sharded across nodes) behind a MikroTik CRS804-4DDQ 400G switch — about 25K CHF. Notable networking finding: internal PCIe limits mean each Spark gets 2×200G, not 400G, so one 200G link carries data plane and management moves to a separate interface; the nodes are memory-rich but bandwidth-poor (~273 GB/s), so MoE models run best. The interesting operational lessons are in data fusion: combine state, signals, inventory, and intent (from a system of record like Infrahub), pair tools with skills instead of exposing raw data, and make every finding verifiable by linking it to source evidence. Security model covers RBAC per role/device/action, MCP Enterprise-Managed Authorization via the identity provider, scoped SSH/API identities for the agent, prompt injection (a malicious ticket can steer tool calls even with a local model), model-trust limits of open weights, audit trails, and human approval gates with rollback.
  • Where applicable: Operators with privacy, sovereignty (CLOUD Act / AI Act), or cost constraints on shipping network data to cloud LLMs — particularly IT/OT and critical infrastructure. The honest trade-offs are stated: you need staff who can run it, the model market moves monthly, and without clear goals it becomes a time sink. Reproducible as a reference architecture; scale is deliberately small (desk-sized), not hyperscaler.
path: On-prem LLM cluster for network and security analyses

items.title: Reality, Rewritten: AI as Forger and Investigator
items.text:
SwiNOG #42 — Operator digest Wildcard pick 21 October 2026

Dominik Haenni - Zurich Forensic Science Institute

  • Why: The opening keynote frames the question the three agentic-AI talks later dance around: when the same technology fabricates evidence and analyzes it, what happens to expert judgment and trust in organizations — which is, in the end, the same question as trusting an agent's root-cause analysis on a production network.
  • What: An exploration of generative AI's dual role — producing convincing fake images, cloned voices, and plausible documents, while also accelerating forensic analysis, research, and software development — with current examples from the Institute's casework, and a look beyond the tool at responsibility and how organizations work when AI compresses timelines.
  • How: Case-example driven (the abstract does not describe a method); the argument is that when AI "changes the rules," business as usual in evidence handling — and by extension, any function that certifies truth — is not affordable.
  • Where applicable: Not a networking talk, but its trust-in-automated-findings framing transfers directly to anyone shipping AI-generated analysis into operational workflows. (from abstract only)
path: Reality, Rewritten: AI as Forger and Investigator

items.title: Retro Networks
items.text:
SwiNOG #42 — Operator digest Wildcard pick 21 October 2026

Slides Recording

Gianpaolo Del Matto - THE PHINTAGE COLLECTOR

VideoPDF

  • Why: Looks like a nostalgia talk and is, for two-thirds of it (10BASE5 vampire taps, PhoneNet, Token Ring developed in Zurich, DOS memory limits) — but it pivots into one of the most honest available case studies of LLM-assisted development in a deeply constrained environment, and the lessons are unusually sharp.
  • What: The speaker reimplemented the 3Com 3C509B configuration utility (3CCFGCLI) in 16-bit real-mode 8086 assembly, because the original needs a 286+ and 232 KB on disk. The result: 0.8.3 is feature-complete and runs on a real 8086 in ≤256 KB RAM, with the binary refactored from 40 KB down to 26 KB.
  • How: Used an LLM as "a very fast, sometimes hallucinating developer" — not an oracle. Concrete episodes: the LLM correctly suggested a full hardware mock early, the speaker refused, and paid for it with an entire 0.6 refactoring branch; separately, the LLM burned three hours chasing a "mysterious" 1-byte offset down into disassembling Turbo Assembler itself when the root cause was that 8086 short jumps can only reach ±127 bytes and the routine had simply outgrown them. Discipline: the ~180-case test harness was human-built, all output reviewed, and continuous refactoring kept the bloat down.
  • Where applicable: As engineering-method takeaways, broadly — "AI can help you build it, but you still need to understand it, review it, and prove that it works." Published at github.com/gpdm/TPC-3CCFGCLI. Only the LLM-methods half generalizes; the vintage-hardware half is for fun (and the ENTER Technikwelt exhibit).

items.title: Small BNGs
items.text:
SwiNOG #42 — Operator digest Adjacent pick 21 October 2026

Slides Recording

Fiona Weber - WDZ GmbH // Wobcom GmbH

VideoPDF

  • Why: A contrarian architecture decision with a completed migration to show for it: instead of the industry trend of terminating subscribers on a few huge central routers, AS9136 pushed small white-box BNGs to the edge. A genuine postmortem-flavored operator story — exactly the kind of hard-won, transferable lesson the PM's field values.
  • What: Migration from 2 central to 25 distributed BNGs on RtBrick software on UfiSpace and EdgeCore hardware (MPLS/IS-IS + SR, BGP, PPPoE/IPoE, QinQ, RADIUS, CGNAT, L2/L3VPN), plus the migration experience: the topology change turned into a major fiber and infrastructure cleanup, strange CPEs in the field, "bugs, bugs, bugs," and subscriber migration pain.
  • How: Distributed termination removes centralized failure points, simplifies backbone/fiber planning, enables direct routing and service flexibility, and avoids "major vendor tax" with pay-as-you-grow boxes. The costs: IP pool management and config automation get harder, and you're running more complex hardware deep in the field with a new software vendor. The speaker's guidance on fit: it depends on physical footprint and org structure, and is especially attractive for medium-sized networks — but even if decentralization isn't right for you, shrink your failure domains ("huge chassis routers need to die").
  • Where applicable: The migration specifics are AS9136/WDZ-specific; the failure-domain reasoning and the honest challenge list are broadly applicable to any access-network operator.

items.title: The Accidental Platform Team: Kubernetes Operators at Swisscom
items.text:
SwiNOG #42 — Operator digest Adjacent pick 21 October 2026

Slides Recording

Fabian Schulz - Swisscom (with Lea Brühwiler)

VideoPDF

  • Why: The organizational counterpart to the SDC and gNMIc talks: what happens when Kubernetes operators for network automation (IPAM, inventory, NETCONF router config — the same Swisscom stack) get adopted beyond their original 5G-core scope and become "Operators as a Service" for a platform team running Kubernetes-as-a-Service.
  • What: An adoption story, not an architecture story. The honest middle section is the value: a wall of real user objections ("I don't understand Kubernetes", "we were faster the old way", "there will always be manual changes on the box", "I just did it myself with a Gitlab pipeline, it's easier") and the incremental answers that overcame them.
  • How: Gradual adoption (pick one easy use case, ship a prototype early, iterate on feedback), then four countermeasures: a graphical UI for people who won't use kubectl; observability and traceability (commit history, provenance of every change) to answer "how do I know where this change came from"; knowledge-sharing initiatives and regular check-ins to build trust. The before/after numbers are striking: 5G-core network provisioning dropped from multi-week sequences (change requests 5–10 days, IP tables 2 days, integration 5–10 days) to minutes-to-hours of intent creation with continuous automated testing. Reference architecture published at architecture.cncf.io.
  • Where applicable: Teams building internal platform/operator tooling — the human-side lessons are the transferable part and generalize well beyond telco. Scale numbers are Swisscom-specific.
path: The Accidental Platform Team: Kubernetes Operators at Swisscom

items.title: The Cloud-Native Advantage: Intent-based Network Automation
items.text:
SwiNOG #42 — Operator digest Core pick 21 October 2026

Slides Recording

Alexander North - Swisscom (with Markus Vahlenkamp - Nokia)

VideoPDF

  • Why: Bridges the PM's two worlds in one talk — Kubernetes resource-model tooling applied to YANG/NETCONF/gNMI device configuration. The core problem is one anyone running CNFs or telco functions has hit: Helm deploys the pod, but the running config is still set with imperative per-instance NETCONF RPCs, outside any reconcile loop.
  • What: Schema Driven Configuration (SDC), an open-source (initiated by Nokia, CNCF Sandbox since 2026) Kubernetes Operator that models device configuration as Config custom resources with priorities, and reconciles them against the device via NETCONF or gNMI. In production at Swisscom for the 5G mobile core — roughly 2000 pods, 5000 interdependent parameters, 14 network functions.
  • How: Config CRs declare only their slice of the YANG tree, tagged with a target and a priority. SDC merges all Configs (priority resolves overlaps — a temporary ops override at prio 50 beats the platform baseline at prio 100, and deleting the override restores the baseline), validates the merged tree against YANG, diffs against the device's running config, and translates only the delta to NETCONF/gNMI with per-NOS rules. Drift is surfaced as Deviation CRs with typed reasons (NOT_APPLIED, OVERRULED, UNHANDLED brownfield config); revertive: true re-applies automatically. A kubectl sdc blame command shows, for every leaf, whether it came from which Config or from brownfield running config — "Config Blame is to Config apply what Git Blame is to commit."
  • Where applicable: Anything with a YANG model — physical routers, VMs, containers. Note the abstract oversells "self-healing": default behavior reports drift rather than fixing it (revertive is opt-in), and RESTCONF is not yet supported. The Swisscom deployment is a large-scale telco core, but the mechanism itself is general and adoptable at docs.sdcio.dev.
path: The Cloud-Native Advantage: Intent-based Network Automation

items.title: 5G and Cellular Network Security
items.text:
USENIX Security '25 (34th USENIX Security Symposium) digest Adjacent pick 13–15 August 2025

Multiple papers/teams — see below — Adjacent

  • Why: A dense cluster of 5G/cellular protocol-security papers this cycle — worth a combined mention as a vertical, even though cellular/RAN isn't explicitly named in the PM's core interests, because the architectural patterns (control/data-plane separation, standardized network functions) echo cloud-native networking design.
  • What: AKMA+ (Singapore Management University et al.) finds and fixes vulnerabilities in 5G's Authentication and Key Management for Applications protocol while preserving standards compatibility. SNI5GECT (SUTD) sniffs and injects into pre-authentication 5G NR messages without a rogue base station, achieving 70–90% attack success within 20m. CoreCrisis (Penn State) is a stateful fuzzer that found 13 crashing and 7 spec-deviation vulnerabilities across three open-source and one commercial 5G core implementation. GLaDoS (ETH Zurich / Oxford) is a full-scale deployed system for geofenced cellular denial-of-service in sensitive areas, neutralizing 99.3% of connections across 100+ commercial cells. (from abstract only)
  • How: Varies by paper — protocol formal analysis (AKMA+), pre-auth sniff-and-inject (SNI5GECT), stateful black-box fuzzing with FSM learning (CoreCrisis), and combined overshadowing + localization (GLaDoS). (from abstract only)
  • Where applicable: 5G core/RAN operators and equipment vendors specifically; GLaDoS is also relevant to physical-security/sensitive-facility contexts wanting legal, geofenced cellular control.

items.title: A Framework for Abusability Analysis: The Case of Passkeys in Interpersonal Threat Models
items.text:
USENIX Security '25 (34th USENIX Security Symposium) digest Adjacent pick 13–15 August 2025

Alaa Daffalla et al., Cornell University / Cornell Tech; University of Wisconsin–Madison; New York University — Adjacent

  • Why: The first analysis of how passkeys — the largest current push toward passwordless authentication — interact with interpersonal threat models (intimate partner violence, elder abuse), a threat class that's easy to overlook when passkey security is evaluated only against remote attackers.
  • What: An abusability-analysis framework applied to 19 passkey-supporting services, finding abuse vectors including flawed implementations that let an abuser maintain ongoing illicit access with no recovery path for the victim, and vectors that let attackers lock victims out or gaslight them. (from abstract only)
  • How: A general framework for identifying how new authentication features can be exploited by an adversary with routine physical device access and partial credential knowledge — applied specifically to passkey account-recovery and device-management flows. (from abstract only)
  • Where applicable: General framework applicable beyond passkeys; the passkey-specific findings are directly relevant to anyone implementing or evaluating passkey account-recovery UX.
path: A Framework for Abusability Analysis: The Case of Passkeys in Interpersonal Threat Models

items.title: An Industry Interview Study of Software Signing for Supply Chain Security
items.text:
USENIX Security '25 (34th USENIX Security Symposium) digest Adjacent pick 13–15 August 2025

Recording

Kelechi G. Kalu et al., Purdue University — Adjacent

Video

  • Why: Software signing is widely recommended by supply-chain security frameworks but adoption remains low — this is the first in-depth practitioner account of why, complementing the technical PKI/cert-validation picks above with the human/organizational side.
  • What: Interviews with 18 experienced security practitioners across 13 organizations on software-signing adoption, surfacing technical, organizational, and human barriers; finds experts disagree on signing's importance and documents how internal/external events (breaches, new regulation) drive adoption. (from abstract only)
  • How: Qualitative interview study producing a refined software-supply-chain factory model highlighting where and why signing practices break down. (from abstract only)
  • Where applicable: General for organizations evaluating or mandating software signing as part of supply-chain security policy.
path: An Industry Interview Study of Software Signing for Supply Chain Security

items.title: Ares: Comprehensive Path Hijacking Detection via Routing Tree
items.text:
USENIX Security '25 (34th USENIX Security Symposium) digest Core pick 13–15 August 2025

Recording

Yinxiang Tao et al., Tsinghua University / Zhongguancun Laboratory / Quan Cheng Laboratory; Congcong Miao, Tencent — Core

Video

  • Why: Path hijacking (manipulating AS-path attributes rather than just the origin) is the stealthier successor to origin hijacking specifically designed to evade existing detection — this is a system that closes that gap with real-event validation, not just simulation.
  • What: Ares, a system detecting path hijacking by tracking changes to an AS's "observed prefix routing tree" (OPRT), validated against 12 real-world hijacking events (detected within 5 minutes each) and large-scale simulation (97.2%–99.3% detection rate, 1.06% false-positive rate). (from abstract only)
  • How: Uses weighted edit distance between routing trees to quantify anomalous change, combined with clustering to accelerate detection and heuristics to reduce false positives; generates ~2.31 alerts/hour across the entire Internet. (from abstract only)
  • Where applicable: General BGP route-hijacking detection for network operators and Tier-1/content ASes; a deployable detection system rather than a protocol change.
path: Ares: Comprehensive Path Hijacking Detection via Routing Tree

items.title: Assessing the Aftermath: The Effects of a Global Takedown Against DDoS-for-hire Services
items.text:
USENIX Security '25 (34th USENIX Security Symposium) digest Adjacent pick 13–15 August 2025

Recording

Anh V. Vu et al., University of Cambridge; University of Edinburgh; University of Strathclyde; University of Illinois Chicago — Adjacent

Video

  • Why: A rare quantitative, multi-year measurement of whether law-enforcement disruption actually works against the DDoS-for-hire ecosystem — useful context for anyone evaluating DDoS threat trends rather than just technical mitigation.
  • What: An assessment of the largest booter takedown effort to date (since December 2022), finding over half of seized sites returned within a day, traffic to re-emerged domains dropped 80–90%, and the first takedown wave cut global DDoS volume 20–40% (with a significant effect specifically on UDP-based attacks) — but the overall market proved resilient, with effects lasting at most ~6 weeks. (from abstract only)
  • How: Combines web traffic data, ground-truth visits to seized sites, millions of DDoS attack records, and underground-forum/Telegram chat analysis. (from abstract only)
  • Where applicable: General threat-intelligence context for DDoS trend forecasting; policy-relevant more than technically actionable for network defenders directly.
path: Assessing the Aftermath: The Effects of a Global Takedown Against DDoS-for-hire Services

items.title: BGP Vortex: Update Message Floods Can Create Internet Instabilities
items.text:
USENIX Security '25 (34th USENIX Security Symposium) digest Core pick 13–15 August 2025

Recording

Felix Stöger, ETH Zurich; Henry Birge-Lee, Princeton University; Giacomo Giuliari, Mysten Labs; Jordi Subira-Nieto and Adrian Perrig, ETH Zurich — Core

Video

  • Why: A new BGP instability attack that neither BGPSEC nor RPKI can prevent, because every message involved is a legitimate, standards-compliant BGP UPDATE — a reminder that route-origin validation alone doesn't close the routing-security gap.
  • What: Discovery of the "BGP Vortex," a configuration where just three legitimate BGP UPDATE messages trigger persistent instability, weaponizable to cause router overload and forwarding loops across the Internet. All major router implementations tested were susceptible. (from abstract only)
  • How: Exploits standards-compliant BGP Communities extensions (used for traffic engineering) that allow route-preference modification; the paper proposes a framework for classifying which BGP extensions are similarly dangerous versus safe to deploy. (from abstract only)
  • Where applicable: General for any BGP-speaking network; the mitigation framework is for router vendors and operators using BGP Communities-based traffic engineering.
path: BGP Vortex: Update Message Floods Can Create Internet Instabilities

items.title: Catch-22: Uncovering Compromised Hosts Using SSH Public Keys
items.text:
USENIX Security '25 (34th USENIX Security Symposium) digest Wildcard pick 13–15 August 2025

Recording

Cristian Munteanu et al., Max Planck Institute for Informatics; Delft University of Technology (Distinguished Paper Award Winner) — Wildcard

Video

  • Why: A clever, minimally-invasive Internet-scale detection technique — using SSH's own public-key-authentication challenge behavior to fingerprint compromise without ever needing valid credentials or touching the compromised system — that found state-actor-associated keys inside sensitive ASes.
  • What: A method identifying 21,700+ compromised SSH servers across 1,649 ASes and 144 countries by checking for the presence of known-malicious attacker public keys, without needing to log in or test passwords; surfaced new context on botnets (fritzfrog), threat actors (teamtnt), and state-actor-linked keys in sensitive networks. (from abstract only)
  • How: Exploits the fact that SSH only sends a public-key-authentication challenge if the corresponding key is actually present on the server — letting a scanner test for known malicious keys' presence with zero access and zero risk of triggering an actual login. (from abstract only)
  • Where applicable: General Internet-scale compromise detection; the technique's elegance (a side effect of protocol behavior, not a vulnerability) is the interesting part, applicable anywhere an authentication protocol leaks presence information.
path: Catch-22: Uncovering Compromised Hosts Using SSH Public Keys

items.title: Deanonymizing Ethereum Validators: The P2P Network Has a Privacy Issue
items.text:
USENIX Security '25 (34th USENIX Security Symposium) digest Wildcard pick 13–15 August 2025

Lioba Heimbach et al., ETH Zurich; University of Bern; IMDEA Networks — Wildcard

  • Why: Not a blockchain-economics paper — a peer-to-peer network privacy/deanonymization finding (any node can link validator identities to peer IP addresses) that's really a P2P protocol design lesson wearing blockchain clothing, relevant to anyone reasoning about identity-unlinkability guarantees in P2P systems generally.
  • What: Demonstrates the Ethereum P2P network fails to provide its intended validator anonymity — any participating node can link a validator's identifier to a peer's IP address. Using data from just four nodes over three days, the authors located 15%+ of all Ethereum validators, including geographic location and hosting organization. Awarded a bug bounty by the Ethereum Foundation. (from abstract only)
  • How: A methodology for any P2P node to correlate validator identifiers with connected peers' network-level metadata, empirically validated at scale rather than theorized. (from abstract only)
  • Where applicable: Directly Ethereum-specific in its finding, but the underlying lesson — that P2P protocols claiming participant anonymity need explicit defenses against peer-correlation attacks, not just identifier obfuscation — generalizes to any P2P system with an unlinkability goal.
path: Deanonymizing Ethereum Validators: The P2P Network Has a Privacy Issue

items.title: Detecting Compromise of Passkey Storage on the Cloud (CASPER)
items.text:
USENIX Security '25 (34th USENIX Security Symposium) digest Core pick 13–15 August 2025

Mazharul Islam et al., University of Wisconsin–Madison; Visa Research — Core

  • Why: Directly addresses a real gap in FIDO2 passkey deployments: cloud-synced passkeys solve the account-recovery problem but reintroduce a breach surface (the passkey management service's cloud storage) that today's defenses can't close without breaking recovery or login UX.
  • What: CASPER, the first framework letting web service providers detect abuse of passkeys leaked from a passkey management service (PMS), even against attackers who strategically adapt to evade detection. (from abstract only)
  • How: Integrates into existing passkey backup/sync/authentication flows with minimal UX impact, negligible performance overhead, and low deployment complexity for participating services. (from abstract only — detection mechanism specifics not given)
  • Where applicable: General for any relying party accepting FIDO2 synced passkeys; directly actionable for services already on the passkey adoption path.
path: Detecting Compromise of Passkey Storage on the Cloud (CASPER)

items.title: Exposing and Circumventing SNI-based QUIC Censorship of the Great Firewall of China
items.text:
USENIX Security '25 (34th USENIX Security Symposium) digest Core pick 13–15 August 2025

Ali Zohaib et al., University of Massachusetts Amherst / GFW Report / University of Colorado Boulder / Stanford University — Core

  • Why: A rigorous measurement of a nation-state QUIC-blocking system reveals a real architectural weakness (decryption overhead collapses effectiveness under load) and a real weaponization risk (it can be triggered to block arbitrary UDP traffic between third parties) — directly relevant to anyone reasoning about QUIC/UDP behavior at the network edge.
  • What: The GFW decrypts QUIC Initial packets at scale to apply SNI-based blocking, using a blocklist distinct from its other censorship mechanisms; the paper finds this decryption is computationally expensive enough to fail under moderate traffic and can be weaponized to block unrelated UDP traffic. Circumvention strategies were integrated into Firefox, quic-go, and major circumvention tools. (from abstract only)
  • How: Active measurement characterizes what triggers GFW QUIC blocking; the weaponization angle exploits the same decryption-at-scale mechanism against arbitrary third-party UDP flows. (from abstract only)
  • Where applicable: General for QUIC/UDP traffic traversing state-level middleboxes; the weaponization finding is a general lesson about any inline-decryption censorship/inspection architecture, not GFW-specific.
path: Exposing and Circumventing SNI-based QUIC Censorship of the Great Firewall of China

items.title: Haunted by Legacy: Discovering and Exploiting Vulnerable Tunnelling Hosts
items.text:
USENIX Security '25 (34th USENIX Security Symposium) digest Core pick 13–15 August 2025

Angelos Beitis and Mathy Vanhoef, DistriNet, KU Leuven — Core

  • Why: The same tunneling encapsulation families underlying datacenter and WAN overlay networking — GRE, IPIP, and IPv4/IPv6 translation tunnels — turn out to have over 4 million open, unauthenticated hosts on the public Internet, directly relevant to anyone running or securing tunnel endpoints.
  • What: An Internet-wide scan finding 4M+ hosts that accept unauthenticated IPIP, GRE, 4in6, or 6in4 tunneling traffic, exploitable as one-way proxies, for source-address spoofing, or for access into private networks — plus two new amplification-based DoS attacks (16x and 75x amplification) and an Economic DoS attack that drains a host's outgoing bandwidth. (from abstract only)
  • How: Seven distinct IPv4/IPv6 scan methods identify hosts accepting unauthenticated tunneling traffic; the amplification attacks work by concentrating traffic in time or looping packets between vulnerable hosts. (from abstract only)
  • Where applicable: General for any network exposing GRE/IPIP/4in6/6in4 tunnel endpoints to the Internet without authentication — directly applicable to DC/WAN overlay and legacy IPv6-transition tunnel deployments specifically, not just an academic curiosity.
path: Haunted by Legacy: Discovering and Exploiting Vulnerable Tunnelling Hosts

items.title: Lemon: Network-Wide DDoS Detection with Routing-Oblivious Per-Flow Measurement
items.text:
USENIX Security '25 (34th USENIX Security Symposium) digest Core pick 13–15 August 2025

Wenhao Wu et al., Institute of Computing Technology / Chinese Academy of Sciences — Core

  • Why: A DDoS-detection system implemented and evaluated on real programmable switch hardware (Tofino), directly relevant to datapath/programmable-networking work, that solves a genuine correctness problem (over-counting from unpredictable routing) rather than just adding another ML classifier.
  • What: Lemon, a network-wide DDoS detection system that stays accurate even when traffic routing is unpredictable and invalidates the operator's assumed network topology — a failure mode that breaks existing sketch-based measurement systems. (from abstract only)
  • How: A novel "Lemon sketch" data structure in the data plane avoids over-counting and mis-allocation across measurement points; a control plane aggregates sketches for network-wide, per-flow DDoS detection and victim identification. Implemented in both software (Bmv2) and programmable hardware (Tofino) switches. (from abstract only)
  • Where applicable: General DDoS-detection deployments on programmable data-plane hardware (P4/Tofino-class switches); the routing-obliviousness is specifically valuable for networks with dynamic or asymmetric routing.
path: Lemon: Network-Wide DDoS Detection with Routing-Oblivious Per-Flow Measurement

items.title: LEO-Range: Physical Layer Design for Secure Ranging with Low Earth Orbiting Satellites
items.text:
USENIX Security '25 (34th USENIX Security Symposium) digest Wildcard pick 13–15 August 2025

Daniele Coppola et al., ETH Zurich; CISPA Helmholtz Center for Information Security — Wildcard

  • Why: Not a fit for the PM's terrestrial DC/WAN focus directly, but LEO satellite constellations are an increasingly real backhaul/connectivity layer, and this is provably-secure physical-layer ranging design for exactly that emerging infrastructure — the kind of "where the physical network is heading" signal worth having on the radar.
  • What: A physical-layer design for secure distance ranging between LEO satellites and ground devices, compatible with OFDM (used by high-bandwidth satellite links), with a formal security proof bounding an attacker's probability of a distance-reduction attack. Tested with a hardware satellite-channel emulator, limiting spoofing to under a 2⁻²⁰ success probability for a 117m distance-reduction attempt in realistic channel conditions. (from abstract only)
  • How: A novel frequency-domain verification scheme provides provable security against arbitrary physical-layer attack strategies, rather than relying on a specific attacker model. (from abstract only)
  • Where applicable: LEO satellite communication systems specifically; general technique for physical-layer secure ranging that could generalize to other wireless ranging contexts.
path: LEO-Range: Physical Layer Design for Secure Ranging with Low Earth Orbiting Satellites

items.title: Post-Quantum Secure Messaging: Signal, MLS, and iMessage PQ3
items.text:
USENIX Security '25 (34th USENIX Security Symposium) digest Adjacent pick 13–15 August 2025

Multiple papers/teams — see below — Adjacent

  • Why: A cluster of formal-methods papers rigorously analyzing post-quantum secure-messaging protocols already in production (Signal's PQXDH, Apple's iMessage PQ3, IETF-standardized MLS) — the identity/crypto-agility theme from the Netflix Enigma talk playing out at the protocol-design layer.
  • What: Bundled Authenticated Key Exchange (AIST/PQShield) formally shows Signal's X3DH and PQXDH don't achieve "optimal" security under a new unified model, and introduces RingXKEM, a fully post-quantum handshake that does. A companion paper does the same for deniability guarantees specifically, building an efficient deniable ring-signature scheme from NIST-standardized Falcon. A third paper machine-verifies Apple's iMessage PQ3 protocol in the TAMARIN prover, including previously-thought-infeasible unbounded-loop ratchet analysis. A fourth explores more efficient post-quantum authentication modes for IETF-standardized MLS group messaging, trading some security for up to 75x lower post-quantum communication overhead. (from abstract only)
  • How: Formal/symbolic verification (TAMARIN) and unified concrete-security models applied to already-deployed or standardized PQ messaging handshakes, rather than proposing yet another new protocol from scratch. (from abstract only)
  • Where applicable: General for anyone implementing or evaluating post-quantum secure messaging; directly relevant given Signal, Apple, and IETF (MLS) are all production deployments, not research prototypes.
path: Post-Quantum Secure Messaging: Signal, MLS, and iMessage PQ3

items.title: Red Bleed: A Pragmatic Near-Infrared Presentation Attack on Facial Biometric Authentication Systems
items.text:
USENIX Security '25 (34th USENIX Security Symposium) digest Wildcard pick 13–15 August 2025

Recording

Bowen Hu, Kuo Wang, and Chip Hong Chang, Nanyang Technological University — Wildcard

Video

  • Why: A practical, sub-$400 hardware attack defeating a widely-deployed commercial biometric authentication system (Windows Hello, confirmed by Microsoft's own security response center) — a concrete demonstration that "commercial-off-the-shelf NIR biometric = secure" is no longer a safe assumption.
  • What: Red Bleed, a presentation attack against near-infrared (NIR) facial biometric authentication (e.g., Windows Hello, Apple Face ID) using a custom-built consumer LCD display costing under $400, converting ordinary visible-light face images/video into convincing NIR spoofs. Confirmed against a commercial Windows Hello module with a CVE scheduled for disclosure. (from abstract only)
  • How: A generative framework (VAE-based) converts RGB/visible-spectrum face images or video into the NIR domain, combined with face-swapping, so attackers can use easily-obtainable RGB material (social media photos, video calls) rather than needing rare NIR footage of the target. (from abstract only)
  • Where applicable: NIR-based facial biometric authentication specifically (a widely deployed modality); a hardware/software technique that generalizes to any NIR liveness-detection system relying on the assumption that commodity displays can't emit convincing NIR.
path: Red Bleed: A Pragmatic Near-Infrared Presentation Attack on Facial Biometric Authentication Systems

items.title: Robustifying ML-powered Network Classifiers with PANTS
items.text:
USENIX Security '25 (34th USENIX Security Symposium) digest Core pick 13–15 August 2025

Minhao Jin and Maria Apostolaki, Princeton University — Core

  • Why: ML-based traffic classification is increasingly load-bearing for resource allocation and intrusion detection in cloud-native networking, and this is a practical, white-box framework for finding and fixing adversarial blind spots in exactly that class of system.
  • What: PANTS, a white-box framework combining adversarial ML with SMT solvers to generate realizable adversarial inputs against ML-based network traffic classifiers (MNCs), plus an iterative adversarial-training process that hardens MNCs against them. Outperforms prior baselines (Amoeba, BAP) by 70%–2x in finding adversarial inputs and improves target-model robustness by 52.7% without sacrificing accuracy. (from abstract only)
  • How: Integrates SMT solving to handle MNC-specific challenges — non-differentiable components like traffic engineering, and semantic/reliability constraints on realizable inputs — that block direct use of standard gradient-based adversarial ML methods. (from abstract only)
  • Where applicable: General for network operators deploying ML-based traffic classification (intrusion detection, resource allocation); a practical robustness-testing and hardening tool, not just an attack demonstration.
path: Robustifying ML-powered Network Classifiers with PANTS

items.title: S/MINE: Collecting and Analyzing S/MIME Certificates at Scale
items.text:
USENIX Security '25 (34th USENIX Security Symposium) digest Adjacent pick 13–15 August 2025

Gurur Öndarö et al., Münster University of Applied Sciences; Fraunhofer SIT / ATHENE — Adjacent

  • Why: The first broad empirical look at S/MIME's real-world PKI health (41M+ certificates), complementing the Verdict/X.509DoS/Trust-Agility picks above with a specific-but-large PKI ecosystem case study.
  • What: Analysis of 41M+ real-world S/MIME certificates collected from public LDAP address books, finding the trust-chain and cryptographic health of the S/MIME PKI is generally improving (weak keys expiring, weak algorithms phasing out) but many certificates are issued by non-publicly-trusted CAs, and RFCs/clients should be more stringent about what counts as a valid S/MIME cert. (from abstract only)
  • How: Large-scale collection and trust-chain construction from public LDAP directories, cross-referenced against CA/Browser Forum S/MIME Baseline Requirements. (from abstract only)
  • Where applicable: General email security / S/MIME PKI ecosystem health; most directly useful to CAs and email client implementers.
path: S/MINE: Collecting and Analyzing S/MIME Certificates at Scale

items.title: STEK Sharing is Not Caring: Bypassing TLS Authentication in Web Servers Using Session Tickets
items.text:
USENIX Security '25 (34th USENIX Security Symposium) digest Core pick 13–15 August 2025

Sven Hebrok et al., Paderborn University — Core

  • Why: A concrete, large-scale-confirmed TLS authentication bypass in virtual hosting — exactly the multi-tenant TLS-termination pattern common in cloud/CDN infrastructure — affecting Apache, nginx, (Open)LiteSpeed, and Caddy, plus real providers including Fastly.
  • What: Session ticket confusion vulnerabilities in TLS session resumption under virtual hosting, where a shared Session Ticket Encryption Key (STEK) across virtual hosts on one physical server breaks isolation, enabling bypass of client and server authentication. All four tested server implementations were vulnerable to client-auth bypass; a large-scale scan found six clusters of providers vulnerable to server-auth bypass. (from abstract only)
  • How: Exploits inconsistent STEK handling across virtual hosts sharing one physical server during TLS session resumption to confuse which host a resumed session actually authenticates. (from abstract only)
  • Where applicable: General for any TLS termination point serving multiple virtual hosts/tenants from shared infrastructure with session-ticket resumption enabled — a direct operational risk for multi-tenant edge/CDN/load-balancer deployments.
path: STEK Sharing is Not Caring: Bypassing TLS Authentication in Web Servers Using Session Tickets

items.title: Towards Internet-Based State Learning of TLS State Machines
items.text:
USENIX Security '25 (34th USENIX Security Symposium) digest Adjacent pick 13–15 August 2025

Marcel Maehren et al., Ruhr University Bochum; Paderborn University — Adjacent

  • Why: Extends TLS state-machine learning (previously only usable in controlled local environments) to work across the real, noisy Internet at scale — a methodology advance more than a single vulnerability finding, though it did surface a real Citrix NetScaler integrity bug and new CBC padding oracles.
  • What: The first large-scale (7,337 domains, 1,304 extracted models) study of TLS implementation state machines learned directly over the Internet, handling jitter, load balancers, and non-determinism that previously confined this technique to lab settings. Found a handshake transcript integrity vulnerability in Citrix NetScaler and new CBC padding oracle vulnerabilities. (from abstract only)
  • How: Extends Mealy-machine state-learning techniques with new handling for large protocol alphabets and automated analysis of the resulting automata, plus support for session resumption, renegotiation, and CBC padding-oracle-relevant features previously excluded. (from abstract only)
  • Where applicable: General TLS implementation testing methodology; directly useful to anyone auditing TLS stacks at scale rather than one implementation at a time.
path: Towards Internet-Based State Learning of TLS State Machines

items.title: Towards Practical, End-to-End Formally Verified X.509 Certificate Validators (Verdict)
items.text:
USENIX Security '25 (34th USENIX Security Symposium) digest Core pick 13–15 August 2025

Zhengyao Lin et al., Carnegie Mellon University; Northeastern University — Core

  • Why: X.509 validation bugs have a long history of real security vulnerabilities precisely because the standards are ambiguous and every validator deviates idiosyncratically — this is the first end-to-end formally verified validator, proven to match Chrome/Firefox/OpenSSL's actual (not just documented) behavior at scale.
  • What: Verdict, a formally verified X.509 certificate validator (parsing, path building, path validation) with customizable, formally-specified validation policies compiled to efficient Rust code; validated against Chrome, Firefox, and OpenSSL policies on over ten million real Certificate Transparency certificates. (from abstract only)
  • How: Validation policy is specified in first-order logic; a proof-producing compiler generates Rust code proven to conform to a subset of RFC requirements, and Verdict is shown to match each baseline's actual behavior and performance. (from abstract only)
  • Where applicable: General; directly relevant to anyone building or auditing a TLS/PKI stack who wants provable conformance rather than "matches OpenSSL's quirks by accident."
path: Towards Practical, End-to-End Formally Verified X.509 Certificate Validators (Verdict)

items.title: Trust Agility in an Era of Transient Ties: Rethinking TLS Trust in a Rapidly Evolving Ecosystem
items.text:
USENIX Security '25 (34th USENIX Security Symposium) digest Core pick 13–15 August 2025

Recording

Hoss Shafagh, Netflix (Enigma track) — Core

Video

  • Why: A practitioner-level look at the most consequential near-term shift in the Web PKI — root programs shortening server certificate lifetimes to a maximum of 47 days by 2029 — from someone who runs PKI and workload-identity infrastructure at Netflix scale, not a standards document.
  • What: An argument for "trust agility" — the ability to rapidly and securely update trust relationships as certificate authorities, cryptographic standards, and threat models evolve — as the operational response to shortening cert lifetimes, slower-upgrading consumer devices, and growing non-browser (machine-to-machine, workload identity) use cases that fall outside traditional browser trust models. (from abstract only)
  • How: Draws on real-world PKI operations at Netflix to describe automation and lifecycle-aware certificate management strategies across diverse endpoints, including preparing for post-quantum cryptographic transitions. (from abstract only)
  • Where applicable: Anyone operating PKI/TLS infrastructure at scale, workload-identity systems, or IoT/embedded fleets with slow upgrade cycles; general but grounded in a large-scale production environment.
path: Trust Agility in an Era of Transient Ties: Rethinking TLS Trust in a Rapidly Evolving Ecosystem

items.title: Universal Cross-app Attacks: Exploiting and Securing OAuth 2.0 in Integration Platforms
items.text:
USENIX Security '25 (34th USENIX Security Symposium) digest Core pick 13–15 August 2025

Recording

Kaixuan Luo et al., The Chinese University of Hong Kong; Samsung Research America — Core

Video

  • Why: A platform-wide OAuth account-linking design flaw affecting Microsoft, Google, and Amazon integration platforms — a concrete, high-severity (CVSS 9.6) example of exactly the kind of OAuth/identity-integration failure that matters at the architecture level, not the implementation level.
  • What: Two new attacks — Cross-app OAuth Account Takeover (COAT) and Request Forgery (CORF) — exploiting the lack of app differentiation in multi-app OAuth account-linking on integration platforms (Workflow Automation, Virtual Assistants, Smart Homes). 11 of 18 tested platforms were vulnerable to COAT and 5 to CORF. (from abstract only)
  • How: Built COVScan, a semi-automated black-box tool that profiles OAuth designs across platforms to find cross-app vulnerabilities; a victim risks account takeover simply by linking any single malicious app, or even clicking a crafted link. (from abstract only)
  • Where applicable: General for any platform supporting third-party app marketplaces with OAuth-based account linking; the architectural lesson (differentiate apps, not just users, in the OAuth trust model) generalizes beyond the specific platforms tested.
path: Universal Cross-app Attacks: Exploiting and Securing OAuth 2.0 in Integration Platforms

items.title: X.509DoS: Exploiting and Detecting Denial-of-Service Vulnerabilities in Cryptographic Libraries Using Crafted X.509 Certificates
items.text:
USENIX Security '25 (34th USENIX Security Symposium) digest Core pick 13–15 August 2025

Recording

Bing Shi et al., Alibaba Group; Luyi Xing, Indiana University Bloomington — Core

Video

  • Why: A systematic study of an underexplored class of cryptographic-library vulnerability — availability, not confidentiality/integrity — finding 18 new and 12 previously known CVEs across seven mainstream crypto libraries, all reachable via crafted certificates rather than exotic inputs.
  • What: X.509DoS, a class of denial-of-service attacks against cryptographic library implementations, launched via specially crafted X.509 certificates; a tool for rapidly generating such certificates and detecting the underlying DoS vulnerabilities. (from abstract only)
  • How: Systematically probes implementations handling X.509 certificates for availability-impacting bugs, showing that spec/standard compliance alone does not guarantee resistance to resource-exhaustion attacks. (from abstract only)
  • Where applicable: General for any service parsing/validating X.509 certificates from untrusted input (TLS servers, mTLS endpoints); the finding that standards-compliance ≠ DoS-safety generalizes beyond the seven libraries tested.
path: X.509DoS: Exploiting and Detecting Denial-of-Service Vulnerabilities in Cryptographic Libraries Using Crafted X.509 Certificates
